This constellation of findings—exudative effusion with increased pleural fluid leukocytes, decreased pH, decreased glucose, and increased lactate dehydrogenase—is characteristic of empyema, which is a known complication of pneumonia. Management includes evacuation via chest tube or surgery in addition to antibiotic therapy. Choice B (Malignancy): May present with exudative pleural effusion and infiltrate on chest x-ray, but would not typically present with acute fever and cough unless superinfection is present. Pleural fluid would likely contain malignant cells rather than being predominantly neutrophilic. Choice C (Rheumatoid arthritis): May cause pleural effusions due to associated serositis. However, fever would be uncommon unless superinfection is present. While pleural fluid in rheumatoid arthritis is exudative with neutrophil predominance (potentially mimicking empyema), the acute presentation with fever, cough, and pulmonary infiltrate is not typical. Choice D (Tuberculosis): Frequently causes pleural effusions, which are among the more common extrapulmonary forms of TB. Effusions are generally exudative, but tuberculosis typically presents more insidiously with constitutional symptoms rather than acute fever and cough, and pleural fluid glucose is usually relatively preserved compared to empyema. Choice E (Viral infection): Would not typically present with such markedly elevated pleural fluid leukocytes with neutrophil predominance, decreased pH, and decreased glucose concentration. Viral effusions are generally less inflammatory.
▶Cardiovascular System Aortic Dissection3 questions
Source: 3A #3
A 55-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of ripping substernal chest pain. She has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. Her blood pressure is 220/128 mm Hg in both arms. Carotid, radial, femoral, and pedal pulses are within normal limits. An x-ray of the chest shows a widened aortic root and dilated ascending aorta. Which of the following is the most likely cause? A) Aortic dissection due to Takayasu arteritis B) Degeneration of the aortic wall from Marfan syndrome C) Medial degeneration of the aorta D) Rupture of a sinus of Valsalva aneurysm E) Traumatic disruption of the aorta from a fall
Correct Answer: C) Medial degeneration of the aorta
A history of chronic hypertension, especially if poorly controlled, along with acute, tearing, substernal chest pain is suggestive of aortic dissection. The tearing of the tunica intima and media in dissection allows for the creation of a false lumen in which blood can accumulate. Further, branch vessels can become occluded by the false lumen leading to end-organ ischemia. In older patients with a history of hypertension, atherosclerotic disease of the vasa vasorum plus breakdown of normal mural collagen and elastin results in accumulation of basophilic ground substance in place of normal tissue architecture. This process is known as cystic medial necrosis of the aorta. This process occurs predominantly in the tunica media—the smooth muscle layer of the arterial wall—and results in progressive weakening that can lead to an increased risk for thoracic aortic aneurysm formation and aortic dissection. Choice A: Aortic dissection due to Takayasu arteritis is less likely than medial degeneration for this patient as it is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis in large arteries and is most commonly seen in younger females, especially those of Asian ethnicity; it is less likely to occur in a patient in the sixth decade of life with a history of chronic hypertension. Choice B: Degeneration of the aortic wall from Marfan syndrome results from a genetic mutation leading to impaired synthesis of collagen. Patients with Marfan syndrome characteristically are diagnosed early in life because of lens dislocation, aneurysmal disease, and joint hypermobility. It can also result in early-onset cystic medial degeneration of the aortic root, which places patients at risk for aortic dissection. Marfan syndrome is less likely the cause of this patient's aortic dissection based on the patient's age and history of hypertension. Choice D: Rupture of a sinus of Valsalva aneurysm would result in exsanguination from the aorta into the surrounding aortic adventitia or mediastinum. Sinus of Valsalva aneurysms occur secondary to a number of pathologies, including syphilis, tuberculosis, and chronic cystic medial degeneration. They are less common than aortic dissection as an explanation of the patient's symptoms. Choice E: Traumatic disruption of the aorta from a fall results from shear forces applied to the aorta during rapid deceleration injury such as a fall or high-energy collision. This typically presents with large-volume acute blood loss and hemorrhagic shock.
Source: 7A #20
A previously healthy 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of severe abdominal and back pain. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 120/min and regular, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 160/105 mm Hg in the right arm and 80/50 mm Hg in the left arm. Breath sounds are normal. Cardiac examination shows a normal S1 and S2. Femoral pulses are normal on the right and absent on the left. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 39%, Leukocyte count 10,500/mm3, Serum Urea nitrogen 32 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL. Liver function tests are within the reference range. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Iliac occlusive disease (Leriche syndrome) B) Renal artery embolus C) Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm D) Ruptured thoracic aneurysm E) Aortic dissection
Correct Answer: E) Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection classically presents with severe, acute, tearing chest or abdominal pain radiating to the back and differential blood pressures between extremities with asymmetric pulses. The clinical presentation in this case is pathognomonic for aortic dissection: severe abdominal and back pain, marked hypertension with differential blood pressures between arms (160/105 mm Hg right vs 80/50 mm Hg left), and asymmetric pulses (normal right femoral, absent left femoral). Dissection begins with a disruption of the tunica intima of the vessel, which permits blood to dissect the layers of the vessel wall with each heartbeat. A dissection flap may advance in any direction within the vessel, occluding or involving branch ostia. If vessel takeoffs supplying the limbs are affected, pulse deficits or differential blood pressures may arise. If splanchnic vessels are involved, end-organ dysfunction such as mesenteric ischemia or acute kidney injury may be seen (reflected by the elevated creatinine of 1.5 mg/dL in this patient). Choice A (Iliac occlusive disease/Leriche syndrome) typically presents with claudication and sexual dysfunction, not acute severe pain with hemodynamic instability. Choice B (Renal artery embolus) would present with flank pain and hematuria, but would not explain differential blood pressures, asymmetric pulses, or abdominal pain. Choice C (Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm) would present similarly but typically with more hemodynamic collapse and a pulsatile abdominal mass; the imaging and vital signs are more consistent with dissection. Choice D (Ruptured thoracic aneurysm) would not typically present with the specific pattern of differential blood pressures and asymmetric limb pulses seen here. Management of aortic dissection depends on the location (Type A vs Type B). All patients require immediate medical management to prevent further progression. Controlling heart rate and blood pressure is the priority. Intravenous beta-adrenergic blocking medications should be used with a goal of lowering heart rate to approximately 60 beats per minute and blood pressure to less than 100-120 mm Hg systolic and 60-80 mm Hg diastolic. Lowering heart rate helps prevent advancement of the dissection flap and resultant occlusion of branch vessels by limiting pulse pressure differential. Complications such as stroke, acute coronary syndrome, and cardiac tamponade may be immediately life-threatening.
Source: 4A #16
A 52-year-old woman with hypertension comes to the emergency department 45 minutes after the onset of tearing pain that starts at the base of her neck and radiates to her back. On arrival, her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 190/110 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. No other abnormalities are noted on physical examination. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia and left ventricular hypertrophy. A chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum. The most appropriate next step in management is administration of which of the following? A) Labetalol B) Morphine C) Nitroglycerin D) Phenylephrine E) Sodium nitroprusside
Correct Answer: A) Labetalol
This patient presents with classic findings of acute aortic dissection: tearing pain starting at the base of the neck radiating to the back, hypertensive emergency (BP 190/110), and a widened mediastinum on chest x-ray. The clinical presentation warrants immediate hypertensive emergency management. Labetalol is the first-line antihypertensive medication for aortic dissection because it is a nonselective adrenoreceptor blocker targeting both alpha-1 and beta-1 receptors. This dual action allows it to reduce both cardiac output (via beta-blockade) and mean arterial pressure (via alpha-1 blockade), which is essential to prevent progression of the dissection flap and occlusion of branch vessels. CT angiography of the thoracic aorta should be performed to determine whether the dissection is Type A or Type B, as this will guide definitive management. Morphine (Choice B) treats pain but does not address the underlying hypertensive emergency and aortic dissection. Nitroglycerin (Choice C) reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand but must be accompanied by a beta-blocker to prevent reflex tachycardia, making it inappropriate as monotherapy. Phenylephrine (Choice D) is a vasopressor that increases vascular resistance and blood pressure through alpha-1 stimulation, which would worsen the patient's hypertensive emergency and aortic dissection. Sodium nitroprusside (Choice E), while a vasodilator that can treat hypertensive emergency, is not the optimal choice because labetalol provides the additional benefit of reducing heart rate and cardiac contractility, both of which are necessary to prevent worsening of aortic dissection.
▶Respiratory System Community-Acquired Pneumonia3 questions
Source: 3A #11
A 27-year-old woman who is HIV positive comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of fever, shortness of breath, right-sided chest pain, and cough productive of yellow-brown sputum. She had previously been feeling well. She is compliant with her antiretroviral medication regimen and follow-up visits. One month ago, her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 400/mm³ (Normal ~500), and plasma HIV viral load was undetectable. She has never used illicit drugs. Her temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 90/40 mm Hg. Bronchial breath sounds and egophony are heard over the lower lobe of the right lung posteriorly; there is dullness to percussion. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. An x-ray of the chest shows a right lower lobe consolidation. A Gram stain of sputum shows many segmented neutrophils and numerous gram-positive diplococci. Cultures of the sputum and blood are pending. In addition to supplemental oxygen and intravenous fluids, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Ceftriaxone B) Gentamicin C) Isoniazid, rifampin, and pyrazinamide D) Penicillin E) Prednisone F) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Correct Answer: A) Ceftriaxone
This patient presents with classic lobar pneumonia characterized by fever, productive cough with yellow-brown sputum, pleuritic chest pain, consolidation on chest x-ray, and Gram stain showing gram-positive diplococci consistent with Streptococcus pneumoniae. Despite being HIV-positive, her CD4+ count of 400/mm³ (above 200/mm³) and undetectable viral load indicate well-controlled disease, making her susceptible to typical community-acquired pathogens rather than opportunistic infections. Ceftriaxone (Choice A) is the correct answer. It is a third-generation cephalosporin and anti-pneumococcal beta-lactam antibiotic that is ideal for empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, or M. catarrhalis in patients with adequate CD4 counts. It provides excellent lung penetration and coverage for common respiratory pathogens. Choice B (Gentamicin) is an aminoglycoside antibiotic that, while effective against some gram-negative organisms, is not appropriate for pneumococcal pneumonia. Its significant toxicities (ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity) make it unsuitable when safer alternatives like cephalosporins are available. Choice C (Isoniazid, rifampin, and pyrazinamide) is the standard treatment regimen for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, not for S. pneumoniae pneumonia. While TB is a concern in HIV patients, there is no clinical or microbiological evidence suggesting tuberculosis in this case. Choice D (Penicillin) is a beta-lactam antibiotic but is suboptimal for empiric therapy due to increasing penicillin resistance rates in S. pneumoniae. Third-generation cephalosporins like ceftriaxone have superior coverage. Choice E (Prednisone) is a glucocorticoid with an adjunctive role in selected pulmonary infections (such as P. jirovecii pneumonia with hypoxia or COPD exacerbations with pneumonia), but it is not indicated as primary therapy for bacterial pneumonia and does not treat the underlying infection. Choice F (Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) serves an important role as prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia when CD4 counts fall below 200/mm³. While this patient is on such prophylaxis based on previous counts, TMP-SMX is not appropriate empiric therapy for suspected pneumococcal lobar pneumonia.
Source: 9A #38
An elderly man living in a nursing home who was previously alert and oriented is now disoriented to time and place. His temperature is 37.5°C. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs or gallops. His neck is supple. There is limited range of motion of the right hip with no erythema or edema noted. Neurologic findings are otherwise normal. His leukocyte count is 10,500/mm³ (90% neutrophils and 10% lymphocytes). Urinalysis shows occasional epithelial cells, bacteria, and 1-3 WBC/hpf. An x-ray of the chest shows blurring of the left cardiac border. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia (100/min) with nonspecific ST-T segment changes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Meningitis B) Myocardial infarction C) Pneumonia D) Septic joint E) Urosepsis
Correct Answer: C) Pneumonia
This patient is presenting with signs of early sepsis with encephalopathy, fever, tachycardia, and borderline blood pressures. The most likely cause of infection is pneumonia, based on the blurring of the left cardiac border on chest x-ray, which suggests a pulmonary infiltrate. Pneumonia classically presents with fever, chills, productive cough, shortness of breath, and occasionally pleuritic chest pain. The diagnosis is based on clinical symptomatology and the presence of an identifiable pulmonary infiltrate on chest x-ray. In older or immunocompromised patients, pneumonia can lead to systemic inflammatory response with fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis or leukopenia, and hypotension. Septic encephalopathy may also occur, explaining this patient's altered mental status. Choice A (Meningitis) is incorrect because meningitis presents acutely with fever, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status in a toxic-appearing patient. This patient has no nuchal rigidity, making meningitis unlikely. Choice B (Myocardial infarction) is incorrect because while myocardial infarction may result in abnormal ST-T segments on ECG, it classically presents with crushing chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis. It would not explain the patient's fever or severely altered mental status. Choice D (Septic joint) is incorrect because although this patient previously had a joint replacement, which increases risk for septic joint, there is no erythema or edema noted around his hip, making this a less likely source of infection than pneumonia. Choice E (Urosepsis) is incorrect because while urosepsis is a common cause of septic encephalopathy in older patients, this patient's urinalysis with epithelial cells and a small number of leukocytes is inconsistent with a urinary tract infection, making urosepsis unlikely. Treatment includes oral or intravenous antibiotics depending on severity of illness, with severe cases potentially requiring mechanical ventilation and/or vasopressor medications.
Source: 8A #21
A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of a 2-day history of progressive shortness of breath, fever, and cough productive of clear sputum. Initially, his shortness of breath occurred with exertion; now, it occurs at rest. He received the diagnosis of non-small cell carcinoma of the lung 1 year ago; since then, he has had stable dyspnea with exertion. He has received chemotherapy and radiation therapy; his last course of therapy was 2 months ago. He takes no medications. On arrival, he is in mild respiratory distress. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 104/min and regular, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 146/74 mm Hg. Crackles are heard at the right lung base. His leukocyte count is 16,800/mm3 (75% segmented neutrophils, 5% bands, 2% eosinophils, 1% basophils, 12% lymphocytes, and 5% monocytes). A chest x-ray shows an increased right perihilar mass and a new right middle lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's pneumonia? A) Airway obstruction secondary to carcinoma B) Aspiration from recurrent laryngeal nerve compression C) Immunosuppression from chemotherapy D) Immunosuppression from radiation therapy E) Impaired mucous clearance
Correct Answer: A) Airway obstruction secondary to carcinoma
This patient has pneumonia supported by fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis, and a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest imaging. In a patient with a history of lung cancer, the most likely underlying cause for pneumonia development is airway obstruction secondary to carcinoma. The presence of a mass results in impaired clearance of mucus, microbes, and foreign debris, which is a risk factor for clinically significant infection of the alveolar space and lung parenchyma. This may be caused by extrinsic compression of the airway or an intrinsic space-occupying lesion in the lumen. The patient should be treated with antibiotics and noninvasive respiratory support and monitored closely for clinical improvement. Obstructive pneumonia has a high risk for recurrence. Choice B (Aspiration from recurrent laryngeal nerve compression) is unlikely because nerve injury commonly results in hoarseness of voice, which is not described in this patient. Choices C (Immunosuppression from chemotherapy) and D (Immunosuppression from radiation therapy) are unlikely given that 2 months have passed since his last treatment. He has an appropriate leukocytosis in response to infection and a reassuring white cell differential. Choice E (Impaired mucous clearance) is a risk factor for developing pneumonia and is associated with tobacco use, exposure to other airway irritants, conditions causing neuromuscular weakness, anatomic deformations, and genetic conditions such as Kartagener syndrome. However, in this patient, the presence of active malignancy and an enlarging perihilar mass are more supportive of obstructive pneumonia as the primary mechanism. Educational Objective: Post-obstructive pneumonia is a common complication of masses that occlude large and medium-sized airways. These are often centrally located primary lung malignancies such as small cell lung cancer and squamous cell carcinoma.
▶Male Reproductive Gonorrhea3 questions
Source: 3A #26
A previously healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever and right knee pain. She has not had cough, abdominal pain, or pain with urination. There is no history of intravenous drug use. She appears uncomfortable. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a few raised erythematous papules on both palms. The right knee is warm, erythematous, and tender to palpation. There is a moderate-sized effusion. Passive flexion of the knee is limited to 30 degrees because of severe pain. Analysis of synovial fluid aspirated from the right knee shows a leukocyte count of 45,000/mm³ (80% segmented neutrophils and 20% lymphocytes). A Gram stain of the synovial fluid and microscopic examination for crystals are negative. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings? A) A contiguous soft tissue infection of the joint by Staphylococcus aureus B) Immunologic-mediated arthritis secondary to Borrelia burgdorferi C) Immunologic-mediated arthritis secondary to group A streptococcus D) Infection of the joint secondary to disseminated Borrelia burgdorferi E) Infection of the joint secondary to disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Correct Answer: E) Infection of the joint secondary to disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) presents with the classic triad of fever, migratory polyarthralgia/arthritis, and a characteristic pustular or papular rash involving the palms and soles. This patient demonstrates all these features: fever (39°C), septic arthritis of the knee with significant effusion and limited range of motion, and the pathognomonic raised erythematous papules on both palms. Synovial fluid analysis shows marked leukocytosis (45,000/mm³) with neutrophilic predominance (80% segmented neutrophils), which is typical of septic arthritis from DGI. Diagnosis is confirmed through clinical presentation, joint aspiration analysis, and further investigation including pelvic examination and cultures in sexually active women. Treatment consists of antibiotics and evaluation for the extent of sexually transmitted infection. Choice A (Staphylococcus aureus contiguous soft tissue infection) would cause septic arthritis but would not explain the disseminated pustular rash on the palms and soles, nor would it present with fever and systemic symptoms without preceding local trauma or skin infection. Choices B and C (Immunologic-mediated arthritis secondary to Borrelia burgdorferi or group A streptococcus) typically demonstrate lymphocytic predominance in synovial fluid analysis (rather than the neutrophilic predominance seen here), lower leukocyte counts (typically <50,000/mm³), and absence of organisms on synovial fluid analysis. These conditions are inflammatory arthritides rather than septic arthritis. Choice D (Disseminated Borrelia burgdorferi infection) would be accompanied by the characteristic erythema migrans rash (not pustular papules on palms/soles), a history of tick exposure, and signs of disseminated Lyme disease including myocarditis, peripheral neuropathy, and meningitis, none of which are present in this case. The clinical presentation of fever, migratory arthritis with septic fluid analysis, and pustular rash on the palms and soles is pathognomonic for disseminated gonococcal infection.
Source: 7A #36
A previously healthy 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 7-day history of vaginal discharge and a 3-day history of pustular lesions over her chest and arms. She has been sexually active with a new male partner for 2 weeks; they do not use condoms. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive. On arrival, her temperature is 38.3°C (101°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Examination shows approximately 10 pustular lesions over the thorax and upper extremities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Azithromycin B) Ceftriaxone C) Nafcillin D) Penicillin E) Vancomycin
Correct Answer: B) Ceftriaxone
Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in women. It can also cause a multifocal dermatitis that typically presents with tender macular and/or pustular lesions along with disseminated and migratory polyarthritis. Risk factors for PID and other sexually transmitted infections include adolescence, multiple sexual partners, and not using barrier contraception such as condoms. Vaginitis typically presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus. Cervicitis presents with similar discharge but also with an erythematous, friable cervix and cervical motion tenderness on examination. When infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, PID with purulent cervical discharge, uterine and adnexal tenderness, and systemic symptoms such as fever can result. If left untreated, PID can be complicated by tubo-ovarian or intra-abdominal abscess, presenting with focal tenderness and a fluctuant mass. The antibiotic treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection involves the use of third generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone, as well as concurrent treatment of Chlamydia trachomatis with doxycycline. Choice A (Azithromycin) would treat an infection from Chlamydia trachomatis or trichomoniasis, as well as bacterial vaginosis. However, it does not provide appropriate antimicrobial coverage for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Choice C (Nafcillin) is used to treat gram-positive organisms, especially methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. It is not the antibiotic of choice to treat Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Choice D (Penicillin) is the treatment of choice for syphilis, which is a sexually transmitted disease from the spirochete Treponema pallidum that can present in multiple stages. Primary syphilis presents with a painless chancre (ulcer) of the genitalia. Secondary syphilis can present with macular, not pustular lesions of the hands and feet. Syphilis would not typically cause vaginal discharge. Choice E (Vancomycin) would not appropriately cover the causative organisms of vaginitis. It is effective in the treatment of resistant organisms such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and ampicillin-resistant Enterococcus spp. It does not have significant activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Educational Objective: Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause vaginitis, cervicitis, PID, and a multifocal dermatitis that typically presents with tender macular and/or pustular lesions. Ceftriaxone is the antibiotic of choice for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Source: 8A #36
Two days after the onset of menses, a 24-year-old woman develops diffuse, migrating pain of her wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles and pustules on her extremities. Examination shows slightly tender pustules on the upper and lower extremities. A photograph of the right fingers is shown. There is moderate swelling of the right knee. Which of the following drugs is most likely to be effective? A) Acyclovir B) Ceftriaxone C) Sulfamethoxazole D) Tetracycline
Correct Answer: B) Ceftriaxone
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus that can present with vaginitis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and disseminated gonorrhea. When causing vaginitis, N. gonorrhoeae typically presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus, although patients may be asymptomatic. Cervicitis presents with an erythematous, friable cervix with cervical motion tenderness. When it spreads to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, it may cause a tubo-ovarian abscess, presenting as adnexal tenderness and an adnexal mass. However, when it enters the bloodstream and spreads hematogenously, it can cause disseminated gonorrhea, as in this patient. Disseminated gonorrhea presents with tenosynovitis, polyarthralgias, and dermatitis, although septic arthritis may be the only finding. The lesions associated with disseminated gonorrhea are typically pustular, painless lesions on the distal extremities. One risk factor for the development of disseminated gonorrhea is recent menstruation, which is present in this patient. Treatment includes intravenous antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone. Empiric treatment for chlamydia with doxycycline is also recommended because of the high risk for coinfection. Empiric testing for other sexually transmitted infections (e.g., HIV) should also occur. Choice A (Acyclovir) is used to treat herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus. Herpes simplex often presents with multiple, painful vesicular lesions, although these more commonly occur on the lips or genitals. Herpetic whitlow can present with lesions on the fingers, but these are often painful and would not be concomitant with polyarthralgias. Varicella most commonly presents with multiple vesicular, pruritic lesions on the trunk and extremities. Gonorrhea infection is more likely in this patient. Choice C (Sulfamethoxazole) is often used in conjunction with trimethoprim to treat a variety of infections, such as urinary tract infections and outpatient methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus skin infections. It is also used as a prophylactic antibiotic in immunocompromised patients to prevent toxoplasmosis and Pneumocystis pneumonia. This patient's symptoms are more consistent with gonorrhea, which would not be treated with sulfamethoxazole. Choice D (Tetracycline) is an infrequently used antibiotic that can be used in the treatment of acne vulgaris and uncommon infections, such as cholera and tularemia. It is not used in the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Educational Objective: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted bacteria that can cause cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and disseminated gonorrhea. Disseminated gonorrhea presents with tenosynovitis, polyarthralgias, and dermatitis, with characteristic lesions being small, painless, pustular lesions on the distal extremities. Treatment is with ceftriaxone.
▶Renal Urinary System Renal Artery Stenosis Due to Atherosclerosis3 questions
Source: 9A #29
An 82-year-old man with hypertension comes to the physician for a routine follow-up examination. He says he has been tired but otherwise feels well. He has a 5-year history of peripheral vascular disease. He had a myocardial infarction 3 years ago and underwent right carotid endarterectomy 2 years ago. Current medications include low-dose atenolol, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, and aspirin. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 55 years but quit 3 years ago. The abdomen is nontender with no masses. His serum electrolyte concentrations are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the deterioration of this patient's renal function? A) Acute interstitial nephritis B) Decreased cardiac output C) Decreased renal blood flow D) Tubular necrosis E) Volume depletion
Correct Answer: C) Decreased renal blood flow
Renal artery stenosis should be suspected in older patients with a history of atherosclerotic disease and worsening renal function, especially if renal function worsens after initiation of ACE inhibitors. This patient's presentation is classic: advanced age, extensive atherosclerotic disease (peripheral vascular disease, prior myocardial infarction, prior carotid endarterectomy), and deteriorating renal function following what would be expected initiation of an ACE inhibitor. Renal artery stenosis causes secondary hypertension through abnormal stimulation of the juxtaglomerular apparatus from decreased afferent blood flow, leading to excessive renin and angiotensin production. When ACE inhibitors are started, they block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which normally causes efferent arteriole vasoconstriction. In patients with renal artery stenosis, the nephron is dependent on this efferent vasoconstriction (mediated by angiotensin II) to maintain adequate filtration pressure. ACE inhibitors block this compensatory mechanism, resulting in a transient acute decrease in glomerular filtration rate that is more pronounced in stenotic kidneys with baseline decreased afferent blood flow. Renal artery stenosis is diagnosed with renal artery duplex Doppler ultrasonography as the initial test, with CT or MR angiography for further evaluation, and catheter angiography reserved for cases where intervention is planned. Choice A (Acute interstitial nephritis) is incorrect because it is usually caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to medications (NSAIDs, diuretics, sulfonamides) and is characterized by rash and eosinophilia, neither of which this patient has. Additionally, he has not been recently initiated on a known offending medication. Choice B (Decreased cardiac output) is incorrect. While decreased cardiac output can cause worsening renal function through impaired renal blood flow, this patient's renal function declined immediately after initiating an ACE inhibitor, not following a recent myocardial infarction. The clinical context points to renal artery stenosis as the underlying problem. Choice D (Tubular necrosis) is incorrect. Tubular necrosis typically occurs following an ischemic or nephrotoxic insult and presents with granular, muddy brown casts on urinalysis. This patient lacks evidence of a clear recent ischemic or nephrotoxic insult. Choice E (Volume depletion) is incorrect. While volume depletion causes worsening renal function through impaired renal blood flow, this patient's decline occurred immediately after ACE inhibitor initiation rather than in the setting of an acute hypovolemic state. His extensive atherosclerotic disease history makes renal artery stenosis the most likely diagnosis. Educational Objective: Recognize renal artery stenosis in elderly patients with atherosclerotic disease who develop worsening renal function after initiating ACE inhibitor therapy. Understand that ACE inhibitors can precipitate acute decline in glomerular filtration rate in patients with renal artery stenosis by eliminating the angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriole vasoconstriction that maintains filtration pressure in stenotic kidneys.
Source: 5A #31
A 47-year-old woman with hypertension comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. One month ago, her blood pressure was 200/120 mm Hg, and daily treatment with an oral ACE inhibitor was started. Examination at that visit showed no other abnormalities, and results of serum electrolyte concentrations and renal function studies were within the reference range. Her blood pressure today is 170/90 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Her serum creatinine concentration is 2.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Measurement of plasma renin activity B) Measurement of urine catecholamine concentration C) Addition of thiazide diuretic therapy to the current regimen D) Increase in the dose of ACE inhibitor E) MR angiography of the renal arteries
Correct Answer: E) MR angiography of the renal arteries
This patient presents with a significant rise in serum creatinine (from normal baseline to 2.5 mg/dL) following initiation of an ACE inhibitor for hypertension management, which is a classic presentation of ACE inhibitor-induced acute kidney injury secondary to renal artery stenosis. ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II production, which can lead to a significant reduction in renal blood flow if an existing renal artery stenosis is present. This reduction in blood flow to the kidneys, if bilateral, can result in prerenal acute kidney injury, which manifests as a rise in creatinine following ACE inhibitor administration. To diagnose the patient's probable renal artery stenosis and guide appropriate therapy, CT or MR angiography is needed to outline the renal artery anatomy. Choice A (Measurement of plasma renin activity) would be indicated if symptoms suggestive of secondary hypertension due to elevations in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system were present, but the clinical picture points to renovascular disease rather than primary hyperaldosteronism. Choice B (Measurement of urine catecholamine concentration) would be appropriate for suspected pheochromocytoma, which is not suggested by this clinical presentation. Choice C (Addition of thiazide diuretic therapy) may eventually be necessary to control hypertension, but a renovascular cause of hypertension must be identified and addressed before determining the appropriate medication regimen. Choice D (Increase in the dose of ACE inhibitor) is contraindicated and inappropriate at this time since it would likely worsen renal function in the setting of renal artery stenosis. The key educational point is that any significant rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor should raise suspicion for underlying renal artery stenosis and warrants imaging evaluation.
Source: 4A #4
A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because she is concerned about her high blood pressure. Two days ago, her blood pressure was 200/105 mm Hg at the drug store. She has a 20-year history of hypertension that had been well controlled with a thiazide diuretic. At her last visit 3 months ago, her blood pressure was 140/75 mm Hg. Today, her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 210/114 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows arteriovenous nicking. A right carotid bruit is heard. Laboratory studies are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Acute glomerulonephritis B) Acute porphyria C) Coarctation of the aorta D) Cushing syndrome E) Hyperaldosteronism F) Hyperparathyroidism G) Hyperthyroidism H) Pheochromocytoma I) Renal artery stenosis
Correct Answer: I) Renal artery stenosis
Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension related to abnormal stimulation of the juxtaglomerular apparatus secondary to stenosis of the renal artery leading to insufficient afferent blood flow. This results in excessive production of renin and angiotensin. Secondary hypertension should be considered in new-onset or treatment-resistant hypertension. There are two main causes of renal artery stenosis: fibromuscular dysplasia and atherosclerosis. In younger patients, fibromuscular dysplasia is the most common cause, while older patients develop renal artery stenosis more commonly from atherosclerosis. This 72-year-old patient exhibits a carotid bruit, likely also secondary to atherosclerosis, supporting this diagnosis. The sudden elevation in blood pressure despite prior good control with a thiazide diuretic suggests a secondary cause of hypertension. Diagnosis is established with renal artery Doppler ultrasonography or magnetic resonance angiography. Treatment involves angioplasty or stenting of the stenosed renal artery to improve flow. ACE inhibitors can be considered for unilateral stenosis but can lead to acute end-stage kidney disease in the setting of bilateral renal artery stenosis. Incorrect answers: Choice A (Acute glomerulonephritis) refers to a variety of glomerular diseases, including nephritic and nephrotic syndromes. While nephritic syndrome can result in hypertension, this is less likely given the patient's risk factors for atherosclerosis and the chronic nature of this presentation. Choice B (Acute porphyria) presents with abdominal pain, polyneuropathy, psychological symptoms, and port wine-colored urine, not resistant hypertension. Choice C (Coarctation of the aorta) is a cause of secondary hypertension related to narrowing of the aorta, although it most commonly presents in childhood with differential blood pressure between upper and lower extremities. It is associated with bicuspid aortic valve and gonadal dysgenesis 45,X (Turner syndrome). Choice D (Cushing syndrome) results from increased cortisol levels and presents with hypertension, moon facies, abdominal striae, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, and amenorrhea. This patient demonstrates risk factors for atherosclerosis with no additional findings to suggest Cushing syndrome. Choice E (Hyperaldosteronism) presents with hypertension and metabolic derangements, including hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. This can occur in the setting of an adrenal adenoma such as in Conn syndrome or from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Laboratory studies were normal, making this unlikely. Choice F (Primary hyperparathyroidism) is a potential cause of secondary hypertension and may also present with hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia, with symptoms such as constipation, renal stones, psychiatric disturbances, and osseous lytic lesions. Laboratory studies are normal. Choice G (Hyperthyroidism) can result in secondary hypertension but also typically presents with heat intolerance, weight loss, diarrhea, hyperreflexia, palpitations, and myopathy. Choice H (Pheochromocytoma) results in episodic hypertension with associated palpitations, diaphoresis, headache, and pallor. The presentation here is more consistent with chronic secondary hypertension from renal artery stenosis.
▶Cardiovascular System Atrial Fibrillation3 questions
Source: 9A #41
A 77-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-week history of palpitations. He reports increased fatigue during the past month. He has not had any recent changes in weight. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not use illicit drugs. On examination, pulse is irregular, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Cardiac catheterization B) Dobutamine echocardiography C) 24-Hour ambulatory ECG monitoring D) Measurement of serum brain natriuretic peptide concentration E) Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration
Correct Answer: E) Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration
Hyperthyroidism is the most likely cause of new-onset atrial fibrillation in this patient presenting with palpitations, fatigue, and an irregular pulse. The diagnosis of hyperthyroidism requires measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration, which would be expected to be decreased in this patient. Signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism include weight loss, insomnia, palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, diaphoresis, pretibial myxedema, and exophthalmos in Graves disease. Atrial fibrillation is a common cardiac dysrhythmia that can present with palpitations, fatigue, shortness of breath, light-headedness, angina, and presyncope or syncope. Risk factors for atrial fibrillation include hyperthyroidism, hypertension, coronary artery disease, structural heart or valve disease, pulmonary embolism, lung disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and stimulant use disorder. Patients with new-onset atrial fibrillation should receive evaluation for potentially reversible causes with measurement of serum TSH concentration and screening for high-risk amounts of alcohol intake. Choice A (Cardiac catheterization) is not appropriate as it is used for assessment of coronary artery disease. While coronary ischemia can present with new-onset atrial fibrillation, other reversible causes should be ruled out prior to proceeding with this invasive test. Choice B (Dobutamine echocardiography) is not appropriate as it is a nonexercise stress test used to diagnose cardiac ischemia. This patient has signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism, which makes this a more likely cause of atrial fibrillation than coronary ischemia. Choice C (24-Hour ambulatory ECG monitoring) is not appropriate because atrial fibrillation has already been diagnosed on the initial ECG. Ambulatory monitoring is used in patients with high suspicion for intermittent dysrhythmias based on symptomatology, not for confirmed dysrhythmias. Choice D (Measurement of serum brain natriuretic peptide concentration) is not appropriate. Brain natriuretic peptide is increased in heart failure, which can cause atrial fibrillation. However, this patient does not have symptoms of heart failure and this test would not address the most likely reversible cause (hyperthyroidism). The educational objective is that TSH measurement should be the first step to evaluate for hyperthyroidism as a reversible cause of new-onset atrial fibrillation.
Source: 7A #21
A 67-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital 2 hours after the acute onset of pain in the left lower extremity. She has mild mitral insufficiency and chronic atrial fibrillation. She takes no medications. Examination shows a cool left lower extremity and mottling of the skin to the knee. Sensation is absent below the midthigh. She is unable to move her left foot. After undergoing left femoral embolectomy, sensorimotor function is intact, and left femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are palpable. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a dilated left atrium without a patent foramen ovale or atrioventricular thrombus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to prevent further embolization in this patient? A) Aspirin therapy B) Digoxin therapy C) Verapamil therapy D) Warfarin or direct oral anticoagulant therapy E) Mitral valve replacement
Correct Answer: D) Warfarin or direct oral anticoagulant therapy
Atrial fibrillation describes the uncoordinated contraction of the cardiac atria and is often the result of chronic left atrial enlargement caused by mitral regurgitation or increased left-sided pressures (such as in left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction). When the atria do not uniformly fill and contract, blood can become stagnant in areas of the atria, especially in the left atrial appendage. Blood in stasis is prone to coagulate, resulting in thrombus formation within the cardiac chambers. If a portion of such a thrombus embolizes, various clinical syndromes can result, including strokes from cerebral circulation occlusion, mesenteric ischemia from mesenteric artery occlusion, and acute limb ischemia from extremity artery occlusion, as demonstrated in this patient. Management of atrial fibrillation includes anticoagulation with warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant (such as apixaban) to prevent the formation of atrial thrombus, which significantly reduces the risk for thromboembolic complications. Choice A (Aspirin therapy) is indicated in the prevention of acute coronary syndromes and cerebrovascular accidents. It has not been shown to reduce the risk for thromboembolic complications in atrial fibrillation, though aspirin may be used in addition to anticoagulation in patients at increased risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Choice B (Digoxin therapy) is indicated in the management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and is sometimes used for rate control in atrial fibrillation when beta-adrenergic blockers or calcium channel blockers are insufficient. However, it does not directly influence the coagulation cascade and does not prevent thrombus formation. Choice C (Verapamil therapy) is indicated in the management of heart rate control in atrial fibrillation but does not act on the coagulation cascade and would not prevent the formation or embolization of thrombi. Choice E (Mitral valve replacement) is appropriate in cases of severe or symptomatic mitral stenosis or regurgitation. However, in the setting of left atrial enlargement and existing atrial fibrillation, replacing the valve generally does not reverse the presence of atrial fibrillation. Additionally, anticoagulation is indicated even in cases of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation because spontaneous conversion from sinus rhythm to fibrillation may be undetected by patients. Educational Objective: Anticoagulation is indicated in cases of atrial fibrillation to prevent the formation of atrial thrombus, which reduces the risk for thromboembolic complications such as strokes, mesenteric ischemia, and limb ischemia. Warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants (such as apixaban) are the commonly employed agents for this purpose.
Source: 8A #16
A 78-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital 2 hours after the sudden onset of shortness of breath, palpitations, and dizziness. She has hypertension and heart failure with diastolic dysfunction. Her medications are lisinopril, metoprolol, hydrochlorothiazide, and aspirin. Her temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 150/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on 50% oxygen by nonrebreather face mask shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Crackles are heard one-third of the way up the lung fields. There is inspiratory and expiratory wheezing. No peripheral edema is noted. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 160/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Administration of adenosine B) Administration of albuterol C) Administration of amiodarone D) Administration of diltiazem E) Administration of esmolol F) Electrical cardioversion G) Placement of a pacemaker
Correct Answer: F) Electrical cardioversion
This patient is presenting with hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation (evidenced by hypotension of 82/50 mm Hg, rapid ventricular rate of 160/min, hypoxia at 88%, and signs of acute heart failure) and requires immediate electrical cardioversion. Atrial fibrillation is a common arrhythmia resulting from uncoordinated electrical activity of the atria. While it can be asymptomatic, rapid ventricular response (RVR) with rates exceeding 120/min causes symptoms including palpitations, fatigue, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, angina, and presyncope or syncope. Physical examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse. ECG shows irregular RR intervals and absent P waves. Complications include tachycardia-induced heart failure, hemodynamic instability, and thromboembolic stroke. In stable patients, treatment involves rate control with beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (like diltiazem) and anticoagulation based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc score. However, emergent electrical cardioversion is the definitive treatment for hemodynamically unstable patients. Choice A (Adenosine) is used for reentrant supraventricular tachycardias through AV node antagonism but is inappropriate for unstable patients requiring immediate cardioversion. Choice B (Albuterol) is not indicated and could worsen the arrhythmia. The wheezing in this patient reflects cardiogenic pulmonary edema rather than asthma. Choice C (Amiodarone) is inappropriate given the patient's hypotension and acute decompensated heart failure. While amiodarone treats refractory ventricular and atrial arrhythmias, it is not first-line for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation. Choices D (Diltiazem) and E (Esmolol) are appropriate intravenous pharmacologic options for rate control in hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation. However, both are contraindicated in this patient due to the risk of further decreasing cardiac output in the setting of hypotension and acute heart failure. Choice G (Pacemaker) is not indicated. Pacemakers are for symptomatic bradycardia, not tachyarrhythmias. Educational Objective: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is a common supraventricular arrhythmia characterized by irregular RR intervals and absent P waves on ECG. When associated with hemodynamic instability (hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, or acute heart failure), immediate electrical cardioversion is the treatment of choice, regardless of medication options.
▶Social Sciences Advance directives3 questions
Source: 5A #20
An 82-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is brought to the emergency department by his children because he has been unresponsive for the past 24 hours. His family reports that he has become increasingly sleepy and confused over the past 2 weeks. His lung cancer was diagnosed 3 years ago and initially treated with palliative radiation therapy to his chest and right femur. Nine months ago, he and his oncologist agreed to discontinue treatment. He has had a 16-kg (35-lb) weight loss over the past 9 months. He has lived in his son's house for the past 6 months and has received palliative care only. The patient has an advance directive indicating that he does not want lifesaving treatment, and the son has stated that his father recently confirmed these wishes verbally. His daughter, who lives out of state, disagrees with the plan to provide palliative care at home only and is concerned about her father's weight loss. After a family meeting, both siblings now request that the physician switch to an aggressive treatment plan. The patient appears cachectic but well groomed. He responds to painful stimuli only. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 52 kg (115 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m². His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 122/min, respirations are 34/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 85/50 mm Hg. Serum studies show: Na+ 142 mEq/L, Ca²+ 13.2 mg/dL, Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, Albumin 3 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? A) Contact the hospital attorney B) Contact the hospital ethics committee C) Follow the advance directive D) Perform lifesaving measures until the family issues can be resolved E) Begin aggressive treatment
Correct Answer: C) Follow the advance directive
Advance directives are formal specifications of a patient's wishes created and executed during a time of decision-making capacity. They are enacted when the patient loses capacity to communicate preferences about healthcare wishes. These documents commonly govern end-of-life care and are frequently used in cases of terminal illness, with late-stage malignancy being a very common application. Advance directives should reflect a patient's wishes as expressed during periods of stable values and preferences. The medicolegal strength of an advance directive is significantly greater when family members or persons who know the patient corroborate the document's accurate reflection of long-standing and stable wishes. In this case, the patient had an advance directive specifically prepared for this scenario, and his son, who lives locally and appears to know the patient and his preferences well, corroborates what the father would have wanted. The patient also recently confirmed these wishes verbally. Following the advance directive is the most appropriate course of action while showing compassion and empathy to the family. Contacting the hospital attorney (Choice A) or ethics committee (Choice B) is unnecessary, as the patient's wishes are clearly stated in his advance directive with no evidence that his preferences have changed since drafting and execution. The patient has explicitly stated he does not want lifesaving measures (Choice D), and both he and his oncology team had agreed that aggressive care (Choice E) would be futile given the extent and aggressive nature of his metastatic malignancy, his poor functional status, and multiple organ involvement evidenced by his abnormal labs (elevated calcium and creatinine, low albumin).
Source: 10A #1
A 76-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up examination to discuss advance directives and general goals of care. She has Alzheimer disease but currently is able to live independently and complete most instrumental activities of daily living without assistance. The only exception is that she needs help managing her financial assets. Vital signs are within normal limits. On mental status examination, she is fully alert and oriented, and she displays normal insight and judgment. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation to this patient at this time? A) Designate a medical power of attorney B) Discontinue driving C) Move to a skilled nursing care facility D) Sign a do-not-attempt resuscitation order E) No recommendation is indicated at this time
Correct Answer: A) Designate a medical power of attorney
Educational Objective: This patient has a history of Alzheimer disease but presents fully alert and oriented with normal insight and judgement. The most appropriate recommendation is to designate a medical power of attorney. Explanation: Though some older or cognitively impaired patients may lack capacity to make decisions about their care, these patients should not be assumed to lack decisional capacity. To meet the criteria for decisional capacity, patients must express a consistent choice, demonstrate an understanding of the risks and benefits of the choice, demonstrate an appreciation of the significance of the choice for their personal circumstances, and illustrate an ability to reason through the options. This patient likely still has capacity as she displays normal insights and judgement. Designating a medical power of attorney while the patient still has capacity is an important aspect of planning for general goals of care. Choice B (Discontinue driving) is incorrect. The patient is currently able to live independently and has normal insight. The more appropriate recommendation is to designate a medical power of attorney. Choice C (Move to a skilled nursing care facility) is incorrect. The patient currently has the ability to live independently and perform most instrumental activities of daily living without assistance. The patient does not require skilled nursing care at this time. Choice D (Sign a do-not-attempt resuscitation order) is not the most appropriate recommendation. If the patient expressed that she would like to have a do-not-attempt resuscitation order, this may be appropriate. Having the patient designate a medical power of attorney would be the most appropriate recommendation. Choice E (No recommendation is indicated at this time) is incorrect. The patient is presenting to discuss goals of care and advance directives. It is most appropriate to recommend that the patient designate a medical power of attorney as she has a diagnosis of Alzheimer disease and will need proxy decision-making in the future.
Source: 8A #50
A 77-year-old woman with a 2-year history of stage IV ovarian cancer is brought to the physician by her children for consultation. Initially, she underwent cytoreduction and combination chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. Six months after completing chemotherapy, testing showed that the cancer had recurred. She now has metastatic disease to the spine despite three different chemotherapy regimens (doxorubicin, topotecan, and cyclophosphamide) over the past year. She has been confined to bed. She appears extremely ill and is in respiratory distress. She is alert and oriented and rates her pain as a 10 on a 10-point scale. Examination shows large supraclavicular lymph nodes and bilateral pleural effusions. Abdominal examination shows distention with ascites and a large, fixed ventral mass. She does not want further cancer therapy, but her family demands further treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? A) Consult with the hospital ethics committee B) Obtain psychiatric assessment C) Initiate intravenous morphine therapy D) Intravenous chemotherapy E) Operative cytoreduction
Correct Answer: C) Initiate intravenous morphine therapy
One of the core tenets of medical care is patient autonomy, or a patient's right to make decisions for themselves. This patient has terminal metastatic cancer and has failed multiple treatment options. At this point, transitioning to a more comfort-focused health care approach would be reasonable and in line with this patient's goals. As a terminally ill patient approaches the end of her life, she may decide to focus on the quality of her remaining life rather than on increasing the quantity of time remaining. This often allows them to avoid further invasive diagnostic and therapeutic interventions and to instead be as comfortable as possible for the remainder of their life when additional therapy would not meaningfully extend the quantity of remaining life. The most appropriate next step is to provide adequate pain control with intravenous morphine therapy so that she can be in as little pain as possible until death. Occasionally, a family's desires are inconsistent with a patient's desires for their care. If the patient has capacity to make medical decisions, her wishes should be honored, rather than those of her family. The physician should explore reasons for the discrepancy, especially in cases where values may have recently changed or in cases of impaired capacity, but barring any ethical uncertainty, patient wishes should be honored. Choice A (Consult with the hospital ethics committee) is not necessary. This patient has a terminal illness and the mental capacity to make her own decisions regarding her care. Her desires for her care going forward should be prioritized over the desires of her family. Choice B (Obtain psychiatric assessment) would be inappropriate. This patient has no signs to suggest that she is incapable of making an informed decision regarding her goals of care going forward. With progressive metastatic terminal cancer, the decision to forego further attempts at life-sustaining treatments to focus on quality of life would be a reasonable decision. Choices D (Intravenous chemotherapy) and E (Operative cytoreduction) would not be in line with this patient's goals of care. She would prefer to abstain from further treatment in the setting of progressive metastatic disease, despite her family's desires, because these treatments would be more likely to diminish quality of life without substantially adding to her quantity or remaining quality of life. Educational Objective: Patients with terminal illness, such as metastatic cancer, may decide to transition to a comfort-focused health care approach as they approach the end of their life. Important aspects of this care include alleviating symptoms of their illness, such as pain and anxiety. A patient's desires to stop invasive diagnostic and therapeutic procedures are not always the same desires shared by their family. However, assuming a patient has medical decision-making capacity, their wishes should be adhered to in caring for them.
▶Gastrointestinal System Crohn disease3 questions
Source: 5A #44
A previously healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of low-grade fever, fatigue, and intermittent diarrhea. She has had one episode of blood in her stool and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this time. She takes no medications. Her father has hypertension, and her older sister has irritable bowel syndrome. The patient does not smoke. She drinks one to two glasses of wine monthly. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 102/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows diffuse tenderness and no rebound; bowel sounds are increased. Rectal examination shows normal sphincter tone. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Celiac disease B) Crohn disease C) Cytomegalovirus colitis D) Giardiasis E) Irritable bowel syndrome
Correct Answer: B) Crohn disease
Crohn disease is the most likely diagnosis. Inflammatory bowel disease comprises both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation that can involve any portion of the gastrointestinal tract, manifesting with skip lesions. It particularly involves the terminal ileum and typically spares the rectum. Clinically, it presents with chronic abdominal pain, low-grade fever, weight loss, and watery or bloody diarrhea. Physical exam findings of Crohn disease include perianal fissures/fistulas, abdominal tenderness, and possible positive fecal occult blood, although bloody stools are not required for diagnosis. Colonoscopy can demonstrate aphthous or linear ulcers with luminal strictures, inflammatory lesions, and cobblestone mucosa. Biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis. Choice A (Celiac disease) is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy resulting from autoimmune-mediated intolerance of gliadin, causing inflammatory damage to the small bowel mucosa primarily affecting the distal duodenum and/or proximal jejunum, leading to decreased mucosal absorption. Choice C (Cytomegalovirus colitis) occurs in patients with immunodeficiency, most commonly AIDS, and typically presents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and fever, often superimposed on the patient's primary condition. This patient is previously healthy with no immunodeficiency noted. Choice D (Giardiasis) presents with foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea and bloating, typically in campers who ingest cysts from standing freshwater. The clinical presentation does not match this patient's symptomatology. Choice E (Irritable bowel syndrome) presents with recurrent abdominal pain that improves with defecation, along with a change in frequency and consistency of stool, without fever, weight loss, or positive occult blood testing as seen in this patient.
Source: 7A #27
A previously healthy 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of abdominal cramps and diarrhea. During this period, she has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss and 8 to 10 loose stools daily that contain a small amount of mucus. Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness of the right lower quadrant. A Sudan black B fat stain of the stool is positive. Colonoscopy with biopsy of the terminal ileum shows inflammation with granuloma formation. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's steatorrhea? A) Bacterial overgrowth B) Coexisting pancreatic exocrine dysfunction C) Defective release of secretin D) Impaired bile salt resorption in the terminal ileum E) Poor mixing of bile salts with dietary lipids
Correct Answer: D) Impaired bile salt resorption in the terminal ileum
This patient presents with a classic presentation of Crohn disease, characterized by transmural inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, most frequently involving the terminal ileum. The clinical features include chronic abdominal cramping, diarrhea, weight loss, and right lower quadrant tenderness. The positive Sudan black B fat stain confirms steatorrhea, and colonoscopic findings of inflammation with granuloma formation in the terminal ileum establish the diagnosis of Crohn disease. Crohn disease causes steatorrhea through impairment of bile salt resorption secondary to inflammation of the terminal ileum. Bile salts are recycled through the enterohepatic circulation, which is dependent on resorption of bile salts through an intact ileal mucosa. These bile salts play a crucial role in the solubilization of fats in the enteric lumen. When ileal inflammation impairs bile salt resorption, it overwhelms the liver's ability to synthesize de novo bile acids, resulting in a deficiency of bile salts available for fat solubilization and leading to steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. Choice A (Bacterial overgrowth) may occur after abdominal surgeries or with prolonged proton-pump inhibitor use, but is not the primary mechanism in this case of Crohn disease. Choice B (Coexisting pancreatic exocrine dysfunction) may rarely occur in inflammatory bowel disease due to direct pancreatic inflammation or inflammation near the pancreatic duct, but this complication occurs less frequently than steatorrhea from ileal inflammation and bile salt deficiency. Choice C (Defective release of secretin) does not commonly occur in Crohn disease. Secretin is produced by duodenal S cells and promotes bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretions and bile release while inhibiting gastric acid production. Choice E (Poor mixing of bile salts with dietary lipids) is incorrect because deficient resorption of bile salts, not defective formation of micelles, is the primary cause of steatorrhea in Crohn disease. Educational Objective: Crohn disease manifests with steatorrhea caused by impairment of bile salt resorption secondary to terminal ileal inflammation. Bile salts are essential for fat solubilization and are recycled through the enterohepatic circulation. Impaired ileal resorption overwhelms hepatic bile acid synthesis capacity, resulting in bile salt deficiency and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption. Patients with Crohn disease require frequent evaluation for fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies.
Source: 8A #27
A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of midabdominal pain after meals. She has a 10-year history of Crohn disease and has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain. She underwent resection of the terminal ileum and cecum 5 years ago and two jejunal strictureplasties 1 year ago. Current medications include an aminosalicylate. Her temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Abdominal examination shows moderate midsupraumbilical tenderness. There is a well-healed surgical scar. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. An upper gastrointestinal series with contrast shows a 10-cm segment of ileum with irregular mucosa and no strictures. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Bowel rest B) Cyclosporine therapy C) Infliximab therapy D) Prednisone therapy E) Surgical exploration
Correct Answer: D) Prednisone therapy
Prednisone therapy is the best next step in management of this patient with signs and symptoms of moderate to severe Crohn disease. Clinical severity is determined based on assessment of symptoms, which in this case include fever and abdominal pain, both consistent with moderate to severe disease. Disease activity is a spectrum from clinical remission to mild, moderate, severe, or fulminant disease. Patients with mild disease may have minimal weight loss but no systemic symptoms, while those with moderate to severe disease present with abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, nausea or vomiting, and fever. Fulminant disease is marked by severe symptoms despite steroids or biologic agents and is often associated with complications including abscess formation, peritonitis, stricture, or bowel obstruction. Risk stratification is based on age, extent of disease, inflammatory markers, history of bowel resections, and extraintestinal manifestations. This patient with a history of numerous bowel resections and mucosal irregularity should be assigned to the high-risk group. For patients with symptoms requiring immediate treatment, oral steroids (prednisone or budesonide) for 4 to 8 weeks is utilized as a bridge prior to initiating medications with fewer long-term side effects. Choice A (Bowel rest) would be appropriate for patients with local peritonitis from microperforation or small bowel obstruction. While this patient has fever, she lacks symptoms suggesting these complications. Choice B (Cyclosporine therapy) is sometimes used for fistulizing Crohn disease, although biologic agents are typically preferred. Cyclosporine does not generally induce remission and should not be used in this case. Choice C (Infliximab therapy) is a first-line choice for inducing remission in moderate to severe Crohn disease, especially with fistulizing disease, but is almost always used with an immunomodulator such as azathioprine, methotrexate, or 6-mercaptopurine. Additionally, these medications take several weeks to work, while steroids induce symptom remission faster. Choice E (Surgical exploration) is not warranted as the patient has no evidence of abscess, bowel obstruction, or complications requiring surgery. Educational Objective: For patients with high-risk, moderate to severe Crohn disease who require immediate improvement of symptoms, a 4-to-8-week course of steroids should be considered. Other options include anti-tumor necrosis factor-alpha medications in combination with immunomodulators, although resolution of symptoms with this combination is often longer than with steroids.
▶Human Development Routine vaccinations in adulthood3 questions
Source: 7A #1
A 42-year-old man who is HIV positive comes to the physician for immunizations prior to a trip to Mexico. He is leaving in 6 weeks during autumn. He plans to engage in typical tourist activities in metropolitan areas. He takes highly active antiretroviral therapy. Three years ago, he had pneumococcal pneumonia and received the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine, 23-valent, at that time. He received a tetanus booster 5 years ago and the hepatitis A and B vaccines 3 years ago. He had all appropriate childhood vaccinations. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count of 643/mm3 (Normal >500) and an undetectable plasma HIV viral load. Which of the following vaccinations is most appropriate at this time? A) Human papillomavirus B) Influenza C) Measles-mumps-rubella virus D) Meningococcal E) Rabies F) No vaccines are indicated at this time
Correct Answer: B) Influenza
Influenza is a respiratory viral illness that can be complicated by lower respiratory tract infections and/or bacterial superinfections, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients. Symptoms include fever, chills, cough, myalgias, malaise, headaches, nausea, and vomiting. The Centers for Disease Control recommends annual influenza virus vaccination for all patients greater than 6 months of age. The influenza vaccine is available as a trivalent or quadrivalent intramuscular injection of inactivated virus or as a nasal spray of live attenuated virus. Inactivated influenza virus vaccine can be safely administered via intramuscular injection to patients with HIV, who may be at a higher risk for severe illness and influenza-related complications. Influenza is a seasonal illness, typically affecting patients from the late fall to early spring months. This patient is traveling during the autumn months and should receive the vaccination for influenza virus. Choice A (Human papillomavirus): HPV is sexually transmitted and is associated with genital warts along with premalignant and malignant lesions of the cervical, anogenital, and oropharyngeal regions. HPV vaccines have significantly decreased the incidence and prevalence of HPV and protect against HPV-related malignancies such as cervical and anal squamous cell carcinoma. The vaccine should ideally be administered before the teenage years because the immune response is most robust, and the onset of sexual activity may occur during the teenage years. HPV vaccine is not specifically recommended prior to travel. Choice C (Measles-mumps-rubella): MMR is a live attenuated vaccine that should be avoided in patients with CD4+ counts less than 200/mm3 due to risk of vaccine-strain disease. While this patient's CD4+ count is 643/mm3, MMR is not specifically indicated for travel to Mexico during autumn and is not recommended prior to travel. Choice D (Meningococcal): Meningococcal vaccine is recommended for HIV patients with CD4+ counts greater than 200/mm3, but there is no specific indication based on the patient's travel plans to metropolitan areas in Mexico. Choice E (Rabies): Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis may be considered for high-risk activities, but this patient is planning typical tourist activities in metropolitan areas, which does not constitute high-risk exposure. Choice F (No vaccines are indicated): This is incorrect because influenza vaccination is specifically indicated given the patient's travel during autumn months, immunocompromised status, and CDC recommendations for annual vaccination.
Source: 4A #23
A 37-year-old woman comes for a routine follow-up examination. She has renal failure secondary to polycystic kidney disease and is receiving hemodialysis. Immunization history includes diphtheria-tetanus toxoid and 23-valent pneumococcal vaccine 3 years ago and influenza virus vaccine 12 months ago. Examination shows no abnormalities. Serum hepatitis B surface antibody assay is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate vaccine to administer at this visit? A) Diphtheria-tetanus toxoid B) Hepatitis B C) Influenza virus D) Meningococcal E) 23-Valent pneumococcal
Correct Answer: C) Influenza virus
Influenza virus vaccine is recommended for all individuals aged 6 months or older on an annual basis. The patient is at high risk for complications from influenza given her underlying renal failure (end-stage kidney disease) from polycystic kidney disease. The patient last received her influenza vaccine 12 months ago, indicating the influenza virus vaccine is the most appropriate vaccine to administer at the current visit. Choice A (Diphtheria-tetanus toxoid): The booster is recommended every 10 years for adults who have previously received the Tdap vaccine. The patient has already received this vaccine recently. Choice B (Hepatitis B): This vaccine is typically administered to newborns or to adults who previously did not receive it. The patient exhibits serum hepatitis B surface antibodies, which implies successful prior immunization or resolved prior infection, indicating she does not require the hepatitis B vaccine. Choice D (Meningococcal conjugate vaccine): This is indicated for all children, with an additional serogroup B vaccine indicated for children over 10 years of age at increased risk for meningococcal disease. It is not indicated for this adult patient without specific risk factors for meningococcal disease. Choice E (23-valent pneumococcal vaccine/PPSV23): This is indicated for all adults over 65 years of age and in patients with high-risk conditions such as chronic heart, renal, and liver disease or chronic smokers. The patient has already received this vaccine 3 years ago.
Source: 8A #1
A 67-year-old woman with non-Hodgkin lymphoma is being prepared for discharge from the hospital after treatment of a hypertensive crisis. She is currently receiving her first course of chemotherapy. One year ago, she received pneumococcal and influenza vaccines. Her blood pressure has responded well to lisinopril. Currently, her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 140/86 mm Hg. Examination shows an enlarged left supraclavicular node. The spleen tip is palpated 5 cm below the left costal margin. Administration of which of the following vaccines is most appropriate for this patient? A) Influenza B) Measles-mumps-rubella C) Meningococcal D) Pneumococcal E) Varicella
Correct Answer: A) Influenza
This patient is immunocompromised due to active chemotherapy for non-Hodgkin lymphoma and requires vaccination against seasonal illnesses that pose significant risk. Annual influenza virus vaccination is recommended beginning at age greater than 6 months. The inactivated influenza vaccine (administered via intramuscular injection) can be safely administered to immunocompromised patients, who are at higher risk for severe illness and influenza-related complications if they forego vaccination and become infected. Influenza is a respiratory viral illness that can be complicated by lower respiratory tract infection (pneumonia) and bacterial superinfection, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients. Choice B (Measles-mumps-rubella) is a live attenuated vaccine involving two doses typically administered in childhood. Patients who are severely immunocompromised should not receive this vaccine because of the risk for viral reactivation and adverse events.
