Choice C (Meningococcal) is a conjugate vaccine that may be safely administered to immunocompromised patients, but routine boosters are not necessary. While this vaccine can be given, it is not the most appropriate choice for this patient at this time. Choice D (Pneumococcal) is a 23-valent conjugate vaccine indicated for all adults over 65 years of age and in patients with high-risk conditions. However, this patient received pneumococcal vaccination one year ago and does not require a booster dose at this time. Choice E (Varicella) is a live attenuated vaccine involving two doses usually administered during childhood. Zoster vaccine (also live attenuated) is recommended for adults over 60 years but is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients due to risk of viral reactivation. Educational Objective: Annual influenza virus vaccination is recommended beginning at age greater than 6 months. Inactivated influenza virus vaccine can be safely administered via intramuscular injection to immunocompromised patients, who are at higher risk for severe illness and influenza-related complications if they forego vaccination.
▶Musculoskeletal System Rotator cuff syndrome3 questions
Source: 7A #14
A 42-year-old man comes to the physician because of right shoulder pain for 24 hours. The pain began 8 hours after he spent the day painting his house. The pain increases when he raises his right arm; he is unable to actively abduct the shoulder beyond 60 degrees. Passive range of motion of the shoulder is full and causes only mild discomfort. An x-ray of the shoulder is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Biceps tendon rupture B) Cervical nerve root compression C) Glenohumeral subluxation D) Supraspinatus tendon tear E) Torn glenoid labrum
Correct Answer: D) Supraspinatus tendon tear
The supraspinatus tendon is the most common location of rotator cuff injury. The supraspinatus muscle lies within the supraspinous fossa along the superior portion of the scapula and inserts on the greater tuberosity of the humerus. The supraspinatus muscle contributes to the initiation of arm abduction prior to the action of the deltoid muscle. Injury to the supraspinatus tendon may occur from degeneration, impingement, overuse, or trauma. The clinical presentation in this patient is classic for supraspinatus tendon injury: pain with active shoulder abduction (which places the tendon under tension) that is relieved with passive abduction (where no tension is generated). The patient's history of repetitive overhead activity (painting) supports an overuse mechanism. Treatment includes rest, ice, anti-inflammatory medications, and physical therapy. The injury can be evaluated through abduction of the shoulder against resistance. Choice A (Biceps tendon rupture) results in weakness of elbow flexion and forearm supination along with a retracted, prominent deformity in the anterior aspect of the proximal arm. The biceps muscle consists of a short head originating from the coracoid process and a long head originating from the intra-articular supraglenoid tubercle, inserting at the radial tuberosity. Choice B (Cervical nerve root compression) presents with pain in a radicular pattern associated with the compressed nerve root, which may be accompanied by paresthesia, numbness, frank muscle weakness and/or paralysis. It generally results from traumatic injury to the cervical spine, disc herniation, tumors, or degenerative joint disease and osteoarthritis of the cervical spine. Choice C (Glenohumeral subluxation), a partial dislocation of the shoulder joint, often arises from acute or chronic disruption of the muscles, ligaments, soft tissues, and bones that comprise the joint. It presents with shoulder pain, deformity, and limited passive and active range of motion, generally following a traumatic injury sustained by the shoulder (e.g., when weightlifting or playing sports). It is generally diagnosable on x-ray. Choice E (Torn glenoid labrum) presents with shoulder pain with range of motion (especially overhead), limited range of motion, catching or locking sensation with motion, and occasional instability of the shoulder joint. It generally results from acute trauma and is diagnosed by physical examination and MRI. Educational Objective: The supraspinatus tendon is most often involved in rotator cuff injury and generally results from overuse and repetitive motion. It presents with pain with shoulder abduction that may be improved with passive range of motion. Treatment includes rest, ice, anti-inflammatory medications, and physical therapy.
Source: 4A #3
An otherwise healthy 30-year-old man has had recurrent aching right shoulder pain initiated by reaching overhead; it also occurs at night in bed. The pain is most prominent in the area of the deltoid muscle. It is elicited by abduction of the shoulder against resistance. Which of the following is the most likely site of the underlying condition? A) Biceps tendon B) Cervical nerve root C) Deltoid muscle D) Proximal humerus E) Supraspinatus tendon
Correct Answer: E) Supraspinatus tendon
The supraspinatus tendon is the most common location of rotator cuff injury. The supraspinatus muscle lies within the supraspinous fossa along the superior portion of the scapula, and its tendon inserts on the greater tuberosity of the humerus. The supraspinatus muscle contributes to initiation of arm abduction prior to the action of the deltoid muscle. Injury to the supraspinatus tendon may occur from degeneration, impingement, or trauma, and can be evaluated through abduction of the shoulder against resistance. The clinical presentation of pain with overhead reaching, night pain, and pain elicited by resisted shoulder abduction is classic for supraspinatus pathology. Choice A (Biceps tendon): The biceps brachii consists of a short head originating from the coracoid process and a long head originating from the intra-articular supraglenoid tubercle, inserting at the radial tuberosity. Injury to the biceps tendon results in weakness of elbow flexion and forearm supination, not the described shoulder abduction pain. Choice B (Cervical nerve root): Cervical nerve root injury would result in neurologic symptoms such as weakness, numbness, and paresthesia along a specific dermatome and myotome distribution. It would not be specifically aggravated by shoulder abduction against resistance. Choice C (Deltoid muscle): The deltoid muscle is not commonly injured compared to the supraspinatus tendon and only contributes to abduction of the shoulder after the first 15 degrees. The supraspinatus initiates abduction, making it the more likely pathologic site. Choice D (Proximal humerus): Injury to the proximal humerus such as a surgical neck fracture can lead to axillary nerve injury, which would result in dysfunction of the deltoid muscle and loss of sensation over the proximal lateral arm, not the isolated rotator cuff presentation described.
Source: 8A #12
A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 12-week history of left shoulder pain that radiates to the middle of his left upper arm. He is awakened at night by pain when he rolls onto the affected shoulder. He does not recall any recent history of trauma. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Examination shows no muscular atrophy. There is tenderness to palpation immediately lateral to the acromion. Active abduction of the left shoulder is limited to 120 degrees without resistance and difficult with minimal resistance. Peripheral pulses are normal. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. X-rays of the left shoulder show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Accessory nerve palsy B) Acromioclavicular separation C) Occult fracture of the proximal humerus D) Rotator cuff tendinitis E) Suprascapular nerve palsy
Correct Answer: D) Rotator cuff tendinitis
The rotator cuff is the group of muscles and tendons that act to seat the humeral head directly into the center of the glenoid during motion of the shoulder. These muscles also act, in concert with other muscles about the shoulder, to internally and externally rotate, abduct, and adduct the shoulder. These muscles include the subscapularis, teres minor, supraspinatus, and infraspinatus. Rotator cuff tendonitis is a common cause of shoulder pain in adults. Pain most commonly occurs with overhead activity that involves raising the affected arm, and commonly occurs at night, especially while lying on the affected side. Athletes that perform overhead motions, such as swimmers or baseball pitchers, may experience pain that limits their ability to participate in their sport. The diagnosis is based on clinical examination with a careful assessment of rotator cuff function. The affected muscle or tendon insertion is often tender to palpation. X-ray is generally unrevealing, although ultrasonography and MRI are sensitive for the detection of tendinopathy. The initial treatment of rotator cuff tendinitis includes rest, ice, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and physical therapy. Choice A (Accessory nerve palsy) results in paralysis of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles on the affected side with drooping of the affected shoulder, which is not present in this patient. Choice B (Acromioclavicular separation) usually occurs following direct trauma to the shoulder and is often accompanied by shoulder deformity that is easily detected on clinical examination and by plain film x-ray. This patient has no trauma history and normal x-rays. Choice C (Occult fracture of the proximal humerus) may occur following trauma but is usually detectable with plain film x-ray. This patient's history of pain and weakness with abduction and pain when laying on the affected shoulder is more consistent with rotator cuff tendinitis. Choice E (Suprascapular nerve palsy) commonly occurs because of compression at the suprascapular notch and results in paralysis of the infraspinatus and supraspinatus muscles with resultant weakness of shoulder external rotation and abduction. While shoulder pain is common, muscle atrophy is often present. Tenderness to palpation of the lateral shoulder is atypical of suprascapular nerve palsy. This patient has no muscular atrophy. Educational Objective: Rotator cuff tendinitis is a common cause of shoulder pain in adults. Patients typically present with localized shoulder pain that is exacerbated with overhead movements and with sleeping on the affected shoulder. The initial treatment of rotator cuff tendinitis includes rest, ice, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and physical therapy.
▶Cardiovascular System Bacterial Endocarditis3 questions
Source: 7A #16
An asymptomatic 47-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine examination. She has hypertension and hypothyroidism. During childhood, she was told she had a heart murmur. Current medications include lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and levothyroxine. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 62 kg (136 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m². Her pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Oral examination shows a dark, cracked, right lower molar with swelling, erythema, and tenderness of the gum. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows a normal S₁ and S₂ with variation of S₂ on respiration. The patient is scheduled to undergo a root canal at the dentist next week. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for antibiotic prophylaxis prior to the scheduled dental procedure? A) Oral amoxicillin 1 hour before the dental procedure B) Oral amoxicillin 24 hours before the procedure C) Intravenous vancomycin 1 hour before the dental procedure D) Intravenous vancomycin 24 hours before the dental procedure E) No prophylaxis is indicated
Correct Answer: E) No prophylaxis is indicated
No prophylaxis is indicated prior to a dental procedure in the case of a no-longer-apparent childhood murmur. Although dental procedures that manipulate oral mucosa can result in hematogenous spread of oral flora, antibiotic prophylaxis is only recommended in specific cardiac conditions. The 2020 American Heart Association guidelines recommend antibiotic prophylaxis in the setting of: prosthetic cardiac valves, prosthetic implanted material such as annuloplasty rings or cords, previous infective endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart defects, repaired congenital heart defects with residual shunts or regurgitation adjacent to the site of a patch or prosthetic device, and in transplanted hearts with structurally abnormal valves. Noncyanotic congenital heart defects such as ventricular septal defects, especially if resolved, do not require antibiotic prophylaxis unless another indication is present. This patient has only a history of a childhood murmur that is no longer apparent on examination (normal S₁ and S₂ with physiologic variation), making her ineligible for prophylaxis. Choice A (Oral amoxicillin 1 hour before) would be correct if prophylaxis were indicated, as amoxicillin is first-line for patients without allergy to penicillins, and should be administered 30-60 minutes before the procedure. Choice B (Oral amoxicillin 24 hours before) is incorrect because peak serum concentrations would have passed by the time of the procedure. Choices C and D (Intravenous vancomycin at 1 hour and 24 hours respectively) are incorrect because vancomycin offers poor coverage of gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, which can also cause infective endocarditis and are commonly found in the oral flora.
Source: 4A #30
A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of extreme fatigue and malaise for 3 weeks. He has felt well except for a toothache 5 weeks ago treated with a root canal procedure. He has a history of a cardiac murmur first noted at the age of 19 years. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur heard best at the right second intercostal space, an S4, and an ejection click. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, Leukocyte count 10,000/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 90%, Bands 10%, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 90 mm/h, Urine blood positive. Blood cultures are obtained. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cardiac abnormality? A) Calcification of a bicuspid aortic valve B) Calcified mitral annulus C) Myxomatous degeneration of the aortic valve D) Myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve E) Myxomatous degeneration of the tricuspid valve F) Rheumatic disease of the mitral valve G) Rheumatic disease of the tricuspid valve
Correct Answer: A) Calcification of a bicuspid aortic valve
Calcification of a bicuspid aortic valve is the most likely diagnosis. Bicuspid aortic valves are congenital, consisting of two leaflets instead of the normal three, and can be associated with genetic disorders such as Turner syndrome (45,X). The altered biomechanics of these valves lead to premature degeneration with dystrophic calcification over time, restricting valve opening and resulting in aortic stenosis. This characteristically produces a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the right second intercostal space, which matches this patient's cardiac findings. The ejection click is also typical of aortic stenosis. Crucially, degenerated bicuspid aortic valves have significantly increased risk for infective endocarditis, especially following dental procedures like root canals. The patient's clinical presentation of fever, fatigue, malaise, elevated ESR, leukocytosis with left shift, and positive blood cultures is consistent with acute endocarditis. Additionally, severe aortic stenosis can cause hemolytic anemia from red blood cell lysis as they traverse the stenotic valve, explaining the low hemoglobin (9.3 g/dL) and positive urine blood (hemoglobinuria). Choice B: Calcified mitral annulus causes diastolic murmurs heard at the left fourth or fifth intercostal space, not systolic murmurs at the right second intercostal space. Choices C, D, E: Myxomatous degeneration is typically associated with connective tissue disorders (Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) and produces regurgitant murmurs rather than the systolic ejection murmur with ejection click seen here. Choices F, G: Rheumatic disease of the mitral or tricuspid valves, whether acute or chronic, does not produce a systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space. Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal infection and predominantly affects the mitral valve, while chronic rheumatic disease may cause stenosis, but neither would explain this patient's clinical presentation and murmur location.
Source: 8A #15
A 54-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-week history of temperatures to 38.3°C (101°F), chills, progressive shortness of breath, and pain and swelling of his right knee. He has a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin and insulin. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Cardiac examination discloses a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex. Scattered crackles are heard throughout the lung fields. The right knee is swollen and tender to palpation. There is a 2-cm ulcer over the bottom of the right foot; no surrounding erythema or soft-tissue swelling is noted. When asked about the ulcer, the patient says it is not painful and that it has been present for 5 months. A chest x-ray is shown. In addition to aspiration of the right knee joint, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Blood cultures B) Bone biopsy C) Culture of the ulcer tissue D) Lung biopsy E) Measurement of serum ACE activity F) Transthoracic echocardiography
Correct Answer: A) Blood cultures
This patient's presentation is concerning for bacterial endocarditis, and the most appropriate next step in diagnosis is to obtain blood cultures. Acute endocarditis is commonly caused by Staphylococcus or Streptococcus species. Patients typically present with fever, chills, and malaise. Extracardiac manifestations include end-organ dysfunction caused by septic emboli to the lung (as seen in the chest x-ray with bilateral, scattered areas of consolidation concerning for multifocal pneumonia) or systemic circulation, vascular and immunologic phenomena such as Roth spots, Osler nodes, and Janeway lesions on the palms and soles, along with conjunctival and subungual splinter hemorrhages. Purpuric lesions may be noted elsewhere on skin examination. Distal sites may be seeded with infection, as with this patient's likely septic arthritis of the right knee. Significant disruption of the heart valves can cause acute heart failure, as seen in this patient with progressive shortness of breath, pulmonary rales, and x-ray of the chest disclosing pulmonary edema and vascular congestion. Potential bacterial sources leading to infective endocarditis include procedures that may disrupt mucocutaneous surfaces, such as dental procedures or cystoscopy. Choice B (Bone biopsy) is not indicated at this time for this patient. Patients with osteomyelitis benefit from biopsy of the affected bone to confirm the diagnosis and isolate a causative organism for targeted antimicrobial therapy. Choice C (Culture of the ulcer tissue) is unlikely to provide further information in this patient with poorly controlled diabetes. Skin and wound cultures are often polymicrobial with common skin and environmental flora, and do not provide useful information for antibiotic selection. Choice D (Lung biopsy) is an invasive procedure that is reserved for the diagnosis of malignancy, interstitial lung disease, and severe unusual infections. Less invasive studies such as blood cultures should be performed first. Choice E (Measurement of serum ACE activity) is useful in the evaluation of sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis most commonly presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and pulmonary opacities. It can be asymptomatic or present with a chronic cough, dyspnea, chest pain, fatigue, malaise, fever, and weight loss. Choice F (Transthoracic echocardiography) and/or transesophageal echocardiography should be performed as soon as possible for this patient to evaluate for vegetations and valvular dysfunction; however, it should not delay collection of blood cultures and prompt administration of antibiotics. Educational Objective: Bacterial endocarditis results from hematogenous seeding of the endocardial valves by a pathogen, which may then spread via septic emboli to additional extracardiac sites. Septic emboli to the lungs can result in multifocal pneumonia, central nervous system emboli can result in stroke, and infection of joints and soft tissue can lead to septic arthritis and soft tissue abscesses.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Acute blood loss as a cause of anemia2 questions
Source: 6A #8
A 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of fatigue. Menses occur at regular intervals with no excessive bleeding. She takes no medications or vitamin supplements. Examination shows no abnormalities except for pale conjunctivae. Her hemoglobin concentration is 9 g/dL. A blood smear is shown. This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following? A) Folic acid B) Iron C) Niacin D) Vitamin B1 (thiamine) E) Vitamin B6
Correct Answer: B) Iron
A premenopausal woman presenting with a 3-month history of fatigue, anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), and pale conjunctivae most likely has iron deficiency anemia. Despite regular menses without excessive bleeding, chronic menstrual blood loss is the most common cause of iron deficiency in women of childbearing age. The blood smear demonstrates hypochromia (pale red blood cells with reduced hemoglobin content), which is the characteristic finding in iron deficiency anemia. The patient has no other history of nutritional deficiencies, and there are no clinical clues suggesting other etiologies. Choice A (Folic acid deficiency) would present with macrocytic anemia, not the hypochromic picture seen here. Choice C (Niacin deficiency/Pellagra) causes dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death ('4 Ds'), but does not typically cause anemia. Choice D (Vitamin B1/Thiamine deficiency) causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi, and would present with macrocytic anemia if anemia develops, not microcytic hypochromic anemia. Choice E (Vitamin B6 deficiency) rarely causes clinically significant anemia and is not consistent with the hypochromic presentation. The key distinguishing feature is the presence of microcytic hypochromic anemia in a premenopausal woman with regular menstrual cycles, making iron deficiency the correct diagnosis.
Source: 10A #45
A 67-year-old man comes to the physician 2 weeks after being rejected as a blood donor because of anemia. He has had mild fatigue during the past 4 months. He has not had black stools or blood in his urine or stool. He eats red meat once every 2 weeks. His pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 136/72 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. His hemoglobin concentration 2 years ago was 14 g/dL. His hemoglobin concentration today is 14 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 75 μm³, and serum ferritin concentration is 5 ng/mL. In addition to beginning treatment with iron supplementation, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Dietary counseling B) Second test of the stool for occult blood C) Urinalysis D) Colonoscopy E) Bone marrow biopsy
Correct Answer: D) Colonoscopy
Educational Objective: New microcytic, iron deficiency anemia requires evaluation for a source of iron/blood loss. Colonoscopy is indicated when there is no other apparent explanation for new-onset iron deficiency anemia, as with this patient. Explanation: Iron deficiency anemia classically presents with symptoms of anemia such as fatigue and pallor. Laboratory studies show hypochromic and microcytic anemia with decreased ferritin, increased total iron-binding capacity, and decreased transferrin saturation, which confirm the diagnosis. Iron is required for the synthesis of heme, which is a necessary component of the hemoglobin molecule and of erythrocytes. Heme functions to shuttle oxygen to and from peripheral tissues. In individuals who chronically lose blood due to occult gastrointestinal bleeding, iron deficiency can develop. Iron deficiency anemia may also develop as a result of chronic blood loss from menstruation, dietary intake, malabsorption syndromes such as celiac disease, or after gastric bypass. Iron deficiency anemia with no apparent explanation requires further evaluation for gastrointestinal blood losses with colonoscopy and/or endoscopy. This patient's history of eating red meat, iron deficiency despite appropriate dietary intake, and no clear source of blood loss raises concern for gastrointestinal blood loss. Choice A (Dietary counseling) is incorrect. This patient eats red meat every 2 weeks, which makes it unlikely that his iron deficiency is coming from lack of intake. The next best step is to obtain a colonoscopy. Choice B (Second test of the stool for occult blood) is incorrect. This repeat test will only delay evaluation of suspected gastrointestinal bleeding. This patient should undergo a colonoscopy to evaluate the gastrointestinal tract for sources of blood loss. Choice C (Urinalysis) is incorrect. This patient has no urinary symptoms, and urinalysis would be unhelpful in diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia. Choice E (Bone marrow biopsy) is incorrect as colonoscopy is the appropriate initial diagnostic test to identify the source of blood loss.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency2 questions
Source: 6A #17
A previously healthy 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of progressive shortness of breath. During this period, she also has had intermittent nonproductive cough and wheezing, especially when she has colds during the winter. She has not had night sweats. She takes no medications. She has smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 9 years. She is employed as a landscape architect. Her 60-year-old father has had emphysema since his early 40s. The patient appears well. Her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Breath sounds are mildly decreased at the lung bases. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Spirometry shows an FEV1 of 45% of predicted. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's lung injury? A) Chronic exposure to environmental allergens B) Chronic infection with Aspergillus fumigatus C) Chronic infection with respiratory syncytial virus D) Chronic irritation and inflammation from cigarette smoking E) Defective chloride secretion from respiratory epithelium F) Insufficient inhibition of neutrophil elastase
Correct Answer: F) Insufficient inhibition of neutrophil elastase
The patient's presentation is classic for emphysema secondary to alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency. Key clinical clues include: early-onset progressive dyspnea (age 37), significant family history of premature emphysema (father at age 40s), markedly reduced FEV1 on spirometry (45% predicted), and relatively mild smoking history (0.5 packs/day for 9 years). Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor that normally protects lung tissue from neutrophil elastase released during inflammation. Deficiency leads to unopposed proteolytic activity causing progressive lung destruction, particularly in basilar lung fields (consistent with findings of decreased breath sounds at bases). Choice A (chronic allergen exposure) causes hypersensitivity pneumonitis with characteristic bilateral ground glass, reticular infiltrates, and centrilobular nodules on imaging—not emphysema. Choice B (Aspergillus fumigatus) presents with transient infiltrates, bronchiectasis, fungal balls, and cavitary disease, typically in immunocompromised or asthmatic patients. Choice C (respiratory syncytial virus) causes subacute/chronic cough in immunocompetent patients but symptoms typically resolve within 8 weeks. Choice D (cigarette smoking) alone typically does not cause spirometric changes until irreversible COPD/emphysema develops, and the relatively mild smoking exposure here is insufficient to explain the severity of disease; the markedly reduced FEV1 with family history of early emphysema points to genetic predisposition. Choice E (defective chloride secretion/cystic fibrosis) presents with chronic recurrent infections, malabsorption symptoms, and characteristic bronchiectasis with mucus impaction on imaging. The correct answer highlights that insufficient inhibition of neutrophil elastase due to AAT deficiency is the fundamental pathophysiologic mechanism underlying this patient's accelerated lung destruction.
Source: 4A #31
A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of progressive shortness of breath. He now has shortness of breath after walking 200 feet. He coaches a soccer team and is unable to keep up with his players on the field. He occasionally has wheezing and a nonproductive cough. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. His wife resumed smoking 18 months ago after quitting for 3 years. He has three healthy children. His father died of alcoholic cirrhosis at the age of 55 years. The patient's temperature is 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. End-expiratory wheezes and occasional rhonchi are heard bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows increased lucency and bullous changes at both lung bases. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition? A) Alpha-1-Antitrypsin deficiency B) Exposure to asbestos C) Exposure to radon D) Exposure to secondhand smoke E) Pulmonary fibrosis
Correct Answer: A) Alpha-1-Antitrypsin deficiency
Alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency results in early development of panacinar emphysema and liver disease. It is a hereditary disease caused by misfolding of alpha-1-antitrypsin, which aggregates in hepatocytes leading to hepatocyte injury and progression to cirrhosis at a young age. The lack of functional alpha-1-antitrypsin release into systemic circulation creates an imbalance of proteases and anti-proteases in lung parenchyma, resulting in destruction of alveolar septa and panacinar emphysema. Panacinar emphysema is characterized by emphysematous destructive changes of pulmonary alveolar tissue beginning in bilateral lung bases with bullous changes and potential diffuse spread. Notably, both cirrhosis and panacinar emphysema can develop in AAT deficiency without significant additional risk factors. The clinical presentation of a young male with progressive dyspnea, bilateral basilar bullous changes on chest x-ray, wheezing, and a family history of early cirrhosis (father died of cirrhosis at age 55) is classic for this condition. Exposure to asbestos (Choice B) occurs in roofing, plumbing, and shipbuilding and causes pulmonary asbestosis with pleural calcified plaques and lower lobe predominant interstitial fibrotic changes—not panacinar emphysema. It increases risk for bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma. Exposure to radon (Choice C) is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking, occurring naturally in homes especially basements. This patient presents with emphysema, not lung cancer. Exposure to secondhand smoke (Choice D) is a risk factor for lung cancer presenting with cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss—not panacinar emphysema. Pulmonary fibrosis (Choice E) from various causes (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis, chemotherapeutics) results in restrictive lung pathology with dyspnea, dry crackles, and shallow breathing, not the obstructive pattern with emphysematous changes seen here. Educational Objective: Recognize that alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency presents with panacinar emphysema (basilar-predominant bullous changes) and early-onset cirrhosis, distinguishing it from other causes of chronic lung disease.
▶Endocrine System Cushing syndrome2 questions
Source: 6A #27
A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has been amenorrheic for 3 months. She has also had increased facial hair growth and multiple episodes of acne over the past year; she has had a 27-kg (60-lb) weight gain during this time despite no change in appetite. Menses had occurred at regular intervals until 1 year ago, when they became increasingly irregular. She is not sexually active. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 36 kg/m². Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg. Examination shows truncal obesity with pink striae. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Urine β-hCG test is negative. Measurement of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate concentration B) Serum estradiol concentration C) Serum progesterone concentration D) Urine catecholamine concentration E) Urine free cortisol concentration in a 24-hour specimen
Correct Answer: E) Urine free cortisol concentration in a 24-hour specimen
This patient presents with secondary amenorrhea with pregnancy ruled out (negative β-hCG). The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of Cushing syndrome, characterized by: rapid weight gain (27 kg over 1 year despite stable appetite), hirsutism and acne (signs of androgen excess), truncal obesity with violaceous (pink) striae, and hypertension (160/100 mm Hg). The relatively recent onset and rapid progression of symptoms in the absence of exogenous corticosteroid use should raise strong suspicion for endogenous Cushing syndrome. First-line testing for suspected Cushing syndrome is measurement of 24-hour urine free cortisol concentration (E is correct). This is the most sensitive and specific outpatient screening test for hypercortisolism. Choice A (serum DHEA-S): While hyperandrogenism could explain hirsutism and acne, an androgen-secreting tumor presenting with elevated DHEA-S is more common in postmenopausal women, not in this 37-year-old. Additionally, the constellation of findings (weight gain, hypertension, truncal obesity, striae) is more consistent with Cushing syndrome. Choice B (serum estradiol): Though estradiol measurement may be warranted in general amenorrhea evaluation, the clinical features of hypercortisolism make Cushing syndrome the primary concern and take diagnostic priority. Choice C (serum progesterone): Similar to estradiol, progesterone measurement may be part of amenorrhea workup but is not the first-line test given the clinical presentation suggestive of Cushing syndrome. Choice D (urine catecholamines): Elevated catecholamines would suggest pheochromocytoma, which presents with hypertension but is NOT associated with amenorrhea, weight gain, hirsutism, or truncal obesity with striae. This does not fit the clinical picture. Educational Objective: Recognize the clinical features of Cushing syndrome (hypercortisolism) including weight gain, hirsutism, amenorrhea, hypertension, truncal obesity, and violaceous striae, and understand that 24-hour urine free cortisol is the first-line diagnostic test for suspected Cushing syndrome.
Source: 5A #16
A 27-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of irregular menses. During this time, she has had vaginal spotting so frequently that she does not know the dates of her actual menstrual periods. Previously, menses occurred at regular 28-day intervals. She also reports increased hair growth over the face, chest, and lower abdomen. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows coarse hair over the upper lip, chin, and abdomen. Abdominal and pelvic examinations show no abnormalities. Her serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate concentration is 75 µg/ml (N=0.5-5.4). An overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows no suppression of cortisol. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Measurement of fasting serum cortisol concentration B) Measurement of serum potassium concentration C) Ultrasonography of the pelvis D) CT scan of the abdomen E) MRI of the brain
Correct Answer: D) CT scan of the abdomen
Cushing syndrome is characterized by excess cortisol production resulting in oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, weight gain, skin changes, osteoporosis, and hyperglycemia. Non-suppression of cortisol on overnight dexamethasone suppression test is diagnostic of Cushing syndrome. The multiple potential etiologies include pituitary adenoma, adrenal tumor, or ectopic paraneoplastic ACTH secretion. The markedly elevated DHEA-S (75 µg/ml, normal 0.5-5.4) is a key finding indicating adrenal origin, as DHEA-S is produced in the zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex. Elevated DHEA-S specifically suggests adrenocortical carcinoma or adrenal hyperplasia rather than pituitary pathology. CT scan of the abdomen is the appropriate next step to visualize the adrenal glands and identify a functional adrenal nodule or hyperplasia. Choice A (Fasting serum cortisol) is inaccurate for Cushing syndrome diagnosis; the appropriate initial tests are 24-hour urine free cortisol, late night salivary cortisol, or low-dose overnight dexamethasone suppression test, which has already been abnormal in this patient. Choice B (Serum potassium) is not the appropriate next diagnostic step. While Cushing syndrome can cause hypokalemia due to cortisol's mild mineralocorticoid activity, potassium levels may be normal or only mildly decreased and this would not help localize the disease. Choice C (Pelvic ultrasound) is unnecessary. The irregular menses are explained by excessive cortisol and DHEA-S from Cushing syndrome of adrenal origin, not from primary pelvic or gonadal pathology. Choice E (MRI of the brain) would be indicated to evaluate for pituitary adenoma in central Cushing syndrome. However, the markedly elevated DHEA-S strongly suggests adrenal etiology rather than pituitary pathology, making adrenal imaging the priority.
▶Renal Urinary System Iodinated Contrast Dye Adverse Effects on Renal and Urinary System2 questions
Source: 6A #34
A 57-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a painful, cold right leg for 4 hours. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia. Medications include metformin, triamterene-hydrochlorothiazide, and atorvastatin. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. His blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Pulses are decreased in the right lower extremity. His serum creatinine concentration is 1.5 mg/dL. Angiography of the right lower extremity shows occlusion of the common femoral artery. Twenty-four hours later, his serum creatinine concentration increases to 3.6 mg/dL. Which of the following measures prior to his angiography is most likely to have prevented this patient's worsening azotemia? A) Discontinuation of metformin B) Hydration C) Pretreatment with mannitol D) Pretreatment with prednisone and diphenhydramine E) There are no known preventive measures
Correct Answer: B) Hydration
Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) is defined as acute kidney injury developing shortly after exposure to intravenous contrast. This patient has multiple risk factors for CIN including chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 1.5 mg/dL), diabetes mellitus, and hypertension. The acute rise in serum creatinine to 3.6 mg/dL following angiography is consistent with CIN. Multiple large clinical trials have demonstrated that pretreatment with intravenous hydration—using either normal saline or sodium bicarbonate—significantly reduces the incidence of CIN. This is the only proven preventive measure among the options presented. Choice A (Discontinuation of metformin): While metformin clearance is impaired in chronic kidney disease and can lead to lactic acidosis with increased mortality risk, metformin use itself is not associated with increased risk of CIN. Discontinuing metformin would not prevent CIN, though it may limit subsequent complications if CIN occurs. Choice C (Pretreatment with mannitol): Multiple studies have shown that mannitol, particularly when used with diuretics, does not reduce the risk of CIN. In fact, diuretics may be deleterious and counterproductive. Choice D (Pretreatment with prednisone and diphenhydramine): These agents are appropriate for preventing allergic reactions to contrast but have no role in preventing CIN. Choice E (No known preventive measures): This is incorrect because hydration is an evidence-based preventive strategy. The educational objective emphasizes recognizing risk factors for CIN (chronic kidney disease, diabetes, advanced age, volume depletion) and implementing proven preventive measures, particularly perioperative hydration, prior to contrast exposure.
Source: 5A #11
A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-day history of fever and severe abdominal pain. His only medication is glyburide. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). Abdominal examination shows moderate left lower quadrant tenderness with guarding but no rebound. His serum creatinine concentration is 1.4 mg/dl. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. This patient should receive which of the following prior to a CT scan of the abdomen with intravenous contrast? A) Atrial natriuretic peptide B) Dopamine C) Furosemide D) Mannitol E) 0.9% Saline
Correct Answer: E) 0.9% Saline
Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) results from the toxic effect of intravenous contrast on the tubular cells of the kidney and may result in impaired renal function. This patient presents with fever and abdominal pain requiring a contrast-enhanced CT scan. His elevated creatinine (1.4 mg/dl) places him at higher risk for CIN development. To prevent or decrease the risk of CIN, intravenous 0.9% saline infusion is the recommended intervention. Intravenous isotonic fluid administration assists in promoting renal excretion and reducing the nephrotoxic effects of iodinated contrast through maintained renal perfusion and dilution of the contrast agent. Choice A (Atrial natriuretic peptide) may promote diuresis but has not been shown to prevent CIN. Choice B (Dopamine) is considered a nephroprotective inotrope that can theoretically increase renal blood flow at low concentrations, but it does not have a role in preventing CIN. Choice C (Furosemide) is a loop diuretic that increases urine production. While loop diuretics were historically thought to reduce CIN risk when used with matched intravenous hydration, they should not be used as sole preventative measures because diuretics may result in hemodynamically significant hypovolemia, which could worsen contrast-associated acute kidney injury. Choice D (Mannitol) is an osmotic diuretic primarily used to lower intracranial and intraocular pressure during acute elevations. Forced diuresis with mannitol is not currently recommended for CIN prevention.
▶Gastrointestinal System Clostridium difficile infection2 questions
Source: 9A #13
One week after undergoing appendectomy for acute appendicitis, a patient's postoperative course was uncomplicated. However, the patient now presents with diarrhea. Current temperature is 38°C (100.4°F). Abdominal examination shows a clean, intact surgical incision and diffuse mild tenderness. Examination of the stool shows numerous leukocytes. Results of additional testing are pending. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's diarrhea? A) Ischemic injury to the colonic mucosa B) Microabscesses in the bowel mucosa C) Stimulation of sodium-potassium pumps D) Submucosal proliferation of lymphocytes in the colon E) Toxin-mediated injury to the bowel mucosa
Correct Answer: E) Toxin-mediated injury to the bowel mucosa
This patient most likely has Clostridioides difficile infection secondary to cefoxitin use during the appendectomy. C. difficile infection causes diarrhea as a result of toxin-mediated injury to the bowel mucosa, which leads to inflammation and pseudomembrane formation. C. difficile infection occurs when there is disruption of normal colonic flora as a result of antibiotic use, which allows C. difficile to proliferate and overgrow. The bacteria then produce toxins (toxin A and toxin B) that damage the bowel mucosa, leading to profuse, watery diarrhea and the leukocytes seen on stool examination. The gold standard for diagnosis is a toxigenic culture; however, a two-step algorithm is often used clinically that tests for positive antigen and positive toxin. Prevention includes careful antibiotic use, strict hand hygiene, and contact precautions. Treatment is with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Choice A is incorrect: Ischemic injury to the colonic mucosa typically results from hypoperfusion of the bowel and presents with sudden-onset hematochezia and severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination. Choice B is incorrect: While microabscesses in the bowel mucosa may be present during C. difficile infection because of ongoing inflammation, they are not the direct cause of diarrhea. Choice C is incorrect: Stimulation of sodium-potassium pumps is characteristic of Vibrio cholerae infection, where cholera toxin activates adenylate cyclase, increasing chloride secretion into the intestinal lumen and stimulating the sodium-potassium pump to maintain the electrochemical gradient. Choice D is incorrect: Submucosal proliferation of lymphocytes in the colon is seen in disease states such as inflammatory bowel disease, where lymphoid aggregates are found on biopsy of the bowel wall. Given the recent surgery and cefoxitin use, C. difficile infection is a more likely explanation than IBD.
Source: 10A #27
57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of severe abdominal cramps and profuse nonbloody diarrhea. During this time, she has passed 10 to 20 watery, nonbloody stools daily. She completed a course of cephalexin for treatment of paronychia 4 days ago. She has not had sick contacts. Five days ago, she dined at a local restaurant. Six months ago, she vacationed in Belize. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is mildly distended, soft, and mildly tender to deep palpation. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's diarrhea? A. Colonization of the colon with Clostridioides difficile B. Colonization of the colon with Salmonella enteritidis C. Colonization of the colon with Shigella sonnei D. Production of an exotoxin by C. difficile E. Production of an exotoxin by S. enteritidis F. Production of an exotoxin by S. sonnei
Correct Answer: D. Production of an exotoxin by C. difficile
Educational Objective: This patient has developed profuse diarrhea after a course of cephalexin, a known trigger for Clostridioides difficile infection. Production of an exotoxin by C. difficile causes diarrhea as a result of toxin-mediated injury to the bowel mucosa, leading to inflammation and pseudomembrane formation. Evaluation: The diagnosis of C. difficile infection should be suspected in patients with acute watery or bloody diarrhea and abdominal discomfort after prior antibiotic use. The gold standard for diagnosis is a toxigenic culture, but often a two-step algorithm is used to test for positive antigen and positive toxin laboratory studies. Definition: C. difficile infection occurs when there is disruption of normal colonic flora because of antibiotic use, which allows C. difficile to proliferate, overgrow, and produce toxins. The toxins, Toxin A and Toxin B, damage the bowel mucosa, which leads to profuse, watery diarrhea. Key Clinical Features: This patient's presentation is classic for C. difficile infection: recent antibiotic exposure (cephalexin), acute onset of watery diarrhea (10-20 stools daily), abdominal discomfort, and constitutional symptoms (tachycardia, tachypnea). The acute 2-day time course following antibiotic use 4 days ago is the key clinical clue. Choice A (Colonization with C. difficile): Incorrect. Colonization alone does not cause disease. It is the production of toxins, not the presence of the organism, that damages the bowel mucosa and leads to profuse watery diarrhea in C. difficile infection. Choice B (Colonization with Salmonella enteritidis): Incorrect. While Salmonella can cause acute bacterial diarrhea, it is typically associated with food contamination (poultry, eggs) and presents within 6-72 hours after ingestion. This patient has no clear exposure 4 days before symptom onset, and more importantly, the recent antibiotic use is the critical risk factor pointing to C. difficile. Choice C (Colonization with Shigella sonnei): Incorrect. Shigella causes dysentery with bloody diarrhea and mucus, not the profuse watery nonbloody diarrhea seen here. Additionally, there is no clear exposure history, and the recent antibiotic use points to C. difficile. Choice E (Exotoxin production by S. enteritidis): Incorrect. While Salmonella does produce enterotoxins, the clinical context (recent antibiotic use) and presentation (profuse watery nonbloody diarrhea without bloody stools typical of Salmonella dysentery) make C. difficile far more likely. Choice F (Exotoxin production by S. sonnei): Incorrect. While Shigella produces toxins, Shigella infection typically presents with bloody diarrhea and tenesmus, not the profuse watery nonbloody diarrhea seen in this patient. The recent antibiotic exposure is the critical clue pointing to C. difficile. Prevention: Prevention of C. difficile includes judicious antibiotic use, hand hygiene, and contact precautions. Treatment: Initial treatment of mild to moderate C. difficile infection is with oral vancomycin, metronidazole, or fidaxomicin. Differential Diagnosis: The differential includes other infectious causes such as viral gastroenteritis, acute bacterial enteritis, parasitic infection, and ischemic colitis. However, given this patient's recent antibiotic use and the acute time course of diarrhea, C. difficile infection is the most likely explanation.
