A previously healthy 5-year-old presents with hematuria. He has not had urinary urgency, burning or pain with urination, or flank or back pain. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 140/86 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, Serum Urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, Urine Protein trace, Casts none, Bacteria none. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Urinalysis in 2 weeks B) Measurement of prothrombin time C) Measurement of serum prostate-specific antigen concentration D) Cystoscopy E) Renal biopsy
Correct Answer: D) Cystoscopy
Bladder cancer is the most common malignant tumor of the urinary tract, with the majority being transitional cell carcinoma. Patients classically present with painless hematuria, which may be grossly visible or microscopic. This patient presents with painless hematuria and a significant smoking history (one pack daily for 40 years), raising concern for bladder cancer. Cystoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of bladder cancer, allowing for direct visualization of bladder tissue and tissue sampling. Risk factors for bladder cancer include schistosomiasis, chronic cyclophosphamide use, aniline dye exposure, and tobacco smoking. Urine cytology showing malignant cells is highly specific for bladder cancer, though this finding is not always present. Choice A (Urinalysis in 2 weeks) is incorrect because the patient has already been identified to have hematuria on initial urinalysis, necessitating further diagnostic evaluation. Choice B (Measurement of prothrombin time) is incorrect as there is no history of bleeding disorder or coagulopathy. Choice C (Serum PSA concentration) is not the most appropriate next step because bladder cancer is more likely than prostate cancer given the presentation of painless hematuria and smoking history. Choice E (Renal biopsy) is incorrect because while renal biopsy may be appropriate for suspected renal malignancy, the clinical presentation and risk factors point toward bladder pathology rather than renal pathology. Treatment of bladder cancer is often surgical, potentially with chemotherapy depending on pathology and staging, with transurethral resection of bladder tumor as a resection option.
Source: 10A #41
A 75-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-month history of intermittent episodes of blood in his urine and a 1-hour history of urinary retention. He has not had urgency, urinary incontinence, or pain with urination, and he has no history of trauma. He has hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Medications are metoprolol and ipratropium-albuterol. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 40 years. Upon admission, a three-way Foley catheter is inserted. Temperature is 37.7°C (99.8°F), pulse is 90/min and regular, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. The patient appears to be in moderate distress. Pulmonary examination discloses decreased breath sounds bilaterally. Abdominal examination discloses moderate suprapubic tenderness. Digital rectal examination discloses mild prostatic enlargement but no other abnormalities. Blood clots are visible in the patient's urine collection bag. Laboratory studies show: Serum urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL; Blood hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, leukocyte count 6600/mm³, platelet count 260,000/mm³. In addition to irrigation of the patient's bladder, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Cystoscopy B) MRI of the pelvis C) Transrectal ultrasonography of the prostate D) Urine culture E) Urine cytology
Correct Answer: A) Cystoscopy
Correct Answer: A. Cystoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis of bladder cancer. Educational Objective: Patients with bladder cancer typically present with painless hematuria, which may be grossly visible or microscopic. Cystoscopy is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis for this patient. Evaluation: Bladder cancer is the most common malignant tumor of the urinary tract, with a majority being transitional cell carcinoma. Urine cytology showing malignant cells is highly specific for bladder cancer, though this finding is not always present. Cystoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis. Definition: Patients with bladder cancer typically present with painless, gross hematuria that may cause urinary retention if blood clots are present within the bladder. In advanced or metastatic cases, patients may present with systemic signs such as fatigue, weight loss, and anorexia. Often, asymptomatic hematuria is the only sign or symptom present. Prevention: Risk factors for bladder cancer include schistosomiasis, chronic cyclophosphamide use, aniline dye exposure, and tobacco smoking. Treatment: Treatment is often surgical with possible chemotherapy depending on pathology and clinical staging. Resection can often be achieved with transurethral resection of the bladder tumor. Differential: This patient with a 40-year history of smoking one pack daily presents with painless hematuria and urinary retention, suggestive of bladder cancer. The most appropriate next step is cystoscopy to allow direct visualization of bladder tissue. Choice B (MRI of the pelvis) is incorrect as MRI may be used for staging but cystoscopy is the most appropriate initial diagnostic step. Choice C (Transrectal ultrasonography of the prostate) is incorrect as this patient has mild prostatic enlargement without other abnormalities, and painless hematuria makes bladder cancer more likely. Choice D (Urine culture) is not the most appropriate next step; while hematuria may be present in urinary tract infections, patients typically report dysuria, urinary frequency or urgency, and possible suprapubic pain, which this patient lacks. Choice E (Urine cytology) is incorrect because although commonly used in bladder cancer evaluation, urine cytology has poor sensitivity, especially for low-grade malignancies.
▶Respiratory System Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome2 questions
Source: 5A #48
Twenty-four hours after nearly drowning, a 24-year-old man in the intensive care unit has not regained consciousness. He was resuscitated at the scene and was intubated and mechanically ventilated en route to the emergency department. In the emergency department, his PO2 was 80 mm Hg on an FiO2 of 30%. An x-ray of the chest showed no abnormalities. Now, his temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 121/60 mm Hg. His respirations are 14/min on the ventilator. Examination shows no edema. Coarse airway sounds are heard on auscultation; there are no crackles. Heart sounds are distant with no gallops. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 8500/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 80%, Lymphocytes 20%, Serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis on an FiO2 of 100% and a positive end-expiratory pressure of 20 cm H2O shows pH 7.42, PaCO2 38 mm Hg, PaO2 60 mm Hg. An x-ray of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current x-ray findings? A) Acute respiratory distress syndrome B) Bronchiolitis obliterans C) Congestive heart failure D) Diffuse interstitial pneumonia E) Idiopathic interstitial fibrosis
Correct Answer: A) Acute respiratory distress syndrome
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the most likely diagnosis in this near-drowning victim. ARDS occurs in response to many etiologies, most commonly infectious, inflammatory, and traumatic. The syndrome results from the effect of cytokines on the pulmonary parenchyma from direct or indirect lung injury. This results in endothelial injury with exudative fluid extending into the alveolar space, resulting in diffuse alveolar damage and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. On chest radiographs, this is characterized by diffuse reticular and airspace opacification. In the case of drowning, aspirated fluid causes local inflammation in the lung, along with the dilution of surfactant, leading to impaired compliance and airspace infiltration. This can result in persistent hypoxia despite rising positive end-expiratory pressure and increased fraction of inspired oxygen (as evidenced by PaO2 of 60 mm Hg on FiO2 of 100% and PEEP of 20 cm H2O). Choice B (Bronchiolitis obliterans) is characterized by chronic inflammation in the bronchioles and, in some cases, alveoli, which leads to deposition of connective tissue and can show an obstructive lung disease pattern on spirometry. This is not acute and does not fit the clinical timeline. Choice C (Congestive heart failure) results from increased filling pressures or impaired forward flow in the heart. This increases hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary venous circulation, resulting in transudation of fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the alveolar space. However, this is not the most likely etiology in a previously healthy young person without cardiomegaly on chest x-ray and a more likely explanation related to recent drowning is present. Additionally, the pulmonary edema in CHF is cardiogenic, not the noncardiogenic pulmonary edema seen here. Choice D (Diffuse interstitial pneumonia) commonly presents with infectious or inflammatory symptoms such as fever and cough productive of sputum, along with infiltrates on chest x-ray. This patient is afebrile and had a normal chest x-ray on arrival that became abnormal during the hospital course, suggesting that prior to presentation he had been healthy and the infiltrates represent acute development. Choice E (Idiopathic interstitial fibrosis), also known as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, is a restrictive lung disease that often presents in older smokers, resulting in chronic and progressive shortness of breath. This is a chronic process that does not explain the acute presentation following drowning.
Source: 10A #10
A previously healthy 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-hour history of progressive shortness of breath. He now has shortness of breath with speaking. He has a 3-day history of temperatures to 39.4°C (103°F), cough productive of yellow sputum, and right-sided chest pain that worsens with cough or deep inspiration. His last visit to a physician was 7 years ago. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 38/min, and blood pressure is 98/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Examination shows no jugular venous distention. Diffuse crackles are heard throughout all lung fields. Cardiac examination shows a discrete, nondisplaced, hyperdynamic point of maximal impulse and a normal S3 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops are heard. A chest x-ray shows diffuse infiltrates in all lobes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute respiratory distress syndrome B) Bronchiectasis C) Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease D) Congestive heart failure E) Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Correct Answer: A) Acute respiratory distress syndrome
This patient presents with worsening dyspnea and hypoxemia in the setting of likely pneumonia with a chest x-ray showing diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. This constellation of symptoms is most consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). ARDS is characterized by acute onset, diffuse, inflammatory lung injury and noncardiogenic, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging leading to hypoxic respiratory failure. There are numerous causes of ARDS, including sepsis, pneumonia, chemical pneumonitis, pulmonary contusion, acute pancreatitis, trauma, transfusions, medications, and amniotic fluid embolism. ARDS results from cytokine-mediated injury to the pulmonary parenchyma, especially the alveolar epithelium and endothelium, resulting in diffuse alveolar damage with consequent exudative fluid filling the alveolar spaces. The patient has fever, hypoxia, and productive cough, making infection the most likely cause, with the presentation having progressed to ARDS. Treatment depends on the underlying cause; however, endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation should occur in patients who are apneic, hypoxic, or hypercapnic and not responding to less invasive means, or are unable to protect their airway. Choice B (Bronchiectasis) is incorrect because it typically presents with frequent cough, excessive sputum production, and frequent respiratory exacerbations, with wheezing on pulmonary auscultation from narrow and obstructed airways. Bronchiectasis does not cause diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. Choice C (Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is incorrect because it classically presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion and productive cough in a patient with a history of cigarette smoking. It does not present as a new diagnosis with acute dyspnea and hypoxemia. Choice D (Congestive heart failure) is incorrect because left-sided heart failure presents with dyspnea on exertion, decreased exercise tolerance, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, and shortness of breath. Right-sided heart failure may present with weight gain and edema. Congestive heart failure does not cause fever or purulent sputum. Additionally, the patient's cardiac examination shows no jugular venous distention and normal heart sounds without gallops. Choice E (Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) is incorrect because it is a chronic, progressive lung disease characterized by scarring of the lung parenchyma with symptoms including shortness of breath especially with physical activity, dry hacking cough, fatigue, and weight loss. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis does not present acutely with fever, dyspnea, or hypoxemia in this manner.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Chronic myeloid leukemia2 questions
Source: 7A #5
An asymptomatic 67-year-old man comes for a routine health maintenance examination. His last visit was 2 years ago, and he has been healthy since then. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 65/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Examination shows mild splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 35% Leukocyte count 20,000/mm³ Segmented neutrophils 50% Bands 10% Eosinophils 5% Basophils 5% Lymphocytes 20% Metamyelocytes 5% Myelocytes 5% Platelet count 700,000/mm³ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia B) Chronic myelogenous leukemia C) Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia D) Plasma cell myeloma E) Reactive leukocytosis
Correct Answer: B) Chronic myelogenous leukemia
Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is the most likely diagnosis in this asymptomatic male with splenomegaly, thrombocytosis, and leukocytosis with a white blood cell (WBC) differential demonstrating cells of different lineages. CML is diagnosed by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, which causes constitutive activation of the ABL kinase protein. Activation of ABL kinase leads to subsequent activation of the JAK/STAT and Ras/MAPK/ERK pathways, resulting in increased hematopoietic proliferation, inhibition of normal checkpoint inhibition, and resistance to apoptosis. Typical laboratory findings in CML include leukocytosis with an increase in nearly all cell lines. Basophilia and eosinophilia are particularly characteristic of CML. Splenomegaly, which at times can be massive, is common. Leukostasis, a condition in which leukocytosis leads to end organ damage from occlusion of capillaries by malignant cells, is uncommon in CML, in contrast to acute leukemias where circulating blasts, which are large and not particularly pliable, easily lodge in capillaries causing pulmonary and neurologic complications. Treatment of CML is with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) such as imatinib or dasatinib, which are effective and often result in complete molecular response within several months of initiation. Choice A (Chronic lymphocytic leukemia) is a malignancy of mature, differentiated B lymphocytes presenting with lymphocytosis and smudge cells on peripheral smear, not the mixed myeloid predominance seen here. Choice C (Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm that presents with increased peripheral monocytes. While myelocytes and monocytes derive from multipotent stem cells, they are distinctly different cell lines. This patient's blood smear does not show increased circulating monocytes. Choice D (Plasma cell myeloma) presents with monoclonal protein, bone lesions, hypercalcemia, and renal dysfunction, not the leukocytosis with multilineage involvement seen here. Choice E (Reactive leukocytosis) occurs in response to infection, inflammation, or stress but would not produce the degree of thrombocytosis (700,000/mm³), basophilia, and eosinophilia characteristic of CML.
Source: 8A #4
A previously healthy 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of progressively worsening fatigue; he has had a 14-kg (30-lb) weight loss during this period. Vital signs are within normal limits. The spleen tip is palpated 8 cm below the left costal margin. Examination shows no other abnormalities. His hematocrit is 40%, leukocyte count is 36,000/mm³, and platelet count is 70,000/mm³. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy show 100% cellularity with an increase in all hematopoietic cell lines. The presence of which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis? A) BCR/ABL fusion protein B) BRCAT7 oncogene C) P-glycoprotein D) p53 Suppressor gene E) t(8,16) Translocation
Correct Answer: A) BCR/ABL fusion protein
The presence of the BCR/ABL fusion protein, the product of an abnormal chromosome known as the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome, will confirm the diagnosis of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). CML is diagnosed by the presence of the Ph chromosome, a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, which causes constitutive activation of the ABL kinase protein. Activation of ABL kinase leads to subsequent activation of the JAK/STAT and Ras/MAPK/ERK pathways, leading to increased hematopoietic proliferation, inhibition of normal checkpoint inhibition, and resistance to apoptosis. While the Ph chromosome is required for the diagnosis of CML, it can also be found in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Typical laboratory findings in CML include leukocytosis with an increase in nearly all cell lines. Basophilia and eosinophilia are characteristic. Leukostasis, a condition in which leukocytosis leads to end organ damage from occlusion of capillaries by malignant cells, is uncommon in CML, in contrast to acute leukemias in which circulating blasts easily lodge in capillaries causing pulmonary and neurologic complications. Treatment of CML is primarily with tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib or dasatinib, which are effective and often result in complete molecular response within several months of initiation. Choice B (BRCAT7 oncogene) is implicated in the development of breast and ovarian cancer and is considered a tumor suppressor gene that aids DNA repair when functioning normally. Mutations render this protein nonfunctional, increasing the risk for breast cancer, but this does not confirm CML. Choice C (P-glycoprotein) is an efflux pump belonging to the ABC class of transporters. Leukemic cells may develop the ability to actively shunt chemotherapeutic agents out of the cell using p-glycoproteins, thereby rendering them resistant. However, the presence of p-glycoproteins does not confirm the presence of CML. Choice D (p53 Suppressor gene) is mutated in nearly half of all cancers and its loss of function would not confirm the diagnosis of CML. Choice E (t(8,16) Translocation) is found in a subtype of AML, not CML. Patients with AML will have circulating myeloblasts present on the peripheral blood smear and in the bone marrow. Educational Objective: CML results from constitutive activation of ABL kinase, which causes unregulated cellular proliferation of multiple lineages of white blood cells. Typical findings include leukocytosis with a diverse array of myeloid lineage cells present on the peripheral smear.
▶Renal Urinary System Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug Adverse Effects on Renal and Urinary System2 questions
Source: 7A #33
A 77-year-old man with osteoarthritis comes to the office because of a 2-week history of increasing right knee pain. He was diagnosed with osteoarthritis 5 years ago. Last year, an x-ray of the right knee showed mild degenerative changes. He has been treated with increasing doses of ibuprofen and now takes 800 mg of ibuprofen three times daily. He tries to avoid walking because of the pain. He has not had abdominal pain, change in appetite, or any other symptoms. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). On examination, flexion of the right knee is limited to 20 degrees. There are no effusions. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, Leukocyte count 8500/mm3, Serum Urea nitrogen 32 mg/dL, Creatinine 3 mg/dL, Urine Blood negative, Protein negative, RBC none, WBC none. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Continue ibuprofen at the current dose and repeat the laboratory studies in 2 weeks B) Continue ibuprofen at the current dose and begin oral hydrocortisone C) Decrease the dose of ibuprofen and begin oral prednisone D) Discontinue ibuprofen E) Switch from ibuprofen to oral celecoxib
Correct Answer: D) Discontinue ibuprofen
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a rapid decrease in renal function that may result from prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal causes. In this patient, the markedly elevated creatinine (3 mg/dL) and elevated BUN (32 mg/dL) with normal urine findings indicate NSAID-induced AKI. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors that block prostaglandin and prostacyclin synthesis. Prostaglandins play critical roles in renal blood flow regulation by promoting renal afferent arteriole vasodilation. High-dose, prolonged NSAID use causes AKI through prostaglandin deficiency, leading to reduced renal afferent arteriole vasodilation and decreased renal blood flow. NSAIDs can also cause acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), characterized by declining urine output and GFR, rising creatinine, eosinophilic infiltrates on renal biopsy, and eosinophiluria. The patient's rising creatinine indicates NSAID-induced kidney injury that requires cessation of the offending agent. Choice A (Continue ibuprofen at current dose and repeat labs in 2 weeks) is inappropriate because ibuprofen is the likely cause of AKI and continuing it will worsen renal function. Choice B (Continue ibuprofen and begin oral hydrocortisone) is inappropriate for the same reason—ibuprofen must be discontinued, not continued, and hydrocortisone does not address NSAID-induced AKI. Choice C (Decrease ibuprofen dose and begin oral prednisone) is inadequate because merely reducing the NSAID dose does not sufficiently address NSAID-induced kidney injury; complete cessation is necessary. Prednisone would not reverse NSAID-induced AKI. Choice E (Switch to celecoxib) is inappropriate because celecoxib is also an NSAID (a selective COX-2 inhibitor) and would perpetuate or worsen the patient's AKI rather than resolve it. Educational Objective: NSAIDs can cause acute kidney injury through prostaglandin deficiency, resulting in reduced renal afferent arteriole vasodilation and renal blood flow. NSAID-induced AKI requires discontinuation of the offending agent, not dose reduction or substitution with other NSAIDs.
Source: 10A #3
A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of dark urine. He reports that he has had a viral illness characterized by nausea, diarrhea, and myalgias and has not been able to eat or drink much over the past week. His only medication is 800 mg of ibuprofen three times daily. The patient appears ill. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 128/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. Examination of the throat shows no erythema. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations show no abnormalities. There is no edema of the extremities. Serum studies show a sodium concentration of 148 mEq/L, urea nitrogen concentration of 60 mg/dL, and creatinine concentration of 3.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's renal failure? A) Cyclooxygenase excess B) Cyclooxygenase inhibition C) Glutathione deficiency D) Glutathione excess E) Prostaglandin excess
Correct Answer: B) Cyclooxygenase inhibition
This patient presents with acute kidney injury (AKI) in the setting of prolonged high-dose NSAID use (800 mg ibuprofen three times daily) combined with volume depletion from a viral illness with decreased oral intake. The correct answer is cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibition. Mechanism: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are nonselective COX inhibitors that work by decreasing the production of inflammatory cytokines and prostaglandins. Within the glomerulus, prostaglandins physiologically induce afferent arteriolar vasodilation and thereby increase glomerular filtration rate and renal perfusion. By inhibiting COX and reducing prostaglandin production, NSAIDs decrease afferent arteriolar vasodilation, leading to decreased glomerular perfusion and AKI. This effect is especially pronounced when high-dose or prolonged NSAID use is accompanied by renal blood flow-limiting insults such as volume depletion (diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration), hypovolemia, or hypotension—all present in this case. Clinical presentation: The patient's laboratory findings reveal elevated creatinine (3.5 mg/dL), elevated BUN (60 mg/dL), hypernatremia (148 mEq/L), and tachycardia with hypotension, all consistent with prerenal AKI from volume depletion exacerbated by NSAID-induced reduction in glomerular perfusion. The dark urine suggests myoglobinuria or hemoglobinuria potentially from rhabdomyolysis due to volume depletion and myalgias. Choice A (Cyclooxygenase excess) is incorrect. NSAIDs inhibit rather than increase COX activity. Choices C and D (Glutathione deficiency and excess) are incorrect. Glutathione is a primary hepatic antioxidant, and glutathione depletion is a hallmark of acetaminophen toxicity, not NSAID toxicity. Choice E (Prostaglandin excess) is incorrect. NSAIDs are COX inhibitors that decrease rather than increase prostaglandin production. Decreased prostaglandin concentration, not excess, is expected in patients taking NSAIDs regularly. Prevention and treatment: The patient's condition could have been prevented with increased fluid intake or decreased NSAID dosing. Treatment includes cessation of NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and angiotensin II receptor blockers, correction of hypovolemia, and management of electrolyte abnormalities.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Lyme Disease2 questions
Source: 10A #9
A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of an expanding red rash on his chest, malaise, and muscle and joint pain. He says that he had a tick bite 2 weeks ago. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/84 mm Hg. Examination shows a 5 × 7-cm, erythematous annular plaque with central clearing on the chest. Treatment with doxycycline is most likely to prevent which of the following? A) Carditis B) Chronic fatigue syndrome C) Fibromyalgia D) Hepatitis E) Inflammatory bowel disease
Correct Answer: A) Carditis
Educational Objective: Lyme disease is a tick-borne illness caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, endemic in the Northeastern United States. It characteristically causes erythema chronicum migrans, an expanding annular rash that may have central ring-like clearing, along with flu-like symptoms in early localized disease. Treatment with doxycycline in early stages would most likely prevent the development of carditis. Evaluation: Early localized Lyme disease presents with erythema chronicum migrans, fatigue, anorexia, headache, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, and arthralgias. Later stages can include carditis, atrioventricular block, facial nerve palsy (often bilateral), migratory arthralgias, and if untreated, encephalopathy and chronic arthritis. Treatment: Early stages of Lyme disease are treated with doxycycline, while later stages affecting the heart or central nervous system are treated with parenteral ceftriaxone. Differential: The patient's tick bite 2 weeks prior, presentation with malaise, myalgias, arthralgias, and characteristic annular erythema chronicum migrans plaque make Lyme disease the most likely diagnosis. Carditis occurs in approximately 1-5% of untreated Lyme disease patients, and early doxycycline treatment would most likely prevent this complication. Incorrect Answers: Choice B (Chronic fatigue syndrome): Incorrect. Some patients with treated Lyme disease may experience posttreatment Lyme disease syndrome with persistent fatigue-like symptoms, but doxycycline treatment in early disease more likely prevents carditis. Choice C (Fibromyalgia): Incorrect. While Lyme disease may trigger fibromyalgia, early doxycycline treatment would most likely prevent the more serious complication of carditis. Choice D (Hepatitis): Incorrect. While Borrelia burgdorferi can cause various complications, hepatitis is not a characteristic complication prevented by early treatment. Choice E (Inflammatory bowel disease): Incorrect. This is not a known complication of Lyme disease that would be prevented by doxycycline therapy.
Source: 8A #41
A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of diffuse joint aches. Over the past 3 months, she has had headache, stiff neck, and progressive numbness, tingling, and weakness of both lower extremities. Neurologic examination shows a mild right facial palsy and mild weakness of the distal lower extremities. Sensation to pinprick and light touch is decreased over the lower extremities; deep tendon reflexes are absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Measurement of serum antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi B) Measurement of serum vitamin B12 (cobalamin) concentration C) Monospot test D) PPD skin test E) Rapid plasma reagin
Correct Answer: A) Measurement of serum antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi
Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease caused by Borrelia burgdorferi that is endemic in the Northeastern United States. In its early stages, it causes erythema chronicum migrans, which is an expanding rash with a central ring-like clearing. It can also be associated with a flulike illness and arthralgia. Later stages of Lyme disease are characterized by carditis, atrioventricular heart block, facial nerve palsy (which is often bilateral), mononeuropathy multiplex, motor or sensory radiculoneuropathy, migratory arthralgias, and if left untreated, encephalopathy and chronic arthritis. The diagnosis is confirmed by measurement of serum antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi. The early stages of Lyme disease can be treated with doxycycline, which acts by preventing the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to ribosomes. Side effects of tetracycline antibiotics include gastrointestinal distress, photosensitivity, and in children, discoloration of teeth and inhibition of bone growth, which contraindicates the use of doxycycline in pregnancy. The later stages of Lyme disease that affect the heart or central nervous system are generally treated with parenteral ceftriaxone. Choice B: Measurement of serum vitamin B12 (cobalamin) concentration is useful in the diagnosis of subacute combined degeneration affecting the spinocerebellar tracts, lateral corticospinal tracts, and dorsal columns. Subacute combined degeneration causes a combination of motor and sensory symptoms including ataxic gait, muscle weakness, paresthesia, and loss of proprioception and vibration sense. This patient's history of arthralgia and facial nerve palsy is not consistent with a diagnosis of subacute combined degeneration. Choice C: Monospot testing is useful for the diagnosis of infection with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). EBV infection causes infectious mononucleosis. While infectious mononucleosis can cause facial nerve palsy, this patient's history of diffuse arthralgias and radiculoneuropathy are more suggestive of Lyme disease. Choice D: PPD skin test is useful for the diagnosis of tuberculosis. Tuberculosis does not generally cause facial nerve palsy and is rarely associated with peripheral neuropathy. Choice E: Rapid plasma reagin is used to screen for infection with Treponema pallidum, which causes syphilis. Neurosyphilis may present with headache, altered mental status, vision changes, cranial neuropathies, progressive dementia, and possible brain gummas (focal areas of inflammation). Neurosyphilis is not commonly associated with facial nerve palsy or radiculoneuropathy. Educational Objective: Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease caused by Borrelia burgdorferi that is endemic in the Northeastern United States. It may present acutely with erythema chronicum migrans, flulike illness, and in late stages, migratory arthralgia, carditis, atrioventricular heart block, facial nerve palsy, mononeuropathy multiplex, motor or sensory radiculoneuropathy, and encephalopathy. The diagnosis is confirmed by measurement of serum antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi.
▶Respiratory System Bronchiectasis2 questions
Source: 10A #15
A 72-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 5-day history of fever, cough productive of bloody sputum, and shortness of breath. He has a 10-year history of chronic cough productive of sputum. He has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. He is in mild respiratory distress. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m2. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 95/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Coarse breath sounds are heard throughout the lung fields bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Airway inflammation B) Alveolar hemorrhage C) Increased elasticity and cell destruction D) Increased pulmonary vascular resistance E) Recurrent pulmonary infection with scarring
Correct Answer: E) Recurrent pulmonary infection with scarring
The most likely cause of this patient's productive cough, hemoptysis, respiratory distress, and hypoxia is bronchiectasis, which is caused by recurrent pulmonary infections with scarring. Bronchiectasis typically presents with frequent cough, excessive sputum production, and frequent respiratory exacerbations. Physical examination classically discloses wheezing on pulmonary auscultation because of narrow and obstructed airways. The chest x-ray shows linear atelectasis, indicative of scarring secondary to recurrent infections, along with thickened dilated airways and peripheral opacities related to multifocal mucous plugs. Bronchiectasis refers to irreversible, abnormal dilatation and thickening of the bronchi that results from recurrent infections and chronic inflammation. Patients often have a history of recurrent episodes of pneumonia with associated conditions, including chronic bronchial obstruction, tobacco use, cystic fibrosis, primary immunodeficiency disorders, Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia), and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Management consists of identification and treatment of the underlying disorder, airway clearance techniques (including chest physiotherapy, expectorants, and bronchodilators), and antibiotics for acute exacerbations. Choice A (Airway inflammation) is incorrect. Airway inflammation occurs in asthma, which presents with episodic wheezing and shortness of breath with or without a cough. Asthma does not classically present with hemoptysis. Choice B (Alveolar hemorrhage) is incorrect. Alveolar hemorrhage can occur as a result of various pathologies but presents with respiratory distress, hemoptysis, and diffuse opacities on chest x-ray. While some of this patient's symptoms are consistent with alveolar hemorrhage, his chest x-ray findings of linear atelectasis and scarring are not. Choice C (Increased elasticity and cell destruction) is incorrect. This is the underlying pathophysiology of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which classically presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion and productive cough in a patient with a history of cigarette smoking. COPD does not cause the linear atelectasis seen on this patient's chest x-ray. Choice D (Increased pulmonary vascular resistance) is incorrect. Pulmonary hypertension presents with signs of right-sided heart failure including dyspnea, dependent edema, jugular venous distension, and hepatic congestion. It does not classically cause hemoptysis and may not be evident on chest x-ray.
Source: 8A #22
An 82-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of cough productive of copious amounts of green sputum. She has had several similar episodes over the past 5 years. She had several episodes of "walking pneumonia" as a child. She does not smoke and has no history of asthma or exposure to sick contacts. She is afebrile. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Examination shows clubbing of the fingers. An x-ray of the chest shows streaky linear bilateral basilar scarring. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) α₁-Antitrypsin deficiency B) Asthma C) Bronchiectasis D) Cystic fibrosis E) Gastroesophageal reflux F) Hereditary angioedema G) Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection H) Postnasal discharge I) Sarcoidosis
Correct Answer: C) Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis refers to dilation and distortion of the bronchi and/or bronchioles that leads to obstructive lung disease. There are numerous causes, including congenital bronchiectasis caused by underlying genetic disorders of cartilage or the airways, cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, recurrent aspiration, airway malignancies, immunodeficiency syndromes with recurrent necrotizing pulmonary infections, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and connective tissue disorders. Children classically present with chronic cough (with or without sputum production) and symptoms of infection (fever, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain) during exacerbations. Patients who were not diagnosed in childhood may report a history of recurrent pneumonia, as this patient does. Chest imaging may show linear atelectasis or scarring, dilated airways with thickened walls, and peripheral opacities related to multifocal mucous plugs. Bronchiectasis may result in a progressive decline in pulmonary function, if untreated, and manifest as a severe, chronic obstructive lung disease that limits a patient's activity. Lung transplantation may be required later in life. Choice A (α₁-Antitrypsin deficiency) presents as early panacinar emphysema and cirrhosis. It is a hereditary disease resulting from the misfolding of or a mutated nonfunctional α₁-antitrypsin, an antiprotease. The misfolded protein accumulates in the liver causing hepatocyte damage and is unable to prevent protease-induced damage to the pulmonary parenchyma. Choice B (Asthma) is a reversible obstruction to airflow that typically presents with shortness of breath, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, poor air movement, wheezing, and accessory muscle use. Chest imaging is generally normal. Choice D (Cystic fibrosis) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the CFTR gene. While it is associated with bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis most commonly presents in childhood, and patients will have additional medical issues related to the condition, such as pancreatic insufficiency. Choice E (Gastroesophageal reflux) can cause chronic lung disease from recurrent microaspiration. Irritation and inflammation tends to cause bronchial wall thickening that is more prominent in the central and proximal airways. A history of reflux should be assessed and treated if present because it is a modifiable risk factor for further lung impairment. Choice F (Hereditary angioedema) results from a deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor and may present with angioedema of the face, extremities, oropharynx, and gastrointestinal tract caused by increased concentrations of bradykinin. Choice G (Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection) leading to secondary pulmonary reactivation disease presents with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis. Apical infiltrates and/or cavitary lesions are typically seen on chest imaging. Additionally, the patient does not have any noted risk factors for exposure to tuberculosis. Choice H (Postnasal discharge) is associated with allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis, and typically causes a chronic cough that worsens at night. It is also commonly associated with cobblestoning of the oropharynx on physical examination. Choice I (Sarcoidosis) may present with a new or chronic cough. X-ray of the chest commonly shows bilateral hilar adenopathy with or without upper-lobe predominant coarse interstitial infiltrates, which are absent in this case. Educational Objective: Bronchiectasis refers to abnormal dilatation of the bronchi that may result from recurrent necrotizing infections and/or chronic inflammation. Risk factors for bronchiectasis are numerous and include cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Patients diagnosed in adulthood often have a history of recurrent pneumonia during childhood or adolescence.
▶Gastrointestinal System Primary peritonitis2 questions
Source: 10A #50
A 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever and increasing abdominal distention. He has a history of cirrhosis and takes spironolactone and lactulose. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 100/55 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%; there is large ascites with a fluid wave. Examination of the abdomen shows diffuse tenderness to palpation. Intravenous access is established, and results of laboratory studies are pending. X-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis is negative. Which of the following additional tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis? A) Ascitic fluid cell count and differential B) Ascitic fluid lactic acid concentration C) Blood culture D) Serum lactic acid concentration E) Serum leukocyte count
Correct Answer: A) Ascitic fluid cell count and differential
This patient presents with classic features of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP): cirrhosis with ascites, fever, abdominal pain and distention, and hemodynamic compromise (hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea). The gold standard for diagnosis of bacterial peritonitis is paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and differential. A PMN count greater than 250 cells/μL in ascitic fluid is diagnostic of SBP, even before culture results are available. This finding allows for prompt initiation of antibiotic therapy. While blood cultures (Choice C) may help identify the organism, they are positive in only 10-20% of SBP cases and results take time. Serum or ascitic fluid lactic acid concentrations and serum leukocyte count are non-specific markers and are not diagnostic for SBP. Ascitic fluid analysis with cell count and differential remains the most direct and reliable confirmatory test for this life-threatening complication of cirrhosis.
Source: 10A #51
A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites presents with fever, abdominal pain, and worsening abdominal distention. Which of the following is the gold standard diagnostic test for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
Correct Answer: A) Paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and differential
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an infection of ascitic fluid that occurs without an obvious inciting event and is thought to result from bacterial translocation from the intestinal lumen into the ascitic fluid. Patients with cirrhosis and ascites who present with new fever, abdominal pain, and worsening distention are at risk for SBP. The gold standard diagnostic test is paracentesis with ascitic fluid analysis. The diagnostic criteria for SBP are met when the ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count is greater than 250/mm³, though other confirmatory findings include positive ascitic fluid culture or overall leukocyte count greater than 1000/mm³. Untreated SBP can progress to hepatic encephalopathy, sepsis, and death. Treatment consists of intravenous third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone. Prevention includes antibiotic prophylaxis in high-risk patients such as those with active gastrointestinal bleeding and cirrhosis. Choice B (ascitic fluid lactic acid concentration) may be elevated but is not diagnostic for SBP. Choices C, D, and E (blood culture, serum lactic acid concentration, and serum leukocyte count) may be abnormal in this patient but do not directly identify the source of infection and therefore do not confirm the diagnosis of SBP. The key distinction is that paracentesis with direct ascitic fluid analysis is essential to diagnose SBP, whereas systemic laboratory values are nonspecific and would not narrow the differential diagnosis adequately.
▶Endocrine System Hypoparathyroidism2 questions
Source: 6A #3
A 53-year-old man notices a lump in his neck. Examination shows a hard 2-cm nodule in the lower left pole of the thyroid gland. Needle biopsy shows papillary carcinoma, and he undergoes total thyroidectomy. Five days later, he reports facial numbness and tingling, muscle pain, and hoarseness. Physical examination shows laryngeal stridor and a positive Chvostek sign. Which of the following is the most appropriate management? A) Hydration with 0.9% isotonic saline intravenously B) Administration of calcium gluconate intravenously C) Administration of glucocorticoids D) Administration of 50,000 U of vitamin D E) Endotracheal intubation
Correct Answer: B) Administration of calcium gluconate intravenously
The patient is exhibiting signs of severe hypocalcemia due to acute hypoparathyroidism, a known complication of thyroidectomy. Clinical manifestations include facial numbness and tingling (paresthesias), muscle pain, laryngeal stridor (from laryngospasm), and a positive Chvostek sign—all pathognomonic for hypocalcemia. Immediate treatment with intravenous calcium gluconate is the most appropriate management to rapidly correct serum calcium and abate symptoms. Choice A (0.9% isotonic saline hydration with diuresis) is appropriate for hypercalcemia management, not hypocalcemia, and would be inappropriate here. Choice C (glucocorticoids) is incorrect because corticosteroids may induce tetany in hypoparathyroid patients and would worsen the clinical presentation. Choice D (high-dose vitamin D) is used in chronic management of hypoparathyroidism to enhance intestinal calcium absorption but is not appropriate for acute, severe hypocalcemia requiring rapid correction. Choice E (endotracheal intubation) is premature. While the patient has laryngeal stridor from laryngospasm, he does not yet demonstrate signs of respiratory compromise. Correcting the hypocalcemia with intravenous calcium gluconate will resolve the laryngospasm and make intubation unnecessary at this time. The educational objective emphasizes recognizing post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism presenting with hypocalcemia and understanding the acute management priorities: immediate calcium repletion takes precedence over definitive airway management or chronic supplementation strategies.
Source: 7A #38
A 42-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-month history of burning and tingling of the skin over all the extremities and fatigue. She has hypertension and chronic low back pain. Her only medication is hydrochlorothiazide. She appears tired but is not in acute distress. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. Tapping over the facial nerve produces an involuntary contraction of the ipsilateral muscles. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show: Na+ 138 mEq/L, K+ 4.1 mEq/L, Cl- 100 mEq/L, Ca2+ 7.1 mg/dL, Phosphate 6 mg/dL, Protein, total 9 g/dL, Albumin 5 g/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's condition? A) Autonomous secretion of aldosterone B) Autonomous secretion of parathyroid hormone C) Deficiency of parathyroid hormone D) Deficiency of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) E) Excess secretion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D F) Excess secretion of magnesium
Correct Answer: C) Deficiency of parathyroid hormone
Deficiency of parathyroid hormone (PTH), also known as hypoparathyroidism, explains this patient's symptomatic hypocalcemia. PTH is a peptide hormone that increases osteoclast activity and bone resorption to maintain calcium homeostasis. It is produced by the four parathyroid glands located on the posterior aspect of the thyroid gland. Primary hypoparathyroidism can occur following unintentional resection of the parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy or from autoimmune destruction. Primary hypoparathyroidism results in decreased PTH concentrations leading to hypocalcemia (serum calcium 7.1 mg/dL) secondary to inadequate bone resorption, hyperphosphatemia (6 mg/dL), and decreased 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) because PTH stimulates renal conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form. Decreased calcitriol substantially worsens hypocalcemia as calcitriol directly stimulates intestinal calcium absorption. Signs and symptoms of severe hypocalcemia include perioral paresthesia (burning and tingling of extremities), carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, and prolonged QT interval. The Chvostek sign (tapping the facial nerve causing ipsilateral facial muscle spasm) and Trousseau sign (inflated blood pressure cuff causing carpopedal spasm) are physical examination findings indicating hypocalcemia. Treatment is with calcium and calcitriol supplementation to achieve a low-normal calcium level. Choice A (Autonomous secretion of aldosterone): Primary hyperaldosteronism results in hypokalemia, alkalosis, and hypertension. This patient has normal potassium (4.1 mEq/L) and normal blood pressure. Choice B (Autonomous secretion of parathyroid hormone): Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia, with symptoms including weakness, constipation, confusion, depression, diffuse bone pain, nephrolithiasis, and polyuria. Choice D (Deficiency of vitamin B12): Cobalamin deficiency causes paresthesia and reduced proprioception from subacute combined degeneration of dorsal and lateral spinal cord columns, presenting with impaired gait, abnormal Romberg test, and macrocytic anemia—not the laboratory findings seen here. Choice E (Excess secretion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D): Not a well-recognized clinical syndrome. Hypersecretion of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D occurs in sarcoidosis or granulomatous disorders and causes hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia. Choice F (Excess secretion of magnesium): Does not explain the clinical presentation or laboratory abnormalities.
▶Gastrointestinal System Acute pancreatitis2 questions
Source: 6A #15
A 42-year-old man with alcoholism is admitted to the hospital 12 hours after the onset of severe epigastric pain that radiates to the back. He has had several episodes of vomiting. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. There is tenderness to palpation in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant of the abdomen; there are no signs of peritonitis. Bowel sounds are decreased. After 2 days, laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 13 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume 102 µm³ Leukocyte count 12,000/mm³ Segmented neutrophils 76% Bands 4% Lymphocytes 20% Serum Ca²⁺ 6 mg/dL Urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL Albumin 3.5 g/dL Amylase 500 U/L His serum electrolyte concentrations are within the reference range. Which of the laboratory findings in this patient is associated with the worst prognosis? A) Leukocyte count B) Mean corpuscular volume C) Serum albumin concentration D) Serum amylase activity E) Serum calcium concentration
Correct Answer: E) Serum calcium concentration
The patient's presentation is strongly suggestive of acute pancreatitis given his history of alcoholism and epigastric pain radiating to the back. Prognosis in acute pancreatitis is best predicted by Ranson's criteria, one of the earliest and most commonly used scoring systems. Ranson's criteria consist of 11 factors measured at admission (5 factors) and at 48 hours (6 factors), with each factor assigned a point value of 1 if present. A Ranson's score of 0-2 is associated with 0-3% mortality; 3-4 with 15% mortality; 5-6 with 40% mortality; and 7-11 with almost 100% mortality. Of the clinical factors present in this patient, hypocalcemia (serum calcium <8 mg/dL at 48 hours) is the greatest predictor of mortality. The patient's serum calcium of 6 mg/dL meets the Ranson's criterion threshold of <8 mg/dL (2 mmol/L) at 48 hours and is a major independent risk factor for severe disease and mortality in acute pancreatitis. Choice A (Leukocyte count): An elevated leukocyte count >16,000/mm³ at admission is associated with higher mortality according to Ranson's criteria; however, this patient's leukocyte count of 12,000/mm³ is only mildly elevated and not associated with increased mortality. Choice B (Mean corpuscular volume): While a fall in hematocrit >10% at 48 hours is associated with increased mortality according to Ranson's criteria, a slightly increased mean corpuscular volume is not an independent predictor of mortality. Choice C (Serum albumin concentration): While some recent studies have shown that hypoalbuminemia in pancreatitis is associated with organ failure and death, the mildly decreased serum albumin in this patient (3.5 g/dL) is well above the cutoff points that have been identified as predictive of severe disease. Choice D (Serum amylase activity): While elevated amylase activity can be helpful in the diagnosis of pancreatitis, elevated levels at 48 hours after admission have not been identified as an independent risk factor for mortality. Amylase levels correlate poorly with disease severity.
Source: 8A #31
A 47-year-old man with a history of alcoholism is brought to the emergency department because of severe abdominal pain, mild nausea, and two episodes of vomiting during the past 16 hours. The pain is located in the epigastrium and radiates straight through to the back. He had a similar episode of pain 2 years ago that was treated with fluid hydration and bowel rest during a 2-day hospital stay, but he left against medical advice. Vital signs are within normal limits except for a temperature of 38.7°C (101.7°F). Abdominal examination shows slight distention and mild epigastric tenderness. The liver is nontender, and the edge is palpable at the costal margin. The spleen is not palpable. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Insertion of a nasogastric tube yields green-tinged fluid. His leukocyte count is 18,000/mm³, and serum amylase activity is 350 U/L. Liver function tests show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) X-rays of the abdomen B) CT scan of the abdomen C) HIDA scan D) MRI of the abdomen E) Endoscopy F) Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography G) Percutaneous aspiration
Correct Answer: B) CT scan of the abdomen
Acute pancreatitis typically presents with epigastric abdominal pain that radiates to the back along with nausea and emesis, often in a patient with a history of gallstones, alcohol use disorder, trauma, hypertriglyceridemia, or hypercalcemia. Laboratory evaluation often discloses increased amylase and lipase concentrations. Treatment of acute uncomplicated pancreatitis is largely supportive and should include intravenous fluids (either normal saline or lactated ringers) and bowel rest in addition to pain control. The pain from acute pancreatitis is typically severe and often requires opioid analgesics. Acute pancreatitis can be complicated by necrosis, hemorrhage, abscess, or pseudocyst formation. This patient with severe pain, leukocytosis, and fever may have a pancreatic abscess. CT scan of the abdomen is the gold standard for diagnosis of pancreatitis-related complications such as abscess or hemorrhage. Treatment of such conditions may require surgical intervention, and abscess should be treated with antibiotics and source control. Choice A (X-rays of the abdomen) are often utilized for evaluation of acute abdominal pathology (e.g., small bowel obstruction) but are insensitive and would not be able to visualize the pancreas or pancreatitis-related complications. Choice C (HIDA scan) is used for diagnosis of acute cholecystitis, not pancreatitis. Choice D (MRI of the abdomen) offers high-resolution detail of soft tissue structures and can evaluate various intra-abdominal pathologies but is expensive, time-consuming, and not always readily available; CT scan is the initial modality of choice for pancreatitis diagnosis. Choice E (Endoscopy) would be indicated for upper gastrointestinal bleeding (e.g., esophageal varices or peptic ulcer disease), not pancreatitis. Choice F (Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) is indicated in gallstone-induced pancreatitis to retrieve an obstructing gallstone; this patient's pancreatitis is more likely caused by alcohol use disorder, and gallstone-induced pancreatitis would show signs of jaundice and increased bilirubin. Choice G (Percutaneous aspiration) would be inappropriate until further diagnostic imaging is obtained to evaluate anatomy and complications; it may be necessary once pancreatic abscess is confirmed. Educational Objective: CT scan of the abdomen is the first-line imaging examination for the evaluation of acute pancreatitis and pancreatitis-related complications.
▶Respiratory System Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis2 questions
Source: 6A #16
A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of fever and cough with increasing production of purulent sputum for 24 hours. She has had asthma since childhood that is characterized by episodes of coughing and wheezing. Treatment with inhaled corticosteroids was begun 8 months ago. She has been hospitalized twice over the past 2 months for low-grade fever, increased sputum production, and a poorly resolving infiltrate in the left lower lobe; sputum cultures at that time grew normal flora and Aspergillus fumigatus. She is in moderate respiratory distress. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 95/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Diffuse expiratory wheezes and crackles are heard at the left lung base. Cardiac examination shows a normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis B) α1-Antitrypsin deficiency C) Cystic fibrosis D) Pertussis E) Wegener granulomatosis
Correct Answer: A) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
The presence of Aspergillus fumigatus on sputum culture, combined with uncontrolled asthma despite treatment with inhaled corticosteroids, and a fixed infiltrate on chest X-ray, makes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) the most likely diagnosis. Laboratory findings in ABPA include a positive skin test against Aspergillus antigen and elevated IgE levels. Bronchiectasis is commonly seen on CT scan. α1-Antitrypsin deficiency typically presents with emphysema and can also cause chronic liver disease, neither of which are present in this patient. Cystic fibrosis may present with chronic recurrent respiratory infections or symptoms of malabsorption; as this patient's symptoms are more subacute, cystic fibrosis is much less likely. Pertussis typically presents as a chronic cough (without fever) after an initial 1-2 week period of mild cough, fever, malaise, and increased sputum production; radiographic infiltrates are not common, except in cases of secondary pneumonia. Wegener granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) may present with cough, pulmonary infiltrates, hemoptysis, and may be associated with renal involvement; however, a positive sputum culture makes the diagnosis of a vasculitic lung disease such as Wegener unlikely.
Source: 9A #2
A patient with long-standing asthma controlled on inhaled long-acting β-adrenergic agonist and inhaled glucocorticoid for 8 years presents with productive cough and wheezing for 3 months. She has no pets, no history of travel abroad, or new occupational exposure. She appears well and is not in respiratory distress. Vital signs show oxygen saturation of 96%. A chest x-ray shows alveolar infiltrates. Laboratory studies reveal peripheral eosinophilia and increased serum IgE concentrations. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Examination of the stool for ova and parasites B) Measurement of serum angiotensin-converting enzyme activity C) Measurement of serum α₁-antitrypsin concentration D) Serum assay for IgE and IgG antibodies to Aspergillus species E) Methacholine challenge test F) Bone marrow biopsy
Correct Answer: D) Serum assay for IgE and IgG antibodies to Aspergillus species
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with long-standing asthma presenting with productive cough, wheezing, eosinophilia, increased IgE concentrations, and alveolar infiltrates. The most appropriate next step in diagnosis is a serum assay for IgE and IgG antibodies to Aspergillus species. ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction caused by Aspergillus fumigatus organisms in the airways. Patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis are at increased risk. Clinical features include constitutional symptoms (fatigue, mild fever), progressive cough, asthma-like symptoms refractory to treatment, brown or black sputum, hemoptysis, transitory pulmonary infiltrates, peripheral eosinophilia, and bronchiectasis. Laboratory findings show eosinophilia and increased serum IgE. Diagnosis is supported by skin testing for Aspergillus antigens and species-specific serum antibody assays, with CT chest showing central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction as the gold standard. Choice A (stool examination for ova and parasites) is incorrect. Strongyloidiasis causes peripheral eosinophilia with transient infiltrates but occurs in endemic regions and is less likely than ABPA in this stable asthma patient. Choice B (serum angiotensin-converting enzyme activity) is incorrect. Sarcoidosis presents with bilateral perihilar lymphadenopathy and progressive interstitial lung disease but does not classically cause productive cough with brown sputum. Choice C (serum α₁-antitrypsin concentration) is incorrect. α₁-antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema and bronchiectasis but would not present with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates in this clinical context. Choice E (methacholine challenge test) is incorrect. This patient has had stable asthma for years, making acute worsening unlikely, and this test is not indicated for her current presentation. Choice F (bone marrow biopsy) is incorrect. While hematologic malignancies may present with cough, they typically include night sweats and weight loss, which are not mentioned in this patient's presentation.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Hypovolemic Shock2 questions
Source: 6A #22
A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after vomiting bright red blood twice in the past hour. He appears robust and comfortable. His pulse is 116/min, and blood pressure is 100/80 mm Hg while supine. There is mild epigastric tenderness. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Hematocrit is 40%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Discharge him with instructions to return if the pain or vomiting recurs B) Repeat the hematocrit C) Measurement of serum amylase activity D) Intravenous administration of 0.9% saline E) Surgical consultation
Correct Answer: D) Intravenous administration of 0.9% saline
In the setting of significant hematemesis and tachycardia, the patient is in class 2 hypovolemic/hemorrhagic shock, with an estimated blood loss of 15-30% of circulating volume. Volume resuscitation is the most appropriate immediate next step in management with intravenous 0.9% saline. Choice A is incorrect because discharging the patient without appropriate evaluation and resuscitation would be inappropriate given active hemorrhage and hemodynamic compromise. Choice B is incorrect because a repeat hematocrit is unlikely to change significantly at this acute time point and would not alter immediate management decisions. Choice C is incorrect because while measurement of serum amylase would be helpful in evaluating for pancreatitis as a potential underlying etiology, it would not be the next best step in acute hemorrhage management. Choice E is incorrect because although surgical consultation may ultimately be required for definitive management, volume resuscitation and stabilization take priority over surgical evaluation in the acute setting. The educational objective is recognizing the signs of class 2 hemorrhagic shock (tachycardia with maintained blood pressure) and understanding that immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline is the critical first step in hemorrhage management.
Source: 3A #5
Immediately after an episode of massive hematemesis, a 50-year-old man feels faint, cold, and sweaty. His pulse is 130/min, and blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg; hematocrit is 40%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in patient care? A) Rapid infusion of 5% dextrose in water B) Rapid infusion of 0.9% isotonic saline C) Insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter via the subclavian vein D) Gastric lavage with ice-cold saline until bleeding stops E) Emergency esophagogastroduodenoscopy
Correct Answer: B) Rapid infusion of 0.9% isotonic saline
Rapid infusion of 0.9% isotonic saline is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient's decompensated hemorrhagic shock. The patient demonstrates classic signs of hemorrhagic shock: tachycardia (130/min), hypotension (80/40 mm Hg), diaphoresis, and feeling faint. In acute blood loss, the circulatory system compensates through fluid retention, increased heart rate, and vasoconstriction. As blood loss continues and these compensatory mechanisms fail, hemorrhagic shock develops. In hemorrhage, both red blood cells and plasma are lost equivalently, resulting in a normal hematocrit despite decreased overall blood volume. Emergent management requires rapid intravascular volume repletion with isotonic saline to prevent circulatory collapse, cardiac arrest, and death. Choice A (5% dextrose in water) is suboptimal because the osmolality of this hypotonic solution results in extravascular losses, making it inferior for intravascular volume repletion. While it may be used if normal saline or blood is unavailable, it is not the best choice. Choice C (pulmonary artery catheter via subclavian vein) would be appropriate for evaluating undifferentiated shock when the cause is unclear, particularly in suspected cardiogenic shock. However, this patient has a clear etiology of hemorrhagic shock from hematemesis and does not require a pulmonary artery catheter for diagnosis or initial treatment. Choice D (gastric lavage with ice-cold saline) does not replace intravascular volume repletion, which is the priority in decompensated shock. While gastric lavage may have an adjunctive role in reducing gastrointestinal blood losses, it should not delay fluid resuscitation. Choice E (emergency esophagogastroduodenoscopy) is the first-line definitive intervention for hemorrhage control in capable centers and should be performed after initial hemodynamic stabilization. However, it should not take the place of emergent intravascular volume repletion as the immediate next step in a patient with decompensated hemorrhagic shock. Stabilization precedes definitive intervention.

Correct Answer: A) Serum protein electrophoresis
This patient presents with the classic triad for multiple myeloma: anemia (hemoglobin 8 g/dL), renal failure (elevated creatinine 2.4 mg/dL), and bone pain (midback pain). Additional supportive findings include hypercalcemia (12.4 mg/dL), impaired cognitive function (possibly from hypercalcemia), and lytic lesions on skull x-ray. The elevated calcium concentration and lytic bone lesions further support the diagnosis of multiple myeloma. The next diagnostic step is serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to detect monoclonal proteins (M-spike) characteristic of myeloma. Choice B (Mammography) would be reasonable as a routine screening study but is not indicated for diagnosing multiple myeloma. Choice C (Bone scan) is not typically performed in myeloma evaluation; a skeletal survey with x-rays is the standard imaging approach for detecting lytic lesions. Choice D (CT scan of the head) is unnecessary because the lytic lesion is already evident on the skull x-ray. Choice E (Renal biopsy) would not be the first diagnostic study in this clinical presentation but could be considered later if electrophoresis is normal and renal failure persists without a clear etiology.
Source: 8A #33
A 72-year-old woman with multiple myeloma is brought to the physician because of a 1-day history of shortness of breath and fatigue. Her respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg with no orthostatic changes. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows decreased heart sounds. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Serum Urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL Creatinine 5.1 mg/dL Urine Protein 3+ RBC 0/hpf WBC 0/hpf Fractional excretion of sodium >1% Postvoid residual volume 50 mL A 24-hour urine collection shows 3.5 g of protein and a creatinine clearance of 10 mL/min. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these laboratory findings? A) Bladder outlet obstruction B) Congestive heart failure C) Interstitial nephritis D) Multiple myeloma E) Renovascular disease
Correct Answer: D) Multiple myeloma
Multiple myeloma causes intrinsic renal parenchymal disease, which is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. Multiple myeloma is a malignancy caused by neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells that overproduce monoclonal immunoglobulin and light or heavy chains. These light chains (Bence Jones protein) deposit in the kidneys, causing direct tubular damage and amyloidosis with mesangial renal deposits. This results in intrinsic kidney injury characterized by elevated creatinine, significant proteinuria (3.5 g/24h), and a fractional excretion of sodium >1%, which distinguishes intrinsic renal disease from prerenal causes. Additionally, the BUN-to-creatinine ratio is low (approximately 7:1), consistent with intrinsic parenchymal disease. The absence of pyuria rules out interstitial nephritis. The normal blood pressure and normal fractional excretion of sodium <1% would be expected with prerenal causes like congestive heart failure or renovascular disease. Bladder outlet obstruction would cause postrenal azotemia with a different pattern. Treatment is supportive, and hemodialysis may be required in severe cases. Choice A (Bladder outlet obstruction) would result in postrenal azotemia from obstruction of urinary outflow, typically from bladder cancer, prostate pathology, urethral stricture, or bilateral ureteral pathology. This would present differently with elevated postvoid residual. Choice B (Congestive heart failure) causes acute kidney injury via decreased renal perfusion, resulting in a fractional excretion of sodium <1%, not >1% as seen in this patient. Choice C (Interstitial nephritis) results in pyuria (predominantly eosinophils) and is often related to medications such as diuretics, penicillin, proton pump inhibitors, NSAIDs, and sulfonamides. This patient has no pyuria (0 WBC/hpf). Choice E (Renovascular disease) such as renal artery stenosis decreases renal blood flow and causes secondary hypertension via renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation. This patient has normal blood pressure. Renovascular disease results in fractional excretion of sodium <1% and a BUN-to-creatinine ratio of 20:1 or higher, neither of which fit this clinical picture. Educational Objective: Multiple myeloma causes intrinsic renal parenchymal disease resulting in proteinuria, fractional excretion of sodium >1%, and BUN-to-creatinine ratio less than 20.
▶Respiratory System Pulmonary Hypertension2 questions
Source: 6A #33
A 62-year-old man with severe obstructive pulmonary disease has chronic disabling dyspnea. His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. He is plethoric, and jugular veins are distended. Breath sounds are distant, and the second component of S2 is accentuated. His FEV1 is 0.5 L. An x-ray of the chest shows prominent pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary hypertension in this patient is most likely the result of which of the following? A) Decreased cardiac output B) Decreased expiratory flow rate C) Increased residual volume D) Severity of hypercarbia E) Severity of hypoxemia
Correct Answer: E) Severity of hypoxemia
Hypoxemia is the primary mechanism for development of pulmonary hypertension in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease due to the potent vasoconstriction induced by hypoxia. Chronic hypoxia leads to vascular remodeling, resulting in chronically elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary hypertension. There is a direct correlation between the severity of hypoxia and the development of pulmonary hypertension, making E the correct answer. The severity of hypercarbia in COPD patients has not been associated with development of pulmonary hypertension (D is incorrect). The severity of obstruction and elevated residual volume do not directly cause pulmonary hypertension (B and C are incorrect). While decreased cardiac output can lead to pulmonary hypertension secondary to left-sided heart failure, this is not the most likely mechanism in this patient (A is incorrect). The clinical presentation of distant breath sounds, accentuated P2 (second component of S2), plethora, jugular venous distension, and prominent pulmonary arteries on imaging all support cor pulmonale from chronic hypoxemia.
Source: 9A #34
A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with dyspnea and lower extremity edema. Vital signs are within normal limits. The nail beds are cyanotic. There is jugular venous distention and a parasternal heave. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Cardiac catheterization B) CT scan of the chest C) MUGA scan D) Paracentesis E) Transthoracic echocardiography
Correct Answer: E) Transthoracic echocardiography
The most appropriate next step in diagnosis is transthoracic echocardiography. This patient with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with clinical findings highly suggestive of pulmonary hypertension leading to right ventricular failure. The key clinical features include dyspnea, dependent edema, cyanotic nail beds, jugular venous distention, parasternal heave, and ascites—all signs of right-sided heart failure. Pulmonary hypertension can be primary (genetic mutations causing smooth muscle hypertrophy and increased pulmonary vascular resistance) or secondary to various causes including obstructive sleep apnea, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic venous thromboembolic disease, pulmonary fibrosis, left-sided heart failure, and autoimmune disorders such as lupus and sarcoidosis. Physical examination in pulmonary hypertension typically reveals a precordial heave, delayed or loud pulmonic S2, and tricuspid or pulmonary insufficiency from chronic right heart hypertrophy. Transthoracic echocardiography is the most appropriate first diagnostic step because it is noninvasive, readily accessible, and can directly visualize right ventricular function, size, and wall motion to confirm right ventricular failure. Choice A (Cardiac catheterization) is not the most appropriate initial choice. While right heart catheterization can measure intracardiac and intrapulmonary pressures to aid in diagnosing pulmonary hypertension, it is invasive and reserved for cases where noninvasive testing is inconclusive. Choice B (CT scan of the chest) may show imaging findings suggestive of pulmonary hypertension such as a dilated or hypertrophic right ventricle or dilated pulmonary arteries, but these findings would be nonspecific and not definitive for the diagnosis. Choice C (MUGA scan) is used to more accurately measure cardiac function in patients whose hearts cannot be adequately imaged with transthoracic echocardiography, but it is not the appropriate first-line imaging modality. Choice D (Paracentesis) involves removal of ascitic fluid and may be performed therapeutically for symptomatic ascites or to evaluate for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, but it does not confirm the underlying diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension-induced right ventricular failure.
