He can carry groceries up two flights of stairs without stopping. He has no history of chest pain or heart disease. Two months ago, his serum total cholesterol concentration was 162 mg/dl. He takes no medications. He is adopted and has no information about his family history. He smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years but stopped 3 years ago. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 93 kg (205 lb); BMI is 30 kg/m². His pulse is 78/min and regular, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. S1 and S2 are normal. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex with radiation toward the left axilla. The abdomen is soft. An ECG shows a normal sinus rhythm and left bundle branch block. Echocardiography shows mitral valve thickening with mild regurgitation. Which of the following diagnostic tests is indicated prior to the operation? A) Exercise stress test B) 24-Hour ambulatory ECG monitoring C) Electron beam (ultrafast) CT scan D) Coronary angiography E) No further tests are indicated
Correct Answer: E) No further tests are indicated
The patient demonstrates good functional capacity, able to climb two flights of stairs without dyspnea, which is equivalent to >4 METs of exercise tolerance. This excellent functional status is the most important predictor of perioperative cardiac risk and indicates low risk for surgery. While the patient has several cardiovascular risk factors (age 62, obesity with BMI 30, former smoker, hypertension with BP 138/84), his clinical presentation does not warrant additional testing. The grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex consistent with mild mitral regurgitation is hemodynamically insignificant; typically, murmurs grade 3/6 or higher suggest significant pathology. He has no symptoms of angina or cardiovascular decline. The ECG finding of left bundle branch block and echocardiographic findings of mitral valve thickening with mild regurgitation do not change immediate preoperative management. Exercise stress testing (A) is not needed given his demonstrated good functional capacity. Twenty-four-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring (B) would not alter perioperative management. Electron beam CT (C) and coronary angiography (D) are not indicated as there are no signs of active myocardial ischemia or unstable cardiac disease. The fundamental principle of preoperative cardiac evaluation is to risk-stratify patients and detect conditions that might change management or contraindicate surgery. This patient's excellent functional capacity and lack of cardiac symptoms indicate he can safely proceed to elective surgery without further diagnostic testing.
Source: 10A #28
A patient presents with chest pain radiating to the jaw and arms, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, and hypertension. Physical examination reveals an S4 gallop on auscultation. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test to confirm acute ischemic heart disease?
Correct Answer: Serum troponin I concentration
Serum troponin I is the most sensitive and specific cardiac biomarker for detecting myocardial ischemia and necrosis, with >99.9% sensitivity for cardiac ischemia. The clinical presentation of chest pain radiating to the jaw and arms, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, and S4 gallop on cardiac auscultation is classic for acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Acute coronary syndrome encompasses three primary categories: unstable angina, non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). While an ECG may be normal early in the disease course, troponin elevation indicates myocardial injury. The patient's risk factors including hypertension further support the diagnosis of ischemic heart disease. Evaluation of suspected ACS should include history, vital signs, physical examination, ECG, and serum troponin I concentration in the emergency department. In confirmed or high-risk suspected ischemic heart disease, patients may undergo further testing with cardiac catheterization, echocardiography, or stress testing. Treatment of ACS involves anticoagulation and dual antiplatelet therapy, often followed by cardiac catheterization for revascularization. While ischemic heart disease has nonmodifiable hereditary factors, modifiable risk factors including hyperlipidemia, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and smoking should be managed to prevent disease progression.
▶Biostatistics Epidemiology Population Health Sensitivity2 questions
Source: 6A #41
A study is conducted to compare a new stool test with mucosal biopsy for diagnosing Helicobacter pylori infection. A total of 400 patients with suspected H. pylori infection are enrolled. Patients are screened using both methods. Results show that of the 100 patients who tested positive for H. pylori infection on biopsy, 80 also tested positive using the new stool test; 120 patients who tested negative for H. pylori infection on biopsy tested positive using the new stool test. Which of the following represents the sensitivity of the new stool test for H. pylori infection in this study? A) 10% B) 20% C) 40% D) 60% E) 80%
Correct Answer: E) 80%
Sensitivity is a measure of the ability of a test to detect disease when present. It represents the percentage of tests that are positive (true positives) among all patients with disease (true positives plus false negatives). Sensitivity is calculated using the formula: Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN), where TP is true positive and FN is false negative. In this scenario: - Disease present (H. pylori positive on biopsy): 100 patients total - True positives (positive stool test AND positive biopsy): 80 - False negatives (negative stool test BUT positive biopsy): 20 - Disease absent (H. pylori negative on biopsy): 300 patients total - False positives (positive stool test BUT negative biopsy): 120 - True negatives (negative stool test AND negative biopsy): 180 Using the formula: Sensitivity = 80/(80+20) = 80/100 = 80% This means the new stool test correctly identifies 80% of patients who actually have H. pylori infection on biopsy. The other answer choices are incorrect because they do not properly apply the sensitivity formula focusing only on patients with disease present.
Source: 7A #47
A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician for HIV screening. She is asymptomatic. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. She has had two lifetime male sexual partners, and they used condoms consistently. Examination shows no abnormalities. An ELISA is positive for HIV; the sensitivity of the ELISA is 95%, and the specificity is 90%. Which of the following represents the most appropriate sensitivity and specificity of an additional test to confirm this patient's diagnosis? A) Sensitivity 95%, Specificity 35% B) Sensitivity 99%, Specificity 90% C) Sensitivity 99%, Specificity 95% D) Sensitivity 99%, Specificity 99%
Correct Answer: D) Sensitivity 99%, Specificity 99%
Sensitivity refers to the ability of a test to correctly identify those with the disease (true positive rate), whereas specificity refers to the ability of a test to correctly identify those without the disease (true negative rate). In a patient population with low prevalence of disease, a negative result on a highly sensitive test can effectively rule out the disease because there is a low rate of false negatives. However, a positive result on a sensitive test must be verified by a highly specific test, which minimizes the risk for false positive results. Therefore, sensitive tests are often used for screening (as ELISA was used in this case), but must be verified by a more specific test. A test with high specificity is most appropriate for confirming diagnosis. Specificity is calculated as true negatives divided by the sum of true negatives and false positives. Therefore, a test with 99% specificity would have only one false positive out of 100 administered tests, making positive results more likely to be true positives. Choice A and B have insufficient specificity to reliably confirm the diagnosis. Choice C has adequate specificity but could be improved. Choice D with both 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity provides the most reliable confirmation of diagnosis with minimal false positives and false negatives.

A 77-year-old man is brought by his wife for a follow-up examination 3 weeks after an episode of right middle lobe pneumonia. The pneumonia is improving with antibiotic therapy. Correct Answer: B) Swallowing study
Recurrent episodes of pneumonia (3 weeks and 3 months ago), combined with a history of increased cough after meals, should significantly increase suspicion for chronic aspiration secondary to dysphagia. This clinical presentation warrants further evaluation with a swallowing study to assess for aspiration risk. The patient's risk factors for dysphagia include multi-infarct (vascular) dementia, dysarthric speech, and poor diaphragmatic excursion, all of which can impair swallowing mechanics and protection of the airway. Choice A is incorrect because dietary recommendations should not be made until swallowing study results are available, as premature dietary modifications without confirmed aspiration data could be inappropriate or ineffective. Choice C is incorrect because while a CT scan of the chest may eventually be appropriate to document resolution of pneumonia, the typical timing for follow-up imaging is 6-8 weeks after initial imaging to allow adequate time for the acute inflammatory process to resolve. Choice D is incorrect because there is no clinical evidence suggesting central airway obstruction or post-obstructive pneumonia, and the patient is currently improving on antibiotic therapy, making bronchoscopy unnecessary at this time. Choice E is incorrect because there is no indication of bronchospasm or reactive airway disease in this patient, so inhaled bronchodilators are unlikely to provide significant clinical benefit.
Source: 7A #22
One week after undergoing appendectomy and peritoneal lavage for ruptured appendicitis, a previously healthy 61-year-old man is evaluated because of fever, chills, cough, and mild shortness of breath. During the procedure, a peritoneal drain was placed. Postoperatively, intravenous ciprofloxacin and metronidazole therapy was begun. A persistent ileus was diagnosed on postoperative day 2, and a nasogastric tube was inserted. Yesterday, the nasogastric tube was removed, and he was advanced to a regular diet. Today, his temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Crackles are heard at the mid left lung field. Abdominal examination shows a clean, dry surgical incision. The peritoneal drain is mostly clear of fluid. Leukocyte count is 15,100/mm3 (65% segmented neutrophils, 10% bands, 25% lymphocytes). Chest x-rays are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Administration of ceftriaxone and azithromycin B) Administration of sulfamethoxazole and cefuroxime C) Administration of vancomycin and ceftazidime D) Bronchoscopy for microbiologic assessment E) CT scan of the chest with pulmonary embolism protocol
Correct Answer: C) Administration of vancomycin and ceftazidime
Pneumonia classically presents with acute onset cough (generally productive of sputum), shortness of breath, chest discomfort, fever, chills, and fatigue. Vital signs may show fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and hypotension (if severe). On examination, rhonchi and rales may be detected in consolidated lung, along with egophony and dullness to percussion. Patients may have increased work of breathing or respiratory distress. The diagnosis is supported radiographically with airspace disease or consolidation visualized on x-ray, as shown here, or on CT. Pneumonia arises because of the presence of bacteria, virus, parasite, or fungi within pulmonary parenchyma, triggering an inflammatory reaction with resultant exudate into airspace. It is common in hospitalized patients because of risk factors for introduction of a pathogen, aspiration, and immunocompromise, including recent surgery, swallowing dysfunction, and intubation. Additionally, resistant pathogens often colonize hospitals and equipment, increasing the risk for refractory infection despite coadministration of antibiotics. Treatment of hospital-acquired pneumonia generally begins with the administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics (especially those covering methicillin resistant S. aureus [MRSA] and P. aeruginosa) while awaiting culture and sensitivity data from sputum samples if obtained. Suitable antibiotics for this purpose include vancomycin and third- or fourth-generation cephalosporins such as ceftazidime or cefepime. Antibiotics should then be narrowed to those that suitably target the infecting agent once a clinical response is achieved. Reduction in risk factors should occur, such as upright positioning of patients, removal of any unnecessary pharyngeal lines or tubes (eg, nasogastric tubes), and frequent respiratory therapy/pulmonary toileting. Postoperative pain, often worse when breathing, should be aggressively managed to permit full chest excursion, promote coughing and respiratory clearance, and limit atelectasis.
▶Endocrine System Diabetic ketoacidosis2 questions
Source: 3A #8
A 32-year-old woman has had polyuria, blurred vision, and rapid breathing for 1 day. Her pulse is 110/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 100/50 mm Hg. Examination is otherwise within normal limits. Serum studies show: Na+ 139 mEq/L Cl- 99 mEq/L K+ 4.7 mEq/L HCO3- 18 mEq/L Glucose 783 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely cause of her acidosis? A) Accumulation of β-hydroxybutyric acid B) Accumulation of lactate C) Decreased renal production of ammonium D) Loss of bicarbonate through the kidneys E) Movement of potassium into the cells
Correct Answer: A) Accumulation of β-hydroxybutyric acid
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) occurs due to the accumulation of serum ketones such as β-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of deficient insulin signaling. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs because of the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. Patients present with fatigue, polyuria, shortness of breath, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Vital signs may show tachycardia and tachypnea. Kussmaul respirations (rapid and deep) is a classic physical exam finding because of respiratory compensation for the underlying metabolic acidosis. Labs typically show increased glucose, ketones, and a high anion gap because of the accumulation of unmeasured anions in serum. The anion gap is calculated as the difference between sodium and the sum of bicarbonate and chloride anions. Treatment is through replacement of insulin, volume repletion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions. Choice B (Accumulation of lactate/lactic acidosis) can occur in multiple different situations such as shock, metabolic derangements, and in response to medications. It can also occur in DKA; however, it is not the primary cause of acidosis. Choice C (Decreased renal production of ammonium) and Choice D (Loss of bicarbonate through the kidneys) are both causes of renal tubular acidosis (RTA). RTAs are not caused by the accumulation of an unmeasured anion and do not present with an increased anion gap. Choice E (Movement of potassium into the cells) occurs because of transcellular potassium-proton exchange. Increased movement of potassium into the cells occurs when the serum is alkalotic, not acidotic. Acidosis in the setting of DKA stimulates movement of potassium out of the cells into the serum.
Source: 8A #45
A 23-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the hospital because of a 2-day history of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He also has had increased thirst and urination. During the past 2 hours, he has become tired and wants to sleep. He has not taken insulin in 24 hours. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 100%. Skin examination shows no abnormalities. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Heart sounds are normal. Bowel sounds are decreased; there is no organomegaly or tenderness. On neurologic examination, the patient is somnolent but easily aroused and fully oriented. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 15.5 g/dL, Hematocrit 50%, Leukocyte count 13,500/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 70%, Lymphocytes 30%, Serum Na⁺ 130 mEq/L, K⁺ 5.8 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 94 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 10 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, Glucose 600 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: pH 7.13, PCO₂ 23 mm Hg, PO₂ 98 mm Hg. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia. This patient most likely has which of the following acid-base disorders? A) Anion gap metabolic acidosis B) Anion gap metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis C) Anion gap metabolic acidosis and respiratory acidosis D) Respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis E) Respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
Correct Answer: A) Anion gap metabolic acidosis
This patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), evidenced by missed insulin doses, hyperglycemia (600 mg/dL), and classic symptoms of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, polydipsia, and polyuria with hemoconcentration. The arterial blood gas and electrolytes confirm anion gap metabolic acidosis: pH 7.13 (acidemia), low HCO₃⁻ (10 mEq/L), and low PCO₂ (23 mm Hg). The low PCO₂ represents appropriate respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis (hyperventilation). The anion gap is calculated as Na⁺ - (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 130 - (94 + 10) = 26, which is elevated (normal 8-12), confirming anion gap metabolic acidosis. The unmeasured anions contributing to the anion gap are ketone bodies produced from accelerated lipolysis due to relative insulin deficiency. Pathophysiology includes: relative absence of insulin preventing glucose utilization, leading to hyperglycemia, osmotic diuresis (polyuria), and compensatory fluid intake (polydipsia); metabolic accumulation of ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone); and volume depletion causing hemoconcentration. Winter's formula can verify appropriate respiratory compensation: Expected PCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2 = 1.5(10) + 8 ± 2 = 23 ± 2, which matches the patient's PCO₂ of 23 mm Hg, confirming this is a single acid-base disorder without secondary abnormality. Treatment requires intravenous hydration, insulin therapy, and electrolyte correction. Choice B is incorrect because the delta-delta ratio (patient's anion gap - normal anion gap)/(normal HCO₃⁻ - patient's HCO₃⁻) = (26 - 12)/(24 - 10) ≈ 1.0, which indicates a single acid-base disorder (ratio <1 suggests concomitant non-gap acidosis; >2 suggests concomitant alkalosis). Choices C, D, and E are incorrect because the PCO₂ is appropriately low (not elevated as in respiratory acidosis or alkalosis), representing appropriate respiratory compensation for the metabolic acidosis. Other causes of anion gap metabolic acidosis include lactic acidosis, uremia, ethylene glycol or methanol ingestion, and salicylate poisoning.
▶Immune System Common Variable Immunodeficiency2 questions
Source: 3A #13
A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She has a 5-year history of mild shortness of breath on exertion and cough productive of copious yellow-to-whitish sputum. She has not had fever or chills. She has reactive airways disease treated with daily salmeterol-fluticasone and albuterol and seasonal allergies treated with fexofenadine. She has a chronic cough that is not controlled by her medications. She has a 20-year history of multiple respiratory tract infections, including three episodes of pneumonia during the past 15 years and two episodes of sinusitis during the past 5 years. She usually requires antibiotic therapy for bronchitis three to four times yearly. She does not smoke. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Examination shows mild lymphadenopathy. There is mild thrush. Coarse breath sounds are heard bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities except for a slightly increased S2. There is no clubbing or edema. In addition to pulmonary function testing and antifungal therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Measurement of CD4+ T-lymphocyte count B) Measurement of serum complement concentrations C) Measurement of serum immunoglobulin concentrations D) Sputum culture E) Ventilation-perfusion lung scans
Correct Answer: C) Measurement of serum immunoglobulin concentrations
A history of multiple sinopulmonary infections in an otherwise healthy adult along with thrush raises the possibility of late-presenting primary immunodeficiency, specifically common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). CVID classically presents in the second to fourth decades of life with recurrent sinus or pulmonary infections, including pneumonia, bronchitis, and sinusitis. The presence of thrush, while potentially related to inhaled corticosteroid use, further raises concern for immunodeficiency. Measurement of serum immunoglobulin concentrations is the most appropriate next diagnostic step to evaluate for antibody deficiency. Choice A (CD4+ T-lymphocyte count) would be appropriate for known or suspected HIV/AIDS, but this patient lacks clear risk factors and her presentation is more consistent with CVID, which involves primarily B-cell/antibody deficiency rather than T-cell deficiency. Choice B (Serum complement concentrations) would be indicated if complement deficiency were suspected, particularly in cases of increased susceptibility to Neisseria species infections related to terminal complement protein deficiencies (C5-C9). Choice D (Sputum culture) may be appropriate for identifying organisms in active pulmonary infection but would not explain her pattern of recurrent infections over many years and does not address the underlying immunologic defect. Choice E (Ventilation-perfusion lung scans) are used to diagnose conditions affecting ventilation or perfusion, particularly pulmonary embolism, and are not indicated for evaluating recurrent infections.
Source: 5A #1
A 32-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up examination. Six weeks ago, she was diagnosed with sinusitis and began a 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate therapy. She has occasional nonproductive cough; she otherwise feels well. During the past 6 years, she has had eight episodes of sinusitis treated with amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and azithromycin. One episode required a 1-month course of amoxicillin therapy. The patient also has had two episodes of bacterial pneumonia during the past 3 years that resolved with moxifloxacin therapy. She currently takes no medications. Her maternal uncle died of pneumonia at the age of 28 years. The patient is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 64 kg (140 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Scattered rhonchi are heard over the right lower lung base. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Results of a complete blood count, liver and kidney function testing, and HIV antibody serologic testing are within the reference ranges. A CT scan of the paranasal sinuses shows mucosal thickening of the maxillary, sphenoid, and ethmoid sinuses. A CT scan of the chest shows bronchial thickening and dilation of the bronchi in the lower lobe of the right lung. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Bone marrow biopsy B) Bronchoalveolar lavage C) Open lung biopsy D) Quantitative serum immunoglobulin testing E) Sputum culture for acid-fast bacilli
Correct Answer: D) Quantitative serum immunoglobulin testing
The clinical presentation of recurrent sinopulmonary infections (eight episodes of sinusitis over 6 years and two episodes of bacterial pneumonia over 3 years) with documented bronchiectasis on imaging strongly suggests an underlying primary immunodeficiency, particularly a B-cell disorder. The patient's normal CBC, liver and kidney function, and negative HIV antibody testing help exclude other causes of immunosuppression. Decreased, absent, or aberrant immunoglobulin production by B-cells results in recurrent sinopulmonary infections, which can progress to bronchiectasis as seen in this patient. Quantitative serum immunoglobulin testing is the appropriate initial diagnostic step to identify the specific immunologic defect and differentiate between primary B-cell immunodeficiencies such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia, selective IgA deficiency, and common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). Given the patient's age (32 years) and presentation pattern, CVID is the most likely diagnosis, as it typically presents in early adulthood and characteristically manifests with recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Choice A (Bone marrow biopsy) is an invasive procedure reserved for suspected bone marrow pathology such as lymphoproliferative disorders or unexplained cytopenias, which are not indicated here given normal CBC findings. Choice B (Bronchoalveolar lavage) is used to definitively identify infectious organisms in severe or persistent pneumonia, but is not necessary for diagnosing an immunodeficiency. Choice C (Open lung biopsy) may be indicated for interstitial lung disease or pulmonary nodules but is not required for immunodeficiency diagnosis. Choice E (Sputum culture for acid-fast bacilli) is used to evaluate for mycobacterial infection and is not the appropriate next step in evaluating suspected immunodeficiency.
▶Cardiovascular System Congestive Heart Failure2 questions
Source: 3A #17
A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of shortness of breath and wheezing for 2 days. He also has had swelling of the lower legs since he returned from a 200-mile car trip 3 days ago. He has a 20-year history of poorly controlled hypertension currently treated with hydrochlorothiazide. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min and regular, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention. Crackles and wheezes are heard in the lower lung fields bilaterally. A prominent S3 gallop is heard at the apex. There is 4+ ankle edema. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly and cephalization of the pulmonary vessels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Aspiration pneumonia B) Bronchiectasis C) Chronic bronchitis D) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis E) Pulmonary edema F) Pulmonary embolism
Correct Answer: E) Pulmonary edema
This patient presents with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema secondary to decompensated heart failure from poorly controlled hypertension. The clinical presentation includes shortness of breath, bilateral crackles and wheezes in lower lung fields, signs of volume overload (peripheral edema, jugular venous distention), physical findings of heart failure (prominent S3 gallop at apex), tachycardia, tachypnea, and imaging findings consistent with heart failure (cardiomegaly and cephalization of pulmonary vessels indicating elevated pulmonary venous pressures). The pathophysiology involves increased left-heart filling pressures from hypertensive heart disease, which elevates pulmonary venous pressure and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to transudation of fluid into the interstitium and alveoli. Treatment includes diuresis to reduce hypervolemia and cardiac filling pressures, venodilators such as nitroglycerin to shift fluid into capacitance vessels and reduce preload, and positive pressure ventilation to reduce alveolar and interstitial edema. Incorrect Answer Rationale: Aspiration pneumonia (A) would present with focal consolidation on chest x-ray (often in the superior segment of the right lower lobe), productive cough with fever, and a history of aspiration risk factors (dysphagia, stroke, malignancy, vomiting). Bilateral crackles and wheezes with cardiomegaly and cephalization are not typical. Bronchiectasis (B) presents with signs of obstructive lung disease and chronic productive cough but typically results from prior necrotizing infections, cystic fibrosis, or Kartagener syndrome. It would not produce bilateral signs of hypervolemia (edema, JVD) or cephalization of vessels unless concomitant heart failure were present. Chest x-ray typically shows bronchial dilatation and wall thickening. Chronic bronchitis (C) presents with chronic productive cough and obstructive lung disease signs (wheezing, air trapping) in smokers as part of COPD. While it can lead to right heart failure from chronic hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (manifesting as JVD, ascites, lower extremity edema), pulmonary edema would be less likely, and the acuteness of this patient's presentation with bilateral pulmonary edema is atypical. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (D) is caused by a type III or IV hypersensitivity reaction to inhaled antigens. The acute form presents with dyspnea, cough, fever, chills, headache, and rash following antigen exposure. Imaging may show interstitial infiltrates, and pulmonary function tests demonstrate a restrictive pattern. Signs of volume overload and cephalization would be unlikely unless heart failure were concomitant. Pulmonary embolism (F) is associated with immobilization (long car trips, plane flights) and presents with rapid-onset chest pain, dyspnea, and possibly pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis if infarction occurs. However, classic PE findings include unilateral lower extremity edema (DVT sign), clear lungs on auscultation, and the absence of cardiomegaly and cephalization. The bilateral crackles, S3 gallop, signs of generalized volume overload, and imaging findings are inconsistent with PE.
Source: 5A #22
A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of shortness of breath on exertion over the past 2 weeks. His last examination was 38 years ago. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. His temperature is 36.?°C (98°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is not increased. Crackles are heard at both lung bases. Cardiac examination shows an S4 gallop. Pulses are symmetric without bruits. There is no peripheral edema. His fasting serum glucose concentration is 130 mg/dL, and fasting serum cholesterol concentration is 270 mg/dL. An x-ray of the chest shows mild cardiomegaly and Kerley B lines. An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. Echocardiography shows a thickened left ventricle and an ejection fraction of 40% without segmental wall abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented the echocardiographic findings? A) Adequate control of blood pressure B) Adequate control of serum glucose concentrations C) β-Adrenergic agonist inhaler therapy D) Low-cholesterol diet E) Smoking cessation
Correct Answer: A) Adequate control of blood pressure
Hypertension is a common cause of chronic systolic and diastolic left-sided heart failure and is considered a modifiable risk factor. This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with chronic left-sided heart failure characterized by: (1) symptoms of dyspnea on exertion; (2) signs of pulmonary edema on chest x-ray (Kerley B lines and mild cardiomegaly); (3) S4 gallop on cardiac exam indicating diastolic dysfunction; (4) left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG; and (5) reduced ejection fraction of 40% on echocardiography indicating systolic dysfunction. The lack of elevated jugular venous pressure makes right-sided heart failure less likely. Adequate blood pressure control decreases afterload and reduces the degree of cardiac myocyte hypertrophy, which directly decreases the risk of developing heart failure. Choice B: Adequate control of serum glucose concentrations reduces the risk of microvascular complications of diabetes mellitus (retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy), but evidence for tight glucose control in significantly reducing macrovascular complications is less clear and has a less direct impact on heart failure development. Choice C: β-Adrenergic agonist inhaler therapy is appropriate treatment for obstructive lung disease such as COPD or persistent asthma, not for preventing heart failure from hypertension. Choice D: Low-cholesterol diet would help treat hypercholesterolemia and reduce atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk, thereby reducing coronary artery disease risk. However, this has a less direct impact on chronic heart failure development compared to blood pressure control. Choice E: Smoking cessation is a modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular and pulmonary disease, but uncontrolled hypertension imparts greater relative risk in this case for developing heart failure.
▶Renal Urinary System Nephrotic Syndrome2 questions
Source: 3A #19
A previously healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of swelling of her face and legs for 2 weeks. As the day progresses, her facial swelling resolves, but her legs become increasingly swollen. Her pulse is 64/min and regular, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. There is 1+ presacral edema and 2+ edema of the lower extremities. Her prothrombin time is 12 seconds (INR=1.1), and serum albumin concentration is 2.3 g/dl. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's edema? A) Cellulitis B) Cirrhosis C) Congestive heart failure D) Deep venous thrombosis E) Lymphangitis F) Lymphedema G) Malnutrition H) Nephrotic syndrome I) Postphlebitic syndrome J) Pulmonary hypertension K) Stasis dermatitis L) Varicose veins
Correct Answer: H) Nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema secondary to excessive proteinuria resulting in hypoalbuminemia and diminished intravascular oncotic pressure. This occurs because of loss of normal size and charge filtration of the glomerular capillary and Bowman's capsule interface. Causes of nephrotic syndrome include minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, and focal segmental glomerular sclerosis. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs; foamy or dark-colored urine; hypoalbuminemia; and proteinuria. Complications include hypercoagulability caused by urinary loss of antithrombin-3 and infection caused by urinary loss of gamma globulins. Workup includes renal biopsy and treating underlying causes such as HIV, hepatitis, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Treatment involves the use of glucocorticoids and immunomodulators, though treatment-refractory disease is common. Patients may ultimately require renal replacement therapy or transplantation. Choice A (Cellulitis) presents with cutaneous erythema, warmth, and induration, often following inoculation from an injury such as an abrasion. It is typically localized and would not present with diffuse dependent edema or hypoalbuminemia. Choice B (Cirrhosis) can present with edema caused by loss of oncotic pressure, though it also presents with ascites, increased bilirubin, jaundice, and signs of portal hypertension such as esophageal varices, splenomegaly, caput medusae, and rectal varices. It typically occurs in patients with preceding conditions such as alcohol abuse or chronic hepatitis. Choice C (Congestive heart failure) presents with edema caused by increased hydrostatic pressure rather than loss of oncotic pressure. Choice D (Deep venous thrombosis) is a common cause of lower extremity edema, though it is often unilateral unless the thrombus is large and proximal or bilateral. It would not be expected to cause facial edema or hypoalbuminemia. Choice E (Lymphangitis) occurs because of infection or inflammation traveling within the lymphatic system and presents with streaking, sometimes traveling away from areas of cellulitis or abscess. It does not generally cause diffuse edema or hypoalbuminemia. Choice F (Lymphedema) occurs because of obstruction or excision of lymphatic channels, such as in cases of lymphoma or after lymph node dissection. It is typically localized to a single upper, single lower, or bilateral lower extremities, and would not be expected to cause hypoalbuminemia. Choice G (Malnutrition) can result in edema because of insufficient dietary protein and resultant impaired synthesis of albumin, as seen in Kwashiorkor syndrome. Kwashiorkor is rare in the developed world and would be noted on exam with signs of malnutrition and muscle loss such as temporal wasting and sunken eyes. Choice I (Postphlebitic syndrome) is characterized by chronic edema following thrombosis. It occurs in an extremity because of valvular insufficiency and chronic venous hypertension following damage from a deep venous thrombosis. Choice J (Pulmonary hypertension) can be primary (e.g., genetic mutation causing smooth muscle hypertrophy and increased pulmonary vascular resistance) or secondary (e.g., chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic venous thromboembolic disease, pulmonary fibrosis, or heart failure). It presents with signs of right-sided heart failure including dependent edema, jugular venous distention, and hepatic congestion. Examination typically reveals a precordial heave, delayed or loud P2, and tricuspid or pulmonary insufficiency caused by chronic hypertrophy of the right heart. Choice K (Stasis dermatitis) presents as erythema, itching, and hyperpigmentation of skin caused by chronic inflammation from third spacing, and is often seen in the bilateral lower extremities in cases of heart failure or impaired venous return. Choice L (Varicose veins) are dilated and tortuous superficial venous segments that often occur in the lower extremities. Patients with varicosities would not be expected to have hypoalbuminemia or migratory, dependent edema.
Source: 7A #31
A 23-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-week history of fatigue and swelling of her eyelids, ankles, and feet. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows 2+ periorbital edema and 3+ pedal edema. No other abnormalities are noted. Fasting serum studies show a total cholesterol concentration of 348 mg/dL and triglyceride concentration of greater than 400 mg/dL. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications? A) Deep venous thrombosis B) Hypothyroidism C) Nephrolithiasis D) Peripheral vascular disease E) Stasis dermatitis
Correct Answer: A) Deep venous thrombosis
Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema secondary to excessive proteinuria resulting in hypoalbuminemia and diminished intravascular oncotic pressure. This occurs because of the loss of normal size and charge filtration of the glomerular capillary and Bowman capsule interface. Causes of nephrotic syndrome include minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and proteinuria. The critical complication is hypercoagulability caused by the urinary loss of proteins such as antithrombin-3, which functions to inhibit coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X, XI, and XII. Deficiency of antithrombin-3 leads to hypercoagulability and puts this patient at high risk for thrombotic conditions such as deep venous thrombosis. Patients with nephrotic syndrome are also at increased risk for infection because of the urinary loss of gamma globulins. Choice B (Hypothyroidism) can present with peripheral edema but typically presents with a constellation of symptoms including cold intolerance, weight gain, hyporeflexia, and dry, cool skin—not the primary presentation here. Choice C (Nephrolithiasis) can occur with increased formation of calcium oxalate, uric acid, cystine, or struvite crystals, but this is not the primary complication in nephrotic syndrome. These conditions have specific etiologies unrelated to nephrotic syndrome. Choice D (Peripheral vascular disease) occurs secondary to decreased arterial blood flow through stenotic arteries and presents with ischemic ulcers on the lower extremities and tips of digits. It is common in older, male smokers with hypertension, diabetes, and/or hyperlipidemia—not the typical presentation in a young woman with nephrotic syndrome. Choice E (Stasis dermatitis) presents as erythema, itching, and hyperpigmentation of skin caused by chronic inflammation from third spacing fluid in the bilateral lower extremities in cases of heart failure or impaired venous return, not from nephrotic syndrome per se. Educational Objective: Patients with nephrotic syndrome classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and proteinuria. Loss of antithrombin-3 in the urine leads to hypercoagulability and a pro-thrombotic state, making deep venous thrombosis the most significant complication risk in these patients.
▶Cardiovascular System Acute Myocardial Infarction2 questions
Source: 3A #32
A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe substernal chest pain for 2 hours and severe shortness of breath for 30 minutes. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with an oral hypoglycemic agent and hypertension treated with a diuretic. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 100/78 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is increased. Bilateral crackles are heard throughout all lung fields. An S3 and S4 gallop are heard. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral perihilar infiltrates and a slightly enlarged cardiac silhouette. An ECG shows ST-segment elevation and T-wave inversion in leads V2 through V5. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute pericarditis B) Myocardial infarction C) Pericardial tamponade D) Pneumonia E) Pulmonary embolism
Correct Answer: B) Myocardial infarction
Myocardial infarction classically presents with acute-onset substernal chest pain, often radiating to the neck, jaw, or arm, along with shortness of breath, nausea, and/or light-headedness. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, smoking, hyperlipidemia, and obesity. When the infarction results in left ventricular dysfunction, patients experience cardiogenic pulmonary edema manifesting as shortness of breath, tachypnea, hypoxia, bilateral crackles, and S3 or S4 gallop—all present in this case. Diagnosis is confirmed by clinical history, cardiac biomarkers, and ECG findings showing ST-segment elevation or depression, inverted T-waves, or Q-waves. The focal ST-segment elevation in leads V2-V5 indicates an anterior wall MI. Treatment requires antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel), anticoagulants (heparin), pain control, and revascularization via angioplasty, thrombolysis, or coronary artery bypass grafting. Complications include dysrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, pulmonary edema, wall rupture, and post-infarction pericarditis. Choice A (Acute pericarditis) presents with pleuritic chest pain exacerbated by lying down, caused by infectious, inflammatory, or malignant precipitants. ECG findings include diffuse (not focal) ST-segment elevations and PR depressions, which do not match this patient's focal ST elevation pattern. Choice C (Pericardial tamponade) presents with hypotension, shortness of breath, distant heart sounds, jugular venous distention, and pulsus paradoxus following accumulation of large-volume or rapid-onset pericardial effusion. ECG typically shows low voltage and electrical alternans, not the focal ST elevation seen here. Choice D (Pneumonia) presents with cough, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, fever, and abnormal breath sounds, often following upper respiratory infection or aspiration. While this patient has crackles and infiltrates, the ECG findings of ST-segment elevation are not typical of pneumonia, and the focal infiltrates pattern and cardiac biomarker elevation would support MI. Choice E (Pulmonary embolism) presents with acute chest pain, shortness of breath, and hypoxia, often in patients with deep venous thrombosis or hypercoagulable states. Small pulmonary emboli are often undetectable on chest x-ray; large emboli may show wedge-shaped infarctions or Westermark sign. The classic ECG findings are sinus tachycardia or the S1Q3T3 pattern indicating right heart strain. ST-segment elevation would not be expected with pulmonary embolism.
Source: 8A #18
A 57-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after a 2-hour episode of shortness of breath and substernal chest pain that radiated to her left shoulder. She rates the episode of pain as a 6 on a 10-point scale. She has a 30-year history of hypertension well controlled with lisinopril and a 20-year history of hypercholesterolemia treated with atorvastatin. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Her pulse is 90/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 160/92 mm Hg. Bilateral basilar crackles are heard. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities except for an S4 gallop. Her serum troponin I concentration is 3.6 ng/mL (N<0.4). An x-ray of the chest shows moderate cardiomegaly. An ECG shows T-wave inversion in the anterior and lateral precordial leads. Which of the following findings is the best evidence of an acute myocardial infarction in this patient? A) Cardiomegaly on x-ray of the chest B) Chest pain pattern C) Serum troponin I concentration of 3.6 ng/mL D) Presence of crackles E) Presence of an S4 gallop F) T-wave inversion in the anterior and lateral precordial leads on ECG
Correct Answer: C) Serum troponin I concentration of 3.6 ng/mL
The patient presents with acute coronary syndrome with characteristic angina (substernal pain radiating to the left arm) and nonspecific ECG changes. Ischemic injury leads to leakage of intracellular proteins from damaged cardiomyocytes. An elevated serum troponin I concentration (3.6 ng/mL, normal <0.4) is strong evidence for active myocardial infarction. Cardiac-specific troponin I is the preferred diagnostic assay because it is sensitive and highly specific for myocardial damage. This patient's presentation is consistent with non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Treatment includes dual antiplatelet therapy and therapeutic anticoagulation, with risk stratification to determine timing of cardiac catheterization (typically within 24 hours). Cardiomegaly on chest x-ray (Choice A) is nonspecific, indicating chamber enlargement and/or pericardial involvement from various causes including cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, ischemic disease, heart failure, or pericardial effusion. Chest pain pattern (Choice B) is consistent with cardiac angina but is suggestive rather than diagnostic, as numerous other conditions produce similar chest pain characteristics. Presence of crackles (Choice D) is a nonspecific lung finding indicating pulmonary edema secondary to impaired forward flow and pulmonary vascular congestion from myocardial damage. Presence of an S4 gallop (Choice E) suggests ventricular hypertrophy or diastolic dysfunction from forceful atrial contraction in presystole, but is not associated with acute myocardial infarction. T-wave inversion in anterior and lateral precordial leads (Choice F) is nonspecific and can have cardiac or noncardiac causes, observed in states of high cardiovascular stress. Educational Objective: Myocardial infarction carries high risk for morbidity and mortality and should be suspected in patients with chest pain. Measurement of serum troponin I concentration is the most specific test used routinely to diagnose myocardial infarction.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Polycythemia vera2 questions
Source: 3A #42
A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain of the fingertips for 1 month. Examination shows plethora and splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 20.2 g/dL, Leukocyte count 14,500/mm³ with a normal differential, Platelet count 400,000/mm³. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: PO2 92 mm Hg, O2 saturation 94%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Administration of chlorambucil B) Administration of heparin C) Thrombopheresis D) Phlebotomy E) Splenectomy
Correct Answer: D) Phlebotomy
Polycythemia vera is a chronic myeloproliferative disorder resulting in increased production of all cell lineages (erythrocyte, leukocyte, and thrombocyte) secondary to a JAK2 mutation. This patient presents with characteristic findings including erythromelalgia (episodic severe, burning pain with red-blue discoloration of extremities secondary to blood clot formation in extremity vessels), plethora (vessel congestion), and splenomegaly. The markedly elevated hemoglobin (20.2 g/dL) and elevated platelet count indicate increased red blood cell and platelet production. The clinical picture is consistent with hyperviscosity syndrome from increased red blood cell mass, which can lead to blurred vision and CNS symptoms related to vascular congestion. Therapeutic phlebotomy results in decreased red blood cell mass and blood volume, making it the best initial treatment for this patient's symptoms. Choice A (Chlorambucil): Used to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia, Hodgkin disease, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, not polycythemia vera. Choice B (Heparin): While this patient may eventually develop thrombosis requiring anticoagulation, there is currently no evident thrombotic complication warranting immediate anticoagulation. Choice C (Thrombopheresis): Selective removal of platelets is performed to treat conditions of excess platelets such as essential thrombocythemia when other cell lines are not similarly increased. This patient has elevation of all cell lines, making this inappropriate. Choice E (Splenectomy): May have a role in treating patients with polycythemia vera if they develop painful splenomegaly or splenic infarction, but barring such complications, it is not a routine next step in management.
Source: 5A #43
A previously healthy 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of episodic memory loss, dizziness, and double vision and a 2-hour history of burning pain in his left great toe. During the past 2 months, he has had a moderate itching sensation over his legs. On arrival, he is conscious and oriented to person, place, and time. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 75/min and regular, and blood pressure is 170/80 mm Hg. Examination shows bluish-red discoloration of the left great toe. There is no pain on movement of the toe. On cardiac examination, no murmurs or gallops are heard. The spleen tip is palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 18.5 g/dL, Hematocrit 62%, Leukocyte count 13,000/mm³, Platelet count 420,000/mm³, Serum Urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, Ferritin 14 ng/mL, Uric acid 12.9 mg/dL. Which of the following interventions will most rapidly correct this patient's visual and memory disturbances? A) Aspirin therapy B) Heparin therapy C) Hydroxyurea therapy D) Infusion of 0.9% saline E) Phlebotomy
Correct Answer: E) Phlebotomy
Polycythemia vera is a chronic myeloproliferative disorder resulting in disordered, increased production of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets secondary to a JAK2 mutation. The clinical presentation in this patient includes multiple classic features: increased pruritus over the past 2 months (often worse after hot showers due to increased mast cell production), erythromelalgia (episodic severe burning pain with red-blue discoloration of the left great toe secondary to blood clot formation in extremity vessels), and hyperviscosity syndrome manifested by blurred vision (double vision) and central nervous system symptoms (episodic memory loss, dizziness) related to vascular congestion from markedly elevated red blood cell mass and hematocrit (62%). The laboratory findings confirm this diagnosis with elevated hemoglobin (18.5 g/dL), hematocrit (62%), elevated platelet count (420,000/mm³), and elevated uric acid (12.9 mg/dL). Therapeutic phlebotomy results in decreased red blood cell mass and blood volume, which is the most rapid intervention to reverse the hyperviscosity symptoms by reducing blood viscosity and improving cerebral and ocular perfusion. Choice A (Aspirin) irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes 1 and 2, resulting in decreased platelet aggregation but has no effect on red blood cell mass and blood volume. Choice B (Heparin) inhibits various clotting factors after binding to antithrombin III, resulting in immediate anticoagulation, but does not affect red blood cell mass or concentration. Choice C (Hydroxyurea) inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and is used primarily for the treatment of sickle cell disease, not for acute symptom reversal in polycythemia vera. Choice D (Saline infusion) would result in decreased red blood cell concentration through dilution but would further increase blood volume, potentially worsening hyperviscosity.
▶Musculoskeletal System Rheumatoid arthritis2 questions
Source: 3A #44
A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of pain and swelling of her knees. She says she also has had stiffness of her knees, which is worse in the morning. During the past month, she has had progressive, generalized fatigue. On examination, the knees are warm, swollen, and tender. Any attempt at passive movement of the knees produces pain. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dl, leukocyte count is 10,000/mm³, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 50 mm/h. X-rays of the knees show osteopenia and subcartilaginous cysts around the joints. The joint spaces are intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Oral alendronate B) Oral colchicine C) Oral ibuprofen D) Intra-articular injection of methylprednisolone E) Intravenous cefazolin
Correct Answer: C) Oral ibuprofen
This patient presents with a classic presentation of inflammatory arthropathy, most consistent with rheumatoid arthritis. Key clinical features include symmetric joint pain and swelling, morning stiffness worse in the morning, progressive fatigue, mild anemia (hemoglobin 10 g/dl), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (50 mm/h), and radiographic findings of periarticular osteopenia and subcartilaginous cysts with intact joint spaces. These findings are characteristic of an inflammatory arthropathy rather than osteoarthritis or other conditions. Once secondary causes such as disseminated gonococcal arthritis, Lyme disease, and septic arthritis have been excluded, first-line treatment for inflammatory arthropathies is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as ibuprofen. NSAIDs provide both anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects, addressing the underlying inflammation and pain. Choice A (Oral alendronate): Alendronate is a bisphosphonate used for osteoporosis and hypercalcemia management. It has no role in treating inflammatory arthropathies and does not address the inflammatory process. Choice B (Oral colchicine): Colchicine is used for gout, pseudogout, and pericarditis. These conditions present with acute, severe, monoarticular symptoms triggered by crystal deposition in the joint space. Diagnosis is confirmed via arthrocentesis showing crystals. This patient's presentation is inconsistent with crystal arthropathy. Choice D (Intra-articular injection of methylprednisolone): While corticosteroid injections may have a role in inflammatory arthritis management, they are typically used after a trial of NSAIDs has been initiated. Additionally, local injections would require repeated administration for bilateral knee involvement, increasing infection risk and patient discomfort. Systemic treatment is more appropriate as first-line therapy. Choice E (Intravenous cefazolin): Antibiotics are appropriate only if septic arthritis is confirmed. This patient lacks the acute presentation, fever, and other features typical of septic arthritis. Empiric antibiotics are inappropriate without clear evidence of infection. Educational Objective: Recognize the clinical presentation of inflammatory arthropathy and initiate appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy with NSAIDs while excluding other diagnoses such as septic arthritis, crystal arthropathies, and infectious etiologies.
Source: 10A #33
A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She received the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis 4 weeks ago and has been treated with naproxen since then. Today, she says that her joint pain has been well controlled and asks what else she can do to prevent disability and protect her bone structure. She is a sales representative at a department store. Examination of the wrist, metacarpophalangeal, and knee joints shows mild effusions and synovial thickening. Range of motion of the affected joints is limited. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation? A. Range-of-motion and aerobic exercises B. Bisphosphonate therapy C. Glucosamine and chondroitin supplementation D. Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation E. Vitamin C supplementation F. Acupuncture
Correct Answer: A. Range-of-motion and aerobic exercises
Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease that causes extensive inflammation in synovial tissues. The patient presents with classic findings of early-stage RA including mild joint effusions, synovial thickening, and limited range of motion affecting multiple joints (wrist, metacarpophalangeal, and knee joints). While her pain is currently controlled with NSAIDs, the most appropriate recommendation to prevent long-term disability and protect bone structure is range-of-motion and aerobic exercises. Physical activity has been shown to decrease fatigue, pain, and disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis. This is a key component of comprehensive RA management alongside disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) such as methotrexate. Choice B (Bisphosphonate therapy) is not appropriate as the primary recommendation for this younger patient. Bisphosphonates are indicated for patients with osteoporosis or osteopenia with high fracture risk, not as a first-line intervention for early RA. While bone loss is a concern in RA, exercise is the more appropriate initial recommendation. Choice C (Glucosamine and chondroitin supplementation) has shown conflicting results in efficacy for treatment of osteoarthritis and is not indicated specifically for RA management. Exercise is the evidence-based recommendation. Choice D (Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation) may possibly modulate disease activity in RA but has not been established as a primary recommendation for preventing disability. Physical exercise is superior for improving functional outcomes. Choice E (Vitamin C supplementation), while potentially protective in high concentrations, is not the most appropriate active intervention for a patient already diagnosed with RA who needs to prevent disability. Choice F (Acupuncture) may help reduce pain associated with RA but does not provide the systemic benefits of range-of-motion and aerobic exercise, which reduce fatigue, pain, and disease activity while improving joint function and preventing disability.

Source: 3A #48
A 77-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of confusion and sleepiness for the past 12 hours. She has mild hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide but is otherwise healthy. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 150/100 mm Hg. On examination, she is obtunded and confused. There is no jugular venous distention when she is supine. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. There are no focal neurologic signs. Serum studies show: Na+ 146 mEq/L, K+ 5.0 mEq/L, Ca2+ 15 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 40 mg/dL, Glucose 105 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, Albumin 3.1 g/dL. Intravenous infusion of which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy? A) Albumin B) Furosemide C) Glucose and insulin D) 0.9% Saline E) Sodium phosphate
Correct Answer: D) 0.9% Saline
Acute hypercalcemia can present with a broad spectrum of symptoms and can be life-threatening because of its effect on neuronal conduction, the cardiac action potential, kidney function, and volume status. It can result from an exacerbation of known hypercalcemia (e.g., in cases of bony metastatic disease with increased osteoclast activity) or as a new diagnosis caused by an acute electrolyte derangement (e.g., excessive intake of calcium in the form of antacid medication). Hypercalcemia can induce nephrogenic diabetes insipidus resulting in excessive renal water losses. Treatment includes fluid resuscitation to prevent renal failure, promoting renal excretion of calcium, reducing intestinal absorption of calcium, inhibiting bony destruction, and, if necessary, renal replacement therapy with dialysis. Treatment therefore begins with infusion of 0.9% saline to restore intravascular volume and dilute serum calcium, followed by administration of osteoclast inhibitors such as bisphosphonates and possibly calcitonin if further medications are required to reduce calcium levels. This patient presents with symptomatic hypercalcemia (serum calcium 15 mEq/L) with altered mental status, and initial management must focus on volume resuscitation and renal perfusion. Albumin (Choice A) is used as a resuscitation colloid in cases of known hypoalbuminemia, such as liver failure or nephrotic syndrome. It supplies minimal intravascular volume directly, but rather draws fluid into the intravascular space through oncotic pressure. Such equilibration takes time, making it a suboptimal colloid in managing symptomatic hypercalcemia. Furosemide (Choice B), a loop diuretic, acts at the kidney to promote fluid and electrolyte losses, including calcium. It has a role in the management of hypercalcemia but would be used following adequate volume resuscitation, not before. Glucose and insulin (Choice C) are a combined therapy used to shift potassium into cells in cases of acute hyperkalemia while maintaining normoglycemia. This patient's potassium level is within normal limits at 5.0 mEq/L; immediate intervention is not required at this time. Oral sodium phosphate (Choice E) has an adjunct role in binding calcium in the GI tract, preventing further absorption, but does not have a role in the abrupt lowering of serum calcium levels. Intravenous phosphate has also been shown to bind calcium in the serum; however, the resulting insoluble calcium-phosphate product can deposit throughout tissues. This treatment may lead to additional organ dysfunction and should be avoided if possible.
Source: 4A #17
A 62-year-old man has had lethargy, weakness, confusion, and constipation for 3 days. Three weeks ago, he was diagnosed with inoperable squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. Examination shows decreased skin turgor. Breath sounds are decreased at the left apex. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count: 8100/mm³ Serum Na+: 142 mEq/L K+: 4.8 mEq/L Ca²+: 15.2 mg/dL Phosphorus: 1.2 mg/dL Albumin: 4.5 g/dL An ECG shows a short QT interval. Intravenous administration of 0.9% saline (200 mL/h) is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Allopurinol B) Cisplatin C) Cryoprecipitate D) Demeclocycline E) Doxycycline F) Fresh frozen plasma G) Heparin H) Hydroxyurea I) Pamidronate J) Tamoxifen
Correct Answer: I) Pamidronate
Pamidronate is a bisphosphonate and is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient's hypercalcemia. The clinical presentation of lethargy, weakness, confusion, and constipation combined with laboratory findings of markedly elevated serum calcium (15.2 mg/dL), short QT interval on ECG, and decreased skin turgor are classic for acute hypercalcemia. The patient's inoperable squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is a common malignancy that produces parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP), which induces osteoclast activity and results in hypercalcemia. Bisphosphonates like pamidronate inhibit osteoclast activity, reducing bone resorption and lowering serum calcium. First-line therapy for hypercalcemia includes isotonic fluid resuscitation (0.9% saline), which has already been initiated, followed by IV bisphosphonate administration with or without calcitonin if further calcium reduction is required. Incorrect answers: Allopurinol (Choice A) is used for gout prevention by inhibiting xanthine oxidase. Cisplatin (Choice B) is a chemotherapeutic agent used for malignancies but does not treat hypercalcemia. Cryoprecipitate (Choice C) contains fibrinogen and coagulation factors and is used for coagulopathic states, not hypercalcemia. Demeclocycline (Choice D) is an ADH antagonist used for refractory SIADH. Doxycycline (Choice E) is a tetracycline antibiotic for bacterial infections. Fresh frozen plasma (Choice F) contains coagulation factors for anticoagulation reversal and hypocoagulable states. Heparin (Choice G) is an anticoagulant for DVT, PE, and ACS. Hydroxyurea (Choice H) is used for sickle cell disease by inducing fetal hemoglobin production. Tamoxifen (Choice J) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator for breast cancer treatment.

Source: 9A #19
A 34-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-day history of intermittent episodes of mild, "colicky" left-sided flank pain associated with blood in his urine. He has not experienced any recent trauma, fever, nausea, vomiting, difficulty urinating, or radiation of the pain. He has no history of serious illness and he takes no medications. He has a family history of kidney disease in his uncle, which requires hemodialysis. Blood pressure is 144/106 mm Hg; remaining vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Ultrasonography of the kidneys shows multiple cysts bilaterally; there are no renal calculi noted. Dipstick urinalysis obtained in the office shows visible hematuria but no other abnormalities. Amlodipine and acetaminophen are initiated. During follow-up examination 1 week later, the patient reports that his flank pain and hematuria have resolved. Blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. The result of serum creatinine concentration from 1 week ago is 0.8 mg/dL. Repeat urinalysis shows 1+ blood. Which of the following conditions is this patient most likely to develop in 30 years? A) Brain aneurysm B) Cerebral infarction C) End-stage kidney disease D) Renal cell carcinoma E) Splenic infarction
Correct Answer: C) End-stage kidney disease
This patient presents with the classic clinical features of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD): flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, and bilateral multiple kidney cysts on ultrasonography, combined with a positive family history of kidney disease requiring hemodialysis. ADPKQ is caused by genetic mutations in PKD1 or PKD2 genes, which result in structural abnormalities of renal tubules leading to cyst development. The kidney cysts generally form in adulthood and progressively compress adjacent normal renal parenchyma, eventually leading to end-stage kidney disease. The majority of patients with ADPKD will require renal replacement therapy within 30 years. Treatment focuses on blood pressure management and dietary modifications, but there is no known way to prevent disease progression. While patients with ADPKD do have an increased risk for associated vascular abnormalities such as cerebral (berry) aneurysms and mitral valve prolapse, end-stage kidney disease is the most likely outcome in 30 years given this patient's presentation and the natural history of ADPKD. Choice A (brain aneurysm) is incorrect because although patients with ADPKD are at increased risk for cerebral aneurysms, end-stage kidney disease is more likely to develop. Choice B (cerebral infarction) is incorrect because this patient lacks risk factors for cerebral infarction such as family history of cerebral aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage, and end-stage kidney disease is more probable. Choice D (renal cell carcinoma) is incorrect because although ADPKD patients have increased risk for renal cell carcinoma, end-stage kidney disease is more likely to develop first. Choice E (splenic infarction) is incorrect because splenic infarcts have not been strongly associated with ADPKD, and end-stage kidney disease is the expected long-term complication.

A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of fatigue, decreased appetite, and occasional episodes of vomiting. She has had hypertension since the age of 35 years but has not been compliant with the prescribed pharmacotherapy. She currently takes only ibuprofen for chronic headaches. Her mother died of a brain hemorrhage, and her brother is receiving dialysis. Her blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows fullness in the left upper quadrant. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 45%, Serum Na+ 138 mEq/L, Cl- 104 mEq/L, K+ 5.5 mEq/L, HCO3- 18 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 81 mg/dL, Creatinine 7.2 mg/dL. Urine shows blood and protein with 5-10 RBC/hpf. A 24-hour urine collection shows 0.7 g of protein and 1.5 g of creatinine. Two years ago, her serum creatinine concentration was 4.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Analgesic nephropathy B) Chronic glomerulonephritis C) Goodpasture syndrome D) Multiple myeloma E) Obstructive nephropathy F) Polycystic kidney disease G) Reflux nephropathy H) Tubulointerstitial nephritis I) Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Correct Answer: F) Polycystic kidney disease
This patient presents with hypertension, progressive chronic kidney disease (serum creatinine increased from 4.5 mg/dL two years ago to 7.2 mg/dL now), and fullness in the left upper abdominal quadrant. Critically, she has a significant family history of kidney disease (brother on dialysis) and brain hemorrhage (mother), which are hallmark features of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). The left upper quadrant fullness likely represents enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts. Polycystic kidney disease is caused by genetic mutations in PKD1 or PKD2 that result in structural abnormalities of renal tubules leading to multiple cyst formation. Patients typically present with flank pain, hematuria (evidenced by blood in urine here), hypertension, and progressive chronic kidney disease. The disease is associated with vascular abnormalities including berry aneurysms (which may explain the mother's brain hemorrhage), mitral valve prolapse, and hepatic cysts. The diagnosis is clinical and based on family history, laboratory findings, and imaging showing multiple renal cysts. Treatment focuses on blood pressure management and dietary modifications, with most patients eventually requiring renal replacement therapy. Choice A (Analgesic nephropathy) is incorrect because while NSAIDs like ibuprofen can cause kidney injury through decreased glomerular perfusion, this patient's presentation and family history are more consistent with ADPKD. Choice B (Chronic glomerulonephritis) is incorrect as it refers to various glomerular diseases and nephritic syndromes, but does not explain the family history of kidney disease or the abdominal findings. Choice C (Goodpasture syndrome) is incorrect because it is characterized by autoantibodies against type IV collagen affecting renal and alveolar basement membranes, typically presenting with hematuria and hemoptysis, without family history or abdominal cyst findings. Choice D (Multiple myeloma) is incorrect as it is a plasma cell malignancy presenting with bone pain, anemia, hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, and renal dysfunction, not chronic progressive kidney disease with cysts and family history. Choice E (Obstructive nephropathy) is incorrect as this represents a postrenal cause of acute kidney injury from obstruction (nephrolithiasis, benign prostatic hyperplasia), not the chronic progressive disease with cysts seen here. Choice G (Reflux nephropathy) is incorrect because it results from vesicoureteral reflux with retrograde urine flow, typically beginning in childhood from ureteric valve abnormalities, and does not account for the family history or characteristic cyst findings. Choice H (Tubulointerstitial nephritis) is incorrect as it does not explain the family history, progressive nature, or the left upper quadrant findings. Choice I (Granulomatosis with polyangiitis) is incorrect as this systemic vasculitis typically presents with upper respiratory tract involvement and pulmonary-renal syndrome, not isolated progressive kidney disease with cysts and characteristic family history.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Allergic Contact Dermatitis2 questions
Source: 9A #20
A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of blisters and redness on the dorsum of her hands for 3 months and generalized urticaria for 1 week. The blisters partially improve with the use of topical corticosteroids. Her work as a scrub nurse requires her to wear latex gloves throughout the day. Examination shows lichenified dermatitis on the dorsum of both hands with several vesicles in various stages of resolution. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? A. Avoidance of all latex-containing materials B. Change to gloves without talcum powder C. Skin testing and desensitization D. Nighttime topical corticosteroid therapy with occlusion for hands E. Daily oral antihistamine therapy
Correct Answer: A) Avoidance of all latex-containing materials
This patient's persistent dyshidrotic eczema despite topical corticosteroid treatment in the setting of occupational exposure to latex is highly suggestive of allergic contact dermatitis. Eczematous rashes should be evaluated for exacerbating factors including occupational or hobby-related exposures. Dyshidrotic eczema may be triggered by irritants and contact allergens, frequently presenting with ill-defined, scaly, vesiculated, and eroded plaques on the lateral and dorsal aspects of the fingers. Improvement during periods away from the triggering allergen suggests contact allergy. Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T lymphocytes. The pathophysiology involves antigen-presenting cells recognizing a target antigen and activating T lymphocytes, which induce cell death and inflammation. This requires an initial sensitizing exposure followed by a reaction on repeat exposure. Common contact allergens include poison ivy, nickel, and latex—particularly relevant in healthcare workers. The most appropriate management is avoidance of the offending material (latex) combined with topical corticosteroids for symptomatic treatment. Since the patient's symptoms persist despite adequate topical corticosteroid therapy, continued exposure to latex is the primary problem. Choice B (change to gloves without talcum powder) is incorrect because talcum powder is not commonly associated with contact dermatitis; the most likely culprit is latex itself. Choice C (skin testing and desensitization) is incorrect because these interventions are used for type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reactions, which are IgE-mediated and involve histamine release. Type IV hypersensitivity reactions require trigger avoidance instead. Choice D (nighttime topical corticosteroid therapy with occlusion) is incorrect because while occlusion is commonly used in dyshidrotic eczema treatment, this patient remains symptomatic despite adequate corticosteroid therapy, indicating an uncontrolled contact allergen exposure. Choice E (daily oral antihistamine therapy) is incorrect because oral antihistamines inhibit H1 receptors and are used for seasonal allergies and type I hypersensitivity reactions, not type IV contact dermatitis. Contact dermatitis management requires avoidance of the causative agent.
Source: 5A #45
A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of a rash over her left wrist. She first noticed the rash after she started wearing a new watch, but the rash has not resolved since she stopped wearing the watch 3 days ago. She has a 2-year history of hypertension treated with atenolol. She is wearing perfume today. Examination of the left wrist shows erythematous papules. There are several nevi over the chest and abdomen. The skin is diffusely dry and flakes easily. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Adverse effect of atenolol B) Allergic reaction to perfume C) Dry skin D) Exposure to nickel E) Impaired T-lymphocyte response
Correct Answer: D) Exposure to nickel
Contact dermatitis is a type IV T cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction following exposure to an allergen, which results in the development of a pruritic, erythematous, and papular rash. It is characteristically distributed along the location of clothing, perfume, plant contact, or nickel jewelry contact. The rashes are often described as linear or angular in shape. In some cases, the rash can spread from the point of initial contact through transfer of the allergen by hand contact. Frequent allergens resulting in contact dermatitis are nickel, topical antibiotics, and poison ivy or oak. Diagnosis for the specific causative allergen can be made through patch testing, with first-line treatments being topical corticosteroids and avoidance of the culprit allergen. Choice A (Atenolol): Atenolol is a beta-1 selective antagonist used in the management of hypertension and supraventricular dysrhythmias. Side effects include bradycardia and atrioventricular block, not a localized dermatologic rash. Choice B (Perfume): While perfume can result in a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, the patient's rash is located specifically at the site of the new watch, which likely contains a component of nickel. The rash does not demonstrate the appropriate location or timeline to be presumed secondary to perfume alone. Choice C (Dry skin): Given the temporal and spatial relationship to the wearing of a new watch, along with erythematous papules, this is unlikely to represent a patch of dry skin. Choice E (Impaired T-lymphocyte response): Contact dermatitis occurs secondary to a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, which is T-cell dependent. An impaired T-lymphocyte response would actually protect against contact dermatitis rather than cause it. The clinical presentation—localized erythematous papules at the site of a new watch worn for 3 weeks—is classic for nickel-induced contact dermatitis.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Septic Shock2 questions
Source: 9A #23
A patient appeared weak and confused before passing out. Pulse oximetry on 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 100%. Crackles are heard at the right lung base with egophony. His fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 130 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
