Transitioning to hospice care represents a transition from diagnostic and invasive procedures to prioritizing comfort and symptom management. Further intervention would not likely prolong life and would only add to the patient's pain and suffering. Educational Objective: Hospice care is a multidisciplinary healthcare model that aims to provide symptom management, emotional and spiritual support, and access to various health care providers. The purpose of hospice care is to alleviate pain and suffering at the end of a patient's life by minimizing hospital admissions and diagnostic and invasive procedures. Medications provided during hospice care are often titrated to patient symptoms, with appropriate pain control being an important tenet of end-of-life care.
Source: 4A #5
A 57-year-old woman with stage IV non-small cell lung carcinoma is admitted to the hospital because of a 2-day history of shortness of breath and fever. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). She receives the diagnosis of postobstructive pneumonia. Treatment with intravenous antibiotics is begun, and her symptoms resolve 3 days later. During a family meeting to discuss her treatment options, the patient states that she wishes to discontinue chemotherapy and requests no resuscitation if she has a cardiac arrest. In addition to obtaining a signed advance directive and durable power of attorney for health care decisions, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient? A) Discharge home with home hospice care B) Discharge home with physical and occupational therapy C) Discharge home with visiting nurse services D) Discharge to a skilled nursing care facility E) Remain in the hospital
Correct Answer: A) Discharge home with home hospice care
Discharge home with home hospice care is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient. Hospice care is indicated for patients with a life expectancy of less than six months in the setting of a terminal diagnosis. This patient has stage IV non-small cell lung carcinoma and has explicitly stated her wish to discontinue aggressive treatment such as chemotherapy, indicating a decision to pursue comfort-focused care rather than curative measures. Hospice care focuses on palliation of symptoms with attention to providing comfort and dignity at the end of life. Choice B (Physical and occupational therapy) is indicated for rehabilitation following hospitalization, surgery, or trauma to improve physical abilities and return to daily activities. This patient's goals are incompatible with rehabilitative care. Choice C (Visiting nurse services) and Choice D (Skilled nursing facility) are appropriate for patients needing nursing care to assist with medications, hygiene, and management of medical conditions, but these services do not focus primarily on palliation and comfort care as hospice does. Choice E (Remain in the hospital) would not allow the patient to receive palliative care in the comfort of her own home, which aligns with her stated wishes to avoid aggressive intervention. The key distinction is that hospice care directly addresses this patient's goals of comfort and dignity while avoiding prolonged hospitalization and aggressive treatments she has explicitly declined.
▶Cardiovascular System Mitral Valve Stenosis2 questions
Source: 10A #13
A 57-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 2-month history of shortness of breath with exertion. He becomes short of breath after walking two level blocks or one flight of stairs. On two occasions during this period, he has awoken during the night with shortness of breath; this symptom resolved after 15 minutes of sitting upright. He does not recall unusual shortness of breath in the past. He has a 3-month history of swelling of his ankles. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He has not seen a physician for 25 years and has a sedentary lifestyle. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years; he does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. On examination, he is sitting upright and appears mildly dyspneic. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 92/min and regular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 135/88 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Jugular venous pressure is 6 cm H2O. Percussion of the lungs shows no abnormalities. Inspiratory crackles are heard at both lung bases. Palpation of the precordium shows no abnormalities. There is a grade 2/6, low-pitched, diastolic murmur at the apex, which lasts throughout diastole and is loudest immediately prior to S4, and an opening snap after S2. No other murmurs are noted. There is pitting edema to the midcalves. Right and left cardiac catheterization is most likely to show which of the following findings in this patient? Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure | Left Atrial Pressure | Left Ventricular End-diastolic Pressure A) Increased | Increased | Increased B) Increased | Increased | Normal C) Increased | Normal | Increased D) Increased | Normal | Normal E) Normal | Increased | Normal
Correct Answer: B) Increased | Increased | Normal
This patient presents with acute decompensated heart failure evidenced by progressive exertional shortness of breath, nocturnal dyspnea (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea), jugular venous distention, inspiratory crackles at the lung bases, and peripheral edema. The cardiac examination is key to diagnosis: the low-pitched, holosystolic diastolic murmur at the apex that is loudest immediately prior to S4, combined with an opening snap after S2, is pathognomonic for mitral stenosis. The opening snap occurs early in diastole when the stenotic mitral valve leaflets abruptly stop closing. The murmur reflects turbulent flow across the narrowed mitral orifice during diastole. Mitral stenosis is a common cause of heart failure, particularly in patients with risk factors such as advanced age and significant smoking history. In mitral stenosis, the pathophysiology involves obstruction to left ventricular filling. The stenotic mitral valve prevents normal blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle during diastole. This obstruction causes: 1. Left Atrial Pressure - INCREASED: Blood backs up in the left atrium, causing elevated left atrial pressure as the atrium works harder to push blood across the narrowed mitral valve. 2. Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure - INCREASED: The elevated left atrial pressure is transmitted backward through the pulmonary veins to the pulmonary capillary bed, resulting in increased wedge pressure (which reflects left atrial pressure). 3. Left Ventricular End-diastolic Pressure (LVEDP) - NORMAL: The left ventricle itself is distal to the mitral valve obstruction. Since blood cannot easily enter the left ventricle from the stenotic mitral valve, the left ventricle remains relatively underfilled and has normal or even low end-diastolic pressure. The left ventricular systolic function is typically normal in isolated mitral stenosis. The differential diagnosis includes other valvular lesions: In mitral regurgitation, the left ventricle would have increased end-diastolic pressure due to regurgitant flow into the ventricle. In aortic stenosis or aortic regurgitation, the left ventricular pressures would be affected differently. In left ventricular systolic dysfunction from other causes (ischemic heart disease, cardiomyopathy), the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure would be increased. Treatment of heart failure in this patient involves supplemental oxygen, diuretics (to reduce pulmonary and systemic congestion), and definitive management with mitral valve replacement or repair. Beta-blockers and other heart failure medications may provide symptomatic relief, while valve replacement addresses the underlying anatomic problem. The patient's clinical presentation, murmur characteristics, and expected catheterization findings all point to mitral stenosis as the primary diagnosis. Educational Objective: Understand the hemodynamic profile of mitral stenosis on cardiac catheterization and recognize the clinical presentation of mitral stenosis as a cause of heart failure. Key Concept: In mitral stenosis, increased left atrial, pulmonary vein, and pulmonary capillary pressures occur proximal to the valve obstruction, while left ventricular end-diastolic pressure remains normal because the left ventricle is distal to the stenotic valve and underfilled.
Source: 8A #19
A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of progressive shortness of breath and blood-tinged sputum over the past 7 days. Examination shows jugular venous distention. There is an increased S2 with a high-pitched extra heart sound after S2. A grade 1/6, low-pitched diastolic murmur is heard at the apex radiating to the anterior axillary line. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Aortic insufficiency B) Aortic stenosis C) Atrial septal defect D) Coarctation of the aorta E) Mitral insufficiency F) Mitral stenosis G) Pulmonic stenosis
Correct Answer: F) Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is classically heard as an opening snap followed by a diastolic rumble, loudest over the cardiac apex and radiating to the axilla. Mitral stenosis occurs because of calcification and fibrosis of the mitral valve. Impaired excursion of the valve leaflets results in increased left atrial filling pressures and impaired diastolic filling of the left ventricle. The fixed obstruction to blood flow may manifest with left atrial enlargement and progression to heart failure. Increased resistance to flow on the left side of the heart can result in pulmonary hypertension. A history of rheumatic fever is the most common cause. Other causes include congenital defects and infective endocarditis. Treatment is through medical optimization followed by surgical valve replacement if severe. Choice A (Aortic insufficiency) presents with an early diastolic decrescendo murmur best heard in the right second intercostal space, and is commonly associated with endocarditis, acute rheumatic fever, and aortic root dilation. Choice B (Aortic stenosis) presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, best heard at the upper right sternal border, and radiates to the carotid arteries. It classically occurs secondary to age-related fibrotic and calcific changes of the valve but can occur earlier in life in cases of bicuspid aortic valve or chronic rheumatic disease. Choice C (Atrial septal defect) results in a left-to-right shunt with abnormal flow of blood from the left atrium to the right atrium. This increased stroke volume of the right ventricle results in delayed closure of the pulmonic valve, which presents as a fixed, split S2 and low-grade physiologic ejection murmur on cardiac auscultation. Choice D (Coarctation of the aorta) often presents in childhood with hypertension in an upper extremity and a systolic murmur. It is associated with weak pulses and relatively decreased blood pressure in the lower extremities. Choice E (Mitral insufficiency) presents with a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left fourth or fifth intercostal space along the midclavicular line and radiates to the left axilla. It is commonly associated with mitral valve prolapse, acute rheumatic fever, endocarditis, and prior myocardial infarction. Choice G (Pulmonic stenosis) presents with a systolic murmur best heard in the second left intercostal region, which is often crescendo-decrescendo, though quieter and with less radiation to the lower neck because of the lower pressure in the pulmonary circulation. This is typically seen in the setting of Tetralogy of Fallot. Educational Objective: Mitral valve stenosis is often associated with a history of rheumatic fever and should be suspected when a patient has a low-pitched diastolic murmur heard at the apex with radiation to the anterior axillary line.
▶Endocrine System Thyroid nodule2 questions
Source: 10A #16
A previously healthy 52-year-old man comes to the physician 2 weeks after noticing a lump in the left side of his neck. He has not had difficulty speaking or swallowing. He has not had any other symptoms. Examination shows a 2-cm, firm, freely mobile mass on the left side of the neck that rises with swallowing. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A. Carotid duplex ultrasonography B. CT scan of the neck C. I131 thyroid scan D. Excisional biopsy of the mass E. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass
Correct Answer: E. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass
The patient presents with a palpable thyroid nodule (2-cm mass that rises with swallowing, indicating thyroid origin). The most appropriate next step in diagnosis is fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass for further characterization. Thyroid masses may be asymptomatic or present with neck pain, difficulty swallowing, or voice changes. Patients with a new thyroid nodule should be evaluated with serum TSH measurement and thyroid ultrasonography. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy is performed for patients with risk factors for malignancy or for nodules with concerning ultrasonography findings, such as being larger than 1.5 cm. Subsequent workup and management depend on serum TSH measurement, ultrasonography characteristics, and biopsy results, which may include monitoring with repeat ultrasonography or surgical intervention. Choice A (Carotid duplex ultrasonography) is incorrect because carotid duplex ultrasonography is useful for evaluating carotid stenosis, not thyroid nodules. Choice B (CT scan of the neck) is incorrect because while CT may help determine size and location of a thyroid mass, ultrasonography is the preferred imaging modality, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy is the most appropriate next diagnostic step. Choice C (I131 thyroid scan) is not the most appropriate next step. A radioactive iodine uptake scan is recommended if serum TSH concentration is decreased, indicating primary hyperthyroidism. This patient does not present with signs or symptoms of hyperthyroidism. Choice D (Excisional biopsy) is incorrect because excisional biopsy is reserved for larger thyroid nodules with concerning features on ultrasonography. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy is the appropriate initial biopsy technique. Risk factors for thyroid malignancy include young age, radiation exposure to the head or neck, and family history of thyroid cancer or associated congenital neoplastic syndromes such as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.
Source: 4A #27
A previously healthy 42-year-old woman comes to the physician 2 days after she noted a mildly tender bump on her neck. She has not had fever, chills, cough, sore throat, or palpitations. She has smoked approximately one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. She underwent a hysterectomy 2 years ago. Her only medication is conjugated estrogen. She is in no acute distress. She is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 57 kg (125 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m². Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 120/78 mm Hg. Examination of the neck shows a 2-cm lesion on the left lobe of the thyroid gland. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Her serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is 1.5 µU/ml, and serum free thyroxine concentration is 1.4 ng/dl (N=0.9-2.1). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Reexamination and repeat thyroid function tests in 1 month B) Measurement of thyroid radioactive iodine uptake C) CT scan of the neck D) Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion E) Partial thyroidectomy
Correct Answer: D) Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion
Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) is the most appropriate next step in management for thyroid nodules greater than 1 cm in dimension with either normal or high TSH levels. This patient presents with a 2-cm thyroid nodule with normal TSH (1.5 µU/ml) and normal free thyroxine (1.4 ng/dl), indicating the nodule is non-hyperfunctioning. Non-functioning nodules have an increased risk of malignancy and require tissue characterization via FNA to determine the underlying pathology and guide further treatment decisions. Choice A (Reexamination and repeat thyroid function tests in 1 month) would be appropriate for subacute thyroiditis, which presents with a tender thyroid and is typically self-limiting. However, this patient's presentation and thyroid function tests are more consistent with a thyroid nodule requiring characterization rather than inflammatory thyroiditis. Choice B (Measurement of thyroid radioactive iodine uptake) is indicated specifically for evaluation of hyperfunctioning thyroid nodules presenting with suppressed TSH levels (e.g., toxic adenoma, multinodular goiter, Graves disease). This patient has normal TSH, making this study unnecessary. Choice C (CT scan of the neck) is reserved for cases with clinical suspicion of local invasion by thyroid malignancy, manifested by symptoms such as dysphagia, hoarseness, or other signs of compression of surrounding structures. This is not indicated in this patient without such concerning symptoms. Choice E (Partial thyroidectomy) is a surgical intervention indicated for treatment of toxic adenomas, debulking of large compressive goiters, or definitive management of thyroid malignancy. It is not an appropriate diagnostic step and would not be performed before tissue characterization via FNA.
▶Gastrointestinal System Irritable bowel syndrome2 questions
Source: 10A #22
A previously healthy 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of episodes of abdominal pain and constipation. The pain is relieved with bowel movements. He frequently feels bloated but has not had weight loss or blood in the stools. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and mild left lower quadrant tenderness. Rectal examination shows no abnormalities; test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Colon cancer B) Crohn disease C) Diverticulitis D) Irritable bowel syndrome E) Ulcerative colitis
Correct Answer: D) Irritable bowel syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by altered bowel habits and recurrent abdominal pain with changes in stool frequency or form. This patient presents with classic features of IBS: a 6-month history of abdominal pain relieved by defecation, constipation, bloating, and no structural abnormalities on examination or testing. Key diagnostic features in this case: - Chronic symptoms (6 months) with pain relief after bowel movements, which is typical for IBS - Absence of alarm features: no weight loss, no blood in stools, negative occult blood test - Normal rectal examination excluding structural pathology - Mild abdominal tenderness and distention without acute findings IBS is diagnosed clinically based on characteristic symptoms after excluding competing diagnoses. The different subtypes include IBS with constipation, IBS with diarrhea, and mixed IBS. This patient has IBS with constipation predominance. Differential diagnosis considerations: - Colon cancer: Would typically present with weight loss, changes in bowel caliber, or positive occult blood test, which are absent here - Crohn disease: Would show elevated inflammatory markers, possible weight loss, and may have extraintestinal manifestations - Diverticulitis: Presents as acute episodes with fever and more severe pain, not chronic constipation - Ulcerative colitis: Would present with diarrhea with blood/mucus and systemic inflammation Treatment of IBS focuses on dietary and lifestyle interventions as first-line management, with pharmacologic agents such as linaclotide available for additional management. IBS is a functional disorder without underlying structural or biochemical abnormalities, distinguishing it from inflammatory bowel disease and other organic causes of gastrointestinal symptoms.
Source: 8A #29
A previously healthy 23-year-old woman, who is a graduate student, comes to the office because of a 4-month history of intermittent diarrhea characterized by copious loose brown stools and moderate abdominal cramps. The cramps are relieved by defecation. She has not had fever, nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. She takes ginger extract and a daily multivitamin. She smokes three to five cigarettes daily. She drinks one to three beers on special occasions. She does not use illicit drugs. She has not traveled recently. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (140 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. Examination, including examination of the oropharynx and abdomen, shows no abnormalities. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for these findings? A) Bacteria overgrowth B) Endomysial antibody formation C) Medication adverse effect D) Smooth muscle hypersensitivity E) Stimulant laxative use
Correct Answer: D) Smooth muscle hypersensitivity
Smooth muscle hypersensitivity is the most likely mechanism responsible for this patient's abdominal pain and diarrhea, which is most consistent with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). IBS is diagnosed using the Rome-IV criteria, which includes the presence of abdominal pain at least once weekly that is associated with (generally relieved by) defecation, along with a change in stool appearance or stool frequency (at least two of three required). IBS is further subdivided into IBS with constipation (IBS-C), with diarrhea (IBS-D), or mixed (IBS-M). IBS often presents with intermittent abdominal pain that is relieved by bowel movements and associated alterations in bowel habits with intermittent episodes of diarrhea and/or constipation. Features that are suggestive of underlying organic pathology rather than IBS include the presence of occult blood or melena, nocturnal diarrhea, ongoing diarrhea despite fasting, worsening abdominal pain, weight loss, or a family history of inflammatory bowel disease or colon cancer. While no consistent or definitive mechanism has been demonstrated to account for all patients with IBS, it is thought that those with IBS may have an increased sensitivity to regularly secreted cholecystokinin, a highly sensitive gastro-colic reflex, and/or a higher rate of baseline peristalsis. Other theories including the role of food sensitivities and mucosal inflammation are being explored as potential contributing factors. Treatment often requires a multimodal approach with dietary modifications, exercise, treatment of underlying anxiety or depression, and the use of medications such as anti-diarrheal medications or anti-spasmodic agents. Choice A (Bacteria overgrowth) occurs in the setting of impaired intestinal peristalsis, which allows for the uncontrolled growth of bacteria caused by the loss of appropriate peristaltic propulsion. This can result in intestinal malabsorption, diarrhea, bloating, and chronic abdominal pain, but would typically present with weight loss and malabsorption that this patient does not have. Choice B (Endomysial antibody formation) is characteristic of celiac disease, which often presents with chronic diarrhea and weight loss secondary to malabsorption. Symptoms may overlap with IBS, but patients with IBS typically do not suffer from weight loss, as seen in this case. Choice C (Medication adverse effect) is unlikely in this case as neither ginger nor multivitamins are associated with chronic diarrhea. Some patients forget to report over the counter medications such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) which, when taken in large quantities, can cause microscopic colitis, but this patient does not report a history of NSAID use. Choice E (Stimulant laxative use) can cause chronic, watery diarrhea in addition to electrolyte derangements such as hypokalemia, but this patient does not report any history of laxative use. Educational Objective: Irritable bowel syndrome is characterized by abdominal pain and a change in stool appearance or stool frequency. Patients with IBS-D have frequent episodes of diarrhea that are not associated with weight loss, malabsorption, or occult gastrointestinal bleeding. Treatment must address underlying psychiatric comorbidities and focus on diet modification. Medications to slow gut motility or relieve bloating are employed in the treatment of IBS-D.
▶Respiratory System Obesity-hypoventilation syndrome2 questions
Source: 10A #23
A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of progressive shortness of breath. He also says that he frequently falls asleep during the day. He becomes short of breath after walking 10 to 15 yards. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 125 kg (276 lb); BMI is 42 kg/m². The lungs are clear to auscultation. Respirations and heart sounds are distant. There is 1+ pedal edema. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: pH 7.36, PCO₂ 60 mmHg, PO₂ 60 mm Hg. A chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Arteriovenous shunting B) Decreased atmospheric partial pressure of oxygen C) Decreased diffusion capacity D) Hypoventilation E) Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
Correct Answer: D) Hypoventilation
This patient's history of chronic shortness of breath with exertion, daytime sleepiness, increased BMI (42 kg/m²), edema, and arterial blood gas showing chronic hypoxia (PO₂ 60 mmHg) and hypercapnia (PCO₂ 60 mmHg) is consistent with obesity-hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) and/or obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Both conditions cause hypoventilation, which results in retention of carbon dioxide, hypoxia, and compensated respiratory acidosis (pH 7.36 with elevated HCO₃⁻ from metabolic compensation). OHS and OSA are chronic conditions that cause apnea and hypopnea, leading to hypoventilation during nighttime and daytime, respectively. The presentation of both elevated CO₂ and low O₂ with clear lungs and normal chest x-ray in an obese patient with hypersomnolence is pathognomonic for hypoventilation. Chronic alveolar hypoventilation leads to both hypercapnia and hypoxemia. Hypercapnia causes respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation, manifesting as increased serum bicarbonate concentration, while chronic hypoxemia can lead to pulmonary and systemic hypertension and polycythemia. OHS is a clinical diagnosis based on increased BMI and abnormal CO₂ and/or O₂ concentrations in the absence of competing diagnoses. OSA is diagnosed using polysomnography. Choice A (Arteriovenous shunting) is incorrect. While it causes hypoxia from deoxygenated blood bypassing the pulmonary circuit, it does not result in retention of carbon dioxide and edema in the setting of obesity. Choice B (Decreased atmospheric partial pressure of oxygen) is incorrect. This causes hypoxia without an abnormal alveolar-arterial gradient and occurs at high altitude. This mechanism would not cause hypercapnia. Choice C (Decreased diffusion capacity) is incorrect. This occurs in chronic lung disease such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and would not cause hypercapnia unless another diagnosis causing hypoventilation were also present. Furthermore, pulmonary function tests are often normal in OHS/OSA. Choice E (Ventilation-perfusion mismatch) is incorrect. While it is the most common cause of hypoxia in various acute and chronic cardiopulmonary pathologies, it does not independently cause edema and does not explain the degree of hypercapnia present. Treatment involves weight loss for OHS (first-line) and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for OSA. Recommendations for both are often made given the clinical overlap.
Source: 8A #26
A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 10-month history of severe fatigue. She awakens four to five times nightly to void. She now takes daily naps and frequently falls asleep while watching television. She has noted swelling of her legs and occasional palpitations during the past 6 months. She has not had fever, night sweats, or change in bowel movements. She has had an 18-kg (40-lb) weight gain during the past year. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and now weighs 145 kg (320 lb); BMI is 57 kg/m². Her pulse is 96/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 160/95 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia and P pulmonale. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's nocturia? A) Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease B) Cystitis C) Hypothyroidism D) Narcolepsy E) Obesity-hypoventilation syndrome
Correct Answer: E) Obesity-hypoventilation syndrome
Obesity-hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) is the most likely cause of this patient's nocturia. OHS is occasionally encountered in patients with a BMI over 30 kg/m², and is common in patients with a BMI over 50 kg/m². This patient's BMI is 57 kg/m², which is consistent with OHS. Chronic alveolar hypoventilation leads to both hypercapnia and hypoxemia. Hypercapnia results in compensatory metabolic alkalosis manifesting as increased serum bicarbonate concentration, while chronic hypoxemia can lead to pulmonary hypertension and polycythemia. Pulmonary function tests are often normal but may disclose varying degrees of restrictive lung disease and reduced diffusing capacity. There is substantial overlap with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but OSA does not cause chronic hypercapnia. Patients commonly exhibit hypersomnolence, morning headaches, fatigue, snoring, and nocturia. Nocturia occurs due to increased circulating atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), triggered either by atrial distention from increasingly negative intrathoracic pressure during sleep or from hypoxia-induced pulmonary vasoconstriction. ANP inhibits antidiuretic hormone release, leading to nocturia through increased free water excretion. Diagnosis is made in patients with BMI over 30 kg/m² with documented alveolar hypoventilation while awake after excluding competing diagnoses. Choice A (COPD) typically presents with exertional dyspnea, coughing, or wheezing, is more common in smokers, and is less likely to present with daytime somnolence and nocturia. COPD is diagnosed using spirometry. Choice B (Cystitis) is unlikely as the patient lacks dysuria, frequency, or urgency. Choice C (Hypothyroidism) can worsen OSA symptoms only in severe cases causing respiratory muscle myopathy. While weight gain could be secondary to hypothyroidism, this patient's clinical signs and symptoms support OHS. Choice D (Narcolepsy) is caused by decreased concentrations of orexins (orexin-A and orexin-B) and presents with cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis, and daytime somnolence. It is more common in patients under age 40. Educational Objective: OHS is a sleep disorder characterized by chronic alveolar hypoventilation with subsequent hypercapnia and hypoxemia. It is more common in morbidly obese patients and may occur concomitantly with OSA. Symptoms include daytime somnolence, morning headaches, and nocturia, with laboratory studies disclosing hypercarbia. Diagnosis is made using polysomnography.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Decubitus Ulcer2 questions
Source: 10A #29
Five days after being hospitalized for treatment of a left hip fracture sustained in a fall, a 78-year-old woman has a 4 x 4-cm area of nonblanchable erythema with excoriation of the epidermis over the sacrum. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this skin lesion? A. Administering topical neomycin and bacitracin B. Changing positions every 2 hours C. Sitting in a chair for most of the day D. Using a donut-shaped cushion over the sacral area
Correct Answer: B. Changing positions every 2 hours
This patient presents with nonblanchable erythema with excoriation of the epidermis over the sacrum 5 days after hospitalization for a hip fracture, consistent with a Stage 1-2 pressure injury (decubitus ulcer). Decubitus ulcers are tissue damage that occurs over bony prominences due to prolonged pressure and shearing forces, commonly affecting immobilized or bedridden patients. The best preventive measure for pressure injuries in dependent patients is frequent position changes (every 2 hours), which relieves pressure on vulnerable areas and prevents tissue breakdown. Prevention of pressure injuries includes frequent position changes for dependent patients and avoidance of a moist environment in areas at risk. Choice A (Topical neomycin and bacitracin): These antibiotics are used for treatment of superficial wounds and infections and provide coverage against common bacterial pathogens. However, they do not prevent the development of decubitus ulcers, as the underlying problem is mechanical pressure rather than bacterial colonization. Choice C (Sitting in a chair for most of the day): While this would transfer some pressure load from the sacrum to the ischial tuberosities and potentially prevent sacral ulceration, it simply shifts the pressure to another area, placing the patient at risk for pressure ulceration at the ischial tuberosities instead. Choice D (Using a donut-shaped cushion): While pressure-relieving devices may provide some benefit, they do not replace the critical need for frequent repositioning. Localized cushioning alone is insufficient to prevent pressure injuries without regular position changes. Educational Objective: Frequent repositioning every 2 hours is the most effective preventive strategy for decubitus ulcers in immobilized patients. Pressure injuries can progress from nonblanchable erythema (Stage 1) to deep ulceration involving muscle, bone, or tendon (Stage 4) and are associated with serious complications including infection, osteomyelitis, and sepsis.
Source: 4A #6
An 87-year-old resident of a skilled nursing care facility is brought to the physician by staff because of a lesion on his left leg for 3 weeks. He has been confined to bed for 3 years because of a left hemiplegia following a cerebral infarction. Examination shows a 5 x 7-cm, grade 3 pressure ulcer over the left greater trochanter; there is an overlying eschar with a small rim of erythema. There are no other areas of ulceration. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Use of an air bed B) Application of wet-to-dry dressings C) Application of silver sulfadiazine cream and a sterile dressing D) Debridement of the ulcer E) Skin graft
Correct Answer: D) Debridement of the ulcer
Debridement of the ulcer is the most appropriate next step in management of a grade 3 pressure ulcer with necrotic tissue. A grade 3 pressure ulcer is characterized by full-thickness tissue loss with visible subcutaneous fat. The presence of an overlying eschar (necrotic tissue) and rim of erythema indicates the need for urgent debridement to remove devitalized tissue and allow proper wound healing. Debridement should be followed by wet-to-dry dressings, pressure offloading, and consistent wound cleaning. Choice A (Use of an air bed) can limit pressure to dependent body regions and serves as a preventive measure, but is only adjunctive management for an existing ulcer with necrosis and insufficient as primary treatment. Choice B (Application of wet-to-dry dressings) and Choice C (Application of silver sulfadiazine cream and sterile dressing) are therapeutic interventions for promoting tissue regrowth and maintaining wound cleanliness, but these are not sufficient in isolation for an ulcer with evidence of necrosis. The eschar must be debrided first before these dressings can be effective. Choice E (Skin graft) is indicated for patients with clean stage 3 or 4 ulcers that do not respond to optimal medical interventions or when rapid wound closure would significantly improve quality of life. Grafting is not appropriate for this ulcer as long as necrotic tissue remains, and optimal medical management has not yet been attempted.
▶Cardiovascular System Ventricular Tachycardia2 questions
Source: 4A #8
A 55-year-old man is admitted to the hospital in a coma following a sudden collapse. He has a history of recent coronary bypass operation for coronary artery disease. ECG shows wide QRS complexes (QRS 160 ms) with a ventricular rate of 170/min and an atrial rate of 110/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management? A) Administration of digitalis B) Administration of verapamil C) Carotid sinus massage D) Direct current countershock E) External pacing
Correct Answer: D) Direct current countershock
Direct current countershock is the most appropriate initial management for this unstable wide-QRS tachyarrhythmia. The patient presents with altered mental status (coma), a wide QRS complex (160 ms), rapid ventricular rate (170/min), and hemodynamic instability—all indications for immediate synchronized cardioversion or defibrillation. The differential diagnosis for wide-QRS tachycardia includes ventricular tachycardia (monomorphic or polymorphic), antidromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, or supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction. Direct current countershock is indicated for any tachyarrhythmia presenting with hemodynamic instability, altered mental status, no pulse, hypotension, or end-organ failure. Choice A (Digitalis) is used for rate control in atrial fibrillation or for inotropic support in heart failure, not for unstable wide-complex tachycardias. Choice B (Verapamil) is a calcium channel blocker used for supraventricular tachyarrhythmias like atrial fibrillation or AVNRT but is contraindicated in wide-complex rhythms of uncertain origin and in unstable patients. Choice C (Carotid sinus massage) increases vagal tone to slow AV nodal conduction and may be used for stable supraventricular tachycardia but has no role in wide-complex tachycardia or unstable arrhythmias. Choice E (External pacing) is reserved for treatment of refractory or unstable bradycardia, not tachycardia. In any hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmia, direct current countershock takes precedence over pharmacologic therapy.
Source: 4A #47
A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a 3-minute episode of unconsciousness. The patient says that the episode began with an impending sense of feeling ill while watching television. He quickly became confused, swayed in his chair, and fell to the floor. He had no bowel or bladder incontinence during this episode. His mental status spontaneously recovered fully within 3 minutes. He has a 10-year history of hypertension well controlled with hydrochlorothiazide. He had a myocardial infarction 4 years ago. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m². His pulse is 86/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 124/86 mm Hg. Neurologic and cardiac examinations show normal findings. An ECG shows Q waves in leads II, III, and aVF. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A) Hypoglycemia B) Paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia C) Pulmonary embolus D) Seizure E) Transient ischemic attack
Correct Answer: B) Paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia
Paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia (VT) refers to the sudden onset of VT, defined as three or more consecutive premature ventricular contractions resulting in a wide QRS complex tachyarrhythmia. This patient has multiple risk factors for VT: history of myocardial infarction 4 years ago (evidenced by Q waves in the inferior leads II, III, and aVF on ECG) and underlying structural heart disease. The clinical presentation is classic for arrhythmogenic syncope: sudden onset while at rest with prodromal symptoms (impending sense of feeling ill), brief loss of consciousness (3 minutes), rapid spontaneous recovery of mental status, and no postictal state. Syncope in the setting of VT typically persists for the duration of the episode. Treatment varies depending on whether the VT is sustained or nonsustained, with options including anti-arrhythmic medications (Class I or III agents) for stable sustained VT, synchronized cardioversion for unstable sustained VT, and defibrillation for pulseless VT. Hypoglycemia (Choice A) is a common cause of syncope, particularly in patients with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus or insulinoma. However, syncope secondary to hypoglycemia would not be expected to spontaneously resolve without treatment (dextrose/glucagon). This patient lacks risk factors for hypoglycemia, and given his significant cardiac risk factors (prior MI, hypertension), arrhythmogenic syncope is far more likely. Pulmonary embolus (Choice C) can result in syncope only in the setting of a massive PE, which would present with tachycardia, hypotension, and right heart strain signs on ECG (e.g., S1Q3T3 pattern). This patient has normal vital signs, normal cardiac examination, and an ECG showing only inferior Q waves consistent with prior MI. Seizure (Choice D), such as generalized tonic-clonic seizure, would present with sudden onset syncope accompanied by characteristic seizure-type movements. Critically, the patient would present in a postictal state with delayed recovery of mental status. This patient had spontaneous, immediate mental status recovery without postictal confusion, making seizure unlikely. Transient ischemic attack (Choice E) is a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without infarction. While TIA can cause transient loss of consciousness, it typically does not present with a true syncopal episode and the rapid spontaneous recovery of mental status without focal neurologic deficits makes this diagnosis unlikely.
▶Immune System Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction1 questions
Source: 6A #2
A 24-year-old woman has had intermittent fever, malaise, and a generalized rash for 2 weeks. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. There is a generalized erythematous maculopapular rash over the palms and soles. She has patchy alopecia of the scalp and eyebrows. Hematocrit is 36%, and leukocyte count is 9000/mm³ (70% segmented neutrophils and 30% lymphocytes). She is given intravenous aqueous penicillin G. Two hours later, she has severe chills, headache, tachycardia, flushing, and hyperventilation. Her temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her acute condition? A) Chronic meningococcemia B) Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction C) Rocky Mountain spotted fever D) Systemic lupus erythematosus E) Toxic shock syndrome
Correct Answer: B) Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
This patient presents with clinical features consistent with a tick-borne infection such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, evidenced by fever, malaise, generalized erythematous maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, and patchy alopecia. However, the acute deterioration occurring within 2 hours of penicillin G administration is pathognomonic for a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. This reaction occurs due to direct bacterial injury from antibiotic therapy, which causes rapid release of bacterial endotoxin and lipopolysaccharides. This triggers an acute inflammatory cascade characterized by fever, chills, headache, tachycardia, flushing, hyperventilation, and potentially hypotension and shock. Although the reaction can be severe and life-threatening, it is typically self-limiting and does not represent worsening of the underlying infection. Choice A (Chronic meningococcemia) can cause similar constitutional symptoms and rash but would not be precipitated by penicillin injection. Choice C (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) is the underlying diagnosis but does not explain the acute worsening after antibiotic administration. Choice D (Systemic lupus erythematosus) can present with rash, fever, and systemic symptoms but would not be exacerbated by penicillin administration and typically presents with different clinical features including photosensitivity and other autoimmune manifestations. Choice E (Toxic shock syndrome) presents with diffuse erythematous rash involving palms and soles but typically progresses to desquamation of these areas one to two weeks later and is accompanied by multiorgan system involvement; the acute temporal relationship to penicillin administration is not consistent with this diagnosis.
▶Gastrointestinal System Constipation1 questions
Source: 6A #4
A 77-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of intermittent mild abdominal pain. He also has had rectal pain with bowel movements and occasionally notices traces of red blood in his stool. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and hypertension. Current medications include insulin, tamsulosin, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide; verapamil was added 4 months ago. A colonoscopy performed 1 year ago showed no abnormalities. He is not in distress. His blood pressure is 108/72 mm Hg. Examination shows moist mucous membranes. The abdomen is slightly distended and nontender. The prostate is enlarged, and there is an external hemorrhoid. Rectal examination shows hard stool in the rectal vault. Sensation to light touch and vibration is intact over the distal lower extremities. An x-ray of the abdomen shows multiple air-fluid levels and stool throughout the bowel. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms? A) Adverse effect of verapamil B) Colon cancer C) Dehydration D) Diabetic neuropathy of the colon E) Metastatic prostate cancer
Correct Answer: A) Adverse effect of verapamil
The clinical presentation of abdominal pain, rectal pain with bowel movements, hematochezia, hard stool in the rectal vault, abdominal distention, and air-fluid levels on imaging is consistent with constipation. Verapamil, a calcium channel blocker, is a well-known cause of dose-dependent constipation, occurring in up to 25% of patients. The temporal relationship between verapamil initiation 4 months ago and symptom onset 3 months ago strongly supports this diagnosis as the most likely cause (A is correct). Choice B (Colon cancer) can present with abdominal discomfort, constipation, and hematochezia; however, a normal colonoscopy performed only 1 year ago makes malignancy much less likely in this timeframe. Choice C (Dehydration) could lead to constipation; however, the presence of moist mucous membranes on examination argues against significant dehydration. Choice D (Diabetic neuropathy of the colon) can cause GI motility dysfunction; however, diabetic neuropathy more commonly manifests as gastroesophageal reflux, gastroparesis, and chronic diarrhea rather than constipation. Furthermore, these complications are more prevalent in type 1 diabetics compared to type 2 diabetics. Additionally, the patient's intact sensation to light touch and vibration in the distal lower extremities argues against significant neuropathy. Choice E (Metastatic prostate cancer) typically presents with bone pain at presentation. Urinary symptoms such as hematuria, inability to void, or incontinence are much more common presenting symptoms than constipation, making this diagnosis unlikely.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Encephalitis1 questions
Source: 6A #5
A 52-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the hospital because of a 2-day history of increasing confusion. She is left-hand dominant. Her medications are lisinopril and metformin. On admission, she is awake and alert. Her temperature is 38.3°C (101°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg. On examination, muscle strength is 5/5 bilaterally. Sensation to light touch and pinprick is intact. Coordination is normal. She cannot recall a name and address after 5 minutes. A T2-weighted MRI of the brain is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Acyclovir B) Ceftriaxone C) Dexamethasone D) Low-molecular-weight heparin E) Mannitol F) Pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine
Correct Answer: A) Acyclovir
This patient presents with encephalopathy, fever, and selective memory impairment (inability to recall name and address after 5 minutes) suggestive of acute encephalitis. The MRI shows hyperattenuation in the temporal lobe, which is characteristic of herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE). HSE classically presents with fever, altered mental status, memory disturbance, and MRI findings of temporal lobe involvement. Acyclovir is the first-line treatment for HSE and should be initiated immediately given the clinical presentation and imaging findings. Choice A (Acyclovir): Correct. This is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for herpes simplex encephalitis. The temporal lobe involvement on MRI is pathognomonic for HSE, and early acyclovir administration is essential to prevent severe neurologic sequelae. Choice B (Ceftriaxone): While ceftriaxone is appropriate empiric therapy for bacterial meningitis and might be considered before neuroimaging in suspected meningitis, the MRI findings of temporal lobe hyperattenuation specifically point to HSE rather than bacterial meningitis. Choice C (Dexamethasone): Dexamethasone is used as adjunctive therapy in bacterial meningitis to reduce inflammation and improve outcomes, but it is not indicated as primary therapy for viral encephalitis. The temporal lobe involvement is diagnostic for HSE, not bacterial meningitis. Choice D (Low-molecular-weight heparin): There is no clinical indication for anticoagulation in this patient. HSE does not typically require anticoagulation therapy. Choice E (Mannitol): While mannitol is used to treat cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure, there is no evidence of significant brain edema or elevated ICP in this case. Her vital signs are relatively stable, and neurologic examination does not suggest herniation. Choice F (Pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine): This combination is used to treat toxoplasmosis, which can present with similar neurologic symptoms. However, toxoplasmosis is primarily a concern in immunocompromised patients (particularly those with CD4 count <100 cells/μL in HIV/AIDS), and this patient has no evidence of immunocompromise. Additionally, the temporal lobe involvement on MRI is more specific for HSE. Educational Objective: Recognize the clinical and radiographic presentation of herpes simplex encephalitis and initiate appropriate antiviral therapy. Temporal lobe involvement on MRI is highly suggestive of HSE and should prompt immediate acyclovir administration.
▶Renal Urinary System Renal Laceration1 questions
Source: 6A #7
A previously healthy 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after he was hit in his right flank by a hockey stick. He reports no blood in his urine. He rates his pain as a 6 on a 10-point scale. His pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows moderate tenderness to palpation over the right flank. His hematocrit is 42%. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Diagnostic laparoscopy B) Renal arteriography C) Retrograde urethrography D) Spiral CT scan of the abdomen E) No further testing is indicated
Correct Answer: E) No further testing is indicated
This patient presents with blunt trauma to the flank from a hockey stick injury. The critical finding is the absence of hematuria on urinalysis, which is the most sensitive indicator of renal trauma. In the absence of hematuria, the likelihood of clinically significant renal injury is low, and no further imaging or evaluation is required. The patient is hemodynamically stable (pulse 100/min, BP 140/90 mm Hg), has an unchanged hematocrit of 42%, and is not showing signs of hemodynamic instability or active bleeding, so urgent surgical intervention is not warranted. Diagnostic laparoscopy (A) would be inappropriate without evidence of visceral injury. Spiral CT scan of the abdomen (D) would be the appropriate imaging modality if hematuria were present, but it is not indicated here given the normal urinalysis. Retrograde urethrography (C) is indicated in the setting of suspected urethral injury, typically following trauma to the penis, scrotum, perineum, or pelvis—none of which apply to this flank injury. Renal arteriography (B) may be considered in cases of ongoing bleeding from renal trauma to allow for angioembolization, but is not warranted in the absence of hematuria. The key educational point is that absence of hematuria effectively rules out significant renal injury in the blunt trauma setting, making conservative management without further testing the appropriate approach.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Subclavian Steal Syndrome1 questions
Source: 6A #9
A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician 8 days after she had loss of consciousness while combing her hair. She says she felt light-headed before she passed out. During the past 3 months, she has had two similar episodes and has noticed that her left arm tires easily. She is left-handed. She has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide and atenolol. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Her pulse is 76/min and regular, and blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg in the right arm. Heart sounds are normal. The radial and brachial pulses are absent on the left and present on the right. Pedal pulses are decreased bilaterally. Muscle strength and sensation are normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Coarctation of the aorta B) Left cervical rib C) Raynaud disease D) Subclavian steal syndrome E) Thromboangiitis obliterans F) Transient ischemic attack
Correct Answer: D) Subclavian steal syndrome
This patient has subclavian steal syndrome, which is a proximal stenosis of the subclavian artery. The diagnosis is supported by the clinical presentation of absent left-sided radial and brachial pulses, a significant smoking history (40 pack-years), hypertension, and decreased pedal pulses bilaterally suggesting peripheral vascular disease. The pathophysiology involves retrograde flow through the vertebral artery to compensate for decreased blood flow to the affected arm. When the left arm is exercised or the patient assumes certain positions (such as combing hair), increased blood demand in the arm causes the vertebral artery to reverse flow, creating a "steal" of blood from the vertebrobasilar circulation. This leads to posterior circulation cerebral ischemia and syncope. Choice A (Coarctation of the aorta): While this could cause weakened pulses in the left arm, it typically presents much earlier in life and would not account for the recurrent syncopal episodes in a 62-year-old patient. Choice B (Left cervical rib): A cervical rib can cause thoracic outlet syndrome and vascular symptoms including weakened left arm pulses, but would not explain the syncope episodes. Choice C (Raynaud disease): This is a vasospastic disorder affecting small vessels and is characterized by color changes (red, blue, and white discoloration) in response to cold or emotional stress, which are absent in this patient. Choice E (Thromboangiitis obliterans): While this is a possibility given the patient's smoking history, it primarily affects medium to small vessels, whereas this patient's symptom distribution clearly indicates large vessel disease (subclavian artery level). Choice F (Transient ischemic attack): Although TIA could explain vertebrobasilar syncope, it would not account for the absent large arm pulses and peripheral vascular findings on examination. Educational Objective: Recognize subclavian steal syndrome as a cause of syncope in patients with proximal subclavian artery stenosis, characterized by absent upper extremity pulses and exercise-induced symptoms due to retrograde vertebral artery flow.
▶Male Reproductive Prostatitis1 questions
Source: 6A #11
A 35-year-old man has had recurrent episodes of dysuria and pelvic pain over the past 2 years. He is sexually active. Examination shows a tender prostate. Urinalysis shows 2-5 WBC/hpf. A urine culture is negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause? A) Chancroid B) Chlamydia trachomatis C) Herpes simplex D) Syphilis E) Trichomonas vaginalis
Correct Answer: B) Chlamydia trachomatis
The presentation of recurrent dysuria and pelvic pain with a tender prostate is consistent with chronic prostatitis. While the most common etiologic agents are gram-negative rods such as E. coli, a negative urine culture should prompt evaluation for Chlamydia trachomatis in sexually active men, making B the correct answer. Choice A (Chancroid): Caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, chancroid presents with painful genital ulcerations and does not cause dysuria and urethritis symptoms. Choice C (Herpes simplex): While primary infection with herpes simplex virus can cause dysuria, chronic recurrent herpes simplex typically presents with small vesicular and ulcerative genital lesions rather than prostatitis with negative urine cultures. Choice D (Syphilis): Caused by Treponema pallidum, syphilis is associated with an ulcerative lesion (chancre) in early infection, which may progress to secondary and tertiary syphilis with systemic involvement of the cardiovascular or nervous systems, not chronic prostatitis. Choice E (Trichomonas vaginalis): While a rare cause of urethritis in men that can be identified in a high proportion of male sexual partners of infected women, the infection is typically asymptomatic and self-limited. Educational Objective: In sexually active men with recurrent dysuria, pelvic pain, and prostatitis symptoms with a negative urine culture, Chlamydia trachomatis should be considered as a likely etiologic agent for non-bacterial chronic prostatitis.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Cubital Tunnel Syndrome1 questions
Source: 6A #12
A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of moderate numbness and weakness of his left hand. There is no history of trauma to the hand. He has hypertension treated with enalapril and type 1 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (140 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m². His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. Examination shows atrophy of the hypothenar muscles. The middle, ring, and small fingers are held in flexion; there is weakness of abduction of the small finger. The patient cannot prevent paper from being pulled through his fingers. All other intrinsic hand muscles are normal. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ at the left brachioradialis, biceps, and triceps muscles. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the palmar aspect of the left ring and small fingers and the hypothenar region of the hand. The remainder of the examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Cervical syringomyelia B) C8 nerve root compression C) Lesion of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus D) Lesion of the medial cord of the brachial plexus E) Ulnar nerve compression
Correct Answer: E) Ulnar nerve compression
This patient presents with classic signs of ulnar nerve compression affecting his left hand. The clinical findings are highly characteristic of ulnar nerve pathology: hypothenar muscle atrophy (innervated by the deep ulnar branch), weakness of small finger abduction (a purely ulnar-innervated function), inability to prevent paper from being pulled through his fingers (positive paper sign, testing intrinsic hand muscles), and sensory loss over the palmar aspect of the ring and small fingers plus the hypothenar region (classic ulnar sensory distribution). The normal function of all other intrinsic hand muscles argues against involvement of the median nerve or more proximal lesions. Choice A (Cervical syringomyelia) might theoretically cause similar symptoms of hand weakness and numbness, but syringomyelia typically affects both hands bilaterally and characteristically causes loss of temperature sensation (suspended sensory level) rather than the isolated pinprick deficit seen here. Choice B (C8 nerve root compression) would likely cause additional symptoms including weakness of wrist extension, finger extension, and other muscles beyond the hypothenar region, along with more extensive sensory changes across the C8 dermatome. Choice C (Lower trunk of brachial plexus lesion) and Choice D (Medial cord lesion) would produce a more widespread pattern of weakness and sensory loss involving multiple muscles and nerve distributions (including median nerve-innervated muscles), which is not present in this patient. The combination of motor findings (hypothenar atrophy, small finger abduction weakness, positive paper sign), isolated sensory loss in ulnar distribution, and normal function of other hand muscles makes ulnar nerve compression the most likely diagnosis.
▶Cardiovascular System Sick Sinus Syndrome1 questions
Source: 6A #13
A 77-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of light-headedness. She states that she feels as if she is going to pass out when she gets out of bed in the morning. She has not had chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations. She has hypertension and hypothyroidism. Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide, enalapril, and levothyroxine. She appears fatigued. She is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 26 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 64/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg while supine and 135/85 mm Hg while standing. Examination shows dry skin. The thyroid gland is symmetrically enlarged, nodular, and nontender. Jugular venous pulsations are present 3 cm above the sternal angle and decrease by 2 cm with inspiration. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 1/6 systolic murmur is heard best at the left sternal border without radiation. There is trace pitting edema of the ankles. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Results of a complete blood count are within the reference range. Her serum potassium concentration is 3.4 mEq/L, and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is 1.5 µU/ml. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 64/min and is otherwise unchanged from an ECG 1 year ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine the cause of this patient's light-headedness? A) Measurement of serum free thyroxine concentration B) Serial measurements of serum creatine kinase activity C) Thyrotropin-releasing hormone stimulation test D) Ambulatory ECG monitoring E) Exercise stress test
Correct Answer: D) Ambulatory ECG monitoring
This patient presents with presyncope and demonstrates an irregularly irregular pulse with atrial fibrillation. The key diagnostic clue is the combination of atrial fibrillation with an unusually slow ventricular rate of 64/min, which suggests atrioventricular dissociation. This finding is most consistent with sick sinus syndrome, a condition where the sinoatrial node fails to generate appropriate impulses, resulting in periods of bradycardia despite the presence of atrial fibrillation. The patient's symptoms of light-headedness upon standing correlate with symptomatic bradycardic episodes. While the patient has hypothyroidism and an enlarged thyroid gland, her TSH is within normal range at 1.5 µU/ml, making primary hypothyroidism an unlikely cause. Additionally, the findings of jugular venous distention and peripheral edema suggest possible heart failure, but the primary rhythm disturbance causing presyncope is the bradycardia from sick sinus syndrome. Ambulatory ECG (Holter) monitoring is the appropriate diagnostic test because it will capture the bradycardic episodes during the patient's symptomatic periods and confirm the correlation between symptoms and the underlying arrhythmia. This diagnosis would then lead to pacemaker implantation as definitive treatment. Choice A (free thyroxine) is unnecessary given normal TSH. Choice B (creatine kinase) is not indicated and would not diagnose the arrhythmia. Choice C (TRH stimulation test) is not needed with normal baseline TSH. Choice E (exercise stress test) would be contraindicated in a patient with symptomatic bradycardia and could precipitate syncope.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Hidradenitis Suppurativa1 questions
Source: 6A #19
A moderately obese 35-year-old woman has a 4-year history of recurrent abscesses in both axillae. These are progressively more frequent and severe. The episodes are interfering with her ability to work. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus that is fairly well controlled by diet and the use of oral hypoglycemic agents. Which of the following is the most appropriate management? A) Institution of insulin therapy to improve glucose control B) Long-term administration of antibiotics C) Surgical excision of apocrine tissue D) Topical application of silver sulfadiazine E) Washing three times daily with pHisoHex and water
Correct Answer: C) Surgical excision of apocrine tissue
This patient likely has hidradenitis suppurativa, an inflammatory condition of apocrine tissue. The patient's disease pattern demonstrates progressive symptoms and exacerbations that are affecting her quality of life and work capacity, indicating need for definitive management. Choice A: Institution of insulin therapy is not appropriate. The patient's type 2 diabetes mellitus is already fairly well controlled by diet and oral hypoglycemic agents. Improving glucose control further would not substantially alter her risk for recurrent abscesses or change the course of hidradenitis suppurativa. Choice B: Long-term administration of antibiotics would not alter the clinical course of hidradenitis suppurativa and carries unnecessary risks of side effects and resistance development. Choice D: Topical application of silver sulfadiazine would not have a meaningful effect on her symptoms or the underlying inflammatory condition. Choice E: Washing three times daily with pHisoHex and water may provide some benefit for hygiene and prevention, but given the progressive nature of her symptoms and significant disease burden affecting her ability to work, this conservative measure alone is insufficient. Choice C: Surgical excision of apocrine tissue is the most appropriate management for this patient with progressive, severe, and frequent recurrent abscesses causing significant morbidity. Surgical intervention is the definitive treatment for hidradenitis suppurativa when conservative measures have failed or disease is significantly impacting quality of life.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Hypercalcemia of Malignancy1 questions
Source: 6A #21
A 77-year-old woman with osteoporosis and hypertension is admitted to the hospital because of progressive confusion during the past 5 days. Her husband reports that she has had constipation for the past week and abdominal pain for the past 3 days. She had right breast cancer treated with lumpectomy and radiation therapy 2 years ago. Medications are alendronate, hydrochlorothiazide, and a calcium supplement containing vitamin D. She is alert. Her temperature is 36.4°C (97.5°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 156/82 mm Hg. Pulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and tenderness throughout; there is no guarding or rebound. Rectal examination shows hard brown stool. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. On mental status examination, she appears anxious and is not oriented to person, place, or time. Her serum calcium concentration is 14.8 mg/dL, and serum albumin concentration is 3 g/dL. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows multiple skull metastases. Which of the following is the strongest contributing factor for this patient's hypercalcemia? A) Alendronate therapy B) Constipation C) Hydrochlorothiazide therapy D) Overuse of calcium supplement E) Postradiation bronchogenic carcinoma F) Recurrence of breast cancer
Correct Answer: F) Recurrence of breast cancer
This patient presents with clinical manifestations of hypercalcemia including altered mental status, constipation, and confirmed elevated serum calcium of 14.8 mg/dL. The multiple skull metastases on CT imaging are the key diagnostic finding pointing toward malignancy as the etiology. Malignancy is the most common cause of hypercalcemia, with breast cancer being the most frequent malignancy in the US. The patient's history of breast cancer treated 2 years ago with recurrence to bone makes recurrence of breast cancer the strongest contributing factor to her hypercalcemia. Choice A (Alendronate) is incorrect because bisphosphonates suppress bone resorption and decrease serum calcium levels; they are used to treat hypercalcemia, not cause it. Choice B (Constipation) is incorrect because constipation is a consequence of hypercalcemia rather than a cause of it. Choice C (Hydrochlorothiazide) is incorrect because while thiazide diuretics do increase renal calcium reabsorption and can mildly elevate serum calcium, a calcium level greater than 12 mg/dL should raise suspicion of an underlying cause such as hyperparathyroidism or malignancy; thiazides alone rarely cause such marked elevation. Choice D (Overuse of calcium supplement) is incorrect because high calcium intake alone rarely causes hypercalcemia except in milk-alkali syndrome; while excessive vitamin D intake can lead to hypercalcemia through increased calcium absorption and bone resorption, this is less common than hypercalcemia of malignancy. Choice E (Postradiation bronchogenic carcinoma) is incorrect because postradiation bronchogenic carcinoma is exceedingly rare, and the imaging already demonstrates bone metastases consistent with recurrent breast cancer.
▶Cardiovascular System Papillary Muscle Rupture1 questions
Source: 6A #25
Two days after a myocardial infarction, a previously asymptomatic 60-year-old woman develops pulmonary edema. A grade 4/6 systolic murmur is heard at the apex. Oxygen saturation in the right atrium and pulmonary artery is 65%, and pulmonary artery diastolic pressure is 35 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Ruptured interventricular septum B) Ruptured left ventricular free wall C) Ruptured papillary muscle D) Ruptured pulmonary valve E) Torn chordae tendineae of the tricuspid valve
Correct Answer: C) Ruptured papillary muscle
This patient presents with acute mitral regurgitation secondary to papillary muscle rupture, a mechanical complication of myocardial infarction that occurs most commonly within 2-3 days post-MI. The clinical findings are consistent with this diagnosis: (1) A holosystolic (grade 4/6) murmur at the apex, characteristic of acute mitral regurgitation; (2) Pulmonary edema from acute decompensation due to regurgitant flow into the left atrium; (3) Lower oxygen saturation (65%) in the right heart chambers due to the left-to-right shunt of deoxygenated pulmonary venous return; (4) Elevated pulmonary artery diastolic pressure (35 mm Hg) reflecting pulmonary hypertension from the regurgitant burden. Choice A (Ruptured interventricular septum): While this could produce similar hemodynamic findings and a systolic murmur, it would cause a left-to-right shunt at the ventricular level. Oxygenated blood from the left ventricle would shunt directly into the right ventricle and pulmonary circulation, resulting in higher oxygen saturation in the right heart (typically >75%), not the low value of 65% seen here. Choice B (Ruptured left ventricular free wall): Rupture of the LV free wall causes acute cardiac tamponade and cardiogenic shock, not the constellation of findings seen in mitral regurgitation. It would not produce the characteristic apical systolic murmur and would not typically lead to pulmonary edema. Right-sided pressures would be lower due to tamponade physiology. Choice D (Ruptured pulmonary valve): Pulmonary valve rupture produces a diastolic murmur (pulmonary insufficiency), not the systolic murmur heard at the apex in this patient. Additionally, it would not lead to the markedly elevated pulmonary artery diastolic pressure seen here. Choice E (Torn chordae tendineae of the tricuspid valve): Tricuspid valve pathology produces a murmur best heard at the sternal border (right lower sternal border), not at the apex. Tricuspid regurgitation would lead to elevated venous pressures (elevated JVP) and typically lower pulmonary artery pressures, which is opposite to what is demonstrated in this case. Educational Objective: Recognize papillary muscle rupture as the most common mechanical complication of myocardial infarction occurring 2-7 days post-MI, presenting with acute severe mitral regurgitation, pulmonary edema, and characteristic hemodynamic findings. Differentiate from other post-MI mechanical complications using clinical and hemodynamic parameters.
▶Immune System Type 4 Hypersensitivity Reactions1 questions
Source: 6A #29
A previously healthy 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an itchy rash on her face, arms, and hands for 2 days. She notes that the rash appeared 2 days after working in her garden. Examination shows urticaria and vesicular lesions over the face, upper extremities, and hands. Which of the following is the most likely pathologic process of this patient's rash? A) Chemotaxis of eosinophils caused by direct antibody reaction with plant sap B) Destruction of adhesion among epidermal cells caused by circulating IgG autoantibodies directed against the cell surface of keratinocytes C) Inflammation caused by release of cytokines by effector and memory T lymphocytes D) Photosensitivity of the epidermis caused by plant sap E) Squamous epithelial cell damage caused by plant sap
Correct Answer: C) Inflammation caused by release of cytokines by effector and memory T lymphocytes
This patient has contact dermatitis most likely caused by a plant toxin such as poison ivy, which is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Type IV hypersensitivity is a cell-mediated immune response involving helper T lymphocytes and cytokine release, not direct antibody-mediated or innate mechanisms. The temporal relationship (2-day delay after exposure) is classic for delayed-type hypersensitivity, which requires time for T cell sensitization and proliferation. Choice A is incorrect because chemotaxis of eosinophils via direct antibody reaction would represent Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity. Choice B is incorrect because IgG autoantibodies against keratinocyte cell surfaces would represent Type II hypersensitivity (cytotoxic antibody-mediated), such as seen in pemphigus vulgaris, and typically involves destruction of cell-cell adhesion, not the clinical presentation here. Choice D is incorrect because plant sap does not cause photosensitivity in typical contact dermatitis (photosensitivity requires systemic absorption and phototoxic or photoallergic reactions). Choice E is incorrect because plant sap causes contact dermatitis through immune-mediated mechanisms rather than direct chemical injury to squamous epithelial cells. The educational objective is to recognize that contact dermatitis represents a Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T lymphocytes and cytokine release, not immediate hypersensitivity (Type I), cytotoxic antibodies (Type II), or direct chemical injury.
▶Cardiovascular System Systolic Dysfunction1 questions
Source: 6A #30
A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of progressive fatigue and shortness of breath with exertion. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 56/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/92 mm Hg. Bilateral basilar crackles are heard on auscultation. Cardiac examination shows a laterally displaced point of maximal impulse. Echocardiography shows left ventricular dilation and an ejection fraction of 32%. In addition to furosemide, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Clonidine B) Diltiazem C) Lisinopril D) Metoprolol E) Nifedipine F) Spironolactone
Correct Answer: C) Lisinopril
This patient presents with systolic heart failure or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), evidenced by left ventricular dilation, ejection fraction of 32%, fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, and signs of congestion (bilateral basilar crackles). ACE inhibitors and select beta-adrenergic blockers (metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, and nebivolol) are first-line agents for HFrEF management. However, beta-adrenergic blockers should not be initiated in newly diagnosed patients in acute decompensated heart failure, making lisinopril the most appropriate choice in this acute setting. Choice A (Clonidine) has no established role in HFrEF treatment except in severe cases of uncontrolled hypertension. Choice B (Diltiazem) is a negative inotropic agent and is contraindicated in HFrEF due to its potential to worsen cardiac function. Choice D (Metoprolol) is a first-line agent but should be avoided in acute decompensated heart failure. Choice E (Nifedipine) may be appropriate for hypertension or heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) but lacks evidence-based benefit in HFrEF. Choice F (Spironolactone) is beneficial only in patients without significant renal dysfunction who are in New York Heart Association class III or IV heart failure despite maximal ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker therapy, making it inappropriate as initial therapy.
▶Immune System AIDS Secondary Infections1 questions
Source: 6A #31
An asymptomatic 32-year-old woman with HIV infection comes to the physician as a new patient. Her last visit to a physician was 14 months ago. She takes no medications. Examination shows hairy leukoplakia and cervical adenopathy. Her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 180/mm³ (Normal ~500), and plasma HIV viral load is 20,000 copies/ml. In addition to antiretroviral therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Mammography and Pap smear B) Mammography, Pap smear, and Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carinii) prophylaxis C) Pap smear and P. jiroveci prophylaxis D) P. jiroveci and Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis E) P. jiroveci prophylaxis only
Correct Answer: C) Pap smear and P. jiroveci prophylaxis
This patient has AIDS, defined as a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count <200/mm³. At this immunosuppression level, prophylaxis for opportunistic infections is essential. Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis is warranted when CD4+ count drops below 200/mm³, which applies to this patient with a count of 180/mm³. Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) prophylaxis is indicated only when CD4+ count falls below 50/mm³, so it is not yet necessary for this patient. Regarding screening: Pap smear screening is appropriate and recommended for all women with HIV as part of routine screening (cervical cancer risk is higher in HIV+ women), but mammography is not indicated for a 32-year-old woman with no other risk factors or family history of early cancer. Therefore, the most appropriate management includes Pap smear for routine screening and P. jiroveci prophylaxis for opportunistic infection prevention at this CD4+ threshold.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Syringomyelia1 questions
Source: 6A #32
A 37-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus and anxiety disorder comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive numbness of her hands that has recently extended to her forearms.
