During the past 2 months, she has burned her fingers numerous times while cooking; she did not know that she had burned herself until she saw the development of blisters. She has no other neurologic symptoms. Her only medication is insulin. Cranial nerves are intact. Muscle strength is 5/5 in the upper and lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ bilaterally. Babinski sign is absent. Sensation to pinprick and temperature is absent over the hands and upper extremities extending to the neck and posterior scalp but is intact over the trunk and lower extremities. Proprioception and sensation to vibration are normal throughout. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Brachial plexopathy B) Cervical stenosis C) Conversion disorder D) Diabetic polyneuropathy E) Syringomyelia
Correct Answer: E) Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia is a cyst that occurs in the spinal cord and is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. The clinical presentation of progressive loss of pinprick and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution (hands, upper extremities, neck, and posterior scalp) with preserved proprioception and vibration sense is classic for syringomyelia. This pattern reflects damage to crossing spinothalamic tract fibers in the anterior commissure of the spinal cord, which preferentially carry pain and temperature sensation. The loss of pain sensation explains the patient's inability to perceive burns until blisters developed. Choice A (Brachial plexopathy) would present with weakness and sensory changes in a specific upper extremity distribution following the brachial plexus anatomy, and would not produce the cape-like distribution or preserve proprioception as seen here. Choice B (Cervical stenosis) can cause upper extremity symptoms but would typically present with weakness (not present in this patient with 5/5 strength), pain, and would not selectively affect temperature sensation while preserving vibration sense. Choice C (Conversion disorder) is ruled out by the objective neurologic findings including hyperreflexia (3+ DTRs bilaterally), which indicates upper motor neuron involvement and is inconsistent with conversion disorder. Choice D (Diabetic polyneuropathy) typically produces distal, symmetrical sensory loss in a stocking-glove distribution and characteristically affects vibratory sensation early, which is preserved in this patient. It also would not produce the selective loss of pain and temperature with preserved proprioception. The presence of hyperreflexia indicates upper motor neuron involvement, supporting the diagnosis of an intraspinal process like syringomyelia rather than peripheral nerve pathology.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Systemic Sclerosis1 questions
Source: 6A #35
A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of increasingly severe pain of the fingers over the past 6 months. She has a 6-year history of cold sensitivity of the hands. On cold exposure, her fingers become initially pale and then turn blue; there is redness with recovery. She has a 3-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease. Examination shows tightening of the skin of the fingers, with erythema, scaling, and telangiectasias. Dry crepitant crackles are heard at both lung bases. X-rays of the hands show loss of tufts of some distal phalanges and scattered soft tissue calcifications. Serum antinuclear antibody testing is most likely to show which of the following? A) Negative findings B) Positive findings for anticentromere antibody C) Positive findings for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody and negative findings for antinuclear antibody D) Positive findings for antiribonuclear protein antibody E) Positive findings for double-stranded DNA
Correct Answer: B) Positive findings for anticentromere antibody
The patient presents with classic features of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), including Raynaud's phenomenon (cold-induced color changes: pale, then blue, then red), sclerodactyly (skin tightening of fingers with erythema and scaling), telangiectasias, gastroesophageal reflux disease (common in scleroderma), and pulmonary involvement (dry crackles at lung bases suggesting interstitial lung disease). The presence of distal phalangeal resorption and soft tissue calcifications further supports this diagnosis. In systemic sclerosis, serology typically shows positive anticentromere antibodies (ACA), which are found in the limited/CREST variant of systemic sclerosis. ANA is also typically positive in systemic sclerosis patients. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are usually positive in patients with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and are associated with a more severe phenotype. Choice A is incorrect because serologies would not be negative in systemic sclerosis; positive ANA and anticentromere antibodies are characteristic. Choice C is incorrect because antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are associated with vasculitis conditions such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not systemic sclerosis. ANA would be expected to be positive in this patient. Choice D is incorrect because antiribonuclear protein (anti-RNP) antibodies are typically positive in mixed connective tissue disease, which presents with overlapping features of lupus, systemic sclerosis, Sjögren syndrome, polymyositis, and dermatomyositis. While this patient has systemic sclerosis features, the clinical presentation is more consistent with systemic sclerosis alone. Choice E is incorrect because anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus, which typically presents with fatigue, fevers, arthritis, malar (butterfly) rash, and photosensitivity—features not prominent in this patient's presentation.
▶Musculoskeletal System Avascular necrosis1 questions
Source: 6A #40
A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-day history of increasingly severe left hip pain. She now has difficulty walking because of the pain. She has temporal arteritis and hypertension. Her medications are prednisone and enalapril. Vital signs are within normal limits. Internal and external range of motion of the left hip is limited by pain. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the left hip shows no abnormalities. An MRI of the hips is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Avascular necrosis B) Hip fracture C) Iliotibial band syndrome D) Osteoarthritis E) Trochanteric bursitis
Correct Answer: A) Avascular necrosis
This patient presents with acute hip pain and is on chronic prednisone therapy for temporal arteritis. Corticosteroids are a well-established risk factor for avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head. The clinical presentation of acute onset hip pain with limited range of motion in both internal and external rotation, combined with imaging findings of lucency/collapse in the femoral head on the left compared to the right on MRI, is classic for AVN. Hip fracture (B) can be excluded because the x-ray shows no abnormalities, and occult fractures on plain films would typically be visible on MRI. Osteoarthritis (D) is unlikely in this acute presentation and would show degenerative changes on x-ray. Iliotibial band syndrome (C) typically presents with lateral hip or thigh pain, follows physical overuse, and would not produce the MRI findings of femoral head lucency seen in this patient. Trochanteric bursitis (E) would present with focal tenderness over the greater trochanter and lateral hip pain, not the global hip pain with limited internal and external rotation seen here. The MRI findings of femoral head lucency/signal change are pathognomonic for avascular necrosis, making this the most likely diagnosis in a corticosteroid-treated patient with acute hip pain.
▶Respiratory System Peritonsillar Abscess1 questions
Source: 6A #42
A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of soreness in the back of her throat and pain on swallowing. She has had recurrent episodes of tonsillitis during the past 2 years. Examination shows massive edema of the soft palate and enlarged tonsils with a purulent discharge from the right tonsil. Without treatment, this patient is at increased risk for which of the following? A) Airway compromise B) Brain abscess C) Necrosis of the tonsils D) Paralysis of the facial nerve E) Rupture of the tympanic membrane
Correct Answer: A) Airway compromise
The patient presents with classic features of peritonsillar abscess: recurrent tonsillitis, massive edema of the soft palate, enlarged tonsils, and unilateral purulent discharge from the right tonsil. Without appropriate treatment—which may include incision and drainage or needle aspiration—progressive swelling of the soft palate and surrounding tissues can lead to airway obstruction and compromise, making airway compromise the most clinically significant immediate risk. The most common causative organism is Group A streptococcus. Choice A is correct. Other potential complications of peritonsillar abscess include aspiration pneumonitis, lung abscess, and hemorrhage due to septic necrosis into the carotid sheath, but these are less likely or less immediate than airway compromise. Extension of infection into deep neck tissue or posterior mediastinum is possible but not the most common or immediate risk. Poststreptococcal sequelae such as rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis may occur but are not direct complications of the abscess itself. Brain abscess (B), necrosis of the tonsils (C), paralysis of the facial nerve (D), and rupture of the tympanic membrane (E) are not typical complications of peritonsillar abscess and are therefore incorrect.
▶Cardiovascular System Coronary Artery Disease1 questions
Source: 6A #44
A 72-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine examination. He has a 1-year history of hypertension controlled by a thiazide diuretic. He smokes one pack of cigarettes and drinks 3 ounces of alcohol daily. He has gained 6 kg (13 lb) since his last visit 1 year ago. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and now weighs 88 kg (195 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m². His blood pressure is 156/88 mm Hg. His serum LDL-cholesterol concentration is 150 mg/dl, and serum HDL-cholesterol concentration is 50 mg/dl. Which of the following is the greatest risk factor for coronary artery disease in this patient? A) Alcohol consumption B) Blood pressure C) Cigarette smoking D) Use of a thiazide diuretic E) Weight
Correct Answer: C) Cigarette smoking
This patient presents with multiple cardiovascular risk factors including hypertension (BP 156/88 mm Hg), elevated LDL-cholesterol (150 mg/dl), low HDL-cholesterol (50 mg/dl), overweight status (BMI 28 kg/m²), cigarette smoking (1 pack daily), excess alcohol consumption (3 ounces daily), and advanced age (72 years). Among these risk factors, cigarette smoking is the greatest risk factor for coronary artery disease. Smoking is a major independent risk factor that significantly increases the risk of myocardial infarction, sudden cardiac death, and other cardiovascular events. While blood pressure elevation and obesity contribute to cardiovascular disease risk, smoking remains the most potent modifiable risk factor in this patient. Excess alcohol consumption can lead to blood pressure elevations and may contribute to cardiovascular risk. Hydrochlorothiazide, the thiazide diuretic being used, is a therapeutic agent aimed at treating hypertension and has been shown to reduce cardiovascular disease risk rather than increase it. The educational objective is to recognize cigarette smoking as the most significant modifiable risk factor for coronary artery disease when multiple risk factors are present.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Hereditary spherocytosis1 questions
Source: 6A #47
A healthy 39-year-old man of German descent comes for a routine examination. He had a cholecystectomy at the age of 25 years. He has had several episodes of mild jaundice over the past 10 years that resolved spontaneously. He appears healthy. Examination shows no abnormalities except for splenomegaly. His hematocrit is 39%, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration is 36% Hb/cell, and mean corpuscular volume is 80 µm³. Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative. A blood smear shows erythrocytes with loss of central pallor. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia? A) Abnormal red blood cell membrane B) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia C) Congenital dihydrofolate reductase deficiency D) Decreased erythropoietin concentration E) Folic acid deficiency F) Globin chain mutation G) Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency H) Lead poisoning I) Pyruvate kinase deficiency J) Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency
Correct Answer: A) Abnormal red blood cell membrane
This patient presents with hereditary spherocytosis, the most likely diagnosis given his northern European descent and classic clinical presentation. The key diagnostic features include: (1) intermittent hemolysis manifested by recurrent episodes of jaundice that resolved spontaneously, (2) mild anemia with splenomegaly, (3) spherocytes on blood smear (erythrocytes with loss of central pallor), (4) negative direct antiglobulin test ruling out immune-mediated hemolysis, and (5) normocytic anemia with normal MCHC. Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by alterations in genes encoding red blood cell membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.2) leading to membrane instability and osmotic fragility. The history of cholecystectomy at age 25 is consistent with gallstone formation from chronic hemolysis. Choice B is excluded by the negative Coombs test. Choices E and J are excluded by the absence of macrocytosis. Choice C is unlikely at this age without supplemental folic acid use. Choice D shows no evidence of chronic kidney disease or other causes of decreased erythropoietin. Choice G (G6PD deficiency) is unlikely in northern European populations and typically manifests only after oxidative stress from drugs like sulfa antibiotics. Choice F (globin chain mutations) would produce microcytosis with more profound anemia and auto-splenectomy rather than splenomegaly at this age. Choice H (lead poisoning) lacks supporting history or laboratory evidence. While choice I (pyruvate kinase deficiency) fits the clinical picture, it typically manifests more severely in childhood and requires transfusions if significant, neither of which is mentioned in the vignette. Hereditary spherocytosis remains the most likely diagnosis.
▶Renal Urinary System Glomerular Disease Due to Hepatitis C1 questions
Source: 6A #48
A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of progressive swelling of both legs and generalized weakness. He says he now has some difficulty performing his usual activities. Last year, he received the diagnosis of hepatitis B and C. He has a long-standing history of intravenous drug use. He refused treatment for hepatitis C and currently takes no medications. He is not in acute distress. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 55 kg (121 lb); BMI is 16 kg/m². His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 160/99 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is nontender. There is no hepatomegaly. Muscle strength is normal. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10 g/dL, Leukocyte count 9000/mm³, Platelet count 260,000/mm³, Serum Urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, Albumin 3.8 g/dL, Total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, AST 70 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, Urine Blood 3+, Protein 4+. Microscopic examination of urine shows numerous RBCs, which are mostly acanthocytes with irregular membrane protrusions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Second set of laboratory studies in 1 month B) Urine protein electrophoresis C) Urine culture D) Cystoscopy E) Renal biopsy
Correct Answer: E) Renal biopsy
The patient presents with untreated hepatitis C and clinical and laboratory evidence of nephrotic syndrome including significant edema, marked proteinuria (4+), and hematuria with acanthocytosis, which indicates glomerulonephritis. Hepatitis C is a well-known cause of renal disease, particularly membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, membranous nephropathy, mixed cryoglobulinemia syndrome, and polyarteritis nodosa. The elevated serum creatinine (2.1 mg/dL) indicates significant renal impairment. Given the severity of clinical symptoms, elevated creatinine, proteinuria, and evidence of glomerular hematuria (acanthocytes), renal biopsy is the most appropriate next diagnostic step to confirm the type of glomerulonephritis and guide treatment decisions. Choice A (repeat labs in 1 month) is inappropriate because the disease is actively progressing and delaying diagnosis risks further deterioration of renal function. Choice B (urine protein electrophoresis) is used to evaluate for monoclonal gammopathy in conditions like multiple myeloma or amyloidosis, not for this presentation of glomerulonephritis. Choice C (urine culture) is not indicated as there are no clinical signs or symptoms of urinary tract infection. Choice D (cystoscopy) may be considered for isolated microscopic hematuria after infectious and renal causes have been ruled out, but in this patient with clear evidence of glomerular disease (proteinuria, elevated creatinine, and acanthocytes), renal biopsy is more appropriate and takes priority. The renal biopsy will establish the definitive diagnosis and help direct specific treatment for hepatitis C-associated glomerulonephritis.
▶Gastrointestinal System Gastric ulcer1 questions
Source: 6A #49
A 37-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of vomiting for the past 3 days. He says that he cannot hold down liquids or solids. For the past month, he has had early satiety and has not been eating as much as he usually does. He has a 2-year history of peptic ulcer disease, diagnosed by upper endoscopy. Infection with Helicobacter pylori was successfully treated with clarithromycin, amoxicillin, omeprazole, and bismuth subsalicylate therapy. Since then, he has had intermittent epigastric pain for which he takes cimetidine when he remembers to do so. He appears ill and anxious. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes and a flat, soft, nontender abdomen. Which of the following sets of laboratory abnormalities is most likely in this patient? A) K+ Increased, Cl- Increased, pH Decreased B) K+ Decreased, Cl- Decreased, pH Decreased C) K+ Increased, Cl- Decreased, pH Increased D) K+ Decreased, Cl- Decreased, pH Increased E) K+ Decreased, Cl- Increased, pH Increased
Correct Answer: D) K+ Decreased, Cl- Decreased, pH Increased
This patient's clinical presentation is strongly suggestive of gastric outlet obstruction (GOO), a known complication of peptic ulcer disease. The key features are: 3-day history of intractable vomiting (cannot hold down liquids or solids), early satiety, and prior peptic ulcer disease diagnosed by endoscopy. Although H. pylori was successfully treated, the patient has intermittent epigastric pain and did not receive adequate acid suppression (only taking cimetidine sporadically), predisposing him to recurrent ulceration and subsequent scarring leading to GOO. While malignancy is now a more common cause of GOO in the modern era, peptic ulcer disease remains an important etiology. The pathophysiology of recurrent vomiting leads to predictable laboratory abnormalities: Recurrent vomiting causes loss of gastric contents, which are rich in hydrochloric acid (HCl). This loss of acid leads to: (1) Metabolic alkalosis (pH increases), (2) Hypochloremia (serum Cl- decreases due to direct loss in gastric fluid). Additionally, volume depletion from ongoing losses of gastric fluid (evidenced by dry mucous membranes) stimulates increased renal sodium reabsorption via activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Aldosterone increases distal renal tubular reabsorption of sodium and water while promoting urinary excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions. Combined with the metabolic alkalosis causing increased renal potassium wasting, this results in hypokalemia (serum K+ decreases). Choice A (K+ Increased, Cl- Increased, pH Decreased) is incorrect because vomiting causes loss of HCl, leading to alkalosis not acidosis, and both K+ and Cl- are depleted. Choice B (K+ Decreased, Cl- Decreased, pH Decreased) is incorrect because while K+ and Cl- are appropriately decreased, the pH should be increased (alkalosis) not decreased, as loss of HCl from vomiting creates metabolic alkalosis. Choice C (K+ Increased, Cl- Decreased, pH Increased) is incorrect because potassium is decreased, not increased, due to renal wasting from aldosterone effects in the setting of volume depletion and metabolic alkalosis. Choice E (K+ Decreased, Cl- Increased, pH Increased) is incorrect because chloride is decreased, not increased, due to direct losses in gastric fluid rich in HCl. Educational Objective: Recognize that recurrent vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction causes a characteristic pattern of hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypochloremia. Understand the mechanisms: direct loss of HCl causes alkalosis and hypochloremia, while volume depletion and secondary aldosteronism cause renal potassium wasting and hypokalemia. This electrolyte pattern is classic for loss of gastric contents and is an important clinical pattern to recognize and treat appropriately with fluid resuscitation, potassium and chloride replacement, and treatment of the underlying cause.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Acne Vulgaris1 questions
Source: 3A #1
A 19-year-old woman comes for a routine follow-up examination for acne vulgaris. She is sexually active and does not use contraception. She has had chronic migraines over the past 3 years. She has a history of early signs of cataracts. There is a family history of hypercholesterolemia and inflammatory bowel disease. Examination shows active acne vulgaris on her face. She says that the various treatments she has received have failed to adequately control her acne, and she asks for a prescription for isotretinoin, a medication that has worked well for many of her friends. Isotretinoin therapy is contraindicated in this patient because of which of the following historic findings? A) Chronic migraines B) Early cataracts C) Family history of hypercholesterolemia D) Family history of inflammatory bowel disease E) Sexual activity without contraception
Correct Answer: E) Sexual activity without contraception
Isotretinoin (retinoic acid), a derivative of vitamin A, is highly teratogenic and causes multiple malformations involving the central nervous and musculoskeletal systems. The most critical contraindication in this patient is her sexual activity without contraception. All patients taking isotretinoin must use reliable contraception—at least one form, ideally two forms—to prevent pregnancy and resulting teratogenic consequences for the fetus. Barrier methods alone are considered inadequate due to higher failure rates; intrauterine devices and oral contraceptive pills are preferred. Since this patient is sexually active without current contraception use, she cannot safely take isotretinoin without first establishing adequate contraceptive coverage. The other historical findings do not represent contraindications to isotretinoin use. Chronic migraines, early cataracts, hypercholesterolemia, and inflammatory bowel disease are not characteristically exacerbated by vitamin A derivatives and would not contraindicate isotretinoin therapy in this patient.
▶Cardiovascular System Wide Complex Tachycardia1 questions
Source: 3A #2
A 73-year-old man with hypertension is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 1 hour after the onset of moderate chest pain and difficulty breathing. Aspirin was administered en route to the hospital. He takes no other medications. On arrival, he is diaphoretic. His temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse is 185/min and thready, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 85/45 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygen by face mask shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Breath sounds are heard bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows a regular rhythm. A rhythm strip shows a wide complex tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management? A) Administration of esmolol B) Administration of nitroglycerin by intravenous drip C) Intravenous administration of morphine D) Endotracheal intubation E) Synchronized cardioversion
Correct Answer: E) Synchronized cardioversion
Patients with wide-complex (QRS greater than 120 msec) tachycardia require emergent medical attention and intervention. Rapid electrical depolarization of the heart and resultant increased heart rate impairs diastolic filling time, resulting in low cardiac output and hypotension. Such a condition carries high likelihood of degeneration to ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. This patient presents with unstable wide-complex tachycardia, as evidenced by hypotension (85/45 mm Hg), diaphoresis, tachypnea (30/min), and signs of hypoperfusion. According to Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) protocols, any unstable patient with wide-complex tachycardia (hypotensive, diaphoretic, tachypneic, with altered mental status) should be immediately synchronized cardioverted to abort the rhythm and restore adequate cardiac output. Stable, perfusing wide-complex arrhythmias can be treated with antiarrhythmic medications, and pulseless rhythms require CPR and defibrillation, but this patient's unstable hemodynamic state mandates immediate electrical therapy. Choice A (Esmolol): While appropriate for refractory ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation following failed conventional ACLS protocols, esmolol is not the initial treatment for unstable wide-complex tachycardia. It is classically used to rapidly lower blood pressure and heart rate in aortic dissection. Choice B (Nitroglycerin IV): Would be appropriate for hypertensive emergency, refractory anginal chest pain, or as an adjunct with beta-blockers in aortic dissection, but is not indicated for unstable tachyarrhythmias and could worsen outcomes by further reducing perfusion pressure. Choice C (Morphine IV): Appropriate for acute pain management, but may worsen hemodynamics in an unstable patient with compromised cardiac output and hypotension. Choice D (Endotracheal intubation): May be necessary for airway protection in patients with depressed mental status or airway compromise. However, this patient shows no immediate signs of airway compromise; the respiratory symptoms are secondary to hypoperfusion and low cardiac output, which should be addressed immediately by restoring adequate perfusion through cardioversion.
▶Cardiovascular System High-output Heart Failure1 questions
Source: 3A #6
A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-month history of progressive shortness of breath and fatigue. She has had no chest pain. There is no history of heart or pulmonary disease. She is in moderate respiratory distress. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention. Crackles are heard halfway up both lungs. A grade 2/6, systolic ejection murmur is heard along the left sternal border. There is an S3. She has 2+ edema of the lower extremities. Rectal examination shows dark stools; test for occult blood is positive. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin: 5 g/dL Leukocyte count: 9000/mm³ Serum Na+: 140 mEq/L K+: 4 mEq/L Cl-: 105 mEq/L HCO3-: 25 mEq/L Urea nitrogen: 28 mg/dL Glucose: 120 mg/dL Creatinine: 1.2 mg/dL Urine protein: 1+ An x-ray of the chest shows a mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette with pulmonary vascular congestion. An ECG shows nonspecific ST-segment changes. Echocardiography shows trace mitral regurgitation and an ejection fraction of 70%; there are no wall motion abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) High-output heart failure B) Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction C) Left ventricular systolic dysfunction D) Nephrotic syndrome E) Valvular heart disease
Correct Answer: A) High-output heart failure
The clinical presentation of shortness of breath, fatigue, tachycardia, tachypnea, jugular venous distention, bilateral basilar crackles, an S3 gallop, ejection murmur, and lower extremity edema are classic signs of heart failure. However, the critical diagnostic clue is the severely depressed hemoglobin of 5 g/dL in conjunction with dark stools and a positive occult blood test, indicating significant anemia from chronic blood loss. In high-output heart failure, the heart must increase cardiac output to compensate for the reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood. Since oxygen delivery is a function of cardiac output and oxygen content, when oxygen content falls due to anemia, cardiac output must rise to maintain equivalent oxygen delivery to tissues. This is accomplished through increased heart rate and potentially increased stroke volume. The preserved ejection fraction of 70% and absence of wall motion abnormalities on echocardiography further support this diagnosis, as systolic dysfunction would typically show a reduced ejection fraction and abnormal contractility. Choice B (Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction) is characterized by impaired relaxation and chamber hypertrophy on echocardiography. While it does present with pulmonary vascular congestion, it is typically a consequence of chronic poorly controlled hypertension or aortic stenosis and would not explain the severely reduced hemoglobin or the need for increased cardiac output. Choice C (Left ventricular systolic dysfunction) typically presents with a reduced ejection fraction and is seen on echocardiography as an enlarged, dilated chamber with poor contractility. This patient's ejection fraction of 70% rules out systolic dysfunction. Choice D (Nephrotic syndrome) does present with edema and proteinuria, but this patient's clinical presentation is better explained by heart failure secondary to anemia rather than a primary renal process. Additionally, the patient would be expected to have more significant proteinuria and additional features like hypoalbuminemia. Choice E (Valvular heart disease) is a common cause of heart failure, but this patient has no significant valvular dysfunction on echocardiography, with only trace mitral regurgitation which is a consequence rather than a cause of the heart failure. Educational Objective: Recognize high-output heart failure as a compensatory state where the heart increases cardiac output to meet metabolic demands, particularly in conditions causing reduced oxygen-carrying capacity such as severe anemia, and distinguish it from primary cardiac dysfunction based on preserved ejection fraction and the severity of anemia.
▶Gastrointestinal System Traveler's diarrhea1 questions
Source: 3A #7
A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of abdominal bloating, increasing flatulence, and diarrhea 6 to 12 times daily despite loperamide therapy. The stool is watery, nonbloody, and foul smelling; he says it is usually brown and occasionally green. He has not had fever. He recently traveled to the Middle East. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows slight distention and mild tenderness with no rebound or guarding; bowel sounds are normal. Rectal examination shows no abnormalities. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Campylobacter jejuni B) Clostridium difficile C) Entamoeba coli D) Entamoeba histolytica E) Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli F) Nontyphoidal Salmonella species G) Norwalk virus H) Rotavirus I) Shigella species J) Yersinia enterocolitica
Correct Answer: E) Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) is the most common cause of travelers' diarrhea and one of the most common causes of bacterial diarrhea in the developing world. It is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. The clinical presentation is classic: acute, diffuse, crampy abdominal pain and bloating with profuse, frequent episodes of watery, nonbloody diarrhea. ETEC causes diarrhea through the production of bacterial exotoxins rather than mucosal invasion. The diagnosis is made via stool culture and microscopy, which typically shows an absence of blood and stool leukocytes. Treatment is supportive with rehydration and electrolyte repletion; the infection is often self-limiting, though antibiotics may be required in prolonged or severe cases. The key distinguishing features in this case are: (1) recent travel to the Middle East (endemic area), (2) watery, nonbloody diarrhea, (3) negative stool for occult blood, (4) no fever, and (5) lack of systemic toxicity. Incorrect Answer Explanations: Choice A (Campylobacter jejuni), Choice D (Entamoeba histolytica), Choice F (Nontyphoidal Salmonella species), Choice I (Shigella species), and Choice J (Yersinia enterocolitica) classically present with mucosal inflammation and invasion, leading to a toxic presentation with bloody diarrhea, which this patient does not have. Choice B (Clostridium difficile) can present with watery or bloody diarrhea depending on infection severity and typically follows antibiotic administration. These invasive, toxin-producing pathogens require antibiotic therapy plus supportive care. Choice C (Entamoeba coli) is a commensal organism that generally does not cause pathologic enteritis or colitis. Choice G (Norwalk virus) causes self-limited viral gastroenteritis with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, commonly detected in outbreaks on cruise ships and during winter months, not in travelers to the Middle East. Choice H (Rotavirus) causes self-limited nausea, vomiting, and watery diarrhea primarily in children, with nearly 100% of children having been affected by age five, making it unlikely in this adult patient.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Hemophilia A1 questions
Source: 3A #9
A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-hour history of muscle swelling and tenderness of the left thigh following minimal trauma. He has severe hemophilia A and has received factor VIII replacement therapy for bleeding episodes since childhood. Over recent months, his bleeding has been poorly controlled; increasing doses of factor VIII have been required to stop bleeding episodes. His platelet count is 125,000/mm³, and activated partial thromboplastin time is greater than 120 sec. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis of this patient's increased bleeding? A) Measurement of bleeding time B) Measurement of factor IX concentration C) Measurement of thrombin time to detect heparin D) Platelet function studies E) Test for factor VIII inhibitor
Correct Answer: E) Test for factor VIII inhibitor
Hemophilia A is an X-linked coagulopathy arising from genetic deficiency in factor VIII synthesis or activity. Patients present with easy bruising and hemorrhage involving muscles and joints, often requiring factor VIII transfusions. With repeated transfusions of the nonnative protein, patients can acquire antibodies (typically IgG) against exogenous factor VIII. This acquired inhibitor binds and neutralizes the transfused factor VIII, requiring increasingly larger transfusions to achieve the same hemostatic effect. The clinical presentation of poorly controlled bleeding despite increasing doses of factor VIII replacement is the classic indicator for testing for a factor VIII inhibitor. Choice A (Bleeding time) measures platelet function and is used in platelet disorders such as thrombocytopenia, von Willebrand disease, and Bernard-Soulier syndrome. It does not correlate with coagulation factor deficiencies and has no role in hemophilia workup. Choice B (Factor IX concentration) is used in the workup of hemophilia B, not hemophilia A. The presence of both hemophilia A and B in the same patient is exceedingly rare. Choice C (Thrombin time to detect heparin) would be appropriate only if the patient were receiving heparin therapy, which is not indicated in this case. Choice D (Platelet function studies) assess qualitative platelet hemostatic defects through bleeding time, platelet aggregation, and platelet activation tests. This patient has a known factor deficiency with progressive under-responsiveness to replacement therapy, suggesting an acquired factor inhibitor rather than a platelet disorder. Educational Objective: Recognize that acquisition of factor VIII inhibitors in hemophilia A patients receiving repeated transfusions presents with progressive resistance to factor VIII replacement therapy, necessitating specific testing for inhibitors to guide subsequent management decisions.
▶Respiratory System Bordetella pertussis Pneumonia1 questions
Source: 3A #10
A previously healthy 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department 2 weeks after the onset of mild cough and runny nose. During the past 3 days, the cough has worsened with episodes so intense that he has vomited. The cough is productive of thick green sputum. He feels well between coughing episodes. He has not had fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath. He takes no medications. He is a college student. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 115/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Pulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Influenza B) Legionnaires disease C) Pertussis D) Psittacosis E) Q fever
Correct Answer: C) Pertussis
Episodes of severe coughing followed by emesis, in the setting of a respiratory illness, raises suspicion for pertussis. Pertussis is caused by infection from Bordetella pertussis and classically presents in three stages. The catarrhal stage is first, which presents with fever, rhinorrhea, and a mild cough. This progresses to the paroxysmal stage after 1 to 2 weeks, in which patients experience violent bouts of extreme coughing, at times violent enough to cause secondary traumatic injury such as rib fractures, urinary incontinence, and pneumothoraces. Often, such coughing fits are followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The paroxysmal stage can last for weeks to months. Symptoms resolve in the convalescent stage, which lasts from 1 to 4 weeks. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization and is treated with antibiotics, typically macrolides. Influenza (Choice A) presents with respiratory, gastrointestinal, and systemic symptoms, including cough, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, chills, headache, myalgias, and arthralgias; it can be complicated by bacterial superinfection causing severe bacterial pneumonia. It typically lasts for less than 1 week and does not have a paroxysmal stage. Legionnaires disease (Choice B) is caused by infection from Legionella pneumophila, which is typically spread through aerosol transmission from a water habitat source (e.g., air conditioning). It often presents with diarrhea and hyponatremia in addition to respiratory symptoms and does not typically have a paroxysmal stage. Psittacosis (Choice D) occurs in persons with exposure to birds, as a vector is typically required to transmit the infection (Chlamydia psittaci). Similarly, Q fever (Choice E) caused by Coxiella burnetii typically requires exposure to sheep, goats, and cattle as a zoonotic source.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Labyrinthitis1 questions
Source: 3A #14
A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of dizziness and progressive difficulty with balance. She has been supporting herself against walls when she walks. She has not had numbness, weakness, or palpitations. She has had nausea and a mild decrease in appetite but is able to drink fluids. There is no history of head trauma. She has mitral valve prolapse. She takes no medications. Her sister has multiple sclerosis. Vital signs are within normal limits. The optic discs appear normal, and ocular movements are full. Tympanic membranes are dull bilaterally. The light reflex is distorted. There are no exudates on the pharynx. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard best at the lower left sternal border. Muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes are normal. Her gait is unsteady. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) B) Cerebral infarction C) Dehydration D) Endocarditis E) Labyrinthitis F) Multiple sclerosis
Correct Answer: E) Labyrinthitis
Labyrinthitis is inflammation of the inner ear, often involving the vestibulocochlear nerve, and is typically preceded by an upper respiratory or ear infection. The classic presentation includes vertigo, ataxia, nausea, vomiting, and hearing loss. This patient's 3-day history of dizziness with gait instability, nausea, and notably dull tympanic membranes with distorted light reflex (indicating middle ear inflammation and fluid) following a presumed upper respiratory infection makes labyrinthitis the most likely diagnosis. Treatment is supportive, and the condition is typically self-limited. Dizziness and gait instability are categorized as central causes (cerebrovascular accidents, brain tumors, demyelinating disorders), peripheral causes (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, labyrinthitis, Meniere disease), or secondary systemic causes (electrolyte imbalances, hypovolemia, cardiac arrhythmia, infections). Choice A (Acoustic neuroma/vestibular schwannoma): While these tumors can cause central vertigo by impinging on the vestibulocochlear nerve at the cerebellopontine angle, they are often subclinical and associated with neurofibromatosis. Preceding infection or dull tympanic membranes would not be expected with acoustic neuroma. Choice B (Cerebral infarction): Although infarction involving the cerebellum, pons, or brain stem can cause vertigo by disrupting equilibrium and proprioception, this typically presents with additional neurologic findings such as nystagmus, motor or sensory deficits, cranial nerve deficits, or signs of vertebrobasilar insufficiency (dysarthria, impaired brain stem reflexes). The acute presentation would not typically include preceding ear findings. Choice C (Dehydration): While dehydration may present with dizziness or ataxia in the setting of orthostatic hypotension with light-headedness on position changes, this patient maintains adequate fluid intake. Dull tympanic membranes would not be a feature of dehydration. Choice D (Endocarditis): Although this patient has mitral valve prolapse and a systolic murmur, endocarditis typically presents with acute or subacute fever, a new or changing heart murmur, septic emboli, and vascular phenomena (Roth spots, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages). The patient is afebrile with vital signs within normal limits and no other signs of endocarditis. Choice F (Multiple sclerosis): MS presents with neurologic symptoms separated in space and time, commonly beginning with optic neuritis. Women are more commonly affected. However, MS would not be expected to follow an acute infection, and tympanic membrane findings (indicating acute middle ear inflammation) would not be present with MS. The rapid 3-day onset following presumed infection is inconsistent with MS.
▶Endocrine System Acromegaly1 questions
Source: 3A #15
A 57-year-old man comes to the physician with his wife because of a headache for 3 days. He has had a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain over the past 6 months. His dentist has told him that the space between his teeth is increasing. His wife says that he has started snoring and his voice has deepened over the past 6 months. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and now weighs 91 kg (200 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m². Examination shows frontal bossing and large feet. Measurement of which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis? A) Hemoglobin A1c B) Serum C-peptide concentration C) Serum growth hormone-releasing hormone concentration D) Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 E) Serum somatostatin concentration
Correct Answer: D) Serum insulin-like growth factor 1
Acromegaly results from excess production of growth hormone (GH), typically from a functional pituitary adenoma. GH upregulates production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which is the key mediator of GH effects. Following fusion of growth plates, stimulus from IGF-1 results in enlargement of bones in the head, face, hands, and feet, sparing the long bones. If the derangement occurs prior to puberty, long-bone enlargement also occurs, resulting in gigantism. The clinical presentation includes enlarged hands, feet, forehead, skull, and jaw, deepening of the voice, frontal bossing, interdental spacing, and sleep apnea from soft tissue enlargement. Complications include diabetes mellitus development. Serum IGF-1 measurement is the most reliable confirmatory test for acromegaly diagnosis, as IGF-1 levels are markedly elevated and correlate with disease severity. Diagnosis is confirmed by clinical presentation, measured hormonal levels (particularly IGF-1), and cross-sectional imaging to detect the culprit adenoma. Surgical resection is the preferred treatment; if surgery cannot be performed, somatostatin analogues (e.g., octreotide) and GH receptor antagonists (e.g., pegvisomant) can be used. Choice A (Hemoglobin A1c) is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus when increased above 6.5% but has no role in the immediate diagnosis of acromegaly, though diabetes is a complication. Choice B (Serum C-peptide concentration) is used in the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus to distinguish between type 1 (low insulin and C-peptide) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (increased insulin and C-peptide), and in diagnosing factitious hypoglycemia, but does not diagnose acromegaly. Choice C (Serum growth hormone-releasing hormone concentration) could be useful if a hypothalamic cause was suspected for acromegaly, but a pituitary adenoma with resultant loss of normal feedback mechanisms is the more common etiology. Choice E (Serum somatostatin concentration) does not play a role in the diagnosis of acromegaly; rather, somatostatin analogues are used therapeutically in treatment of the condition.
▶Respiratory System Silicosis 1 questions
Question #25
A 70-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath with exertion. Six months ago, he was able to walk five blocks before having shortness of breath. He now has shortness of breath after walking one block. He has not had chest pain, palpitations, swelling of his legs, or shortness of breath at night. He has hypertension. His medications are lisinopril and aspirin. He does not smoke cigarettes. He is a retired foundry worker. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². His pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows no other abnormalities. There is no edema of the extremities. Results of pulmonary function testing show an FVC of 65% of predicted and an FEV₁:FVC ratio of 70%. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Asbestosis B) Aspergillosis C) Asthma D) Bronchiectasis E) Chronic bronchitis F) Silicosis
Correct Answer: F) Silicosis
Pneumoconiosis describes interstitial lung disease arising because of inhalation of small solid particulate matter such as dust or powder (eg, talc, silica, beryllium, and ores) that leads to the development of fibrosis with resultant restrictive lung disease. It is often seen in patients with chronic exposures, such as foundry workers, miners, shipyard workers, cotton workers, farmers, stone drillers, and sandblasters. The disease's progress is often worsened by smoking. It generally presents with chronic symptoms of cough and shortness of breath on exertion; when severe or advanced, it can be associated with the need for supplemental oxygen and symptoms of heart failure (eg, cor pulmonale). Diagnosis is based on clinical history, symptoms, examination, exposure history, characteristic imaging tests that show fibrosis (x-ray may show honeycombing and fibrosis, especially in the apices), and pulmonary function tests that disclose a restrictive pattern of lung disease marked by decreased overall volumes and capacities but a preserved or increased ratio of FEV₁:FVC. This ratio is a key distinguishing feature from obstructive lung disease, which generally presents with a decrease in the ratio.
▶Renal Urinary System Pyelonephritis1 questions
Source: 3A #18
A previously healthy 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of fever, chills, and left flank pain. She also has had nausea and vomited four times during this period. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft with tenderness to percussion over the left flank. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 39%, Leukocyte count 22,000/mm³, Urine RBC 10-20/hpf, WBC 20-50/hpf. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Oral amoxicillin B) Oral azithromycin C) Intravenous amoxicillin D) Intravenous ceftriaxone E) Intravenous metronidazole
Correct Answer: D) Intravenous ceftriaxone
This clinical presentation is classic for pyelonephritis, an upper urinary tract infection that commonly results from retrograde spread of a lower urinary tract infection. The patient presents with fever, chills, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension, and costovertebral angle tenderness, along with laboratory findings of leukocytosis and significant pyuria with hematuria. These findings indicate a severe systemic infection requiring parenteral antibiotic therapy with adequate gram-negative coverage. Intravenous ceftriaxone is the most appropriate choice as it is a third-generation cephalosporin with excellent broad coverage against gram-negative rods, which are the most common pathogens in pyelonephritis (particularly E. coli). Given the patient's systemic toxicity (hypotension, high fever, tachycardia), parenteral therapy is indicated rather than oral agents. Incorrect answers: Oral amoxicillin (Choice A) and intravenous amoxicillin (Choice C) have limited coverage of gram-negative bacteria unless paired with a beta-lactamase inhibitor such as clavulanic acid, making them inadequate monotherapy for pyelonephritis. Oral azithromycin (Choice B) has limited spectrum against gram-negative pathogens and is not reliably concentrated in urine; it is used for sinusitis, pharyngitis, respiratory infections, and sexually transmitted infections. Intravenous metronidazole (Choice E) is used for anaerobic bacterial and parasitic infections (such as Clostridium difficile, Giardia, Clostridia, Gardnerella, Trichinella species, and amebic infections) and does not have a primary role in treating pyelonephritis or urinary tract infections.
▶Gastrointestinal System Colon malignant neoplasms1 questions
Source: 3A #22
A 65-year-old man has a positive test of the stool for occult blood during a routine examination. He has no personal or family history of gastrointestinal disorders. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation? A) Repeat test of the stool for occult blood in 6 weeks B) Measurement of serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) concentration C) CT scan of the abdomen D) Flexible sigmoidoscopy E) Colonoscopy
Correct Answer: E) Colonoscopy
Occult blood in stool is sensitive but not specific for many malignant, vascular, infectious, and inflammatory gastrointestinal (GI) conditions, including colorectal carcinoma (CRC), arteriovenous malformation, polyposis, diverticulosis, inflammatory bowel disease, gastritis, and peptic ulcer disease. Blood may also be detectable from extraintestinal sources such as swallowed blood during epistaxis. The test can be confounded by oral iron supplementation, which can lead to false positive results. Colonoscopy is indicated when a lower GI tract source is suspected because it allows visualization, biopsy, excision, or cautery of any suspicious lesions, making it both diagnostic and therapeutic. CRC is a common cause of occult GI bleeding, especially in persons over age 50 years and should be investigated via colonoscopy. Choice A (Repeat test in 6 weeks) could delay a life-threatening diagnosis; there is no reason to suspect this was a transient event or false positive. Choice B (CEA measurement) is incorrect because CEA is measured once a CRC diagnosis is made to follow disease progression and screen for recurrence after treatment, but it should not be used for primary screening as it is nonspecific. Choice C (CT scan of the abdomen) has a role in diagnosis and staging of CRC but may miss sessile lesions and stage 1-2 tumors. Colonoscopy is superior because it permits both visualization and concomitant sampling for biopsy. Choice D (Flexible sigmoidoscopy) is inadequate because it does not permit evaluation of the transverse and ascending colon, which must be investigated during occult GI bleeding workup. For a 65-year-old with occult GI bleeding and risk factors for CRC, colonoscopy is the standard of care providing both diagnostic and therapeutic capability.
▶Renal Urinary System Urethral Obstruction1 questions
Source: 3A #23
An 82-year-old man has been mechanically ventilated in the hospital for the past 48 hours because of an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has passed no urine since removal of a urinary catheter 12 hours ago. Current medications include intravenous methylprednisolone and albuterol, ipratropium, and fluticasone by inhalation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute interstitial nephritis B) Acute urethral obstruction C) Contrast-induced nephropathy D) End-stage renal disease E) Hepatorenal syndrome F) Ischemic acute tubular necrosis G) Myoglobinuric acute renal failure (rhabdomyolysis) H) Prerenal azotemia
Correct Answer: B) Acute urethral obstruction
Acute urethral obstruction is the most likely diagnosis in this 82-year-old man who has failed to void for 12 hours following removal of an indwelling urinary catheter. Urethral obstruction can result from obstructive, malignant, infectious, structural, or inflammatory lesions in the penile or prostatic urethra, or at the urethral origin at the bladder. Common causes include urethral stricture, urethral trauma, urethritis, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), prostatitis, prostatic abscess, tumor, hematoma, cystitis, bladder tumors, intraluminal thrombus, indwelling catheter malfunction, kinking, or obstruction, and from inflammation following removal of an indwelling catheter. Failure to void following catheter removal raises strong suspicion for post-catheter urethral inflammation with resultant acute urinary obstruction. This is particularly common in older male patients with diminished caliber of the prostatic urethra secondary to baseline BPH. Acute urinary obstruction is a urologic emergency and should be treated with placement of a Foley catheter to prevent bladder rupture or post-renal azotemia. Choice A (Acute interstitial nephritis) is an intrinsic renal failure secondary to toxin exposure from medications like NSAIDs, antibiotics, and sulfas. It presents with decreased GFR, rising creatinine, and eosinophils on biopsy and urinalysis—not acute inability to void following catheter removal. Choice C (Contrast-induced nephropathy) is intrinsic renal failure from nephrotoxicity of intravenous contrast dye, presenting with rising creatinine and decreased GFR following contrast administration. There is no history of contrast exposure in this patient, and this would not cause acute urinary retention. Choice D (End-stage renal disease) results from prolonged natural history of chronically uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes, inflammatory diseases, or glomerulonephritis. It would not present with acute inability to void immediately after catheter removal. Choice E (Hepatorenal syndrome) occurs with concomitant liver failure and splanchnic vessel shunting. This patient has no evidence of liver failure. Choice F (Ischemic acute tubular necrosis) is intrinsic acute renal failure leading to low GFR and decreased urine production with muddy brown casts on urinalysis. Without a history of hypoxia or hypotension, this is unlikely, and it results in decreased urine production, not urinary retention. Choice G (Myoglobinuric acute renal failure/rhabdomyolysis) causes intrinsic renal failure from myoglobin toxicity, presenting with low GFR, decreased urine production, and muddy brown casts on urinalysis—not acute urinary retention. Choice H (Prerenal azotemia) describes increased blood urea nitrogen and creatinine from insufficient renal blood delivery in states of hypoperfusion. While this patient may have diminished cardiac output from positive pressure ventilation, prerenal azotemia would present with diminished urine production and low urine output, not rapid anuria following abrupt catheter removal.
▶Biostatistics Epidemiology Population Health Randomized Controlled Trial1 questions
Source: 3A #24
A 52-year-old man with a 5-year history of essential hypertension comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He has read about a clinical trial for a new medication, drug X, which has shown promise in controlling difficult cases of hypertension, and inquires about participation. His hypertension is moderately controlled with a thiazide diuretic, β-adrenergic blocking agent, and calcium-channel blocking agent. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate study design? A) Prospective observational cohort B) Retrospective observational cohort C) Randomized controlled trial of drug X versus a placebo D) Randomized controlled trial of drug X versus standard therapy
Correct Answer: D) Randomized controlled trial of drug X versus standard therapy
To evaluate the effectiveness of a new therapy, it should be compared against the current standard of care using a randomized, double-blinded controlled trial. In this design, patients are randomly enrolled into two groups: experimental and control. The experimental arm receives the new drug X, while the control arm receives standard antihypertensive therapy (the current standard of care). Both groups have their outcome measures assessed, and neither participants nor researchers should be aware of which therapy patients are receiving or assessing to prevent bias. Analysis is then performed to measure the efficacy of drug X compared to standard care by examining differences in outcomes. A well-executed randomized controlled trial represents one of the highest levels of clinical evidence. Perspective observational cohort studies (Choice A) and retrospective observational cohort studies (Choice B) are not appropriate for this scenario. These study designs evaluate outcomes with respect to exposures within groups sharing common characteristics and are primarily used in epidemiology. They assess relative risk rather than directly comparing treatment efficacy and cannot establish causation as effectively as RCTs. A randomized controlled trial comparing drug X to placebo (Choice C) is suboptimal for several reasons. First, it would answer whether drug X is effective as an antihypertensive, but not whether it is equivalent to or better than current standard therapy already in use. Second, comparing a new drug to placebo when effective treatments exist raises ethical concerns, as patients randomized to placebo would experience unnecessarily poorly controlled hypertension and increased cardiovascular risk.
▶Gastrointestinal System Foreign body in digestive system1 questions
Source: 3A #25
A 27-year-old man with moderate mental retardation is brought to the physician by his caretaker because of increasingly frequent episodes of intermittent vomiting over the past 3 weeks. The vomiting typically occurs within an hour after eating and usually contains partially digested food; no blood is noted in the vomitus. The patient's appetite seems unaffected, but he stops eating before he completes the meal. He has had a 3.6-kg (8-lb) weight loss since his last visit 6 months ago. He takes phenytoin for a seizure disorder but is otherwise healthy. His vital signs are within normal limits. His speech is not intelligible. Examination shows a 3 x 4-cm area of alopecia in the right occipitoparietal area of the scalp. Bowel sounds are present. The abdominal musculature voluntarily contracts with palpation; no organomegaly or masses are palpated. There are minimal contractures in both upper and lower extremities and increased muscle tone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Achalasia B) Brain tumor C) Bulimia nervosa D) Cholecystitis E) Diabetic gastroparesis F) Drug toxicity G) Food poisoning H) Gastric bezoar I) Gastric carcinoma J) Pyloric channel ulcer K) Small-bowel obstruction L) Uremia
Correct Answer: H) Gastric bezoar
A history of mental retardation/intellectual disability, early satiety, post-prandial emesis, weight loss, and focal alopecia raises the possibility of hair ingestion, which can result in development of a gastric hair bezoar. Bezoars are space-occupying masses of indigestible matter, often hair or chewing gum. Occasionally, large-volume pill ingestion can lead to a pill bezoar. Because of the space-occupying nature of the lesion in the stomach, much smaller amounts of food can be consumed prior to feelings of satiety. If large enough, a bezoar can lead to a gastric outlet obstruction which results in vomiting of undigested food with resultant weight loss from malnutrition. The presence of alopecia raises suspicion for hair ingestion and provides a clue to the contents of the bezoar. Treatment includes supportive care to correct fluid, electrolyte, and nutritional deficiencies, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy or surgery to diagnose and remove the bezoar. Choice A (Achalasia) is a type of esophageal dysmotility disorder resulting from deficient peristalsis along the length of the esophagus and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter. It manifests as dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, halitosis, and regurgitation of undigested food, diagnosed through barium swallow plus esophageal manometry. Choice B (Brain tumor), especially if causing increased intracranial pressure, can result in vomiting and weight loss; however, this patient manifests no additional signs of increased intracranial pressure such as somnolence or altered mental status, headaches when supine, papilledema, and/or new or changing neurologic deficits. He has positive symptoms to suggest an alternate cause such as a bezoar, making brain tumor less likely. Choice C (Bulimia nervosa) is marked by binge-purge behaviors such as eating a large meal, then inducing vomiting, which does not match this clinical presentation. Choice D (Cholecystitis) presents acutely with fever, nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant pain, and a Murphy sign on exam, often in the presence of gallstones. Choice E (Diabetic gastroparesis) occurs secondary to neurologic dysfunction of the enteric nervous system and typically presents late in the course of chronically uncontrolled diabetes as epigastric and left upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Choice F (Drug toxicity) has many manifestations. Several medications have known gastrointestinal adverse effects. Phenytoin does have gastrointestinal adverse effects which can include nausea, vomiting, and occasionally hepatitis; however, toxicity can also include nystagmus, ataxia, vertigo, peripheral neuropathy, megaloblastic anemia, gingival hyperplasia, dysrhythmia, and hirsutism. Choice G (Food poisoning) commonly refers to ingestion of a preformed toxin or food contaminated with a gastrointestinal pathogen. Symptoms are typically acute and include nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea, and are often self-limited. Choice I (Gastric carcinoma) presents with early satiety, weight loss, nausea, and vomiting if the lesion creates an obstruction to peristalsis. Physical exam may show a palpable mass or a Sister Mary Joseph nodule. Symptoms are chronic and often occur in older persons, smokers, or those who have frequently ingested nitrate-containing foods. Choice J (Pyloric channel ulcer) can cause gastric outlet obstruction; however, peptic ulcers often present with coffee-ground or frankly bloody emesis and are classically associated with Helicobacter pylori infections. Choice K (Small bowel obstruction) is typically acute, occurring because of adhesions, inflammatory bowel disease, strictures, malignancies, or hernias, and presents with abdominal pain, nausea, nonbloody and sometimes bilious emesis, hyperactive and high-pitched bowel sounds, and abdominal distention. Choice L (Uremia) can present with gastrointestinal symptoms but is preceded by renal failure, of which this patient has no evidence.
▶Gastrointestinal System Primary sclerosing cholangitis1 questions
Source: 3A #27
A 36-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, chills, abdominal pain, and dark urine for 1 day. He was hospitalized for treatment of a similar episode 1 year ago; ultrasonography and CT scan of the abdomen at that time showed no abnormalities. His symptoms resolved after administration of intravenous fluids and antibiotics. He has an 8-month history of pruritus and a 6-year history of ulcerative colitis treated with sulfasalazine. His temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 125/84 mm Hg. Examination shows jaundice and epigastric tenderness without masses or rebound. The liver is firm and slightly tender and has a span of 12 cm. Laboratory studies show: Prothrombin time 18 sec (INR=1.8), Serum Protein Total 8.0 g/dL, Albumin 4.0 g/dL, Globulin 4.0 g/dL, Total cholesterol 320 mg/dL, Bilirubin total 3.0 mg/dL, Direct 2.5 mg/dL, Alkaline phosphatase 300 U/L, ALT 120 U/L, HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs negative, Anti-HBc negative, Anti-HCV negative. A) Acute cholecystitis B) Acute pancreatitis C) Autoimmune chronic active hepatitis D) Budd-Chiari syndrome E) Chronic hepatitis B F) Chronic hepatitis C G) Drug-induced hepatitis H) Hepatolenticular degeneration (Wilson disease) I) Primary biliary cirrhosis J) Sclerosing cholangitis
Correct Answer: J) Sclerosing cholangitis
Sclerosing cholangitis is the correct diagnosis. This patient presents with fever, chills, abdominal pain, dark urine, jaundice, and epigastric tenderness with a history of recurrent similar episodes and ulcerative colitis. Laboratory findings show direct hyperbilirubinemia (2.5 mg/dL direct out of 3.0 mg/dL total), markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (300 U/L), mildly elevated transaminases (ALT 120 U/L), and elevated INR (1.8), consistent with cholestasis and hepatic synthetic dysfunction. Sclerosing cholangitis is a progressive inflammatory condition of the biliary tree resulting in scarring and obstruction of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. It is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis as in this patient. The condition presents with chronic fatigue, pruritus (present for 8 months), jaundice, and epigastric abdominal discomfort. Laboratory evaluation characteristically shows obstructive direct hyperbilirubinemia and increased transaminases. Examination may reveal excoriation from pruritus and/or jaundice. The repeated episodes of symptoms with fever suggest recurrent episodes of ascending cholangitis, which develops due to the increased susceptibility to infection from the biliary obstruction and stricturing. Definitive diagnosis requires biopsy and is supported by clinical history. The INR elevation indicates compromised hepatic synthetic function, possibly from developing cirrhosis. Choice A (Acute cholecystitis) presents with right upper quadrant pain and tenderness, often preceded by biliary colic and history of gallstones, which this patient lacks. Jaundice is uncommon unless complicated by choledocholithiasis or ascending cholangitis. Choice B (Acute pancreatitis) presents with epigastric pain, nausea, and emesis, often in patients with gallstones, alcohol use, trauma, hypertriglyceridemia, or hypercalcemia. It is not commonly associated with inflammatory bowel disease and would show elevated lipase rather than this pattern of cholestasis. Choice C (Autoimmune hepatitis) typically presents in females of middle age with nonspecific symptoms including fatigue, weight loss, jaundice, and pruritis. Laboratory evaluation shows transaminase elevation and anti-smooth muscle antibodies. The cholestatic pattern and association with ulcerative colitis make sclerosing cholangitis more likely. Choice D (Budd-Chiari syndrome) presents with acute severe right upper quadrant pain and congestive hepatopathy from hepatic vein thrombosis. The clinical presentation and lack of findings consistent with acute Budd-Chiari syndrome make this unlikely. Choice E (Chronic hepatitis B) and Choice F (Chronic hepatitis C) would show abnormal serologic studies (HBsAg, Anti-HBs, Anti-HBc, or Anti-HCV). This patient's negative serology excludes these diagnoses. Choice G (Drug-induced hepatitis) typically shows increased transaminases rather than the prominent cholestatic pattern seen here. There is no mention of hepatotoxic medications. Choice H (Hepatolenticular degeneration/Wilson disease) results from impaired copper metabolism and presents with liver dysfunction and neuropsychologic impairment (parkinsonism, ataxia, tremors, dystonia, dementia). There are no neurologic findings in this patient. Choice I (Primary biliary cirrhosis) presents with cholestatic symptoms and anti-mitochondrial antibodies and is more common in women in the fourth to sixth decades of life. While it can present with similar symptoms, the strong association with ulcerative colitis and the recurrent acute episodes with fever are more characteristic of primary sclerosing cholangitis.
▶Gastrointestinal System Hepatitis C1 questions
Source: 3A #28
A 65-year-old man comes to the physician because of easy fatigability for 2 months. In 1985, he had loss of appetite, mild nausea, and fatigue approximately 2 months after receiving a transfusion for a bleeding peptic ulcer. The liver has a span of 12 cm. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Prothrombin time 12 sec (INR=1.1), Serum Protein Total 7.8 g/dL, Albumin 4.5 g/dL, Globulin 3.3 g/dL, Total cholesterol 185 mg/dL, Bilirubin total 0.8 mg/dL, Direct 0.2 mg/dL, Alkaline phosphatase 70 U/L, ALT 125 U/L, HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs positive, Anti-HBc positive, Anti-HCV positive. A) Acute cholecystitis B) Acute pancreatitis C) Autoimmune chronic active hepatitis D) Budd-Chiari syndrome E) Chronic hepatitis B F) Chronic hepatitis C G) Drug-induced hepatitis H) Hepatolenticular degeneration (Wilson disease) I) Primary biliary cirrhosis J) Sclerosing cholangitis
Correct Answer: F) Chronic hepatitis C
This patient has chronic hepatitis C. The clinical presentation is consistent with hepatitis C acquired via transfusion in the prescreening era (1985). The patient presented with nonspecific chronic symptoms including fatigue, nausea, and easy fatigability over months. The serologic findings are diagnostic: Anti-HCV antibody is positive, confirming hepatitis C exposure. HBsAg is negative (ruling out active hepatitis B), while Anti-HBs and Anti-HBc are positive, indicating previous hepatitis B infection that has been cleared. The ALT is mildly elevated at 125 U/L, which is consistent with chronic hepatitis C. Hepatitis C is commonly transmitted via blood transfusions, especially in the prescreening era before 1992. Chronic hepatitis C can present with nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. If left untreated, it can eventually lead to cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease. Anti-HCV antibodies indicate exposure to hepatitis C virus but do not confer immunity. Acute cholecystitis presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain and tenderness, often with a history of gallstones, not with chronic fatigue months after transfusion. Acute pancreatitis presents with epigastric pain, nausea, and elevated lipase, not with this clinical picture. Autoimmune hepatitis typically occurs in females in middle age with autoimmune markers like anti-smooth muscle antibodies. Budd-Chiari syndrome presents with acute severe right upper quadrant pain, congestive hepatopathy, and liver failure from hepatic vein thrombosis. Chronic hepatitis B would require HBsAg positivity, which is negative in this patient; the positive Anti-HBs and Anti-HBc indicate previous cleared infection. Drug-induced hepatitis requires a medication history and does not fit this transfusion-acquired picture. Wilson disease presents with neuropsychologic symptoms in addition to liver disease. Primary biliary cirrhosis presents with cholestasis symptoms (itching, jaundice), anti-mitochondrial antibodies, and occurs primarily in women. Sclerosing cholangitis is associated with inflammatory bowel disease and presents with obstructive hyperbilirubinemia.
▶Renal Urinary System Acute Interstitial Nephritis1 questions
Source: 3A #29
A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever and rash for 2 days. He just completed a 6-week course of nafcillin for treatment of staphylococcal bacterial endocarditis. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F). Examination shows a faint maculopapular rash. Cardiac examination shows an unchanged murmur of aortic insufficiency and no embolic lesions. Laboratory studies and an x-ray of the chest show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely set of findings on urinalysis? A) Specific Gravity: 1.003, Glucose: negative, Protein: 1+, WBC/hpf: 30, RBC/hpf: 5, Other Casts/Findings: muddy brown tubular epithelial cells B) Specific Gravity: 1.005, Glucose: trace, Protein: 2+, WBC/hpf: 30, RBC/hpf: 3, Other Casts/Findings: rare WBC eosinophils C) Specific Gravity: 1.012, Glucose: negative, Protein: negative, WBC/hpf: 2, RBC/hpf: 5, Other Casts/Findings: none D) Specific Gravity: 1.012, Glucose: 1+, Protein: negative, WBC/hpf: 3, RBC/hpf: 2-3, Other Casts/Findings: WBC 2+ bacteria E) Specific Gravity: 1.012, Glucose: negative, Protein: 3+, WBC/hpf: 100, RBC/hpf: 5, Other Casts/Findings: RBC casts F) Specific Gravity: 1.030, Glucose: 4+, Protein: 3+, WBC/hpf: 30, RBC/hpf: 30, Other Casts/Findings: none, 2+ bacteria
Correct Answer: B) Specific Gravity: 1.005, Glucose: trace, Protein: 2+, WBC/hpf: 30, RBC/hpf: 3, Other Casts/Findings: rare WBC eosinophils
Interstitial nephritis is a cause of intrinsic renal failure that often occurs secondary to medication use, with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics (including nafcillin), and sulfa drugs being common precipitants. In this case, the patient presents with the classic triad of drug-induced interstitial nephritis: low-grade fever, diffuse maculopapular rash, and renal dysfunction occurring after antibiotic exposure. Interstitial nephritis is characterized by decreased glomerular filtration rate, rising creatinine, and eosinophilic infiltrates on biopsy. On urinalysis, it typically reveals eosinophiluria (WBC eosinophils), occasional WBC casts, increased WBC/hpf, and proteinuria. Treatment involves discontinuing the inciting agent (nafcillin in this case). Choice A reflects acute tubular necrosis, which typically follows an ischemic or nephrotoxic insult and presents with muddy brown casts and tubular epithelial cells on microscopy. While this is a form of intrinsic renal failure, it is not the classic presentation associated with drug exposure in this clinical context. Choice C represents a normal urinalysis with specific gravity, glucose, protein, white cells, red cells, and casts all within normal limits. This does not fit the clinical presentation of renal dysfunction. Choice D may reflect pyelonephritis, as it shows WBC casts and bacteria. Pyelonephritis classically presents with elevated WBC per high power field along with leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and pyuria; however, this patient has no symptoms of urinary tract infection and the intact cardiac exam makes this unlikely. Choice E reflects nephritic syndrome, which typically presents with red blood cell casts and hematuria, not the eosinophiluria characteristic of drug-induced interstitial nephritis. Choice F suggests poorly controlled diabetes or sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitor use with concurrent urinary tract infection based on glucosuria, elevated WBCs, and bacteria. This does not fit the clinical picture.
▶Cardiovascular System Aortic Valve Prolapse1 questions
Source: 3A #30
A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. He has not had difficulty breathing at night or chest pain. In addition to a heart murmur that was diagnosed when he was in high school, he has diverticulosis and mild osteoarthritis. He takes no medications except a daily multivitamin. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 135/90 mm Hg. There is no jugular venous distention. The carotid pulse has a slow upstroke. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard best at the right sternal border and radiates to the apex. There is no change in the murmur with the Valsalva maneuver. There is a paradoxical splitting of S2 and a prominent apical impulse. An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy; there is no evidence of infarction. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's heart murmur? A) Atrial septal defect B) Congenital bicuspid aortic valve C) Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy D) Myxomatous degeneration of mitral valve E) Rheumatic heart disease
Correct Answer: B) Congenital bicuspid aortic valve
Congenital bicuspid aortic valve is the correct answer. This condition classically presents with early signs and symptoms of aortic stenosis and left-sided diastolic heart failure. Patients may complain of fatigue, shortness of breath, cough, diminished exercise tolerance, or syncope with exertion—all consistent with this patient's presentation. Key exam findings include a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur best heard at the upper right sternal border (as described in this case), and pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed carotid upstroke) may be noted on examination of peripheral pulses, which correlates with the documented slow carotid upstroke. Because of the chronic increased afterload from a fixed obstruction by the valve, left ventricular hypertrophy and resultant diastolic dysfunction can occur, matching the ECG findings.
