Paradoxical splitting of S2 occurs in aortic stenosis due to prolonged left ventricular ejection time. If early aortic stenosis occurs, the patient may be a candidate for aortic valve replacement. Choice A (Atrial septal defect) presents with fixed splitting of the S2 heart sound and is caused by a failure of closure of the embryologic connection between the right and left atria. Blood generally flows from the left atrium into the right atrium, increasing the amount within the right heart and pulmonary circuit. This would not explain the slow carotid upstroke or left ventricular hypertrophy. Choice C (Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy) classically presents with a systolic murmur loudest in the lower left sternal border, which is quieter with increased preload and afterload (opposite of this case, where no change occurs with Valsalva). It is caused by hypertrophy of the septum, creating an outflow obstruction within the left ventricular outflow tract. It classically presents with syncope or sudden cardiac death in an exercising young athlete with a family history of a similar event, not a 47-year-old with a long-standing murmur. Choice D (Myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve) can eventually lead to mitral insufficiency, which presents with a holosystolic murmur; however, this condition would not be expected to cause left ventricular hypertrophy or pulsus parvus et tardus (slow carotid upstroke). Choice E (Rheumatic heart disease) commonly causes insufficiency murmurs in the acute phase and stenotic murmurs later in life, predominantly affecting the mitral valve. Rheumatic fever typically presents with joint inflammation, pancarditis, subcutaneous inflammatory nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea. Mitral stenosis itself presents with a diastolic murmur radiating to the axilla. This patient has neither a history of acute rheumatic fever nor findings consistent with mitral involvement.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Mild Cognitive Impairment1 questions
Source: 3A #33
An 87-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for treatment of a right femoral neck fracture sustained when he fell down a staircase. He has osteoarthritis of the knees treated with ibuprofen (400 mg three times daily). He takes no other medications. He also reports memory loss, particularly in remembering the names of people he has met recently. He first noted the problem 4 years ago, and he states that it is slowly becoming worse. There is no family history of dementia. He lives alone, drives a car, does his own shopping and cooking, and manages his own finances. He does not smoke cigarettes. He drinks one beer daily. His blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Examination shows shortening and external rotation of the right lower extremity. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. His Mini-Mental State Examination score is 27/30. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's memory loss? A) Dementia, Alzheimer type B) Medication adverse effect C) Mild cognitive impairment D) Multi-infarct (vascular) dementia E) Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency
Correct Answer: C) Mild cognitive impairment
Mild forgetfulness without significant impairment in ability to perform instrumental activities of daily living, with a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 27/30, is most consistent with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). MCI is often seen prior to a diagnosis of dementia, especially Alzheimer type, and includes amnestic (memory-related) and non-amnestic (language, spatial, executive functional impairment) forms with generally preserved ability to function independently without significant impairment. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice A) is defined by the DSM-5 as loss of intellectual function within multiple domains: language, memory, perception, motor skills, attention, orientation, problem solving, and executive function. This patient maintains instrumental activities of daily living and has a relatively preserved MMSE score of 27/30, which is inconsistent with dementia diagnosis. Medication adverse effect (Choice B) is a well-recognized cause of cognitive impairment that is often reversible in elderly persons. Anticholinergics and sedative-hypnotics are frequently cited as causing depressed mental status or delirium. However, this patient is only taking ibuprofen for osteoarthritis, and there is no abrupt cognitive decline correlated with initiating such medications. Additionally, the 4-year slowly progressive course is more consistent with MCI. Multi-infarct (vascular) dementia (Choice D) is characterized by a stepwise decline in cognitive functioning following vascular phenomena, with progressive loss of function after each cerebrovascular accident in a series of ischemic strokes. This patient lacks evidence of strokes and shows gradual rather than stepwise decline. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency (Choice E) presents with dementia resulting from nutritional deficiency and is often accompanied by megaloblastic anemia. There is no evidence of B12 deficiency in this patient's presentation, and his dietary intake appears adequate given his independence in shopping and cooking.
▶Cardiovascular System Unstable Angina Pectoris1 questions
Source: 3A #34
A 64-year-old woman with a 4-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with insulin comes to the emergency department because of exertional chest pressure for 3 weeks. The first episode occurred while she was walking upstairs and was relieved by 5 minutes of rest. The second episode occurred 1 week ago while she was mowing the lawn and was relieved after 10 minutes of rest. She had two episodes yesterday, each lasting 15 minutes; both occurred with exertion and were accompanied by shortness of breath and nausea. Today she had a 10-minute episode starting while she was in the shower and another while she was walking into the emergency department. Examination and an ECG show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Self-monitoring of blood glucose concentration during the next episode of chest pain B) Dipyridamole-thallium-201 scintigraphy C) Exercise stress test within 24 hours D) Antianginal drug therapy now and an exercise stress test in 5 days E) Admit the patient to the hospital
Correct Answer: E) Admit the patient to the hospital
This patient presents with unstable angina, an acute coronary syndrome characterized by worsening anginal symptoms that are new, occur at rest, or are increasing in severity and frequency. Her initial exertional chest pressure relieved by rest represents stable angina, but the progression to more frequent episodes (two yesterday, two today), longer duration (up to 15 minutes), occurrence at rest (in the shower), and associated symptoms (shortness of breath, nausea) indicate unstable angina. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate hospital admission for urgent diagnostic workup and management. Hospitalization allows for serial ECGs, troponin testing, continuous cardiac monitoring, cardiology consultation, and risk stratification using the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) score to guide further management, which may include stress testing and/or coronary angiography with revascularization. Choice A (Self-monitoring of blood glucose) is inappropriate because this patient's symptoms are unlikely related to hyper- or hypoglycemia, and blood glucose monitoring does not address the acute coronary syndrome requiring hospital admission. Choice B (Dipyridamole-thallium-201 scintigraphy) is a nonexertional perfusion test used in patients unable to exercise, but it is not the appropriate initial management for acute unstable angina requiring urgent admission and risk stratification. Choice C (Exercise stress test within 24 hours) may eventually be indicated, but the patient requires urgent hospital admission first for diagnostic workup and stabilization before stress testing can be safely performed. Choice D (Antianginal therapy now with stress test in 5 days) would inappropriately delay urgent diagnostic evaluation of this acute coronary syndrome, potentially missing the opportunity for timely coronary angiography and revascularization.
▶Biostatistics Epidemiology Population Health Primary Prevention1 questions
Source: 3A #37
A 27-year-old man is found to have a total serum cholesterol concentration of 190 mg/dL at a routine examination. He has no family history of hypertension or premature coronary artery disease. His grandmother was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus at the age of 65 years. Examination shows no abnormalities. In addition to general dietary advice and education concerning risk factors, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Repeat measurement of serum cholesterol concentration in 5 years B) Recommend the American Heart Association Step 2 cholesterol-lowering diet C) Glucose tolerance test D) X-ray of the chest E) ECG
Correct Answer: A) Repeat measurement of serum cholesterol concentration in 5 years
Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) has multiple risk factors including uncontrolled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, obesity, excess alcohol consumption, family history, age, and smoking. According to the 2019 AHA/ACC Guideline on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease, persons with known ASCVD should be started on high-intensity statin therapy. For those ages 40 to 75 years at risk for ASCVD, moderate or high-intensity statin therapy is recommended based on personal medical history, family history, and laboratory evaluation. However, routine screening for persons under age 40 years is generally not recommended apart from reasonable surveillance every 4 to 6 years. For persons ages 20 to 39 years who are not at increased risk (below 7.5% risk in the next 10 years), a lifetime or 30-year risk target is reasonable in deciding whether to initiate lipid-lowering therapy. This 27-year-old patient has a total cholesterol of 190 mg/dL (borderline high) but no other obvious personal or family risk factors for ASCVD—no hypertension history, no family history of premature coronary artery disease, and his grandmother's type 2 diabetes diagnosis at age 65 is not a strong immediate risk factor. Lifestyle modifications should be recommended with routine screening; lipid-lowering therapy should be initiated only if his risk subsequently rises. Choice B (AHA Step 2 diet): While aligned with 2019 AHA recommendations, general dietary advice and education have already been provided to this patient, making additional specific diet recommendations premature without demonstrated need or higher risk. Choice C (Glucose tolerance test): Although appropriate for patients in whom diabetes diagnosis is questionable, the 2015 USPSTF Grade B recommendation for diabetes screening applies to adults ages 40 to 70 years. This patient does not meet screening criteria at this time despite family history of type 2 diabetes in his grandmother. Choice D (Chest X-ray): Historically used for various cardiothoracic diagnoses but is no longer recommended for routine screening in asymptomatic individuals. Choice E (ECG): Used to diagnose cardiac arrhythmias, conduction deficits, and myocardial ischemia. ECGs are occasionally used for preoperative screening but are not currently recommended for routine screening in asymptomatic individuals not under investigation for cardiovascular disease. Educational Objective: Understand current guidelines for cardiovascular disease screening and primary prevention in asymptomatic individuals under age 40 with borderline cholesterol and no significant risk factors. Recognize when lifestyle modification and surveillance are appropriate versus when pharmacologic intervention is indicated.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Cobalamin Deficiency1 questions
Source: 3A #38
A 65-year-old woman has fatigue, pallor, and glossitis. Hemoglobin concentration is 8 g/dL, and mean corpuscular volume is 115 µm³. Leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. A blood smear is shown. Which of the following is the most likely primary pathophysiologic mechanism causing her anemia? A) Defective porphyrin metabolism B) Faulty protein transcription C) Impaired DNA synthesis D) Inadequate erythropoietin E) Unbalanced synthesis of α- and β-globulin chains
Correct Answer: C) Impaired DNA synthesis
Impaired DNA synthesis is the primary pathophysiologic mechanism in megaloblastic anemia. This condition is characterized by the presence of hypersegmented neutrophils, anemia, and increased mean corpuscular volume (macrocytosis). The impairment is commonly due to deficiency of required cofactors such as folic acid and cobalamin (vitamin B12). Malnutrition and alcohol use disorder are common causes of folic acid deficiency, while conditions such as pernicious anemia, Crohn disease, and veganism can result in cobalamin deficiency. Clinical presentation includes fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance, with pallor and glossitis found on physical examination. Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia with increased mean cell volume and normal white cell and platelet indices. The presence of hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral blood smear is a characteristic and diagnostic finding in megaloblastic anemia. Treatment involves replacing the deficient vitamin and resolving underlying nutritional deficiencies. Choice A (Defective porphyrin metabolism) is seen in porphyria, which can arise from genetic mutations, heavy metal poisoning, or adverse medication effects. It presents with anemia and often blistering of the skin with sunlight exposure, but does not produce the characteristic megaloblastic picture. Choice B (Faulty protein transcription) can cause various types of anemia, such as sickle cell anemia and pyruvate kinase deficiency, but these typically result in hemolytic, normocytic anemias rather than megaloblastic macrocytic anemia. Choice D (Inadequate erythropoietin) occurs in chronic end-stage kidney disease due to insufficient production from peritubular capillary interstitial cells. This results in normocytic, non-hemolytic anemia without the macrocytosis or hypersegmented neutrophils seen here. Choice E (Unbalanced synthesis of α- and β-globulin chains) defines thalassemia, which classically presents as a microcytic anemia in persons of Mediterranean, Asian, and African descent, not the macrocytic anemia described in this case.
▶Cardiovascular System Stable Angina Pectoris1 questions
Source: 3A #39
A 77-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 3-month history of shortness of breath when she climbs stairs. Her shortness of breath resolves after 5 minutes of rest. Her last episode was 3 days ago. She has not had chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, cough, wheezing, swelling, or difficulty sleeping. She has hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide, omeprazole, and a multivitamin. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (140 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 144/92 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. There are jugular venous pulsations 3 cm above the sternal angle. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An ECG shows a left bundle branch block and no primary T-wave changes, which is unchanged from an ECG 1 year ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine the cause of this patient's dyspnea? A) Measurement of serum troponin I concentration B) ECG exercise stress test C) Exercise stress echocardiography D) Ventilation-perfusion lung scans E) Coronary angiography
Correct Answer: C) Exercise stress echocardiography
The patient presents with exertional dyspnea that resolves with rest over a 3-month period, consistent with stable angina (anginal equivalent without chest pain). She has risk factors for coronary artery disease (age, hypertension) and baseline ECG abnormalities (left bundle branch block unchanged for 1 year). The goal is to diagnose inducible cardiac ischemia noninvasively. Exercise stress echocardiography is the most appropriate next step because it is designed for patients who can exercise but have baseline ECG abnormalities that would prevent accurate interpretation of ST-segment changes during an exercise stress test. The stress echocardiogram evaluates for regional wall motion abnormalities that develop with stress-induced ischemia, providing both functional assessment and direct visualization of cardiac performance. Choice A (Serum troponin I) is used to diagnose acute coronary syndromes, myocardial infarction, or myocarditis. It has no role in diagnosing stable angina without evidence of acute injury or infarction. Choice B (ECG exercise stress test) is a first-line screening test for cardiac ischemia in patients with normal baseline ECGs. However, in patients with baseline ST-segment abnormalities (including left or right bundle branch block, left ventricular hypertrophy, early repolarization, or ventricular aneurysm), the ECG stress test lacks sensitivity and specificity because the baseline abnormalities obscure interpretation of ischemic ST changes. Choice D (Ventilation-perfusion lung scans) assess for mismatches between ventilation and perfusion and are used primarily to evaluate for pulmonary embolism when CT angiography cannot be performed. They are not indicated for evaluating coronary artery disease. Choice E (Coronary angiography) is an invasive procedure used to visualize coronary arteries and is reserved for definitive diagnosis and potential intervention in coronary artery disease. It is performed after initial noninvasive testing in stable patients and is not the first-line diagnostic approach.
▶Gastrointestinal System Boerhaave syndrome1 questions
Source: 3A #40
Immediately after undergoing an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and dilatation for achalasia, a 32-year-old woman has moderate substernal and midback pain. She has no history of serious illness. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The abdomen is soft and nondistended. Esophagography shows a small leak of contrast from the distal esophagus into the left chest. In addition to intravenous antibiotic therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Placement of an intraluminal esophageal stent B) Placement of a left chest tube C) Nissen fundoplication D) Esophagogastrectomy E) Operative repair of the esophageal injury
Correct Answer: E) Operative repair of the esophageal injury
Esophageal perforation is a serious complication of endoscopic procedures, particularly during esophageal dilation for achalasia. The procedure stretches smooth muscle and connective tissue, which can lead to perforation, especially if chronic inflammation has compromised the stromal strength of the esophageal wall. The diagnosis is confirmed by water-soluble contrast esophagography showing contrast leak into the mediastinum, as seen in this case. An esophageal perforation permits translocation of gastrointestinal contents (food, gastric acid, and bacteria) into the mediastinum, which can rapidly lead to fatal mediastinitis if untreated. Management requires emergent surgical repair combined with intravenous antibiotic therapy to prevent mediastinal infection. Choice A (Intraluminal esophageal stent) is used for esophageal obstruction from webs, strictures, or malignancy, not for acute perforation repair. Choice B (Placement of a left chest tube) may be needed later if an empyema develops from translocated gastric contents; however, this complication would not be evident for several days and may be prevented entirely with prompt antibiotics and surgical repair. A chest tube is not the primary intervention. Choice C (Nissen fundoplication) is a surgical treatment for gastroesophageal reflux disease involving plication of the gastric fundus around the lower esophagus. It has no role in managing acute esophageal perforation. Choice D (Esophagogastrectomy) involves removal of portions of the esophagus and stomach and is typically reserved for malignancy, not for acute perforation management. The educational objective is to recognize that esophageal perforation is a surgical emergency requiring immediate operative repair to prevent life-threatening mediastinitis and sepsis.
▶Endocrine System Hyperprolactinemia1 questions
Source: 3A #45
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of spontaneous discharge from her nipples during the past 3 months. She discontinued breast-feeding her child 1 year ago. She takes no medications. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. On physical examination, a milky white discharge can be expressed from both nipples. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Her fasting serum prolactin concentration is 40 ng/ml, and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is within the reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient? A) Application of ice packs to the breasts B) Wearing tight bras C) Bromocriptine therapy D) Tamoxifen therapy E) Vitamin E therapy
Correct Answer: C) Bromocriptine therapy
An inappropriate elevation in serum prolactin is defined as hyperprolactinemia and causes production of breast milk and growth of glandular breast tissue. After cessation of breast-feeding, serum prolactin levels typically return to pre-pregnancy levels. Inappropriate elevation of prolactin often arises from a hyperfunctioning anterior pituitary microadenoma and presents with unexpected production of breast milk. Prolactin is negatively regulated by dopamine. Various dopaminergic blocking medications can have galactorrhea as an adverse effect. Further, prolactin is positively regulated by thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), and in states of hypothyroidism with upregulated TRH, galactorrhea can also occur. With exclusion of thyroid dysfunction and any contributions from dopamine antagonists, further diagnostic evaluation should include an MRI of the brain to assess for the presence of a pituitary adenoma. Treatment is with dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine or cabergoline, and if such medications fail or if a macroadenoma is found, surgical resection of the adenoma is required. Choice A (Application of ice packs to the breasts) and Choice B (Wearing tight bras) are recommendations offered to lactating women approaching the end of breast-feeding or for postpartum women who do not wish to pursue breast-feeding. These measures provide relief of discomfort from engorged breast tissue but have no role in treating hormonal dysregulation from pathologic hyperprolactinemia. Choice D (Tamoxifen therapy), a selective estrogen receptor modulator, is used in the treatment of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer by blocking the trophic action of estrogen on the tumor. It has no role in treating hyperprolactinemia or a pituitary prolactinoma. Choice E (Vitamin E therapy) has been shown to lower prolactin levels in patients with uremia on hemodialysis and has been shown to have an inhibitory effect on pituitary gland hypertrophy; however, it has not been shown to be as effective when compared to dopamine agonists and surgical resection.
▶Cardiovascular System Venous Thromboembolism1 questions
Source: 3A #46
Four days after undergoing a left total hip replacement, a 75-year-old woman has the rapid onset of chest pain, severe dyspnea, and confusion. Her pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 94/60 mm Hg. A pleural rub is heard at the right lung base. The surgical incision appears to be healing well. There is moderate edema of the left leg. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: pH 7.46, PcO2 28 mm Hg, PO2 62 mm Hg. Which of the following postoperative treatments is most likely to have prevented this condition? A) Administration of aspirin B) Administration of cefoxitin C) Administration of oxygen D) Administration of warfarin E) Use of incentive spirometry
Correct Answer: D) Administration of warfarin
The clinical presentation is consistent with a massive pulmonary embolism (PE) secondary to deep venous thrombosis (DVT). Key findings include: sudden onset of chest pain, severe dyspnea, confusion, tachycardia (120/min), tachypnea (28/min), hypotension (94/60 mm Hg—indicating massive PE), moderate edema of the left leg (site of likely DVT), and arterial blood gas showing hypoxemia (PO2 62 mm Hg) with acute respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.46, PcO2 28 mm Hg). This clinical picture fits the classic presentation of PE in a post-operative orthopedic patient. DVT can occur following surgery due to venous stasis from immobilization combined with the hypercoagulable state induced by the surgical inflammatory response. If a DVT embolizes to the pulmonary circulation, it causes PE. When the embolus is large enough to obstruct right heart outflow, hemodynamic compromise and shock result (massive PE). Postoperative anticoagulation with pharmacologic agents like warfarin (an anticoagulant) or mechanical prophylaxis (frequent ambulation, sequential lower extremity compression devices) significantly reduces the incidence of DVT and PE. Warfarin is an anticoagulant that prevents thrombus formation and is used for VTE prophylaxis post-operatively, particularly in high-risk patients undergoing hip replacement. Incorrect choices: Aspirin (Choice A) is an antiplatelet agent used for prevention of arterial thrombotic events (MI, CVA), not venous thromboembolism. Cefoxitin (Choice B), a second-generation cephalosporin, is for treating bacterial infections and has no role in VTE prevention. Oxygen (Choice C) treats hypoxemia from established PE but does not prevent DVT/PE formation. Incentive spirometry (Choice E) prevents post-operative atelectasis and pneumonia but does not prevent VTE.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Peripheral Nerve Injury1 questions
Source: 3A #47
A 57-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. She was the restrained front seat passenger. Her neck was immobilized in a cervical collar at the scene. On arrival, she reports neck pain and pain in her right forearm. Her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/70 mm Hg. Examination of the right upper extremity shows swelling and crepitus. She is able to actively extend the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints but not the metacarpophalangeal joints of her right hand or wrist. The remainder of the examination shows no other abnormalities. Plain x-rays show a midshaft fracture of the humerus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Brachial plexus injury B) Compartment syndrome C) Herniated cervical disc D) Median nerve injury E) Radial nerve injury
Correct Answer: E) Radial nerve injury
The radial nerve courses posterior to the humerus at the midshaft within the radial groove and is frequently injured in displaced midshaft humerus fractures. This patient's inability to extend the metacarpophalangeal joints of the right hand and wrist (wrist drop) is pathognomonic for radial nerve injury. The radial nerve supplies motor fibers to the triceps brachii and extensor muscles of the posterior forearm, as well as sensory fibers to the dorsum of the forearm, wrist, and hand. Injury at the mid-diaphyseal humerus causes extensor muscle loss at the hand and wrist, weakness of forearm supination, wrist drop, and sensory loss over the posterior forearm, dorsum of the hand, and posterior thumb through the radial half of the ring finger. Choice A (Brachial plexus injury) would result in motor and sensory loss of multiple nerves rather than a isolated mononeuropathy, making this unlikely given the focal presentation. Choice B (Compartment syndrome) presents with the classic pentad of pain, paresthesia, paresis, poikilothermia, pallor, and pulselessness due to increased pressure within a fixed myofascial compartment. With an otherwise normal examination and localized findings consistent with radial nerve distribution, compartment syndrome is less likely. Choice C (Herniated cervical disc) can cause cervical radiculopathy with pain in a radicular pattern. However, weakness of muscles innervated by multiple cervical spinal levels would be expected, and this patient's findings localize precisely to the radial nerve distribution. Choice D (Median nerve injury) would present with weakness of the flexor compartment of the forearm, thenar eminence, and first two lumbricals, with sensory loss over the anterior forearm and lateral hand—a pattern not consistent with this patient's presentation.
▶Respiratory System Lung Abscess1 questions
Source: 3A #49
A 40-year-old man with alcoholism has had a low-grade fever, malaise, and cough productive of purulent sputum for 2 weeks and hemoptysis for 24 hours; during this period, he has had a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F). Hematocrit is 33%, and leukocyte count is 15,000/mm³. An x-ray of the chest shows a large cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level in the superior segment of the right lower lobe of the lung. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Aspergilloma B) Bronchiectasis C) Lung abscess D) Lung cancer E) Tuberculosis
Correct Answer: C) Lung abscess
The clinical presentation is classic for lung abscess secondary to aspiration pneumonia. The patient has multiple risk factors for aspiration, including alcohol use disorder which impairs airway-protective reflexes and increases risk of forceful emesis. The key clinical features include: low-grade fever, productive cough with purulent sputum, malaise, weight loss, anemia (Hct 33%), and leukocytosis (15,000/mm³). Most importantly, the chest x-ray finding of a cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level in a dependent segment (superior segment of right lower lobe, a typical location for aspiration while supine) is pathognomonic for lung abscess. Aspiration pneumonia results from bacterial seeding with gastrointestinal or oral flora and, if untreated or complicated, progresses to abscess formation, often involving pathogens like Klebsiella pneumoniae. Treatment involves antibiotics, prevention of recurrent aspiration, and source control with drainage or surgical resection. Incorrect answers: Aspergillomas (Choice A) are fungal masses that arise within pre-existing cavitary lesions from tuberculosis or lung cancer, not acute infections with air-fluid levels in a previously normal lung. Bronchiectasis (Choice B) is chronic bronchial dilatation from recurrent infections associated with cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and does not typically present with acute cavitary lesions and air-fluid levels. Lung cancer (Choice D) presents with hemoptysis and weight loss but would show a solitary nodular mass-like opacity rather than an air-fluid level within a cavity unless superinfection occurred. Tuberculosis (Choice E), while presenting with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis, classically shows cavitary lesions in the lung apices with evidence of a Ghon complex, not in dependent lower lobe segments with acute air-fluid levels in an alcoholic patient without classic TB risk factors.
▶Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Hyponatremia1 questions
Source: 9A #1
A patient with a history of coronary artery disease presents during vacation with peripheral edema. He is on furosemide, spironolactone, benazepril, and atorvastatin. Serum studies show a sodium concentration of 131 mEq/L and glucose concentration of 102 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's serum sodium concentration? A) ADH excess B) Adrenal insufficiency C) Diabetes insipidus D) Glomerular hyperfiltration E) Hypothyroidism F) Primary aldosteronism G) Sodium deficiency
Correct Answer: A) ADH excess
This patient with acute decompensated heart failure secondary to ischemic cardiomyopathy presents with mild hyponatremia (131 mEq/L), which is most likely explained by excess ADH (vasopressin). The decreased cardiac output and arterial underfilling from heart failure stimulate baroreceptors, leading to increased ADH release. Increased ADH causes water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, diluting serum sodium and accumulating fluid, which worsens the heart failure exacerbation. This results in hypotonic hyponatremia in the context of volume overload. Prevention centers on optimal heart failure management, diuretic optimization, and guideline-directed medical therapy. Treatment includes fluid restriction and diuretic titration, with sodium normalizing as cardiac output improves and circulating ADH falls. Choice B (Adrenal insufficiency) is incorrect. While adrenal insufficiency can present with hyponatremia, this patient's presentation is more consistent with ADH excess in acute decompensated heart failure. Adrenal insufficiency generally causes euvolemic hyponatremia. Choice C (Diabetes insipidus) is incorrect. Diabetes insipidus results from ADH deficiency or renal resistance to ADH, causing inability to concentrate urine and leading to hypernatremia, not hyponatremia. Choice D (Glomerular hyperfiltration) is incorrect. Glomerular hyperfiltration is seen in renal pathology such as early-stage diabetic nephropathy and does not inherently change serum sodium concentrations. Choice E (Hypothyroidism) is incorrect. While hypothyroidism can present with hyponatremia, this patient's clinical context is more consistent with ADH excess from heart failure. Hypothyroidism-induced hyponatremia is generally euvolemic. Choice F (Primary aldosteronism) is incorrect. Primary aldosteronism typically presents with treatment-resistant hypertension and does not cause hyponatremia. Patients are generally euvolemic with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Choice G (Sodium deficiency) is incorrect. Sodium deficiency is not a common cause of hyponatremia. Hyponatremia more often results from water excess relative to total body sodium, not from impaired sodium intake or excess sodium loss. The key pathophysiology involves free water retention, not sodium loss.
▶Biostatistics Epidemiology Population Health Ascertainment Bias1 questions
Source: 9A #3
A physician wants to assess the frequency of medical disorders among the residents of a local community exposed to airborne toxins from a manufacturing plant. In a recent journal article, researchers reported a retrospective case series where participants with a history of work absence because of illness were selected from health records, and concluded that 20% of the residents within the local community are likely to have toxin-related medical disorders. This conclusion is invalid because of which of the following features of this study? A) Ascertainment bias B) Lack of randomization C) Prospective analysis D) Retrospective analysis E) Sample size
Correct Answer: A) Ascertainment bias
Ascertainment bias, a form of selection bias, occurs when there is nonrandom (biased) selection of individuals for inclusion in a particular study group. In this study, participants with a history of work absence due to illness were selected from health records, which imposes bias as the study includes only those with a history of illness—not representative of the community at-large. Ascertainment bias may occur when the participants studied differ from the target population. This biased selection led to the false conclusion that 20% of residents likely have toxin-related disorders, when the true prevalence in the community may be different. Choice B (Lack of randomization) is incorrect because randomly selecting participants from the target population would help decrease ascertainment bias by increasing the likelihood that study participants are representative of the local community. Choice C (Prospective analysis) is incorrect. A prospective study identifies a group and follows them over time to determine if an exposure is associated with an outcome. Ascertainment bias is the more likely invalidating feature here. Choice D (Retrospective analysis) is not an invalidating feature. Retrospective studies identify patients and review them historically to assess exposure-outcome associations. The retrospective design itself is not problematic; the biased selection method is. Choice E (Sample size) is not an invalidating feature. Inadequate sample size increases the risk of Type II error (false negative), but the primary issue here is the selection bias in who was chosen for the study, not the number of participants. Educational Objective: Understanding ascertainment bias and recognizing how nonrandom selection of study participants can invalidate study conclusions and make results non-generalizable to the target population.
▶Female Reproductive Breast Non-Lymphogranuloma Venereum Chlamydia Trachomatis1 questions
Source: 9A #5
A patient with urethral discharge and dysuria was treated with intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline, with symptom resolution within 2 days. He is sexually active with three female partners without contraception use. His partners were asymptomatic and treated with ceftriaxone intramuscularly but did not fill their doxycycline prescriptions. The patient denies illicit drug use. Examination reveals no genital ulcerations, vesicles, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. HIV antibody testing is negative. A Gram stain of the discharge shows many leukocytes and no bacteria. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's recurrence of symptoms? A) Ceftriaxone-resistant gonococcal infection B) Inappropriate treatment for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection 3 weeks ago C) New infection with Chlamydia trachomatis D) The patient had Chlamydia trachomatis, not Neisseria gonorrhoeae, infection 3 weeks ago E) Reinfection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Correct Answer: C) New infection with Chlamydia trachomatis
This patient has likely acquired a new infection with Chlamydia trachomatis due to unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners and incomplete treatment of his sexual partners. While coinfection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis is common, and combination therapy with intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline or azithromycin is the standard regimen, this patient's partners did not complete their doxycycline prescriptions. The doxycycline component is specifically needed to treat C. trachomatis, as ceftriaxone primarily targets N. gonorrhoeae. Since the partners were asymptomatic but untreated for chlamydia, they likely remained infected and transmitted the organism back to the patient through continued unprotected sexual contact. C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae are the most common causes of sexually transmitted urethritis in men, presenting with urethral discharge and dysuria. C. trachomatis is often asymptomatic, particularly in sexual partners, and causes intracellular infection that may not be visible on Gram stain (which shows leukocytes without bacteria in chlamydial infection). Diagnosis is confirmed with urine nucleic acid amplification testing. Risk factors include adolescence, multiple sexual partners, and absence of barrier contraception. Choice A is incorrect because the patient received appropriate ceftriaxone therapy, and single-dose ceftriaxone adequately treats uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis in most cases. Additionally, N. gonorrhoeae is an extracellular organism visible on Gram stain, and this patient's Gram stain showed no bacteria. Choice B is incorrect because the patient received appropriate diagnostic testing and treatment for N. gonorrhoeae initially. The issue is inadequate treatment coverage for C. trachomatis among his sexual partners. Choice D cannot be assumed because the patient received appropriate diagnostic testing for N. gonorrhoeae initially. While possible, this explanation does not account for why symptoms recurred after appropriate initial treatment. Choice E is unlikely because the patient and his partners received appropriate ceftriaxone treatment for N. gonorrhoeae. While reinfection with gonorrhea is theoretically possible, new C. trachomatis infection is more likely given the incomplete partner treatment with doxycycline and the high prevalence of chlamydial transmission among untreated partners. Key learning points: Empiric combination therapy targeting both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis is standard for suspected STI. All sexual partners must complete both antibiotic components to prevent reinfection. C. trachomatis often remains asymptomatic in partners and causes intracellular infection not visible on Gram stain. Prompt identification and treatment of both organisms prevents spread and complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility.
▶Gastrointestinal System Hepatitis B1 questions
Source: 9A #7
A 25-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of persistent, right-sided, sharp abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting of clear fluid and undigested food. His medications include hydrocodone. On examination, obturator, psoas, and Rovsing signs are negative. Laboratory studies show: Prothrombin time 17.2 sec (INR=1.3), Serum bilirubin total elevated, Alkaline phosphatase 80 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant shows a 13-cm, heterogenous liver. Serum acetaminophen and blood alcohol concentrations are 0 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A. Measurement of alpha-fetoprotein concentration B. Serologic testing for hepatitis C. CT scan of the abdomen D. HIDA scan E. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy F. Liver biopsy
Correct Answer: B. Serologic testing for hepatitis
This young male patient presenting with right-sided abdominal pain, scleral icterus, and an enlarged liver along with marked elevation in AST and ALT enzymes most likely has acute hepatitis B infection. The gold standard for diagnosing hepatitis B infection is positive serologic testing. Hepatitis B is caused by infection of hepatocytes by the hepatitis B virus, a DNA virus transmitted through exposure to bodily fluids. It presents with nonspecific symptoms such as malaise, nausea, and right-sided abdominal pain, often accompanied by jaundice and right upper quadrant tenderness. The patient's clinical presentation—elevated bilirubin, markedly increased liver enzymes (AST, ALT >1000 U/L), tender enlarged liver, and elevated INR—is consistent with acute hepatitis. In cases without fulminant hepatitis, treatment is supportive; severe cases may require nucleotide analogue therapy. The differential diagnosis includes other hepatitis infections, cholecystitis, and appendicitis, but the laboratory findings pointing to hepatic inflammation make serologic testing the appropriate next diagnostic step. Choice A (Alpha-fetoprotein measurement) is used for surveillance and detection of hepatocellular carcinoma, typically in patients with chronic hepatitis B, not for acute diagnosis. Choice C (CT scan of the abdomen) would be useful for evaluating undifferentiated abdominal pain, but serologic testing for hepatitis should be performed first when clinical suspicion is high. Choice D (HIDA scan) is used to dynamically assess the biliary system and gallbladder function, not for hepatic inflammation or viral hepatitis diagnosis. Choice E (Esophagogastroduodenoscopy) evaluates the esophagus, stomach, and small bowel but does not evaluate hepatic pathology. Choice F (Liver biopsy) would be unnecessarily invasive given that serologic testing is the gold standard for diagnosing hepatitis B and does not require tissue confirmation.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Reactive Arthritis1 questions
Source: 9A #8
A patient presents with fever, chills, joint pain, and a sparse rash on arms and trunk for 4 days. Temperature is 38.3°C, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Other joints appear normal. Joint fluid analysis is pending culture. This patient most likely has which of the following types of arthritis? A) Gonococcal B) α-Hemolytic streptococcal C) Psoriatic D) Rheumatoid E) Staphylococcal septic
Correct Answer: A) Gonococcal
Gonococcal arthritis is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with septic arthritis. The clinical presentation of fever, chills, joint pain, and an associated rash are characteristic features of gonococcal arthritis due to disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Evaluation: Patients with suspected septic arthritis require thorough history to identify infection risks, assessment of vital signs for fever/tachycardia, and physical examination findings of limited range of motion with warm, tender, swollen joints. Arthrocentesis with bacterial culture is essential for diagnosis. Definition: Gonococcal arthritis presents with fever, joint effusion, and pain on range of motion in patients with untreated N. gonorrhoeae infection. Joint aspirates typically show leukocytosis with moderate counts around 50,000 leukocytes/mm³ and an often-negative Gram stain because bacteria exist intracellularly within neutrophils. Serum studies show leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR). Definitive testing uses nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT). Treatment: Gonococcal arthritis is treated with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin to cover possible Chlamydia co-infection. Incorrect Answers: Choice B (α-Hemolytic streptococcal arthritis): Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus viridans are examples of α-hemolytic streptococci, but neither is associated with septic arthritis. Choice C (Psoriatic arthritis): Associated with salmon-colored plaques with micaceous scale characteristic of psoriasis, typically involving distal digits. This presentation does not match this patient's acute septic arthritis with fever and rash. Choice D (Rheumatoid arthritis): Presents with insidious-onset arthritis of distal extremities, morning stiffness, fatigue, and weight loss. Commonly involves metacarpophalangeal, proximal interphalangeal, and wrist joints. Not consistent with this acute febrile presentation. Choice E (Staphylococcal septic arthritis): While presenting similarly with fever, joint pain, limited motion, and leukocytosis on aspiration, Gram stain would show gram-positive cocci in clusters, distinguishing it from the typically gram-negative or negative Gram stain findings in gonococcal arthritis. Additionally, the rash is more characteristic of gonococcal disease.
▶Behavioral Health Cocaine Intoxication1 questions
Source: 9A #9
A patient presents with progressive agitation, paranoid delusions about receiving messages from God and the president, checking windows and doors for intruders, and pressured speech. Physical examination reveals moderate psychomotor agitation and mildly pressured speech. He refuses to answer questions about his medical history claiming "it's all confidential." Serum studies show urea nitrogen concentration of 40 mg/dL and creatinine concentration of 2.5 mg/dL. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia and mild ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads. Use of which of the following substances is the most likely cause of this patient's condition? A) Alcohol B) Cocaine C) Ecstasy (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine) D) Heroin E) γ-Hydroxybutyrate F) Ketamine
Correct Answer: B) Cocaine
This patient's presentation is consistent with cocaine intoxication, a sympathomimetic toxidrome characterized by agitation, paranoia, chest discomfort with ECG ST-segment changes, tachycardia, hypertension, and pressured speech. Cocaine mechanism: Cocaine blocks presynaptic reuptake of dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine. Excess dopamine leads to addiction, hallucinations, and paranoia; excess serotonin causes euphoria; excess norepinephrine activates sympathetic adrenoreceptors causing tachycardia, hypertension, and pupillary dilation. Cocaine causes coronary vasospasm and/or atherosclerotic plaque rupture, explaining the ST-segment elevation and chest discomfort. Key features supporting cocaine use: mood symptoms (agitation, paranoia), hyperadrenergic signs (tachycardia, presumed hypertension, ECG changes), and acute coronary syndrome presentation. Incorrect choices: - Alcohol: CNS depressant causing depression, sedation, ataxia, and slurred speech; does not cause hyperadrenergic state or ECG changes - Ecstasy: Stimulant causing euphoria and agitation but characteristic effects include bruxism, diaphoresis, and blurry vision; associated with hyponatremia, not coronary vasospasm - Heroin: Opioid causing sedation, respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils, and constipation; opposite of this patient's presentation - γ-Hydroxybutyrate: CNS depressant causing disinhibition, amnesia, sedation, and coma; does not cause hyperadrenergic state - Ketamine: Causes hallucinations, dissociation, and nystagmus with hyperadrenergic vital signs, but does not characteristically cause coronary vasospasm and patient lacks nystagmus Treatment involves supportive care and benzodiazepines to counterbalance hyperadrenergic symptoms. If acute coronary syndrome is present, appropriate cardiac management is indicated. The diagnosis is clinical and supported by toxicology testing.
▶Social Sciences Informed consent to treatment1 questions
Source: 9A #11
A patient who speaks only Spanish is awake and oriented but in moderate respiratory distress due to an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Discuss a DNR order with the patient when he is clinically stabilized B) Document the discussion with the daughter in the patient's chart and implement a DNR order C) Make the patient's status a full code D) Use an interpreter to discuss a DNR order with the patient and document the patient's decision in his chart
Correct Answer: D) Use an interpreter to discuss a DNR order with the patient and document the patient's decision in his chart
An alert and oriented patient must be included in conversations regarding medical decision making and life-support intervention preferences. When a language barrier exists between physician and patient, a medical interpreter should be used to ensure neutral and accurate communication of these complex preferences. This is especially important in this case given the patient's increased risk for intubation due to COPD exacerbation. Clarifying the patient's wishes while alert and oriented, prior to any emergency, is critical. Choice A is incorrect because while discussing the DNR order after clinical stabilization may seem prudent, clarification of preferences with the alert and oriented patient must occur promptly, and an interpreter is necessary for accurate communication. Choice B is incorrect because the patient is competent and alert; his own wishes should be obtained directly through an interpreter rather than relying on the daughter's input or making decisions without the patient's participation. Family members should not substitute for the patient's own preferences when the patient can communicate. Choice C is incorrect because making the patient a full code without discussing his preferences violates his autonomy and right to participate in medical decision making. The patient's preferences for life-support interventions must be elicited and documented. The key concept is that life-support decision making requires thorough conversation using professional medical interpreters when language barriers exist. This is best practice to ensure the patient's autonomous wishes are accurately documented and honored.
▶Social Sciences Healthcare proxy designation1 questions
Source: 9A #16
A patient with end-stage renal disease has been receiving hemodialysis for the past 5 years. On examination, he is diffusely weak and spastic and disoriented, unable to speak or identify family members. Placement in a nursing home is being pursued. His wife, who is his health care proxy, wishes to discontinue maintenance hemodialysis. His primary care physician, neurologist, and nephrologist involved in his care agree with this decision. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Obtain a court order to determine whether maintenance hemodialysis may be terminated B) Obtain an ethics team consultation and follow their decision concerning discontinuation of maintenance hemodialysis C) Discontinue maintenance hemodialysis as his wife wishes D) [Not fully specified in source material] E) [Not fully specified in source material]
Correct Answer: C) Discontinue maintenance hemodialysis as his wife wishes
A healthcare proxy, also known as a durable power of attorney or health care agent, is someone who has been legally designated as a representative to make healthcare decisions for a patient when they are unable to do so. In this case, the patient's wife is his designated health care proxy. Since the patient lacks the ability to make medical decisions due to being disoriented and unable to communicate or identify family members, his wife has the authority to make medical decisions on his behalf. This authority includes the ability to discontinue maintenance hemodialysis. The most appropriate next step is to honor the wife's wishes and discontinue the hemodialysis treatment, as she is the designated healthcare proxy and has the legal and ethical authority to make this decision. Choice A is incorrect because a court order is not necessary when a healthcare proxy has already been designated. The wife's designation as healthcare proxy gives her the authority to make medical decisions without requiring court involvement. Choice B is incorrect because while ethics consultation can be helpful in complex cases, it is not the most appropriate next step when a healthcare proxy has already been designated and is ready to make a decision. The healthcare proxy's decision takes precedence and does not require an ethics committee to override or validate it. The key concept is that a healthcare proxy, which may be established through advance directives, is an individual who has been legally allowed to make medical decisions on a patient's behalf when the patient is unable to do so. This includes decisions about life-sustaining treatments such as hemodialysis.
▶Endocrine System Diabetic neuropathy1 questions
Source: 9A #17
A patient with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with sensory abnormalities consistent with peripheral neuropathy. Her current medications include lisinopril, metformin, metoprolol, and glipizide. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 35 kg/m². Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. Examination shows decreased sensation in a stocking-glove distribution. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Begin a protein-restricted diet B) Exercise regularly C) Add an angiotensin II receptor blocking agent to the regimen D) Add a calcium-channel blocking agent to the regimen E) Add long-acting insulin to the regimen F) Discontinue metoprolol
Correct Answer: E) Add long-acting insulin to the regimen
Diabetic neuropathy is a microvascular complication of long-standing diabetes mellitus that typically presents in a stocking-glove distribution of the hands and feet, with symptoms including burning pain and decreased sensation in the extremities. Chronic hyperglycemia leads to glycosylation of axon proteins and sorbitol-related osmotic damage to neurons, causing progressive sensory and motor neuropathy that primarily affects distal nerves initially and progresses proximally over time. The condition impairs healing in distal extremities and decreases awareness of injuries, increasing foot trauma risk. Motor innervation can lead to muscle wasting and decreased deep tendon reflexes. The most effective way to prevent diabetic neuropathy development is to ensure adequate blood glucose control with a goal hemoglobin A1c of less than 7.0%. While type 2 diabetes mellitus is initially managed with oral antihyperglycemics, injectable insulin should be added to the patient's regimen if blood glucose concentrations are not adequately controlled on one to two oral medications. This patient is clearly on inadequate oral regimen (metformin and glipizide) and requires insulin intensification. Choice A (protein-restricted diet) is incorrect as diet modifications like the Mediterranean diet are helpful but are not specifically protein-restricted and are less effective than insulin for preventing neuropathy. Choice B (exercise regularly) is incorrect; while regular exercise improves glycemic control, weight loss, and cardiovascular outcomes, expeditious management of poorly-controlled hyperglycemia with insulin is more critical. Choices C and D (adding angiotensin II receptor blocker or calcium-channel blocker) are incorrect; although the patient's blood pressure is suboptimal at 146/88 mm Hg (goal <130/80 mm Hg for diabetic patients) and these agents may reduce retinopathy, nephropathy, and cardiovascular complications, they do not reduce diabetic neuropathy risk. Choice F (discontinue metoprolol) is incorrect as the patient's hypertension remains poorly controlled and metoprolol should not be removed; this medication does not increase neuropathy risk.
▶Cardiovascular System Aortic Valve Stenosis1 questions
Source: 9A #18
An 82-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 3-day history of worsening shortness of breath. She is now unable to walk because of the dyspnea and has needed to use three pillows for sleeping. She has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure, and osteoarthritis of the knees. Her medications are lisinopril, metoprolol, furosemide, simvastatin, and acetaminophen. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 154/98 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Examination shows jugular venous distention 6 cm above the sternal angle. Crackles are heard over the lower halves of both lung fields posteriorly. On cardiac examination, a grade 3/6, harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that decreases with Valsalva maneuver is heard best at the upper right sternal border; S2 is soft. The point of maximal impulse is sustained at the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Pitting edema is present to the middle of the shins. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly, small pleural effusions, and bilateral pulmonary vascular congestion. Echocardiography is most likely to show which of the following abnormalities? A) Stiffened, narrowed, calcified aortic valve with limited opening B) Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve C) Prolapsed mitral leaflets with regurgitation D) Patent foramen ovale E) Ventricular septal defect
Correct Answer: A) Stiffened, narrowed, calcified aortic valve with limited opening
Aortic stenosis (AS) results from fibrosis and calcification of the aortic valve, causing narrowing and stiffening. This patient presents with classic features of severe AS: a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border that decreases with Valsalva maneuver, signs of left-sided heart failure (dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary crackles), cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion and pleural effusions on imaging, displaced point of maximal impulse, and soft S2. The chronic increased afterload from the fixed obstruction causes left ventricular hypertrophy and subsequent heart failure with pulmonary edema and pleural effusion. Echocardiography definitively diagnoses AS and reveals a stiffened, narrowed, calcified valve with limited opening, a pressure gradient across the valve, and increased flow velocity through the valve. Choice B (Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy) is less common than AS in older patients and does not typically present with signs of heart failure and cardiomegaly; HOCM more frequently presents with sudden symptoms during exertion or dehydration. Choice C (Mitral regurgitation) presents with a holosystolic murmur best heard at the fourth or fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line with radiation to the left axilla, not a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right upper sternal border. Choice D (Patent foramen ovale) is an atrial septal defect that may present with a subtle diastolic murmur, not the systolic murmur heard in this patient. Choice E (Ventricular septal defect) is characterized by a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border and is most common in children as a congenital defect. The combination of heart failure signs, older age, and the characteristic crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the upper right sternal border that decreases with Valsalva maneuver definitively points to aortic stenosis.
▶Endocrine System Thyrotoxicosis1 questions
Source: 9A #21
A 45-year-old woman presents with palpitations, anxiety, and heat intolerance. She has a history of hypertension, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, hyperlipidemia, major depressive disorder, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She takes enalapril, amiodarone, simvastatin, paroxetine, and metformin. She appears anxious and diaphoretic. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 165/90 mm Hg. Physical examination discloses periorbital edema and 1+ pretibial edema. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Amiodarone B) Enalapril C) Metformin D) Paroxetine E) Simvastatin
Correct Answer: A) Amiodarone
This patient presents with classic signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism, including palpitations, anxiety, heat intolerance, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and edema. Of the medications listed, amiodarone is the most likely cause of thyroid dysfunction and thyrotoxicosis. Amiodarone is a potent antiarrhythmic agent with high iodine content that can cause both amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) and amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism. The diagnosis of hyperthyroidism is confirmed by decreased or undetectable TSH with elevated free thyroxine (FT4) and/or triiodothyronine (T3). Treatment typically includes methimazole and/or glucocorticoids, with consideration for discontinuing amiodarone. Prevention involves minimizing cumulative amiodarone dose and avoiding use in patients with pre-existing thyroid disease. Choice B (Enalapril): An ACE inhibitor used for hypertension management. While common adverse effects include dry cough, hypotension, and renal dysfunction, enalapril does not affect thyroid function and would not cause hyperthyroidism. Choice C (Metformin): A first-line antidiabetic medication. Its adverse effects include nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, and rarely lactic acidosis. Thyrotoxicosis is not classically associated with metformin use. Choice D (Paroxetine): A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor used for anxiety and depression. Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, sexual dysfunction, and rarely serotonin syndrome. While paroxetine can cause various side effects, amiodarone is far more likely to induce hyperthyroidism in this clinical context. Choice E (Simvastatin): A statin used for hyperlipidemia management. Its primary adverse effects involve myopathy with muscle pain and stiffness. Statins are not associated with hyperthyroidism or thyroid dysfunction.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Von Willebrand disease1 questions
Source: 9A #22
A patient presents with a lifelong history of easy bruising and had protracted bleeding with a tooth extraction 2 years ago. Her mother has a history of similar symptoms. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Platelet count: 190,000/mm³ Bleeding time: 12 min Prothrombin time: 12 sec (INR=1) Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hemostatic abnormality? A) Autoimmune thrombocytopenia B) Bone marrow suppression C) Hemolytic-uremic syndrome D) Hemophilia E) Hypersplenism F) von Willebrand disease
Correct Answer: F) von Willebrand disease
von Willebrand disease is one of the most common hereditary bleeding disorders caused by quantitative or qualitative abnormalities of von Willebrand factor (vWF). This patient's presentation is classic for von Willebrand disease: lifelong history of easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after tooth extraction, and family history of similar symptoms (autosomal dominant inheritance). Laboratory findings are characteristic with normal platelet count (190,000/mm³), normal prothrombin time, normal bleeding time, and increased partial thromboplastin time (PTT, not shown but implied by the coagulation abnormality). vWF is essential for platelet adhesion and binds platelets to subendothelial collagen during primary hemostasis. Deficiencies cause platelet dysfunction presenting with mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia). Confirmatory testing includes assays for vWF activity and antigen concentrations, ristocetin cofactor activity, and platelet aggregation studies. Treatment depends on severity and may include desmopressin, which promotes release of vWF from endothelial cells. Choice A (Autoimmune thrombocytopenia) is incorrect because the platelet count is normal; thrombocytopenic disorders present with reduced platelet counts. Choice B (Bone marrow suppression) is incorrect because the platelet count is normal and the patient does not have pancytopenia. Choice C (Hemolytic-uremic syndrome) is incorrect because it classically presents with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. This patient has normal platelets and no systemic illness or diarrheal prodrome. Choice D (Hemophilia) is incorrect because hemophilia typically presents with deep tissue bleeding such as joint bleeding (hemarthrosis) and intramuscular hematoma, whereas von Willebrand disease presents with mucocutaneous bleeding. Choice E (Hypersplenism) is incorrect because hypersplenism causes bleeding through thrombocytopenia from splenic sequestration of platelets; this patient does not have thrombocytopenia.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Disseminated intravascular coagulation1 questions
Source: 9A #27
A 60-year-old woman presents with fever, tachycardia, right flank tenderness, and altered mental status. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, Hematocrit 30.6%, Leukocyte count 21,200/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 68%, Bands 20%, Lymphocytes 10%, Monocytes 2%, thrombocytopenia, Prothrombin time (INR=1.6), Partial thromboplastin time 40 sec. A blood smear shows numerous fragmented erythrocytes and helmet cells. Additional laboratory studies are most likely to show which of the following? A) Decreased reptilase time B) Decreased thrombin time C) Increased fibrin degradation products D) Increased partial thromboplastin time E) Increased serum fibrinogen concentration
Correct Answer: C) Increased fibrin degradation products
This patient presents with fever, tachycardia, right flank tenderness, and altered mental status most suggestive of sepsis secondary to pyelonephritis. The laboratory findings of thrombocytopenia, increased prothrombin time, and a blood smear with fragmented erythrocytes (schistocytes) and helmet cells are diagnostic of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The most likely finding in additional laboratory studies would be increased fibrin degradation products (fibrin split products), which reflects ongoing thrombin generation and consumption of coagulation factors. DIC results from thrombin generation and tissue factor exposure, which widely activate the coagulation cascade throughout the vasculature. This activation results in coagulation factor proteins occluding the arterial and venous intravascular space, leading to platelet microthrombosis and mechanical shearing of red blood cells. Common triggers include severe and widespread burns, infection/sepsis, trauma, amniotic fluid embolism, and malignancy. The characteristic laboratory findings in DIC include thrombocytopenia, prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin time, increased fibrin split products, decreased fibrinogen, and increased D-dimer. Choice A (Decreased reptilase time) is incorrect. Reptilase time is a laboratory study that measures the function of fibrinogen. In DIC, fibrinogen is consumed, leading to decreased fibrinogen concentrations and therefore an increased (not decreased) reptilase time. Choice B (Decreased thrombin time) is incorrect. Thrombin time represents the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin. In DIC due to consumption of fibrinogen, the thrombin time would be increased (not decreased). Choice D (Increased partial thromboplastin time) is incorrect. While the partial thromboplastin time is already elevated at 40 seconds in this patient's presentation, it is not the most characteristic finding that would be expected in additional laboratory studies specifically looking for further evidence of DIC. Choice E (Increased serum fibrinogen concentration) is incorrect. In DIC, fibrinogen is consumed as it is activated and converted to fibrin throughout the vasculature, resulting in decreased (not increased) fibrinogen concentrations. Treatment is supportive and includes blood product and factor replacement, with the mainstay focused on treating the triggering conditions—in this case, antibiotic treatment for pyelonephritis. The differential diagnosis for DIC includes hemolytic uremic syndrome and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, but in this patient with septic shock secondary to pyelonephritis, DIC is the most likely diagnosis.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Vascular Dementia1 questions
Source: 9A #28
A 4-year-old woman is brought to the office. She has had trouble walking because of weakness in an extremity; the weakness later resolves spontaneously. She can no longer remember names and becomes confused when in unfamiliar settings. She is no longer interested in socializing with friends. She is oriented to place and self only, and recall is 1 out of 3 objects at 1 minute. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease B) Dementia, Alzheimer type C) Hepatolenticular degeneration (Wilson disease) D) Multi-infarct (vascular) dementia E) Parkinson disease
Correct Answer: D) Multi-infarct (vascular) dementia
Multi-infarct (vascular) dementia presents with a stepwise cognitive decline occurring over a chronic time course, generally in association with recognized stroke or transient ischemic attack symptoms. This patient, with episodes of trouble speaking and walking, has likely experienced multiple transient ischemic attacks leading to loss of cognitive and executive function. Vascular dementia is a clinical diagnosis featuring stepwise cognitive decline following cerebral infarctions that have been either overt, transient, or silent. MRI supports diagnosis, showing acute, subacute, or chronic infarction with resultant loss of cerebral parenchyma. A hallmark of vascular dementia is the existence of persistent neurologic deficits; however, some patients may have a normal neurologic examination apart from executive function testing if they had small or multiple strokes. In this case, the patient has had multiple episodes of difficulty speaking and walking, hyperreflexia (indicating upper motor neuron disease), and disorientation, suggestive of chronic and recurrent cerebral infarctions. Prevention and treatment focus on minimizing stroke risk factors. Patients without contraindications should be treated with antiplatelet agents and statins to minimize stroke risk, and those with atrial fibrillation or other hypercoagulable states should receive anticoagulants. Risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus should be managed. Once vascular dementia occurs, there is no way to reverse the condition; however, treatment to prevent further cerebral infarctions should be initiated. Physical and occupational therapy referrals may help as lost executive function may be regained with appropriate intervention in some cases. Choice A (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease) is incorrect. This is a prion disease caused by a misfolded protein with disease progression through aggregation and misfolding of prion peptides in the central nervous system, leading to progressive neurologic deterioration including myoclonus followed by rapid decline and death usually within 1 year of symptom onset. This patient's chronic presentation argues against this diagnosis. Choice B (Dementia, Alzheimer type) is not the best choice. Although it is the most common cause of dementia in older persons and presents with cognitive decline over a chronic timeframe, this patient's concurrent neurologic deficits (episodes of weakness, difficulty speaking and walking, hyperreflexia) argue for vascular dementia as a more likely cause. Choice C (Hepatolenticular degeneration/Wilson disease) is incorrect. This results from impaired metabolism of copper and presents with liver dysfunction and neuropsychologic impairment including parkinsonism, ataxia, tremors, dystonia, dementia, hallucinations, and personality changes. This patient does not have symptoms of liver dysfunction or parkinsonism. Choice E (Parkinson disease) is incorrect. This neurologic syndrome features bradykinesia, resting tremors, rigidity (frequently associated with cogwheeling), and postural instability. While dementia is a common endpoint of Parkinson disease, this patient does not have the characteristic motor symptoms of Parkinson disease, making vascular dementia more likely. Note: The fragment about DIC and serum factor V and fibrinogen concentrations appears to be from an unrelated question and has been excluded from this analysis.
▶Musculoskeletal System Leiomyosarcoma1 questions
Source: 9A #31
A previously healthy 42-year-old woman comes to the physician 10 weeks after she noticed a painful bruise on her right thigh. She has difficulty walking because of the pain. She has no history of trauma to the right leg. She recently underwent an uncomplicated operative dental procedure. Examination of the right lower extremity shows a mildly tender mass with central areas of necrosis on ultrasonography. Muscle strength and sensation are normal. Platelet count is 150,000/mm³, prothrombin time is 14 sec (INR=1.1), and partial thromboplastin time is 25 sec. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Measurement of serum factor VIII concentration B) Measurement of serum factor IX concentration C) X-ray of the right femur D) MRI of the right thigh E) Excisional biopsy
Correct Answer: D) MRI of the right thigh
This patient presents with a gradually enlarging, mildly tender mass in the right thigh with ultrasonography showing central areas of necrosis, findings highly suggestive of a soft tissue sarcoma. An MRI of the right thigh is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis to characterize the soft tissue mass, assess its extent, and guide further management. Soft tissue sarcomas are a heterogenous group of tumors derived from mesenchymal tissue such as skeletal or smooth muscle, adipose, or fibrous tissue. While a gradually enlarging, painless mass within an extremity is the most common presentation, this patient's tender mass with imaging findings of central necrosis is also concerning for sarcoma. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (previously known as malignant fibrous histiocytoma) is the most common type, and metastasis tends to occur via hematogenous spread rather than lymphatic spread. Choice A (Measurement of serum factor VIII concentration) is incorrect. Hemophilia A is an inherited condition of factor VIII deficiency that presents with recurrent hemarthrosis and cutaneous bleeding early in childhood. It would present with a very prolonged partial thromboplastin time and very decreased or absent serum factor VIII concentration, none of which are present in this patient. Choice B (Measurement of serum factor IX concentration) is incorrect. Hemophilia B is an X-linked bleeding disorder caused by factor IX deficiency, leading to increased partial thromboplastin time. While this could explain bruising, the patient's coagulation studies are normal, and the imaging findings of a mass with central necrosis point to a structural lesion, not a bleeding disorder. Choice C (X-ray of the right femur) is incorrect. X-rays are useful in evaluating bony lesions but are not optimal for evaluating soft tissue masses. MRI provides superior soft tissue contrast and characterization. Choice E (Excisional biopsy) is incorrect. While a needle biopsy may be performed later for pathological evaluation and definitive diagnosis, the most appropriate next step in diagnosis is imaging with MRI to fully characterize the mass before biopsy. Educational Objective: Recognize that soft tissue sarcomas typically present as painless or mildly tender masses in the extremities and that MRI is the imaging modality of choice for characterizing soft tissue lesions and guiding further diagnostic and therapeutic decisions.
▶Endocrine System Diabetes insipidus1 questions
Source: 9A #32
A patient on postoperative day 3 after neurosurgery has intravenous fluids discontinued and a regular diet started. Morning laboratory studies show hypernatremia. Intravenous administration of 0.45% saline is resumed. Twelve hours later, his serum sodium concentration is 144 mEq/L. Intravenous fluids are stopped, and he does not consume any liquids overnight. The following morning, his serum sodium concentration is 152 mEq/L. Which of the following sets of laboratory values is most likely in this patient? | | Serum Osmolality (mOsmol/kg H2O) | Urine Osmolality (mOsmol/kg H2O) | Urine Sodium (mEq/L) | |---|---|---|---| | A | 296 | 206 | High | | B | 298 | 806 | 38 | | C | 296 | 300 | High | | D | 315 | 200 | 30 | | E | 315 | 200 | 110 | | F | 345 | 300 | 38 |
Correct Answer: D) Serum Osmolality 315 mOsmol/kg H2O, Urine Osmolality 200 mOsmol/kg H2O, Urine Sodium 30 mEq/L
Diabetes insipidus may occur as a complication of neurosurgical operations, especially those involving the pituitary gland. The clinical presentation in this case—progressive hypernatremia despite attempts to correct it with hypotonic fluid administration, followed by further hypernatremia when fluids are withheld—is classic for central diabetes insipidus. Pathophysiology: Diabetes insipidus results from inadequate secretion of ADH (vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary, leading to an inability to absorb an appropriate amount of free water. The main physiologic function of ADH is to reclaim water, thereby maintaining serum osmolarity and sodium balance in addition to plasma volume. ADH binds vasopressin-2 (V2) receptors of the late distal convoluted tubule and collecting tubule cells, resulting in the insertion of aquaporin channels in the luminal surface. This increases free water absorption and allows tight regulation of serum osmolality. In ADH deficiency, decreased concentrations of aquaporin channels are inserted within the principal cells of the collecting tubule, leading to an inability to absorb adequate amounts of free water.
