This results in: - Increased serum osmolality (due to free water loss): Expected osmolality >300 mOsmol/kg - Dilute urine with low osmolality: Inability to concentrate urine results in osmolality typically <300 mOsmol/kg - Decreased urine sodium: Dilute urine has low solute content including sodium Choice A (296/206/High): Serum osmolality is normal, which is inconsistent with progressive hypernatremia to 152 mEq/L. Choice B (298/806/38): Urine osmolality is very high, suggesting normal or enhanced ADH function. This would be seen in appropriate responses to hypernatremia (SIADH or normal response), not diabetes insipidus. Choice C (296/300/High): Serum osmolality is normal and urine osmolality is too high for diabetes insipidus. Choice D (315/200/30): Elevated serum osmolality consistent with hypernatremia, dilute urine with low osmolality reflecting inability to concentrate urine, and low urine sodium. This matches diabetes insipidus. Choice E (315/200/110): While serum and urine osmolality are appropriate, urine sodium is elevated. In diabetes insipidus with free water loss, urine sodium would be diluted out and decreased, not elevated. Choice F (345/300/38): Urine osmolality is inappropriately high for diabetes insipidus, suggesting retained ADH responsiveness. The correct answer is D because it demonstrates the characteristic laboratory pattern of diabetes insipidus: increased serum osmolality reflecting free water depletion and hypernatremia, dilute urine reflecting the inability to concentrate urine due to ADH deficiency, and decreased urine sodium reflecting the dilute nature of the urine.
▶Renal Urinary System Nephrolithiasis1 questions
Source: 9A #35
A patient presents with severe right lower abdomen and groin pain. She denies fever, rectal bleeding, pain with urination, vomiting, diarrhea, or vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and was normal. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F). Abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds and voluntary guarding of the right lower quadrant. Pelvic examination shows no cervical motion tenderness or adnexal masses. Stool test for occult blood is negative. Laboratory studies show urine with 3+ blood and 8-10 RBC/hpf. Serum pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Blood cultures B) Urine culture C) X-ray of the abdomen D) CT scan of the abdomen E) Colonoscopy F) Cystoscopy
Correct Answer: D) CT scan of the abdomen
Nephrolithiasis or ureterolithiasis describes formation of calculi within the urinary collecting system (kidney or ureteral stones). The typical presentation includes severe, intermittent, sharp flank pain with either gross or microscopic hematuria, leukocytosis, and occasionally evidence of concomitant urinary tract infection. This patient's clinical presentation and urinalysis findings (3+ hematuria) are classic for urolithiasis. Calcium-containing stones are most common, though stones may also be composed of cystine, struvite, and uric acid. While abdominal x-rays were traditionally used for diagnosis, urate stones are radiolucent and would not be visualized on plain film. Noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is now the preferred imaging modality for definitive diagnosis of urolithiasis due to superior availability and sensitivity. Choice A (Blood cultures) is incorrect because the patient lacks fever and other signs of infection despite mild leukocytosis. Choice B (Urine culture) is not appropriate as the hematuria is most likely from urolithiasis rather than urinary tract infection. Choice C (X-ray of abdomen) is suboptimal because radiolucent urate stones would not be visualized. Choice E (Colonoscopy) is unnecessary as stool occult blood is negative and urolithiasis is the likely diagnosis. Choice F (Cystoscopy) may be used in combination with ureteroscopy for evaluation and treatment but is not the appropriate diagnostic first step. Acute management depends on stone size and location; stones larger than 6 mm often require intervention as they are unlikely to pass spontaneously. For smaller stones in clinically stable patients, treatment includes oral hydration and analgesia. Risk for nephrolithiasis may be decreased with increased fluid intake and dietary modifications.
▶Renal Urinary System Urinary Incontinence1 questions
Source: 9A #36
An 82-year-old woman with Meniere disease, hypertension, and mild generalized anxiety disorder comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. Several years ago, she had interstitial cystitis. She reports good control of her anxiety and no dizziness or problems with hearing. She notes that during the past 8 months, she has experienced occasional urinary leakage. Her medications are atenolol, diltiazem, and buspirone. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol, but she drinks one cup of coffee daily. She walks 1 mile daily for exercise and enjoys relaxing afterward in a hot tub. Her blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's urinary incontinence? A. Adverse effect of diltiazem B. Diuretic effect of caffeine C. Recurrent interstitial cystitis D. Urinary tract infection E. Normal age-related changes
Correct Answer: E. Normal age-related changes
Normal age-related changes are the most likely cause of this patient's urinary incontinence. Stress incontinence is common in older female patients due to weakness of the muscles and connective tissues of the pelvic floor. With age, connective tissue loses tone as collagen degrades and muscle atrophies, resulting in weakness of the pelvic floor, urinary bladder, and sphincters, which can cause stress incontinence—loss of urine with increased intra-abdominal pressure, such as when laughing or coughing. Stress incontinence is commonly associated with urethral hypermobility, as evidenced by deviation greater than 30 degrees from the horizontal of an inserted cotton-tipped applicator with straining. The diagnosis is made on a clinical basis. In female patients, stress incontinence arises from pelvic floor weakness due to aging, multiparity, obesity, connective tissue disease, and urethral or cystoceles. This weakness compromises the support of pelvic structures including the uterus, bladder, urethra, and rectum. Increased abdominal pressure causes the vesicourethral junction to move out of its normal position, preventing sphincter closure and resulting in urine leakage. Choice A (Adverse effect of diltiazem): Diltiazem, a calcium channel blocker used for arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, has adverse effects such as light-headedness, hypotension, and bradycardia. Diltiazem has a primary effect on cardiac calcium channels and is not commonly recognized to influence the urinary bladder or micturition. Choice B (Diuretic effect of caffeine): While caffeine is a recognized diuretic, this patient drinks only one cup of coffee daily and does not report symptoms following caffeine consumption in a clear time course pattern. Choice C (Recurrent interstitial cystitis): Interstitial cystitis presents with suprapubic pain and lower urinary symptoms such as frequency and urgency. Though this patient has a history of interstitial cystitis, she does not currently report any such symptoms. Choice D (Urinary tract infection): UTI presents with dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, suprapubic pain, and may include discolored or foul-smelling urine. While fever is uncommon in older patients with lower UTI, this patient does not present with any other symptoms suggestive of urinary tract infection. Her laboratory studies are within reference ranges, further excluding this diagnosis. Educational Objective: Recognize that stress incontinence due to normal age-related pelvic floor weakness is the most common cause of urinary incontinence in elderly women and distinguish it from incontinence caused by infection, medication effects, or inflammatory conditions based on clinical presentation.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Protein-Calorie Malnutrition1 questions
Source: 9A #37
A 72-year-old man presents with a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss over the past year. He says that he has not been trying to lose weight. He has not had nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. He has osteoarthritis of the hips, which causes pain when arising from a chair or with prolonged walking. There is no family history of serious illness. His only medication is a multivitamin, and he has no known allergies. He lives alone, enjoys home projects, and drinks one to two beers weekly. He appears comfortable. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 62 kg (137 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m². Examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he states that he misses his wife greatly but continues to socialize with friends and remains active. He recalls two of three words after 5 minutes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's weight loss? A) Body image perception B) Major depressive disorder C) Memory difficulties D) Poor diet/inadequate nutritional intake E) Proximal muscle symptoms
Correct Answer: D) Poor diet/inadequate nutritional intake
This patient presents with a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss most suggestive of malnutrition. The cause of poor diet in older individuals is often multifactorial: eating prepared food, living alone, and skipping meals are all risk factors present in this patient. While medical causes such as malignancy and endocrinopathies must be ruled out, poor diet is the most likely cause of this patient's weight loss. Choice A (Body image perception) is incorrect. This patient does not show any signs of body dysmorphia or poor body image perception. Choice B (Major depressive disorder) is incorrect. This patient does not have a depressed mood and does not meet criteria for major depressive disorder. He continues to socialize with friends and remains active, which are inconsistent with major depressive disorder. Choice C (Memory difficulties) is incorrect. While this patient may have mild cognitive decline based on recalling two of three words after 5 minutes, this is not the most likely cause of his weight loss. Choice E (Proximal muscle symptoms) is incorrect. While this patient may be less active due to proximal muscle symptoms from osteoarthritis, poor diet is most likely to be the primary cause of his weight loss. Evaluation: Malnutrition in the older population has complex and multifactorial causes. Insufficient intake can present with unintentional weight loss and can overlap in presentation with frailty and functional impairment. The gold standard for diagnosis is excellent history taking and evaluation to rule out other conditions that may present similarly, such as malignancy. In this case, risk factors for inadequate nutritional intake include living alone (since his wife's passing), likely difficulty preparing meals due to hip osteoarthritis, and possible social isolation related to mobility limitations. Prevention of malnutrition in older individuals involves weight check-ins at primary care appointments, identification of risk factors, maintaining or developing adequate social support, and ensuring access to nutrient-dense food. First-line treatment for malnutrition is addressing risk factors and mitigating them as best as possible, dietary counseling, and providing oral nutritional supplementations if needed. It is crucial in a patient with unintentional weight loss to ensure they do not have a 'can't miss' diagnosis such as malignancy, endocrinopathy, or chronic infection.
▶Musculoskeletal System Adhesive capsulitis of shoulder1 questions
Source: 9A #42
A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of moderate pain and stiffness of her left shoulder for 6 weeks. The stiffness prevents her from raising her arm over her head, and she now has difficulty dressing and is unable to wash her own hair. She has type 1 diabetes mellitus well controlled with insulin. She takes no other medications. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (154 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m². On examination, the left shoulder is nontender. Passive glenohumeral motion with scapular stabilization is markedly decreased compared with range of motion of the right shoulder. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. X-rays of the left shoulder show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Observation only B) Physical therapy C) MRI of the shoulder D) Opioid therapy E) Arthroscopy of the shoulder
Correct Answer: B) Physical therapy
This patient presents with adhesive capsulitis, characterized by progressive development of severe limitations of both active and passive shoulder motion. The key clinical findings are markedly decreased passive glenohumeral range of motion in the setting of type 1 diabetes mellitus (a known risk factor) and normal imaging studies, making adhesive capsulitis the most likely diagnosis. Adhesive capsulitis typically involves an initial phase of severe pain followed by months of progressive loss of motion in all planes, followed by a long recovery phase. The most appropriate next step in management is physical therapy and range of motion exercises, which have been shown to improve range of motion and functional abilities. Treatment is typically conservative, with corticosteroid injections available for moderate-to-severe pain to facilitate physical therapy participation. Surgery is reserved for those with severe persistent range of motion deficits around 1 year of failed conservative treatment. Observation only (Choice A) is incorrect because although adhesive capsulitis is often self-limited, physical therapy actively improves range of motion and functional outcomes, making it the preferred initial approach. MRI of the shoulder (Choice C) is not indicated. This patient has markedly decreased passive glenohumeral range of motion without history of trauma and with normal x-rays. MRI would not change management in suspected adhesive capsulitis. Opioid therapy (Choice D) is not the most appropriate next step. Initial pain management should consist of NSAIDs or acetaminophen. Alternatively, glenohumeral joint and/or subacromial bursa corticosteroid injections are more appropriate options to facilitate physical therapy participation. Arthroscopy of the shoulder (Choice E) is incorrect because adhesive capsulitis is often self-limiting, and physical therapy is the appropriate initial management. Surgical intervention is not indicated at this stage.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Pernicious Anemia1 questions
Source: 9A #43
A patient with a history of total gastrectomy five years ago presents with macrocytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated serum methylmalonic acid (0.08-0.56 μmol/L), and borderline decreased vitamin B12 (cobalamin) concentration of 180 pg/mL (N=160-950 pg/mL). She is otherwise healthy, takes no medications, has never smoked, and has a BMI of 20 kg/m². Physical examination shows a well-healed midline surgical scar with no masses, no jugular venous distention, normal cardiopulmonary examination, and no edema. ECG and chest x-ray are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time? A) Intravenous iron supplementation B) Oral pyridoxine supplementation C) Subcutaneous erythropoietin D) Intramuscular cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12) E) Oral iron supplementation
Correct Answer: D) Intramuscular cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12)
A history of gastrectomy with macrocytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, increased serum methylmalonic acid concentration, and borderline decreased vitamin B12 (cobalamin) concentration is consistent with pernicious anemia secondary to surgical resection of the stomach. Pernicious anemia arises due to loss of gastric parietal cells from autoimmune disease or surgical resection, leading to deficiency of intrinsic factor. Intrinsic factor is necessary for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Without intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 deficiency develops, resulting in megaloblastic anemia. The diagnosis is confirmed by elevated serum methylmalonic acid (a marker of B12 deficiency) and the clinical presentation following gastrectomy. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy is lifelong parenteral vitamin B12 replacement, typically given subcutaneously or intramuscularly. Oral supplementation is ineffective in pernicious anemia because the defect is in intestinal absorption due to lack of intrinsic factor, not dietary intake. Incorrect Answers: Choice A & E (Intravenous and oral iron supplementation): Iron deficiency presents with microcytic anemia, not macrocytic. Iron supplementation does not affect vitamin B12 concentrations or methylmalonic acid levels. Choice B (Oral pyridoxine): Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation is used for vitamin B6 deficiency prevention (e.g., in patients taking isoniazid), not for B12 deficiency. Choice C (Subcutaneous erythropoietin): Erythropoietin is indicated for anemia of chronic kidney disease stemming from decreased erythropoietin production by the kidneys, not for vitamin B12 deficiency.
▶Cardiovascular System Atheroembolic Disease1 questions
Source: 9A #44
A patient presents with petechiae and discoloration of the distal extremities following instrumentation via the aorta. Which of the following is the most likely cause? A. Acute bacterial endocarditis B. Arteriolar vasospasm caused by hypertension C. Atheroemboli from the aorta D. Paradoxical emboli through a patent foramen ovale E. Vasculitis from an allergy to contrast material
Correct Answer: C. Atheroemboli from the aorta
Cholesterol embolization syndrome (atheroemboli from the aorta) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with petechiae and cyanotic discoloration following aortic instrumentation. This syndrome occurs when mechanical disruption during catheterization or surgery causes a shower of atherosclerotic material (cholesterol crystals and plaque contents) to embolize from a proximal large artery (such as the aorta) to distal small arteries and arterioles, resulting in occlusion and localized inflammatory response. Dermatologic manifestations include petechiae, livedo reticularis, and blue toe syndrome. Cholesterol embolization can also affect other organs including kidneys (kidney injury), colon (ischemia), brain (cerebral infarction), and skeletal muscle. The diagnosis is clinical, though imaging via CT or MR angiography can confirm macroscopic occlusions. Risk factors include aortic procedures such as aneurysm repair, cardiac catheterization via femoral approach, and aortic valve replacement. Treatment is supportive as no specific medical or surgical therapy reverses this syndrome. Choice A (Acute bacterial endocarditis) is incorrect because while endocarditis presents with fever, chills, rash (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, petechiae, purpura), and new murmur typically in patients with intravenous drug use or following bacteremia-causing procedures, this patient lacks fever and the preceding clinical context. The rash pattern is consistent with noninfectious arteriolar occlusion rather than immunologic phenomena. Choice B (Arteriolar vasospasm caused by hypertension) is incorrect because hypertension-related vasospasm would present with diffuse cyanosis affecting the entire extremity rather than localized petechiae limited to a single finger or area, and would not produce petechial lesions. Choice D (Paradoxical emboli through a patent foramen ovale) is incorrect because while paradoxical embolization from deep venous thrombosis can cause stroke, organ ischemia, or limb ischemia, this patient has no signs or symptoms of stroke and the clinical presentation more directly follows aortic instrumentation. Choice E (Vasculitis from allergy to contrast material) is incorrect because while vasculitis can present with petechiae and discolored toes, allergies to contrast material typically present as hypersensitivity reactions with urticaria or diffuse rubor rather than petechiae or cyanosis. The temporal relationship to aortic instrumentation makes cholesterol embolization the more likely triggering cause.
▶Cardiovascular System Coronary Artery Spasm1 questions
Source: 9A #45
A patient presents with substernal chest pain that resolves spontaneously. On arrival, she is asymptomatic with pulse 70/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 110/84 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. An ECG shows normal sinus rhythm. Ten minutes later, she sits up in bed and says that her symptoms have returned. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Drug-induced myocardial injury B) Hypovolemic shock C) Myocardial infarction D) Prinzmetal angina E) Viral myocarditis
Correct Answer: D) Prinzmetal angina
Prinzmetal angina, also known as vasospastic angina or variant angina pectoris, describes chest pain due to transient coronary vasospasm. The clinical presentation in this case is classic for this condition: substernal chest pain that occurs without exertion, resolves spontaneously, and recurs. The key diagnostic feature is that ECG changes (ST-segment changes) appear during the episode and resolve when symptoms abate, with normal troponin levels. Prinzmetal angina results from coronary artery vasospasm, not fixed coronary artery disease. It is often associated with coronary endothelial dysfunction characterized by increased intercellular adhesion molecules, heightened sensitivity to vasoconstrictive stimuli, increased inflammatory mediators, and atherosclerosis. Patients may present with chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, diaphoresis, abdominal pain, lightheadedness, or jaw or arm pain. Symptoms are brief, lasting seconds to minutes. Patients experiencing variant angina are often younger or without traditional cardiac risk factors. Smoking and cocaine use may trigger vasospasm. Diagnosis is made via ECG showing transient ST changes that normalize when vasospasm resolves, normal troponin levels, and cardiac catheterization showing no fixed coronary lesions. Treatment includes nitroglycerin for acute episodes and calcium channel blockers for long-term management. Choice A (Drug-induced myocardial injury) is incorrect because there is no disclosed drug use and the history is consistent with regional ischemia from a single artery, characteristic of Prinzmetal angina rather than diffuse myocardial injury. Choice B (Hypovolemic shock) is incorrect because hypovolemic shock presents with hypotension in the setting of clear fluid or blood loss, and does not typically cause territorial ECG changes. This patient has acute, brief symptoms that spontaneously resolve with no evidence of fluid or blood loss. Choice C (Myocardial infarction) is incorrect because MI typically presents with crushing substernal chest pain, territorial ECG changes, and a culprit lesion visible on catheterization. This patient had no coronary artery occlusions, and symptoms resolved completely with normalization of ECG findings. Choice E (Viral myocarditis) is incorrect because viral myocarditis presents with acute to subacute chest pain, shortness of breath, heart failure signs/symptoms, nonspecific ECG changes, elevated troponin, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers in the context of a preceding viral illness. This patient has none of these features.
▶Behavioral Health Alcohol Withdrawal1 questions
Source: 9A #46
A hospitalized 37-year-old man is hostile and fearful 5 days after undergoing operative repair of multiple fractures of the left upper and lower extremities sustained in a fall. He reports seeing "green aliens" in his room and accuses the nursing staff of trying to poison him; he removes his intravenous catheter and insists on leaving. Arterial blood gas analysis and an x-ray of the chest show no abnormalities. A) Brief psychotic disorder B) Cocaine withdrawal C) Alcohol withdrawal D) Delirium, anticholinergic E) Opioid withdrawal
Correct Answer: C) Alcohol withdrawal
Alcohol withdrawal presents with confusion (delirium), hallucinations, autonomic instability (hyperadrenergic states), and tremors, usually beginning 12 to 24 hours after cessation of use. This patient's agitation, hallucinations, paranoia, tachycardia, hypertension, and tremors are consistent with severe alcohol withdrawal, likely resulting from inadvertent discontinuation in the hospital setting. Alcohol, like benzodiazepines and barbiturates, increases the central nervous system activity of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol leads to sympathetic (excitatory) excess. Uncomplicated withdrawal typically presents with tremors, anxiety, restlessness, headache, nausea, and diaphoresis occurring hours after cessation. Alcohol withdrawal can be complicated by seizures and hallucinosis (auditory or visual hallucinations). Severe alcohol withdrawal can present with life-threatening complications including confusion and disorientation, fluctuations in consciousness, agitation, visual hallucinations, and autonomic instability (fluctuations in heart rate and blood pressure). Alcohol withdrawal is a clinical diagnosis based on symptoms and signs plus history of cessation of alcohol within 12 to 24 hours of symptom onset. Prevention includes avoiding cessation or substituting alcohol with tapering, symptom-triggered doses of benzodiazepines. Treatment consists of supportive care with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines, fluid resuscitation, and vitamin/electrolyte repletion for patients with a history of heavy alcohol use. Choice A (Brief psychotic disorder) is incorrect because brief psychotic disorder is characterized by acute onset of psychotic symptoms lasting less than 1 month without the abrupt onset, tremors, and hyperadrenergic state evident in this patient. Choice B (Cocaine withdrawal) is incorrect because cocaine withdrawal presents with depressed mood, fatigue, and slowing of activity. While cocaine intoxication causes hypertension, tachycardia, restlessness, hallucinations, and paranoia, the patient's tremors and presentation are more consistent with alcohol withdrawal. Choice D (Delirium, anticholinergic) is incorrect because anticholinergic delirium more commonly affects older patients or those with pre-existing dementia, typically presenting within 1 to 6 hours of anticholinergic medication administration. Choice E (Opioid withdrawal) is incorrect because opioid withdrawal causes restlessness, tachycardia, hypertension, tremors, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection, and yawning—a different constellation of symptoms without the hallucinations and paranoia seen here.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Metabolic Alkalosis1 questions
Source: 9A #47
A 53-year-old man comes to the emergency department 24 hours after the onset of vomiting. He has had early satiety for 6 months resulting in a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss. Serum studies show: Na+ 125 mEq/L Cl- 80 mEq/L K+ 2.0 mEq/L HCO3- 38 mEq/L Passage of a nasogastric tube recovers 3 L of clear fluid from the stomach. Initial fluid replacement therapy should begin with which of the following? A) 5% dextrose solution B) 5% dextrose solution and 0.45% saline solution with 30 mEq/L of potassium chloride C) 0.3% saline with 30 mEq/L of potassium chloride D) 0.5N HCl solution with 30 mEq/L of potassium chloride E) 0.9% saline solution with 30 mEq/L of potassium chloride
Correct Answer: E) 0.9% saline solution with 30 mEq/L of potassium chloride
This patient presents with symptoms suggestive of gastric outlet obstruction secondary to malignancy and has had frequent vomiting complicated by hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. This is chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis and should be treated with isotonic saline resuscitation and potassium chloride supplementation. Metabolic alkalosis from vomiting occurs through multiple mechanisms: (1) Direct loss of protons and potassium ions secreted by the stomach results in an imbalance of bicarbonate ions, leading to increased serum pH; (2) Volume contraction triggers the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, resulting in renal retention of sodium and excretion of potassium and protons in urine. The clinical presentation includes signs of volume depletion (early satiety, weight loss), elevated serum bicarbonate (38 mEq/L), decreased serum pH, hypokalemia (K+ 2.0 mEq/L), hyponatremia (Na+ 125 mEq/L), and hypochloremia (Cl- 80 mEq/L). Choice A (5% dextrose solution) is incorrect because it is hypotonic and provides no potassium repletion, which is critical in this case. Choices B (5% dextrose and 0.45% saline with KCl) and C (0.3% saline with KCl) are incorrect because they involve hypotonic fluid. The patient requires isotonic (0.9%) saline for proper volume resuscitation. Choice D (0.5N HCl with KCl) is incorrect because hydrochloric acid is corrosive and can damage tissue; it should never be administered to patients. Choice E is correct: 0.9% isotonic saline provides appropriate volume resuscitation and restores the intravascular volume, which decreases aldosterone secretion and allows renal excretion of bicarbonate. The addition of 30 mEq/L of potassium chloride repletes the significant potassium deficit and provides chloride to enhance renal bicarbonate excretion. Definitive treatment involves relieving the gastric outlet obstruction to permit normal peristalsis and enteric fluid absorption.
▶Gastrointestinal System Salmonella species gastrointestinal infection1 questions
Source: 9A #49
A patient presents with temperatures to 38.3°C (101°F) for the first 5 days of illness with diarrhea. She has hypertension and peptic ulcer disease. She has no known sick contacts and frequently dines at restaurants. Stool culture confirms Salmonella enteritidis infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy? A. Oral ciprofloxacin B. Oral metronidazole C. Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin D. Intravenous cefotaxime E. No antibiotic therapy is indicated at this time
Correct Answer: E) No antibiotic therapy is indicated at this time
This immunocompetent patient presents with diarrhea and is found to have Salmonella enteritidis infection. First-line treatment for this infection is supportive care with fluid and electrolyte repletion therapy. No antibiotic therapy is indicated at this time, though it may be appropriate for patients with severe disease or in immunocompromised patients. S. enteritidis infection occurs via ingestion of contaminated food products and results in gastrointestinal infection and diarrheal illness. The infection presents with acute onset of watery diarrhea and fever. Symptoms often last 5 to 7 days before resolution. The gold standard for diagnosis is a stool culture positive for Salmonella species. Choices A, B, C, and D (oral ciprofloxacin, oral metronidazole, intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin, and intravenous cefotaxime) are incorrect because antibiotic treatment is not indicated in this otherwise healthy patient with uncomplicated, nonsevere infection. Antibiotics may be considered only in patients with severe disease or those who are immunocompromised. Proper food handling, specifically including thorough cooking of poultry and eggs, is crucial to prevent this food-borne gastrointestinal illness.
▶Musculoskeletal System Osteoporosis1 questions
Source: 5A #3
A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because she is concerned about her risk for osteoporosis. She has hypertension and deep venous thrombosis. Current medications include metoprolol and warfarin. There is no personal or family history of fractures. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her blood pressure is 132/82 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. A DEXA scan shows findings consistent with osteoporosis. In addition to calcium and vitamin D supplementation, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Alendronate B) Calcitonin C) Estrogen D) Isoflavone E) Raloxifene
Correct Answer: A) Alendronate
Osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease characterized by diffusely low bone density, defined as a T-score more than 2.5 standard deviations below the mean for a young, normal population on DEXA scan. Common risk factors include age, smoking, chronic inflammatory disease, corticosteroid use, and estrogen-depleting conditions in women. The disease is often asymptomatic but significantly increases fracture risk, particularly involving the hip, vertebrae, and distal radius. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation represent first-line treatment and prevention. Bisphosphonates such as alendronate inhibit osteoclast activity and are the standard pharmacologic agents used once osteoporosis is diagnosed to prevent further bone mineral density loss and reduce fracture risk. Weight-bearing exercises are also recommended to slow bone deterioration. Choice B (Calcitonin) is a native hormone that inhibits osteoclast activity and renal calcium reabsorption but is rarely used due to cost and side effects, with application limited mainly to severe symptomatic hypercalcemia. Choice C (Estrogen) does promote positive bone remodeling and increase bone mineral density; however, this patient has a history of deep venous thrombosis, making estrogen therapy contraindicated due to significantly increased risk of life-threatening venous thrombosis. Choice D (Isoflavones) are postulated to improve postmenopausal symptoms and delay osteoporosis, but insufficient data exists regarding their effectiveness and safety. Choice E (Raloxifene) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator with agonist activity for osteoblast-mediated bone remodeling and is useful for osteoporosis prevention, but due to off-target effects, it is generally reserved as third-line therapy following bisphosphonates. Given this patient's contraindication to estrogen-based therapy and the established efficacy of bisphosphonates as first-line pharmacotherapy for diagnosed osteoporosis, alendronate is the most appropriate choice.
▶Musculoskeletal System Osteomyelitis1 questions
Source: 5A #4
A 57-year-old homeless man is admitted to the hospital because of a 5-day history of moderate neck pain and fever. He has HIV infection and hepatitis C. He takes no medications. He uses intravenous heroin three times weekly. He does not smoke cigarettes and drinks alcohol occasionally. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. There is no photophobia. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows a regular rhythm; a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex. The neck is tender over the lower cervical spine with no warmth or erythema. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 400/mm³ (Normal ~500), and HIV viral load is 75,000 copies/ml. A chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the cervical spine shows destructive changes in C5 and C6 and collapse of the intervening disc space. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's neck pain? A) Contiguous spread of organism from adjacent soft-tissue process B) Direct inoculation of the soft tissues of the neck C) Granulomatous inflammation D) Hematogenous dissemination of distant infection E) Reactivation of latent organism
Correct Answer: D) Hematogenous dissemination of distant infection
Discitis-osteomyelitis refers to acute infection of a vertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies, most commonly caused by S. aureus. In adults, it typically occurs from direct spread from adjacent soft tissue infection. However, in intravenous drug users and children, hematogenous seeding is more common due to propensity for bacteremia and distant bacterial seeding. In intravenous drug users, S. aureus and Pseudomonas are the two most common pathogens. On imaging, discitis-osteomyelitis presents with destructive changes of vertebral bone with collapse of the disc space. This patient's clinical presentation is highly suggestive of infective endocarditis (fever, IV drug use, holosystolic apical murmur) and possible concurrent discitis-osteomyelitis from hematogenous bacterial seeding from the infected heart valves to the vertebral column. Choice A (Contiguous spread from adjacent soft tissue infection) is the most common mechanism in immunocompetent adults, but this patient lacks evidence of prior soft tissue infection. Choice B (Direct inoculation) occurs with penetrating trauma or surgery, neither present in this case. Choice C (Granulomatous inflammation) could suggest tuberculosis (Pott's disease), but the clinical context of IV drug use with possible endocarditis makes hematogenous seeding more probable. Choice E (Reactivation of latent organism) may apply to tuberculosis or herpes simplex viruses, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with acute hematogenous seeding from infective endocarditis rather than reactivation of a latent process.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Subarachnoid Hemorrhage1 questions
Source: 5A #7
A 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because she says that she is having "the worst headache of my life." It began abruptly while she was eating dinner 2 hours ago. She has a history of hypertension treated with diuretics. She is lying quietly with her eyes closed. She has difficulty talking and concentrating because of the pain, but is fully oriented. Her blood pressure is 180/98 mm Hg. Examination shows moderate nuchal rigidity. Cranial nerves, reflexes, and sensory examination are normal. Examination of cerebrospinal fluid shows an opening pressure of 170 mm Hg, erythrocyte count of 86,000/mm³, and leukocyte count of 5/mm³. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Arterial hypertension B) Epidural hematoma C) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension D) Meningitis E) Migraine F) Ruptured congenital aneurysm G) Subdural hematoma
Correct Answer: F) Ruptured congenital aneurysm
Nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage most often presents from a ruptured intracranial aneurysm in the setting of hypertension. The classic presentation in this case is the pathognomonic "thunderclap" worst-headache-of-life that began abruptly during a Valsalva maneuver (eating), accompanied by neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity) and elevated blood pressure. These aneurysms are often berry aneurysms located in the Circle of Willis. The aneurysm rupture may have been precipitated by an event increasing mean arterial pressure, which increases stress on the aneurysmal vascular wall. Lumbar puncture demonstrates a markedly elevated erythrocyte count (86,000/mm³) with normal leukocytes (5/mm³), which is characteristic of subarachnoid hemorrhage. The opening pressure of 170 mm Hg reflects elevated intracranial pressure from the hemorrhage. CT scan of the head without contrast is typically obtained in the acute setting to confirm subarachnoid blood, and if confirmed, angiographic imaging is necessary to identify the aneurysm location. Incorrect answers: Hypertensive urgency/emergency (Choice A) can present with headache but hemorrhagic cerebrospinal fluid makes subarachnoid hemorrhage more likely. Epidural and subdural hematomas (Choices B and G) typically occur following trauma and would show different imaging patterns; they cause headache and signs of elevated intracranial pressure from an expanding lesion, but the CSF pattern here is more consistent with subarachnoid hemorrhage. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice C) presents most commonly in younger, overweight females taking vitamin A, oral contraceptives, or danazol, usually with holocephalic headache and blurry vision, not the acute thunderclap presentation. Meningitis (Choice D) classically presents with acute headache, fever, photophobia, and neck stiffness, but would show elevated leukocytes in cerebrospinal fluid analysis (not 5/mm³), and the patient lacks fever. Migraine headaches (Choice E) characteristically recur over time, present with pulsatile unilateral or bilateral headache with photophobia or phonophobia, are triggered by specific factors (foods, medications, noises, menses, illness), and would not produce hemorrhagic CSF with this acute thunderclap presentation.
▶Cardiovascular System Venous Insufficiency1 questions
Source: 5A #8
A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of progressive swelling of her left calf. Ten years ago, she had a thrombus in her left leg and was treated with anticoagulants for 4 months. She currently takes no medications. Her pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Examination shows mild edema and prominent varicose veins of the distal left lower extremity. There is an 8-cm area of hyperpigmentation over the left ankle. Examination of the right lower extremity shows no abnormalities. Peripheral pulses are normal. Ultrasonography of the lower extremities shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's edema? A) Cellulitis B) Obstruction of the iliac vein C) Obstruction of lymph channels D) Saphenous vein reflux E) Valvular insufficiency of deep veins
Correct Answer: E) Valvular insufficiency of deep veins
Valvular insufficiency is a common complication of deep venous thrombosis. As a thrombus occludes the cross-sectional area of a deep vein, the valves, which originate from the walls of the veins, become involved in the thrombus either through compression against the wall of the vessel or through incorporation into the thrombus during propagation. When the thrombus resolves, the residual valve may be dysfunctional from damage to the leaflets, annulus, or diameter of the native vessel. This prevents the valve from functioning effectively and results in retrograde venous flow secondary to gravity. Inadequate venous drainage of the lower extremities can result in varicose veins, chronic edema, and stasis dermatitis (evidenced by the hyperpigmentation noted on examination). Choice A (Cellulitis) is characterized by inflammation in the skin and demonstrates erythema, induration, warmth, and edema. It is most commonly acute and results from bacterial infection; this patient has chronic symptoms without acute inflammatory signs. Choice B (Obstruction of the iliac vein) would present with edema of the entire left lower extremity as opposed to the calf in isolation. Furthermore, the patient's ultrasound was normal without evidence of obstruction. On duplex ultrasound, while iliac vessels may not be fully visualized, doppler venous waveforms would suggest a proximal obstruction if present. Choice C (Obstruction of lymph channels) results in nonpitting edema of the affected extremity and would be less likely given the patient's anatomically correlated history of deep venous thrombosis and lack of infectious (e.g., filariasis), surgical, malignant, or traumatic history to explain lymphatic system injury. Choice D (Saphenous vein reflux) could explain lower extremity edema and varicose vein development; however, the saphenous vein is a superficial vein and this patient has no known history of thrombosis or structural damage to it. The clinical presentation is most consistent with post-thrombotic syndrome from deep vein insufficiency.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Malignant Otitis Externa1 questions
Source: 5A #9
A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of severe left ear pain. At the onset of pain, he flushed his ear with water; the pain has become increasingly severe since then. He has no history of ear problems. He has a 30-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus poorly controlled with insulin. Examination shows moist debris and edema of the left ear canal. Granulation tissue is seen on the floor of the ear canal. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 18,000/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 78%, Lymphocytes 22%, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 100 mm/h, Serum glucose 450 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute mastoiditis B) Acute otitis media C) Angiocentric T-cell lymphoma D) Chronic otitis media with effusion E) Fungal otitis externa F) Necrotizing otitis externa
Correct Answer: F) Necrotizing otitis externa
Necrotizing otitis externa refers to infection of the external ear canal typically caused by Pseudomonas or Enterobacteriaceae, both of which thrive in moist environments. It is frequently seen in patients with poorly controlled diabetes and immunocompromised states, as in this case with a 30-year history of poorly controlled type 1 diabetes and elevated serum glucose of 450 mg/dL. The classic presentation includes severe external ear pain exacerbated with movement of the tragus or pinna, purulent discharge, edematous and erythematous external ear canal, and granulation tissue—all present in this patient. The elevated leukocyte count (18,000/mm³), elevated ESR (100 mm/h), and left shift in differential neutrophilia (78%) support acute bacterial infection. When infection is severe and has infiltrated beyond the external ear canal causing extensive tissue destruction, it is termed necrotizing (or malignant) otitis externa, which requires intravenous antibiotics. Non-necrotizing otitis externa ('swimmer's ear') presents with mild pain, watery discharge, and swelling, and is treated with ear canal cleaning, acidification, and fluoroquinolone ear drops. Choice A (Acute mastoiditis) presents with erythema and tenderness posterior to the ear over the mastoid bone and typically results as a complication of otitis media, not from external ear canal pathology. Choice B (Acute otitis media) classically occurs in children and presents with ear pain, fever, and an erythematous tympanic membrane with retrotympanic pus or middle ear effusion. The exam findings here are consistent with external ear canal disease, not middle ear disease. Choice C (Angiocentric T-cell lymphoma) is a rare cutaneous malignancy often involving natural killer cells and typically presents as single or multiple plaques or nodules that may ulcerate. The acute presentation with infection and inflammatory markers makes malignancy unlikely. Choice D (Chronic otitis media with effusion) presents with chronic middle ear pain and retrotympanic effusion, neither of which were documented on this patient's examination. Choice E (Fungal otitis externa) would present similarly but is less likely than bacterial causes in this acute presentation with prominent systemic inflammation and leukocytosis. Fungal infections tend to be more subacute and indolent.
▶Endocrine System Hyperparathyroidism1 questions
Source: 5A #10
A previously healthy 57-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital for evaluation of a 3-week history of increasing fatigue, constipation, urinary frequency, and increased thirst. She appears lethargic. Her pulse is 116/min, and blood pressure is 150/70 mm Hg. Examination shows dry mucous membranes. Serum studies show a calcium concentration of 15.2 mg/dl, phosphorus concentration of 2.1 mg/dl, and parathyroid hormone concentration of 800 pg/ml. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's polyuria and volume depletion? A) Allergic interstitial nephritis B) Central diabetes insipidus C) Chronic pyelonephritis D) Glycosuria E) Hypertensive nephropathy F) Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Correct Answer: F) Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Primary hyperparathyroidism results in hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia secondary to aberrant increased production of parathyroid hormone (PTH). The most common cause is a parathyroid adenoma, with parathyroid hyperplasia and carcinoma as additional possibilities. Common symptoms of primary hyperparathyroidism are secondary to resultant hypercalcemia and include recurrent nephrolithiasis, bone pain from osseous resorption, polyuria, dehydration, constipation, and psychiatric disturbances. Polyuria and associated volume depletion in this patient are secondary to the direct effects of hypercalcemia on the kidney, which results in renal resistance and lack of response to anti-diuretic hormone (ADH), known as nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. The resistance to ADH results in insufficient aquaporin expression in the collecting tubules of renal nephrons, leading to increased urine volume, which manifests clinically as polyuria and volume depletion. Incorrect choices: Allergic interstitial nephritis (Choice A) results in pyuria (predominantly eosinophils) and azotemia often related to medications such as diuretics, penicillins, proton pump inhibitors, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and sulfonamides. Central diabetes insipidus (Choice B) results in polyuria and volume depletion secondary to insufficient production of ADH from a brain injury or lesion. Chronic pyelonephritis (Choice C) often occurs in patients prone to recurrent episodes of acute pyelonephritis, with risk factors such as chronic obstructing renal stones or vesicoureteral reflux. Glycosuria (Choice D) refers to glucose in the urine, often in patients with hyperglycemia secondary to diabetes mellitus. Hypertensive nephropathy (Choice E) is a common cause of chronic renal failure, resulting from glomerular damage from chronic hypertension.
▶Renal Urinary System Chronic Kidney Disease1 questions
Source: 5A #12
A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She has chronic renal failure secondary to glomerulonephritis. She has received hemodialysis three times weekly for 2 years. She is on a waiting list for a renal transplant. Examination shows no abnormalities. Her serum calcium concentration is 8.2 mg/dl. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's hypocalcemia? A) Decreased absorption due to decreased serum 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol concentration B) Decreased absorption due to decreased serum magnesium concentration C) Decreased absorption due to increased serum ionized calcium concentration D) Increased calcium binding by phosphate in the small bowel E) Increased suppression of parathyroid hormone due to increased serum ionized phosphorus concentration
Correct Answer: A) Decreased absorption due to decreased serum 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol concentration
Active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) is synthesized through cutaneous, hepatic, and renal routes, with the final conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol occurring in the kidney via 1-alpha hydroxylase. Patients with chronic kidney disease have diminished capacity for native vitamin D synthesis because of underlying renal parenchymal damage. The decreased production of active vitamin D results in impaired gastrointestinal uptake of dietary calcium, leading to hypocalcemia. This, in turn, leads to elevations in parathyroid hormone and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Choice B (Magnesium): Magnesium is commonly coabsorbed in the small intestine, notably facilitating absorption of potassium, but does not have a prominent role in the absorption of calcium in patients with renal failure. Choice C (Ionized Calcium): Patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal failure are most commonly hypocalcemic, including both bound and free ionized calcium, so increased ionized calcium would not be the mechanism. Choice D (Phosphate Binding): Patients with renal failure typically develop elevated serum phosphate because of impaired renal excretion of phosphate from tubular dysfunction, which does not necessarily relate to increased intraluminal phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract. Choice E (PTH Suppression): Serum parathyroid hormone in renal failure is characteristically elevated by hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, not suppressed.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Hypomagnesemia1 questions
Source: 5A #13
A 47-year-old man with alcoholism is transferred from the hospital to a drug rehabilitation facility. On arrival, examination shows hyperreflexia and a tremor in both hands when they are outstretched. His serum calcium concentration is 8.1 mg/dl. Which of the following is the most likely additional serum electrolyte abnormality in this patient? A) Hypochloremia B) Hypokalemia C) Hypomagnesemia D) Hyponatremia E) Hypophosphatemia
Correct Answer: C) Hypomagnesemia
Patients with alcohol use disorder often develop multiple vitamin, mineral, and electrolyte deficiencies due to malnutrition from lower dietary intake and the concomitant diuretic effect of alcohol, leading to excessive urinary losses. This patient's examination demonstrates neurologic symptoms, including hyperreflexia and tremor in the setting of alcoholism, which are classic presentations of magnesium deficiency. Magnesium is essential for neuromuscular function and cellular metabolism. Deficiency presents with hyperreflexia, tremor, seizures, muscle spasms, and dysrhythmias (such as Torsades de Pointes). Choice A (Hypochloremia) infrequently occurs in isolation and when present is usually associated with imbalances in sodium, acid-base, or volume status. Most patients do not have symptoms of hypochloremia independent of the presenting condition. Choice B (Hypokalemia), while often occurring in alcoholism, presents commonly with cardiac conduction abnormalities such as acquired long-QT syndrome or dysrhythmias, but does not typically present with peripheral neurologic deficits like the hyperreflexia and tremor described. Choice D (Hyponatremia) is often asymptomatic if chronic and slowly developing. When acute, it is associated with central nervous system symptoms such as headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, delirium, weakness, seizures, and coma—not the peripheral neurologic findings seen here. Choice E (Hypophosphatemia) can occur in nutritional deficiency states such as anorexia nervosa or bulimia, with symptoms resulting from ATP depletion including muscle weakness, cardiorespiratory depression, and neurologic depression. This is less specifically associated with alcoholism and hyperreflexia/tremor.
▶Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Asymptomatic urinary tract infection in pregnancy1 questions
Source: 5A #14
A previously healthy 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of frequent pain with urination and episodes of loss of urine. She has no history of similar symptoms, and she has not had pelvic pain or change in bowel function. Menses occur at regular intervals and last 4 days; her last menstrual period was 10 days ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. The external genitalia, vagina, and cervix appear normal. There is no cervical motion or uterine tenderness, but the bladder is tender to palpation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Nitrofurantoin therapy B) Oxybutynin therapy C) Intermittent self-catheterization D) Sacral nerve stimulation E) Midurethral sling procedure
Correct Answer: A) Nitrofurantoin therapy
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) affect women more frequently than men and may present with lower and/or upper urinary tract symptoms. Lower urinary tract symptoms include increased urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and dysuria. Upper urinary tract symptoms include flank pain, costophrenic angle tenderness, and systemic signs/symptoms such as fevers and rigors. This patient presents with classic lower UTI symptoms: dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic tenderness on examination. Diagnosis of a lower urinary tract infection should be made based on clinical symptoms and supported by increased leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urinalysis along with growth of culprit organisms on urine culture. Uncomplicated UTIs should be treated with nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, cephalexin, or a fluoroquinolone depending on local sensitivity and resistance patterns. This patient meets criteria for uncomplicated UTI treatment. Choice B (Oxybutynin) is an anti-muscarinic medication used to treat urge incontinence from an overactive bladder and detrusor instability, not acute UTI. Choice C (Intermittent self-catheterization) is utilized for the treatment of overflow incontinence from incomplete emptying secondary to detrusor underactivity or bladder outlet obstruction. Additionally, catheterization increases the risk of urinary tract infection, although intermittent self-catheterization imparts less risk than an indwelling Foley or suprapubic catheter. Choice D (Sacral nerve stimulation) is used for the treatment of bladder and bowel incontinence. The S2-S4 nerve roots are modulated to allow for improved voiding, as these play a crucial role in the autonomic regulation of micturition. Choice E (Midurethral sling procedure) is used to treat stress incontinence and entails a surgical procedure utilizing synthetic mesh to support the urethra.
▶Gastrointestinal System Primary biliary cirrhosis1 questions
Source: 5A #18
A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue over the past 6 months. She has had a decreased appetite and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss over the past year. She has not had nausea or vomiting, abdominal pain, changes in bowel movements, diarrhea, or blood in the stool. She has a 2-year history of pruritus. She has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. She has no known allergies. Her mother has Graves disease, her sister has systemic lupus erythematosus, and a paternal uncle has hemochromatosis. Her pulse is 80/min and regular, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 120/85 mm Hg. Examination shows excoriations over the upper and lower extremities and trunk with no lesions. There are xanthomas around the eyelids. Abdominal examination shows a liver span of 12 cm; there are no palpable masses or tenderness. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, Leukocyte count 3500/mm³, Platelet count 100,000/mm³, Total cholesterol 350 mg/dL, Total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, Alkaline phosphatase 450 U/L, AST 30 U/L, ALT 35 U/L. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows hepatomegaly and no evidence of a biliary obstruction. There is a large gallstone in the gallbladder and mild splenomegaly. Which of the following is most likely to suggest the diagnosis? A) Serum antimitochondrial antibody assays B) Serum antinuclear antibody assay C) Serum hepatitis B surface antigen and antibody and core antibody assays D) Oral cholecystography E) HIDAscan F) No further testing indicated
Correct Answer: A) Serum antimitochondrial antibody assays
Primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) is an autoimmune disease of the biliary tree resulting in destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts that classically affects middle-aged women. The clinical presentation of this patient is classic for PBC: fatigue, pruritus (2-year history with excoriations), weight loss, anorexia, hepatomegaly, xanthomas around the eyelids (from hypercholesterolemia), and elevated cholesterol (350 mg/dL). Laboratory findings consistent with PBC include elevated alkaline phosphatase (450 U/L) and mildly elevated bilirubin (2.2 mg/dL) with relatively normal transaminases (AST 30 U/L, ALT 35 U/L). The serum antimitochondrial antibody is the hallmark serologic finding, though liver biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line therapy to improve biliary excretion, with liver transplantation reserved for progressive, severe disease. Choice B (Serum antinuclear antibody) is elevated in many autoimmune and inflammatory diseases and is classically associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, not PBC. While the patient has a family history of SLE, the clinical presentation and lab pattern are not consistent with SLE. Choice C (Serum hepatitis B serology) is used to identify active acute or chronic hepatitis B infection. Acute hepatitis B presents with nausea, vomiting, anorexia, hepatomegaly, and jaundice with markedly elevated transaminases—a pattern not seen in this patient whose transaminases are normal. Choices D (Oral cholecystography) and E (HIDA scan) are used to evaluate gallbladder function when cholecystitis or obstruction is suspected, presenting with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. While the patient has a gallstone on imaging, her presentation and laboratory abnormalities point to a hepatic/biliary disease rather than a primary gallbladder problem. Choice F (No further testing) is incorrect because the patient has multiple biliary laboratory abnormalities (elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase) and symptoms requiring diagnostic clarification to guide appropriate therapy.
▶Renal Urinary System IgA Nephropathy1 questions
Source: 5A #19
A 25-year-old man comes to the physician 1 day after noticing pink-tinged urine. Two days ago, he had an upper respiratory tract infection with a nonproductive, hacking cough; his symptoms are now resolved. He has not had pain, fever, or chills. He has no history of serious illness. Current medications include over-the-counter cough syrup. He does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 114/68 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows a pH of 5.5, 4+ blood, and greater than 50 RBC/hpf. His serum creatinine concentration is 1.1 mg/dL, and serum complement concentration is within the reference range. Ultrasonography of the kidneys and bladder shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cystitis B) IgA nephropathy C) Nongonococcal urethritis D) Postinfectious glomerulonephritis E) Renal cell carcinoma
Correct Answer: B) IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is a type of nephritic syndrome characterized by episodic gross hematuria often following an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. The clinical presentation in this case is classic: recent upper respiratory infection followed within days by pink-tinged (gross) hematuria. On urinalysis, there will be a significant quantity of red blood cells (RBCs) and the possibility for RBC cast formation. A key distinguishing feature is that serum complement levels, including C3, are typically normal in IgA nephropathy. This is critical because it differentiates IgA nephropathy from postinfectious glomerulonephritis. Additionally, anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers will be negative in IgA nephropathy. Choice A (Cystitis): Inflammation of the urinary bladder secondary to acute bacterial urinary tract infection. Presents with increased urinary white blood cells, elevated leukocyte esterase, and possibly elevated nitrites. Does not typically follow upper respiratory infection and does not present with this degree of hematuria. Choice C (Nongonococcal urethritis): Typically secondary to Chlamydia trachomatis infection. Presents with characteristic gram stain findings of numerous neutrophils but no bacteria (sterile pyuria). Not associated with recent respiratory infection. Choice D (Postinfectious glomerulonephritis): Also a nephritic syndrome presenting with urinary RBCs and RBC casts, but typically occurs 2-6 weeks after infection (not 2 days), usually following group A beta-hemolytic streptococci infection. Critically, serum C3 levels are LOW (depressed), not normal as seen here. Additionally, anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers are positive, which would help differentiate from IgA nephropathy. Choice E (Renal cell carcinoma): An adenocarcinoma of tubular epithelial cells. Patients may present with gross hematuria but typically without RBC casts, and usually with associated flank pain and palpable flank mass. Diagnosis requires contrast-enhanced CT or MRI and biopsy confirmation. This does not follow a recent infection and is extremely rare at age 25. Educational Objective: Recognize IgA nephropathy as the most common primary glomerulonephritis presenting with episodic gross hematuria following upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. Distinguish it from postinfectious glomerulonephritis by normal complement levels (particularly C3) and negative anti-streptococcal antibodies in IgA nephropathy versus low C3 and positive titers in postinfectious glomerulonephritis.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Sarcoidosis1 questions
Source: 5A #21
A 42-year-old African American woman comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of cough and fatigue. She has long-standing hypertension well controlled with atenolol. Her blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Serum studies show: Ca2+ 11.8 mg/dL Phosphorus 3.4 mg/dL Globulin 4.8 g/dL Parathyroid hormone, intact 7 pg/mL (N=10-65) Parathyroid hormone-related protein 1.0 pmol/L (N<1.3) An x-ray of the chest shows several nodules throughout both lung fields. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Calcitriol therapy B) Divalproex sodium therapy C) Gallium nitrate therapy D) Glucocorticoid therapy E) Plicamycin therapy F) Dialysis G) Parathyroidectomy
Correct Answer: D) Glucocorticoid therapy
Sarcoidosis is an immune-mediated systemic disease resulting in formation of noncaseating granulomas in a variety of involved organs. It is most common in African American females and is often asymptomatic except for lymphadenopathy, with radiographs potentially demonstrating bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and reticulonodular opacities of bilateral lungs. This patient presents with classic findings: African American female, pulmonary symptoms (cough, fatigue), chest x-ray showing nodules throughout both lung fields, and laboratory evidence of hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH. Granulomatous inflammation can result in autonomous production of 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxy-vitamin D3 to the active form 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D3. This granulomatous expression of the enzyme results in increased production of active vitamin D3, which leads to increased intestinal absorption of calcium, resulting in hypercalcemia. This vitamin D3-dependent hypercalcemia results in physiologic suppression of parathyroid hormone. Glucocorticoids are the first-line therapy for sarcoidosis, utilized to suppress the granulomatous inflammation characteristic of the disease. Choice A (Calcitriol) refers to the active form of 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D3, which would worsen this patient's hypercalcemia and is contraindicated. Choice B (Divalproex sodium) is used in the treatment of seizures, migraine headaches, and psychiatric disturbances such as bipolar disorder, not sarcoidosis. Choice C (Gallium nitrate) treats symptomatic cancer-associated hypercalcemia through inhibition of osteoclast activity, not the underlying sarcoidosis pathology. Choice E (Plicamycin) inhibits RNA synthesis and serves as an anti-neoplastic antibiotic, rarely used for hypercalcemia treatment, and does not address the underlying disease. Choice F (Dialysis) is utilized for removal of excess solutes, toxins, and/or water in emergent settings of acute renal failure or chronic end-stage renal disease. While dialysis may be indicated in cases of severe hypercalcemia where native renal clearance is insufficient, it is not the primary management for sarcoidosis. Choice G (Parathyroidectomy) is indicated for the treatment of hypercalcemia caused by primary hyperparathyroidism, not sarcoidosis-associated hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.
▶Cardiovascular System Third-degree Atrioventricular Block1 questions
Source: 5A #23
A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of severe chest pressure and nausea. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He has smoked three packs of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He is employed as a truck driver and has a sedentary lifestyle. He appears anxious and diaphoretic. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 107 kg (235 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m². His pulse is 44/min and regular, and blood pressure is 160/94 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Peripheral pulses are normal. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cardiac rhythm? A) Complete heart block B) First-degree atrioventricular block C) Mobitz type I (Wenckebach type) block D) Mobitz type II block E) Sinus bradycardia
Correct Answer: A) Complete heart block
Complete heart block is characterized on an ECG by complete dissociation of P waves from the QRS complex, with each maintaining its own unique, separate rate per minute with no one-to-one relationship. This ECG shows an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The inferior wall of the heart and the atrioventricular (AV) node often share a common blood supply from the right coronary artery (RCA). When the RCA is blocked, infarction of both the inferior wall and the AV node can occur, leading to complete AV block with a junctional escape rhythm. The ECG shows an escape rhythm with a constant R-R interval and narrow QRS complex, indicating a pacer focus located in the common bundle or just distal to the AV node within the His-Purkinje system. Choice B (First-degree AV block) results in a prolonged P-R interval (>200 milliseconds), but maintains a consistent P-QRS relationship, which is absent in this case. Choice C (Mobitz type I/Wenckebach) is diagnosed when the PR interval progressively lengthens resulting in a non-conducted beat and grouped beating on ECG. Choice D (Mobitz type II) shows a consistent P-R interval with normal beats followed by dropped QRS complexes in discrete ratios (often 3:2 or 2:1). Choice E (Sinus bradycardia) is characterized by a one-to-one P to QRS ratio with ventricular rate less than 60 beats per minute, which is not present here given the complete dissociation of P waves and QRS complexes.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Spinal Cord Compression1 questions
Source: 5A #24
A previously healthy 25-year-old graduate student comes to the physician because of numbness of her left leg, stiffness of her right leg, and urinary urgency. Examination shows increased tone and deep tendon reflexes in the right lower extremity. Babinski sign is present on the right. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the left lower extremity and below the level of T9 on the left. Sensation to vibration and proprioception is intact. Gait testing shows stiffness and circumduction of the right lower extremity. This patient is most likely to have a lesion at which of the following locations? A) Brain stem B) Cerebral hemispheres C) Peripheral nerves D) Spinal cord E) No lesion (conversion reaction)
Correct Answer: D) Spinal cord
A lesion within the spinal cord can result in injury to a single or multiple spinal cord tracts, leading to asymmetric physical exam findings depending on the location of the lesion. This patient demonstrates a Brown-Séquard syndrome pattern with ipsilateral motor findings (right leg stiffness, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) and contralateral sensory findings (left-sided decreased pinprick sensation). Fine touch and temperature are transmitted by the anterolateral spinothalamic tract (ALS), motor function by the lateral corticospinal tract (CST), and vibration/proprioception by the dorsal columns-medial lemniscus pathway (DC-ML). A lesion in the anterior and lateral fascicles of the spinal cord white matter would injure both the ALS tract and lateral CST. The contralateral loss of fine touch and temperature occurs because the primary sensory neuron for the ALS tract decussates within the spinal cord at the ventral white commissure before ascending in the anterolateral tract. The ipsilateral motor weakness and upper motor neuron findings (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) result from lateral CST injury, as motor decussation occurs in the brainstem. Brainstem lesions (Choice A) typically result in ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits and contralateral long-tract findings (e.g., Wallenberg syndrome), not this asymmetric lower extremity pattern. Cerebral hemisphere lesions (Choice B) cause contralateral focal deficits without bilateral asymmetric findings. Peripheral nerve lesions (Choice C) present with lower motor neuron weakness, paresthesias, and numbness in a specific dermatome or nerve distribution, not upper motor neuron signs. Conversion reaction/functional neurologic symptom disorder (Choice E) is a diagnosis of exclusion involving loss of motor or sensory function without physical explanation; patients often display 'la belle indifférence' regarding their symptoms, which is not described here.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Transfusion reaction1 questions
Source: 5A #27
During transfusion of a second unit of crossmatched packed red blood cells for lower gastrointestinal bleeding, a 67-year-old woman has the onset of fever and chills. Six months ago, she had gastrointestinal bleeding and had no complications after transfusion of 3 units of crossmatched packed red blood cells. She appears anxious. Her temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), pulse is 105/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 135/75 mm Hg. Examination of the skin shows no abnormalities. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Serum studies of a post-transfusion sample show no free hemoglobin. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative. The ABO blood groups of the patient and donor are verified, and a second crossmatch reconfirms compatibility. In addition to intravenous administration of crystalloid solution, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Acetaminophen B) Dantrolene C) Epinephrine D) Penicillin E) Prednisone
Correct Answer: A) Acetaminophen
Acute febrile transfusion reactions occur during blood transfusion secondary to preformed cytokines in the transfused blood. This reaction is not related to inaccurate crossmatching or administration of an incorrect blood type. The clinical presentation includes fever and chills without hemolysis (negative Coombs test and absent free hemoglobin in serum), which distinguishes this from acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. Treatment consists of acetaminophen plus intravenous fluids to blunt the hypothalamic response to cytokines. Dantrolene (Choice B) is used for malignant hyperthermia, which presents with rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability, typically triggered by anesthetic medications or nitrates—not transfusion. Epinephrine (Choice C) is indicated for anaphylactic transfusion reactions, which would present with tachycardia, wheezing, hypotension, angioedema, itching, urticaria, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea—symptoms absent in this case. Penicillin (Choice D) is an antibiotic for gram-positive and spirochete infections; the abrupt time course makes infectious causes unlikely despite blood product exposure. Prednisone (Choice E) is used for various inflammatory, atopic, infectious, and autoimmune conditions but has no specific role in managing acute febrile transfusion reactions.
▶Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Tracheomalacia1 questions
Source: 5A #30
A 42-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-month history of progressive shortness of breath, cough, and intermittent wheezing. Her cough usually is nonproductive but occasionally has produced white sputum. She is otherwise asymptomatic. Nine months ago, she was intubated and mechanically ventilated for 2 weeks for management of Guillain-Barre syndrome. Her only medication is a daily multivitamin. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. She smokes marijuana two times monthly. She does not drink alcohol. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. High-pitched, end-expiratory wheezes are heard in the anterior aspect of the lungs. No crackles are heard. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Asthma B) Guillain-Barre syndrome C) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis D) Paradoxic vocal cord motion E) Tracheomalacia
Correct Answer: E) Tracheomalacia
Tracheomalacia refers to softening and deterioration of the tracheal cartilage, which results in excessive end-expiratory collapse due to atrophy and/or reduction of the tracheal elastic fibers and decreased integrity of tracheal cartilage. In adults, this most commonly occurs after prolonged intubation with an endotracheal tube, which results in direct damage to the tracheal cartilage. Clinically, this presents with shortness of breath, nonproductive cough, and expiratory stridor, which can sound like wheezing on lung auscultation. This patient's recent 2-week history of mechanical ventilation for Guillain-Barre syndrome 9 months ago is the key risk factor for developing tracheomalacia. Choice A (Asthma): The patient has no reported prior history of asthma, and her symptoms and physical examination findings are more consistent with an obstructive airway mechanism from tracheomalacia rather than reactive airway disease. Choice B (Guillain-Barre syndrome): This condition is typically self-limited and affects the lungs through diaphragmatic paralysis, not through an obstructive airway mechanism as seen in this patient. The acute presentation of Guillain-Barre syndrome would not explain her chronic progressive symptoms 9 months after initial intubation. Choice C (Hypersensitivity pneumonitis): This condition results in shortness of breath, cough, and fever after exposure to a specific antigen. There is no history of antigen exposure, and the patient does not have fever. Additionally, hypersensitivity pneumonitis typically presents with interstitial findings, not expiratory wheezes. Choice D (Paradoxic vocal cord motion): This occurs when the vocal cords close during breathing, resulting in an obstructed airway. While it can cause similar symptoms, there are many causes including exercise, coughing, and acid reflux, but it is not typically a direct consequence of prolonged intubation. The high-pitched end-expiratory wheezes are more characteristic of tracheomalacia with expiratory stridor.
▶Renal Urinary System Renal Tubular Acidosis1 questions
Source: 5A #34
A 57-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine examination. He feels well. He has rheumatoid arthritis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Current medications include methotrexate, metformin, lisinopril, simvastatin, and 81-mg aspirin. He drinks one to two glasses of wine each evening. His temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/78 mm Hg. Examination shows an abdominal bruit. Laboratory studies show: Serum: Na+ 142 mEq/L K+ 3.5 mEq/L Cl- 120 mEq/L HCO3- 10 mEq/L Urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL Glucose 134 mg/dL Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL Urine pH 6.5 Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A) Alcohol use B) Diabetic ketoacidosis C) Lactate production D) Renal tubular acidosis E) Salicylate intoxication
Correct Answer: D) Renal tubular acidosis
Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) results in a hyperchloremic, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from dysregulation of the renal tubules. There are three types of RTA, varying in etiology and pathophysiology, but all result in a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. This patient demonstrates a low bicarbonate level (10 mEq/L) with a normal anion gap of 12, consistent with a non-anion gap acidosis. The anion gap is calculated as Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) = 142 - (120 + 10) = 12, which is normal (8-16). Distal RTA (type 1) results from a defect in renal secretion of H+, which results in the lack of generation of HCO3-, ultimately leading to metabolic acidosis.
