It is characterized by a urine pH >5.5 (this patient has a urine pH of 6.5, indicating inability to acidify urine appropriately). The most common causes of type 1 RTA include analgesic nephropathy, congenital obstructive urinary tract anomalies, drugs (e.g., amphotericin), and autoimmune diseases resulting in hypergammaglobulinemia (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome). This patient's rheumatoid arthritis is a significant risk factor for developing RTA. Incorrect choices: A) Alcohol use does not independently alter acid-base pathology outside of extremes such as alcoholic ketoacidosis or consumption of volatile alcohols metabolized to organic acids. B) Diabetic ketoacidosis typically occurs in patients with type 1 diabetes and results in a metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap, not a normal anion gap as seen here. C) Increased lactate production results from hypoperfusion, deficiency in the TCA cycle, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, or vitamin deficiencies and is associated with an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis. E) Salicylate intoxication initially results in respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, followed by a delayed anion gap metabolic acidosis, not a non-anion gap acidosis.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Candidiasis1 questions
Source: 5A #35
A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of difficulty swallowing for 6 days. He says that food becomes stuck in his throat. Over the past 2 weeks, he has had low-grade fever and fatigue. He has had an 11-kg (25-lb) weight loss over the past year. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He uses intravenous heroin. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 110/78 mm Hg. Examination shows anterior and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. There are thick white plaques over the buccal mucosa and soft palate. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's dysphagia? A) Bacterial endocarditis B) Esophageal cancer with nodal metastases C) HIV infection with candidal esophagitis D) Oral cancer with nodal metastases E) Tertiary syphilis
Correct Answer: C) HIV infection with candidal esophagitis
Dysphagia has many structural, malignant, neurologic, infectious, and inflammatory causes. In the setting of weight loss, fatigue, low-grade fever, and intravenous drug abuse, the white oropharyngeal plaques are consistent with esophagitis from Candida species as a cause of dysphagia, a common opportunistic infection in an immunocompromised host such as a person with HIV. The patient's cervical lymphadenopathy is likely reactive to the adjacent esophageal infectious process. Herpes simplex virus and cytomegalovirus are also common infectious etiologies of esophagitis in this population, but these typically present with esophageal ulcers rather than plaques. Choice A (Bacterial endocarditis) presents classically with fevers, a new heart murmur, evidence of disseminated infection such as septic emboli, and vascular/immunologic phenomena such as Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, and splinter hemorrhages. This patient has none of these classic stigmata. Choice B (Esophageal cancer with nodal metastases) could explain the patient's dysphagia, weight loss, and vague systemic symptoms; however, it would not classically present with white oropharyngeal plaques, but rather esophageal narrowing with irregular borders from an infiltrative neoplastic mass. Choice D (Oral cancer with nodal metastases) could present with a white oral plaque (such as squamous cell carcinoma); however, this would typically be a solitary plaque as opposed to the multiple, thick plaques observed in this patient. Choice E (Tertiary syphilis) would not be expected to present with multiple white oral plaques; it classically presents with neurologic symptoms, gummas, and aortitis. The combination of IV drug abuse (risk factor for HIV), oropharyngeal candidiasis (thick white plaques), constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue, weight loss), and dysphagia strongly suggests an opportunistic infection in the setting of advanced HIV disease.
▶Respiratory System Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis1 questions
Source: 5A #36
A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-hour history of shortness of breath and nonproductive cough. She has had similar episodes, which typically last 18 hours, two to three times weekly during the past 3 months. She is asymptomatic when she runs outside for 45 minutes, five times weekly. She has not had chest pain. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is an oral contraceptive. She does not smoke cigarettes. She smokes marijuana once monthly. She moved to a new apartment building 4 months ago and she often uses the communal pool and hot tub. She appears to be in mild respiratory distress. Her temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. She is not using accessory muscles of respiration. Diffuse, fine crackles are heard prominently at the lung bases; no wheezes are heard. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Type of contraceptive use B) Hot tub use C) Illicit drug use D) Swimming pool use E) Type of exercise
Correct Answer: B) Hot tub use
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis represents a mixed type III and IV hypersensitivity reaction to various environmental antigens. This typically results in episodic dyspnea, fever, and cough that starts a few hours after exposure to the antigen. Classically, it occurs in farmers and individuals exposed to bird droppings, but can also occur secondary to hot tub use due to antigen exposure, as seen in this patient. Her symptoms may also represent chemical pneumonitis or bronchitis from inhaled chlorine. The temporal relationship between hot tub use and symptom onset (moved 4 months ago, symptoms for 3 months, episodic pattern) strongly suggests hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Treatment requires avoidance of the specific inciting antigen. Chronic exposure can result in alveolar thickening, noncaseating granuloma formation, and possible upper lobe predominant pulmonary fibrosis. Choice A (Type of contraceptive use): Estrogen-based contraceptives may increase the risk of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, which typically presents with acute-onset chest pain and shortness of breath. Pulmonary embolism would be less likely to present as episodic symptoms as seen in this patient. Choice C (Illicit drug use): Marijuana, when smoked, can result in tracheobronchial inflammation and/or pneumonitis, but she only smokes once monthly, which does not correlate with the frequency of her symptoms (two to three times weekly). Choice D (Swimming pool use): Swimming pool use is not directly associated with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, though it could be associated with chemical pneumonitis from chlorine exposure. Choice E (Type of exercise): The type of exercise may impact asthma symptoms, but would not play a role in hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Notably, the patient is asymptomatic during outdoor running, which actually argues against exercise-induced conditions.
▶Respiratory System Pulmonary Tuberculosis1 questions
Source: 5A #37
A 32-year-old homeless man is admitted to the hospital and placed in respiratory isolation because of a 2-week history of fever, chills, and cough productive of blood-tinged sputum. He also has had shortness of breath after walking approximately 100 feet. He has had a 13.6-kg (30-lb) weight loss during the past 6 months. He takes no prescription medications but has a history of intravenous drug use. He is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 45 kg (100 lb); BMI is 16 kg/m². His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. He is using accessory muscles of respiration. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Examination shows shotty cervical lymphadenopathy. There is bilateral wasting of the temporal and supraclavicular muscles. Diffuse crackles are heard throughout both lung fields. His leukocyte count is 11,500/mm³ (70% segmented neutrophils, 1% eosinophils, 1% basophils, 25% lymphocytes, and 3% monocytes). A PPD skin test is negative. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Aspiration pneumonia B) Bronchiectasis C) Sarcoidosis D) Septic pulmonary embolism E) Tuberculosis F) Wegener granulomatosis
Correct Answer: E) Tuberculosis
Pulmonary tuberculosis can present in various stages. Primary tuberculosis results from initial exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, leading to hilar lymphadenopathy and Ghon complex formation. Reactivation tuberculosis (secondary) typically results in apical pulmonary opacity with fibrocaseous cavitary lesions and presents clinically with prolonged fever, night sweats, weight loss (including skeletal muscle wasting), and hemoptysis. A PPD skin test can be negative in immunocompromised patients with tuberculosis infection. This case is highly suggestive of reactivation tuberculosis given the patient's risk factors (homelessness, IV drug use, immunocompromised state), classic presentation with constitutional symptoms, hemoptysis, weight loss, and radiographic findings. Reactivation tuberculosis requires combination antimicrobial treatment including rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, along with initial respiratory isolation. Incorrect answers: A) Aspiration pneumonia occurs in patients at risk for aspiration (elderly, stroke, dementia) and typically presents with consolidation in dependent portions of right middle or lower lobes following an aspiration episode, not matching this clinical picture. B) Bronchiectasis refers to chronic dilation of bronchi/bronchioles from chronic necrotizing infection, obstruction, cystic fibrosis, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, but does not explain the acute febrile presentation and hemoptysis. C) Sarcoidosis is a chronic non-caseating granulomatous inflammatory condition affecting hilar lymph nodes and lungs with coarse reticular opacities, but acute fever and hemoptysis are rare presentations. D) Septic pulmonary emboli typically occur with endocarditis (tricuspid valve) or infected thromboemboli sources, which are not suggested by this clinical presentation. F) Wegener granulomatosis can cause multifocal cavitary pulmonary nodules but typically presents with upper respiratory tract symptoms (perforated nasal septum, chronic sinusitis) and glomerulonephritis (hematuria), which are absent here.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Lymphangitis1 questions
Source: 5A #41
A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of swelling of his left hand and redness of his left forearm, wrist, and hand after being involved in a grease fire while working at a restaurant yesterday. After emptying the fryers, a small amount of grease splattered and left small burns on his arms. He does not take any medications. He has a history of "abnormal liver tests" and condylomata acuminata. He has had multiple sexual partners during the past 10 years and does not use condoms. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.9°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 138/68 mm Hg. A photograph of the left upper extremity is shown. There is no crepitus or fluctuance. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 18,000/mm³ with a left shift. X-rays of the left hand show diffuse soft-tissue edema. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Brown recluse spider bite B) Disseminated gonococcal infection C) Erysipelas D) Fasciitis E) Gout F) Lymphangitis G) Sporotrichosis
Correct Answer: F) Lymphangitis
Lymphangitis refers to inflammation or infection of the lymphatic channels, which often occurs secondary to an infectious source at a location distal to the lymphatic channel. In this case, it correlates with the location of the patient's burns. The most common cause of lymphangitis is Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A), with Sporothrix schenckii representing the most common fungal lymphangitis. Clinically, it presents with erythema in a linear, longitudinal band appearance, which correlates with the associated lymphatic drainage channel. There is also typically painful lymphadenopathy along the associated lymphatic drainage channel, resulting in pain and swelling with the possibility of high fevers. Choice A (Brown recluse spider bite) is associated with dermatonecrosis due to cytotoxic venom. Systemic illness is possible but more common in children, elderly, and chronically ill individuals, manifesting with fever, rashes, and myalgias, and rarely disseminated intravascular coagulation and end-organ damage. The patient's injury was from a grease fire, not a spider bite. Choice B (Disseminated gonococcal infection) presents with pustular skin lesions, migratory polyarthralgia, and tenosynovitis. While the patient's sexual history is notable, the clinical presentation with localized linear erythema and edema along lymphatic drainage is not consistent with disseminated gonococcal infection. Choice C (Erysipelas) results from infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, most commonly from S. pyogenes. On exam it appears as a well-defined region of raised induration and erythema. However, erysipelas typically affects the face or lower extremities and does not present with the characteristic linear lymphangitic streaking seen in this patient. Choice D (Fasciitis) refers to infection spreading along a deep fascial plane, most commonly from mixed flora (anaerobic and aerobic bacteria). It typically presents with acute onset of pain that progresses to anesthesia at a site of prior trauma or surgery. Evidence of gas production (crepitus), bullae, and severe pain out of proportion to the physical exam are indications of necrotizing infection. This patient has no crepitus or fluctuance, making fasciitis less likely. Choice E (Gout) results from monosodium urate crystals causing inflammatory monoarticular arthritis, classically affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint fluid analysis shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Gout does not present with fever, leukocytosis, or linear erythematous streaking along lymphatic channels. Choice G (Sporotrichosis) results from infection by Sporothrix schenckii, a fungus that grows within the rosettes of conidia plants and is typically introduced through traumatic breakage of the skin from thorns. It results in a local pustule and ulcer formation with ascending lymphangitis. The patient's injury was from a grease fire, not from vegetation, limiting the likelihood of sporotrichosis as the causative agent for lymphangitis.
▶Cardiovascular System Hyperlipidemia1 questions
Source: 5A #42
A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. She feels well. She has a 3-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Current medications include metformin and lisinopril. Her pulse is 68/min, and blood pressure is 116/74 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin A1c of 6.4%, serum creatinine concentration of 0.7 mg/dL, and serum LDL-cholesterol concentration of 112 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy? A) Add rosiglitazone to her current regimen B) Add simvastatin to her current regimen C) Increase the dosage of lisinopril D) Increase the dosage of metformin E) No change in therapy is indicated
Correct Answer: B) Add simvastatin to her current regimen
Simvastatin is a lipid-lowering agent that primarily reduces LDL cholesterol in patients with hypercholesterolemia through inhibition of hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA reductase. General recommendations for individuals with diabetes mellitus center around target LDL <100 mg/dL, HDL >40 mg/dL, and triglycerides <150 mg/dL. This patient's LDL of 112 mg/dL is above the target range for diabetic patients. Patients with diabetes mellitus exhibit higher incidence of cardiovascular disease with increased morbidity and mortality secondary to macrovascular complications including myocardial infarction, peripheral arterial disease, and stroke. It is critical to implement lipid-lowering agents to achieve target ranges for lipoprotein levels. Treatment of LDL cholesterol is considered the first priority for pharmacologic therapy, and statins are the first-line treatment for dyslipidemia in the setting of diabetes mellitus. Choice A (Rosiglitazone) is an oral hypoglycemic agent that binds to PPAR-gamma to increase insulin sensitivity; however, this patient's HbA1c of 6.4% is already at goal (target <7% for patients <70 years), so additional glucose-lowering therapy is not indicated. Choice C (Increasing lisinopril) is not appropriate as the patient's blood pressure is well-controlled at 116/74 mm Hg. While lisinopril inhibits ACE and is useful for hypertension management, diabetic nephropathy prevention, and heart failure management, dose escalation is unnecessary in this patient. Choice D (Increasing metformin) is not indicated because the patient's glycemic control is adequate with current therapy, as demonstrated by HbA1c of 6.4%. Choice E (No change) is incorrect because the patient's LDL cholesterol requires treatment with a statin to reduce cardiovascular risk and achieve the target LDL <100 mg/dL for diabetic patients.
▶Gastrointestinal System Inguinal hernia1 questions
Source: 5A #46
A 67-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-month history of a mass in his right groin that intermittently appears and disappears spontaneously; over the past 3 hours, the mass has become increasingly painful, and he has not been able to make it disappear. He also has had a decreased urinary stream and terminal dribbling with urination. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. He has a daily nonproductive morning cough. Abdominal examination shows no distention or tenderness. There is a nonreducible right groin mass; the testes are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) CT scan of the abdomen with contrast B) Fine-needle aspiration biopsy C) Cystoscopy and urodynamic studies D) Incision and drainage E) Immediate groin exploration
Correct Answer: E) Immediate groin exploration
This patient presents with an acute incarcerated or strangulated inguinal hernia requiring immediate surgical intervention. Inguinal hernias are classified into three categories: (1) Reducible hernias—contents easily return to native position with gentle pressure or resolution of triggering maneuver such as Valsalva; (2) Incarcerated hernias—contents become trapped within hernia defect and will not return despite counterpressure, potentially causing bowel obstruction; (3) Strangulated hernias—herniated contents lose blood supply with risk of necrosis or perforation. This patient's 3-month history of intermittent appearance and disappearance suggests a previously reducible hernia. His acute presentation over 3 hours with increasing pain and inability to reduce the mass indicates incarceration or strangulation. When a hernia cannot be manually reduced in the setting of acute symptoms, surgical reduction is required immediately to prevent life-threatening complications such as bowel necrosis and perforation. Choice A (CT scan of the abdomen with contrast) would provide additional diagnostic information but is unnecessary here. The diagnosis can be made clinically with reasonable confidence based on history and physical examination alone. Imaging would delay definitive therapy without adding pertinent information or advancing treatment. Choice B (Fine-needle aspiration biopsy) would be appropriate if the mass suggested lymphadenopathy; however, lymphadenopathy would not explain the 3-month history of intermittent symptoms. Choice C (Cystoscopy and urodynamic studies) may eventually be necessary to evaluate the patient's urinary symptoms (decreased stream, terminal dribbling), but these represent non-urgent issues. The patient requires immediate treatment for his acutely urgent surgical presentation related to the incarcerated inguinal hernia. Choice D (Incision and drainage) would be appropriate for an abscess, but the presentation is more consistent with an incarcerated hernia rather than an abscess. An abscess would typically present with erythema, fluctuance, and signs of local or systemic infection.
▶Respiratory System Pulmonary contusion1 questions
Source: 5A #49
A 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was the unrestrained driver of a car without an air bag. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 15 years. On arrival, he has severe chest pain that is most severe on inspiration. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 113 kg (250 lb); BMI is 38 kg/m². His pulse is 130/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Examination shows an ecchymosis over the anterior chest; there is no evidence of fractures. The lungs are clear to auscultation. An x-ray of the chest shows interstitial infiltrates of the lungs bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's respiratory symptoms? A) Fat embolism B) Flail chest C) Pulmonary contusion D) Pulmonary edema E) Pulmonary thromboembolism
Correct Answer: C) Pulmonary contusion
Pulmonary contusions occur after blunt or penetrating trauma to the chest. They underlie the region of trauma to the chest wall and result from damage to capillaries with associated leakage of intravascular and extravascular fluid into the pulmonary interstitium and alveolar airspaces. This can result in hypoxia if it involves a large enough region of the lung. On chest radiographs, pulmonary contusions appear as interstitial infiltrates and/or patchy alveolar opacities. The extent and distribution depend on the mechanism, location, and force of trauma to the chest wall. Management is supportive with control of pain, pulmonary toilet, lung expansion, and maintenance of adequate ventilation/oxygenation. Choice A (Fat embolism) typically occurs following a long-bone fracture with resultant fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, petechiae, and conjunctival hemorrhage. This patient has no evidence of fractures, making this unlikely. Choice B (Flail chest) generally results when two or more adjacent ribs are fractured at two or more locations, resulting in paradoxical movement of that chest wall segment. The patient's examination showed no evidence of fractures. Choice D (Pulmonary edema) often occurs secondary to a hypervolemic state (e.g., heart failure, renal failure, cirrhosis) or inflammatory state (e.g., pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome). While it can present with tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, cough, respiratory distress, and interstitial/alveolar opacities, there is no indication of heart failure, renal disease, or infection in this acute trauma setting. Choice E (Pulmonary thromboembolism) presents with tachycardia, tachypnea, and pleuritic chest pain. While PE can result from prolonged immobilization following trauma, it is unlikely to be related to trauma acutely, as the patient was injured only 2 hours prior to presentation.
▶Cardiovascular System Cor Pulmonale1 questions
Source: 5A #50
A 27-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of progressive shortness of breath. Examination shows decreased lung expansion, neck vein distention, and a parasternal heave; diffuse inspiratory crackles are heard on auscultation. She has 3+ pedal edema bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Angioedema B) Superior vena cava obstruction C) Biventricular heart failure D) Cirrhosis of the liver E) Cor pulmonale F) Idiopathic membranous nephropathy G) Lymphedema H) Myxedema I) Venous insufficiency
Correct Answer: E) Cor pulmonale
Cor pulmonale refers to isolated right heart failure secondary to chronic pulmonary pathology with increased pulmonary vascular resistance and right-sided heart pressures. This patient has systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) with decreased lung expansion and inspiratory crackles on examination, indicating underlying interstitial lung disease (ILD) with restrictive pulmonary pathophysiology. Chronic ILD is a major risk factor for developing pulmonary hypertension, which leads to right heart failure. The clinical presentation of right heart failure includes venous congestion manifested as jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, and a parasternal heave (indicating right ventricular hypertrophy). This patient exhibits all of these findings, making cor pulmonale secondary to ILD the most likely diagnosis. Incorrect answers: Angioedema (Choice A) is rapid subdermal or submucosal swelling from histamine or bradykinin release (allergic exposure, ACE inhibitors, C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency). Superior vena cava obstruction (Choice B) presents with obstruction of venous drainage from head and upper extremities, typically from underlying malignancy or thrombosis. Biventricular heart failure (Choice C) affects both ventricles and presents with left heart failure symptoms (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary edema) not seen in this patient. Cirrhosis of the liver (Choice D) presents with ascites, anasarca, jaundice, elevated transaminases, and impaired hepatic synthetic function, which are not evident in this case. Idiopathic membranous nephropathy (Choice F), the most common primary nephrotic syndrome, presents with massive proteinuria, edema, hyperlipidemia, and hypercoagulability. Lymphedema (Choice G) results from abnormal lymphatic drainage secondary to surgery, radiation, or parasitic infection. Myxedema (Choice H) causes facial and periorbital swelling in hypothyroidism. Venous insufficiency (Choice I) follows deep venous thrombosis and presents with stasis dermatitis and cutaneous ulcers. Educational Objective: Recognize that systemic sclerosis commonly causes interstitial lung disease, which through chronic pulmonary hypertension leads to cor pulmonale with characteristic right heart failure findings (JVD, peripheral edema, parasternal heave, and pulmonary crackles from pulmonary congestion).
▶Immune System Terminal Component Deficiency (C5b-C9; terminal complement complex)1 questions
Source: 7A #3
A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of fever and confusion for 4 hours. She has a 5-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus. She had Neisseria meningitidis meningitis 3 years ago. Current medications include hydroxychloroquine. Her temperature is 40°C (104°F). Examination shows nuchal rigidity. Kernig sign is present. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows cloudiness. A Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Common variable immunodeficiency B) Deficiency of terminal complement components C) Impaired cell-mediated immunity D) Leukocyte adhesion deficiency E) Phagocytic cell oxidative metabolism deficiency
Correct Answer: B) Deficiency of terminal complement components
Deficiency of terminal components of complement is the most likely cause of this patient's recent and recurrent infection with Neisseria meningitidis. The clinical presentation of fever, nuchal rigidity, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrating gram-negative diplococci is diagnostic for bacterial meningitis. Deficiency of terminal complement factors (C5-C9) impairs the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) and predisposes patients to infection with Neisseria species, particularly with uncommon serotypes. The complement cascade converges at C3, which is cleaved to release C3a and C3b. The C3 convertase complex subsequently leads to activation of C5, with formation of C5a and C5b. C5b then complexes with C6, C7, C8, and C9 to form the MAC. The MAC creates a transmembrane pore that interferes with cellular membrane integrity, leading to cell lysis and bacterial death. Screening for terminal complement deficiency typically begins with determination of the CH50, a diagnostic test measuring the ability of the patient's serum to lyse antibody-coated sheep erythrocytes. This test measures the activity of factors C1-C9; any deficiency will produce an abnormal result, and terminal complement deficiency results in very decreased or zero CH50 concentration. Treatment includes vaccination against N. meningitidis, H. influenzae, and S. pneumoniae in addition to management of acute infections. Choice A (Common variable immunodeficiency) classically presents in the second to fourth decades of life with recurrent sinopulmonary infections but does not predispose patients to N. meningitidis infection; diagnosis involves measuring decreased serum immunoglobulin concentrations. Choice C (Impaired cell-mediated immunity) refers to a broad range of conditions from acquired lymphocyte dysfunction such as HIV to genetic conditions, and does not specifically predispose to recurrent meningococcal infection. Choice D (Leukocyte adhesion deficiency) causes recurrent bacterial infections but not specifically meningococcal disease. Choice E (Phagocytic cell oxidative metabolism deficiency) is associated with chronic granulomatous disease, which predisposes to catalase-positive organisms, not N. meningitidis.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Delayed hemolysis from transfusion1 questions
Source: 7A #7
Prior to discharge to a skilled nursing care facility, an 80-year-old woman is evaluated in the hospital because of a decreased hemoglobin concentration. She underwent hemicolectomy 10 days ago for gastrointestinal bleeding secondary to diverticulosis. Four units of packed red blood cells were transfused during the procedure. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her medications are lisinopril and metformin. Today, her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mucosal pallor and conjunctival icterus. Abdominal examination shows a well-healing incision. Baseline hemoglobin concentration on postoperative day 3 was 10.0 g/dL. Hemoglobin concentration today is 7.5 g/dL. Laboratory studies are most likely to show which of the following additional findings? A) Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test: negative; Serum Bilirubin Concentration: increased direct B) Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test: negative; Serum Bilirubin Concentration: increased indirect C) Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test: negative; Serum Bilirubin Concentration: normal D) Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test: positive; Serum Bilirubin Concentration: increased direct E) Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test: positive; Serum Bilirubin Concentration: increased indirect F) Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test: positive; Serum Bilirubin Concentration: normal
Correct Answer: E) Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test: positive; Serum Bilirubin Concentration: increased indirect
This patient presents with anemia 10 days post-transfusion with evidence of hemolysis (mucosal pallor and conjunctival icterus), consistent with a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR). Unlike acute hemolytic transfusion reactions from ABO incompatibility, DHTRs typically result from autoantibodies against minor erythrocyte antigens (such as Rh antigens) and occur days to weeks after transfusion. DHTR requires prior exposure to the antigen for antibody production, though antibodies may not be detected during routine blood bank screening. Laboratory findings show: (1) Positive Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) Test: The direct Coombs test detects antibodies or complement bound to the surface of erythrocytes. Incubating patient erythrocytes with anti-IgG and anti-complement Coombs reagent causes agglutination if these are present. In DHTR, autoantibodies bind to red cell surfaces, resulting in a positive test. (2) Increased Indirect Bilirubin: Complement fixation causes intravascular hemolysis, releasing hemoglobin that is converted to unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin. Antibody binding marks erythrocytes for removal by the reticuloendothelial system, also leading to hemolysis and elevated indirect bilirubin. Choice A is incorrect because negative Coombs would not support immune-mediated hemolysis. Choice B is incorrect because the Coombs test should be positive in DHTR. Choice C is incorrect because bilirubin would be elevated with active hemolysis. Choice D is incorrect because direct hyperbilirubinemia occurs with hepatic or biliary dysfunction, not hemolysis. Choice F is incorrect because bilirubin levels would be elevated with hemolysis. Treatment of DHTR is primarily supportive, as it is typically milder than acute hemolytic reactions.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Transient Ischemic Attack1 questions
Source: 7A #8
A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after a 30-minute episode of weakness in the right arm and leg and difficulty speaking. The symptoms resolved spontaneously. His last visit to a physician was 35 years ago. His pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 160/96 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a diffuse point of maximal impulse and an S4 gallop. A left femoral bruit is heard. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, Serum Glucose (nonfasting) 156 mg/dL, Creatinine 3.2 mg/dL, Total cholesterol 210 mg/dL. An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. Treatment of which of the following is most likely to have prevented these findings? A) Congestive heart failure B) Hypercholesterolemia C) Hypertension D) Renal insufficiency E) Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Correct Answer: C) Hypertension
This patient presents with a transient ischemic attack (TIA), defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without evidence of infarction. His presenting symptoms of transient weakness and dysarthria indicate TIA. Additionally, he demonstrates signs of congestive heart failure (enlarged point of maximal impulse, S4 gallop), peripheral vascular disease (femoral bruit), and chronic kidney disease (elevated creatinine of 3.2 mg/dL), along with left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG. This patient has multiple risk factors for TIA and ischemic stroke including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and atherosclerotic disease. Hypertension is the single most important modifiable risk factor for TIAs and ischemic strokes and is a major contributor to the development of CHF, CKD, and peripheral vascular disease. Choice A (Congestive heart failure) is associated with stroke risk factors such as hypertension and dyslipidemia but is not an independent risk factor for stroke itself. Choice B (Hypercholesterolemia) has not been consistently demonstrated as a risk factor for all stroke subtypes and may only play a modest role in large vessel or lacunar ischemic strokes. Choice D (Renal insufficiency) may result from chronic hypertension but is not an independent risk factor for ischemic stroke. Choice E (Type 2 diabetes mellitus) is an important risk factor for ischemic stroke but is not as significant as hypertension in stroke prevention. Educational Objective: Hypertension is the single most important preventable risk factor for TIAs and ischemic strokes. It is also a critical contributor to the development of CHF, CKD, and peripheral vascular disease.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Alzheimer Disease1 questions
Source: 7A #9
An otherwise healthy 92-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her family because of a 1-year history of cognitive decline. Her daughter reports that the patient seems to "fish for words" and often repeats questions. The patient's 94-year-old husband has not noticed a problem. Twenty years ago, she sustained a concussion after falling off a horse. She is a high school graduate. Her 90-year-old sister has significant memory problems; her two younger brothers have no memory problems. The patient takes no medications. On examination, she is pleasant and cooperative. She knows the year, but not the month or date. She can recall a recent holiday. She has no difficulty naming objects by sight, but when asked to name as many animals as she can in 1 minute, she can only name five. She recalls one of three items after 5 minutes. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing factor for this patient's condition? A) Age B) Education level C) Family history D) Gender E) History of head trauma
Correct Answer: A) Age
Alzheimer disease (AD) is the most common type of dementia, presenting with progressive cognitive deterioration that begins with short-term memory impairment and decline in visuospatial abilities, progressing to apraxia, language abnormalities, and dysexecutive syndrome. The disease culminates in behavioral and personality changes that prevent the patient from performing basic activities of daily living. Age is the strongest risk factor for AD, with the incidence approximately doubling every 5 years after age 65. This patient's age of 92 years is the most significant predisposing factor. Less significant risk factors include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and a sedentary lifestyle. AD may be treated with drugs that increase acetylcholine in synaptic clefts, such as donepezil and cholinesterase inhibitors, which non-competitively and reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Though these drugs may slow cognitive decline and modestly improve functionality, they are not curative. Education level (Choice B) has been linked to AD with lower incidence in populations with higher education, but this relationship is not as significant as age. Family history (Choice C) is a mild risk factor; patients with first-degree relatives with AD have modestly increased risk, though most cases are sporadic and rare cases involve dominantly inherited mutations causing early-onset familial AD. Gender (Choice D) does not directly impact AD incidence, though it is more prevalent in women due to their longer life expectancy. History of head trauma (Choice E) has not been consistently demonstrated as an independent risk factor for AD.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Cluster Headache1 questions
Source: 7A #10
A previously healthy 42-year-old man comes to the office because of severe right-sided headaches for the past 3 weeks. He says that he awakens every night at 3 AM with a sharp stabbing pain behind the right eye that usually lasts about 30 minutes. There is no associated nausea. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 25 years and drinks a six-pack of beer daily. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination during an episode shows ptosis on the right and tearing and conjunctival injection; the right pupil is 2 mm, and the left is 4 mm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cluster headaches B) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension C) Migraine D) Subdural hematoma E) Temporal lobe glioma F) Tension-type headache
Correct Answer: A) Cluster headaches
Cluster headaches are primary headaches that typically present with brief (<120 minutes), unilateral, severe pain in the orbital, supraorbital, or temporal region of the head and are accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms. The pathogenesis is incompletely understood but likely involves activation of sensory fibers of the trigeminal nerve and parasympathetic nerves. Autonomic symptoms commonly include ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, and/or nasal congestion. Patients typically present between the ages of 20 and 50 years and are often male. Cigarette and alcohol use may be triggers for patients with a history of cluster headaches. The headaches often recur over a series of weeks to months, sometimes at the same time each year. Oxygen therapy with 100% oxygen is the most effective first-line abortive treatment, and verapamil is the first-line prophylactic treatment. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice B) presents with headache, nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, and transient visual obscuration or blurry vision secondary to increased intracranial pressure. External ocular appearance is normal. The presence of tearing and conjunctival injection in this patient suggests an alternate diagnosis. Migraine (Choice C) is a common cause of headache in adult patients. It often presents with a visual aura of scintillating scotoma or fortification spectra but is not associated with signs of autonomic hyperactivity such as lacrimation or conjunctival injection. Subdural hematoma (Choice D) may result from head trauma and the tearing of bridging veins in the subdural space, and it often presents with an acute or subacute onset headache, nausea, vomiting, and potentially with focal neurologic deficits or seizures caused by mass effect. A history of episodic symptoms over several weeks is less suggestive of an intracranial hemorrhage or hematoma. Temporal lobe glioma (Choice E), such as a glioblastoma, are tumors of the temporal lobe and often present with headache, seizures, and vomiting. Involvement of the temporal lobe visual pathway may cause a contralateral superior quadrantanopia. Tension-type headache (Choice F) typically presents with bilateral dull, pressure-like or band-like pain across the frontal and temporal areas. A tension-type headache does not present with signs of autonomic hyperactivity. The clinician should always distinguish primary headache types (e.g., tension, cluster, migraine) from secondary headache types (e.g., intracranial bleeding, tumors, glaucoma) because the treatment and prognosis differ greatly. Educational Objective: Cluster headaches typically present with brief, unilateral, severe pain in the orbital, supraorbital, or temporal region of the head accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms such as ptosis, miosis, conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, and nasal congestion.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Seborrheic Keratosis1 questions
Source: 7A #11
A 58-year-old man comes to the office because of a 1-year history of a slowly enlarging, painless, non-itchy lesion on his right inner thigh. He notices the lesion only when he bathes and believes he might be developing a similar one on his right forearm. He has HIV infection well controlled with antiretroviral therapy. He also takes a daily multivitamin. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. He used illicit intravenous heroin for 5 years but stopped 35 years ago. He has worked on a farm for 40 years. Vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of the lesion over the right thigh is shown. Examination of the right forearm shows a 3-cm, raised lesion with well-demarcated borders and dark pigmentation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following historical factors most likely increased this patient's risk for developing these lesions? A) Age B) Gender C) Medical history D) Medication history E) Occupation
Correct Answer: A) Age
Seborrheic keratosis is a benign proliferation of the epidermis, characterized histologically by a benign, acanthotic proliferation of keratinocytes with absence of cellular atypia. The lesions are typically round, raised, brown or tan in color, and sharply demarcated with an adherent or stuck-on appearance. Seborrheic keratosis is common in middle-aged and older adults and is most associated with increasing age. While seborrheic keratosis is benign, the sudden appearance of numerous seborrheic keratosis lesions on the back and trunk, known as the Leser-Trélat sign, can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of gastrointestinal malignancy. No treatment is necessary for seborrheic keratosis, although lesions that are cosmetically bothersome may be removed with cryotherapy or simple excision. Gender (Choice B) is not a significant predisposing factor for seborrheic keratosis, which affects men and women in equal proportion. Medical history (Choice C), such as HIV in this patient, does not result in an increased risk for seborrheic keratosis. While Kaposi sarcoma is associated with AIDS, these lesions are red or purple in color and commonly occur on the face, oral mucosa, legs, and torso. Medication history (Choice D), such as the use of antiretroviral therapy in this patient, does not result in an increased risk for seborrheic keratosis. Occupation (Choice E) is not a significant risk factor for seborrheic keratosis. While several zoonotic diseases can affect farmworkers, such as anthrax and tularemia, these lesions are typically characterized as black eschars or ulcerations, respectively. Educational Objective: Seborrheic keratosis is a benign proliferation of the epidermal keratinocytes. Lesions are typically round, raised, brown or tan in color, and sharply demarcated with an adherent or stuck-on appearance. The main risk factor for seborrheic keratosis is increasing age. Treatment is not usually required.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Actinic Keratosis1 questions
Source: 7A #12
A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of persistent actinic keratosis despite treatment with 5-fluorouracil. Examination shows a 0.5 x 0.5-cm lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Observation only B) Excisional biopsy C) Punch biopsy D) Radiation therapy E) Systemic chemotherapy followed by surgical excision
Correct Answer: B) Excisional biopsy
Actinic keratosis is a premalignant lesion that may progress to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Clinically, lesions typically appear as light pink, ill-defined macules with a gritty texture in areas of prolonged sun exposure, such as the face, ears, and dorsal hands. Actinic keratosis may be treated with topical medications such as 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod, excision, cryotherapy, or dermabrasion. Ablative therapies are best used when the diagnosis is relatively certain and a histopathologic specimen is not required. However, lack of response to topical therapy should raise suspicion for possible SCC and should prompt an excisional biopsy. Excisional biopsy is preferable because of its ability to assess for invasive disease and curative potential if the entire lesion is removed. A low threshold of suspicion for SCC should be maintained, particularly in patients with a history of immunocompromise or solid organ transplantation. Choice A (Observation only) is not appropriate because this patient's actinic keratosis has failed to respond to prior topical treatment, which raises suspicion for possible SCC. Choice C (Punch biopsy) is not preferred for the diagnosis and treatment of lesions concerning for SCC because it does not allow for the complete removal of the lesion. SCC lesions that are incompletely excised usually require further excision with careful assessment of margins. Choice D (Radiation therapy) is not typically used for lesions concerning for SCC. Radiation is sometimes used in conjunction with surgical excision in high-risk SCC tumors or in lesions that are not amenable to complete excision. Choice E (Systemic chemotherapy followed by surgical excision) is not necessary for the treatment of either actinic keratosis or SCC, both of which are usually amenable to local, topical chemotherapeutic or ablative treatments. Educational Objective: Actinic keratosis is a premalignant lesion that may progress to SCC. Lack of response to topical therapy should raise suspicion for possible SCC and should prompt an excisional biopsy. Excisional biopsy is preferable because of its ability to assess for invasive disease and curative potential if the entire lesion is removed.
▶Cardiovascular System Atherosclerosis1 questions
Source: 7A #17
A 48-year-old man has a 6-month history of pain in both buttocks when he walks and erectile dysfunction. He has been a heavy smoker for 20 years. His blood pressure in the lower extremities is less than half of that in his arms. His serum cholesterol concentration is 286 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Aortic aneurysm B) Aortic dissection C) Aortic atherosclerosis D) Coarctation of the aorta E) Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)
Correct Answer: C) Aortic atherosclerosis
Aortic atherosclerosis commonly occurs at the aortic arch and in the abdominal aorta distal to the renal arteries. It leads to ischemia of the lower extremities, presenting with claudication of the buttocks and legs, lower extremity pain, paresthesia, paraplegia, shiny hairless skin, and erectile dysfunction. The clinical presentation fits this patient's 6-month history of buttock pain with exertion, erectile dysfunction, significantly reduced lower extremity blood pressures (less than half of arm pressures), and major risk factors including heavy smoking for 20 years and elevated cholesterol (286 mg/dL). A careful examination with attention to lower extremity pulses is crucial. Diagnosis is supported by CT or MR angiography and ankle-brachial blood pressure indices. Treatment includes modification of risk factors (smoking cessation, management of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes) and prompt reperfusion via balloon or stent angioplasty, aortic endarterectomy, vascular bypass surgery (e.g., aortofemoral bypass grafting), or thrombolysis/thrombectomy in acute cases. Choice A (Aortic aneurysm) typically presents with a palpable pulsatile abdominal mass and is generally asymptomatic until rupture, which causes acute abdominal pain and hypotension. Claudication is not typical. Choice B (Aortic dissection) presents with tearing chest or abdominal pain radiating to the back, peripheral pulse or blood pressure deficits, and neurologic symptoms such as numbness or tingling. It may involve mesenteric ischemia or renal infarction. Choice D (Coarctation of the aorta) is a congenital narrowing commonly associated with bicuspid aortic valve and Turner syndrome. It typically presents in childhood with a systolic murmur, differential pulses, and blood pressure differences between extremities. If untreated, it leads to left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure. Choice E (Thromboangiitis obliterans/Buerger disease) is a small-vessel vasculitis associated with smoking presenting with claudication that may progress to painful ulceration, gangrene, and autoamputation of digits, with ulcerations typically occurring at fingertip and toe tips. Educational Objective: Aortic atherosclerosis may present with claudication of the buttocks and lower extremities as well as lower extremity pain, paresthesia, paraplegia, and erectile dysfunction. Treatment includes medical modification of risk factors along with reperfusion by surgical or endovascular methods.
▶Cardiovascular System Pericardial Tamponade1 questions
Source: 7A #18
A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of progressive shortness of breath. He has not had chest pain, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He completed chemotherapy for small cell carcinoma of the lung 10 months ago. He has a long-term history of nocturia twice nightly that resolved over the past 3 days. He smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years but quit 1 year ago. His pulse is 116/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. There is jugular venous distention to the angle of the jaw. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Heart sounds are distant. The liver is tender and has a span of 12 cm. There is no pedal edema. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10 g/dL Serum Na+ 135 mEq/L Cl- 110 mEq/L K+ 4.2 mEq/L HCO3- 22 mEq/L Urea nitrogen 40 mg/dL Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL An ECG shows decreased QRS voltage. An x-ray of the chest shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette. The most likely cause of these findings is an abnormality of which of the following? A) Aorta B) Endocardium C) Myocardium D) Pericardium E) Pulmonary artery F) Pulmonary veins
Correct Answer: D) Pericardium
Fluid that accumulates within the pericardial space in a rapid-onset or large-volume fashion can result in pericardial tamponade. Compression of the cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle, impairs cardiac filling with resultant decreased cardiac output caused by low stroke volume. Severe cases result in obstructive shock, manifest by tachycardia and hypotension. Physical examination findings include Beck triad (hypotension, distended jugular veins, and distant heart sounds). ECG may disclose low voltage and/or electrical alternans, and there may be pulsus paradoxus on evaluation of blood pressure. Treatment requires emergent pericardiocentesis to restore diastolic filling and cardiac output. Predisposing conditions include but are not limited to malignancy, infectious or inflammatory states such as tuberculosis, viral pericarditis, and systemic lupus erythematosus, traumatic injury, and aortic dissection. Choice A (Aorta): Can be implicated in cases of pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade if retrograde travel of an aortic dissection results in rupture into the pericardial space. Such cases generally present with acute chest pain radiating to the back, asymmetric pulses or extremity blood pressures, and potential neurologic deficits. This patient lacks these features. Choice B (Endocardium): Involved in endocarditis, typically from an infectious and inflammatory state. Right-sided endocarditis often involves the tricuspid valve following seeding during intravenous drug abuse. It classically presents with fever, septic emboli, vascular and immunologic phenomena such as splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, and Janeway lesions. Inflammatory endocarditis can occur in systemic lupus erythematosus (Libman-Sacks endocarditis), but is less common than pericarditis as a cardiac manifestation. Choice C (Myocardium): Implicated in myocarditis, which may be infectious or inflammatory, and generally presents with chest discomfort, shortness of breath, tachycardia, and signs of heart failure on examination. This patient has clear lungs, which makes pulmonary edema from myocardial dysfunction unlikely. Choice E (Pulmonary artery): Involved in pulmonary embolism, which presents with chest discomfort, shortness of breath, signs of right heart failure or strain such as lower extremity edema, hepatomegaly, and jugular venous distention. Signs of deep venous thrombosis are also often present. While this patient has some overlapping features, the clear lungs, absence of chest pain, and classic tamponade findings make tamponade more likely. Choice F (Pulmonary veins): May be affected by left-sided heart failure, congestion of which leads to cardiogenic pulmonary edema. This presents with shortness of breath, cough often associated with frothy sputum, and crackles on lung examination. This patient has clear lungs, making pulmonary edema unlikely. Educational Objective: The presence of a large-volume or rapidly accumulating fluid in the pericardial space can cause cardiac tamponade, an obstructive shock state resulting from impaired venous return and poor right ventricular filling. Malignancy is a common predisposing condition and treatment includes emergent pericardial decompression to restore chamber filling.
▶Cardiovascular System Pericardial Effusion1 questions
Source: 7A #19
A 52-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of progressive shortness of breath and right upper abdominal pain. She has been unable to sleep while supine because of difficulty breathing. She underwent chemotherapy 1 year ago for breast cancer. She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 104/80 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous pulsations at the angle of the jaw with the patient sitting upright. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Heart sounds are distant. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard. Abdominal examination shows diffuse hepatomegaly. There is 2+ pedal edema. Her serum urea nitrogen concentration is 42 mg/dL, and serum creatinine concentration is 1.6 mg/dL. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A) Anterior myocardial infarct B) Cor pulmonale C) Pericardial effusion D) Pulmonary emboli E) Right ventricular myocardial infarct
Correct Answer: C) Pericardial effusion
The clinical presentation is classic for pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade. The patient's history of chemotherapy for breast cancer (known risk factor for pericardial effusion) combined with acute onset shortness of breath, orthopnea, and right upper quadrant pain (hepatic congestion) are key features. Physical examination findings demonstrate Beck's triad: distant heart sounds (fluid muffling sound conduction), jugular venous pulsations (increased right heart pressure), and hepatomegaly with pedal edema (systemic venous congestion from impaired right ventricular filling). The elevated BUN and creatinine reflect decreased renal perfusion from low cardiac output. Tachycardia and tachypnea are compensatory responses. Compression of the cardiac chambers, particularly the right ventricle, by pericardial fluid impairs diastolic filling and decreases cardiac output. The clear lungs on auscultation help exclude primary pulmonary pathology. Choice A (Anterior MI) would typically present with chest pain and ST elevation in precordial leads; choice B (Cor pulmonale) develops chronically from pulmonary hypertension and would not present acutely; choice D (Pulmonary embolism) would present with chest pain and hypoxia with clear lungs but lacks the constellation of Beck's triad; choice E (RV MI) could cause right heart failure but would show ST elevation in right-sided leads and lack the acute fluid accumulation findings. Diagnostic confirmation requires echocardiography to visualize the effusion. Management of hemodynamically significant effusion includes pericardiocentesis or pericardial window.
▶Respiratory System Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Bronchus and Lung1 questions
Source: 7A #23
A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of nonproductive cough, hemoptysis, and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss over the past month. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years. Breath sounds are decreased over the right posterior hemithorax. Laboratory studies show no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows collapse of the right lower lobe of the lung. Which of the following is the most likely pathophysiology of this patient's condition? A) Endobronchial obstruction with distal atelectasis B) Increased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure C) Pleural inflammation with fluid formation D) Proximal airway inflammation E) Pulmonary parenchymal necrosis F) Pulmonary vascular obstruction
Correct Answer: A) Endobronchial obstruction with distal atelectasis
This patient presents with classic features of advanced lung cancer with endobronchial obstruction. Lung cancer often remains asymptomatic until advanced stages when the tumor locally invades or metastasizes, leading to nonspecific symptoms including weight loss and fatigue. Once the tumor invades neurosensory and vascular structures, patients develop coughing and hemoptysis. When a lesion is large enough to invade or obstruct a bronchus, it causes post-obstructive or recurrent pneumonia in the distal parenchyma due to atelectasis and impaired endobronchial clearance of mucus, secretions, and inhaled pathogens. In this patient, decreased breath sounds over the right posterior hemithorax indicate endobronchial obstruction to airflow, further supported by the x-ray finding of atelectasis in the corresponding area. The 50-year smoking history, heavy smoking burden (two packs daily for 50 years), and presentation with hemoptysis and weight loss are consistent with centrally-located squamous cell carcinoma or small cell carcinoma, which are common in smokers. Choice B (Increased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure) describes cardiogenic pulmonary edema pathophysiology, which presents with bilateral airspace edema, rales in dependent areas, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions, and cardiomegaly on imaging—findings not present here. Choice C (Pleural inflammation with fluid formation) describes pleurisy, mesothelioma, or empyema. While reduced lung sounds may occur, a pleural effusion would be visible on imaging rather than focal atelectasis. Choice D (Proximal airway inflammation) describes bronchitis, typically presenting with acute productive cough, chest discomfort, and fever following viral upper respiratory infection. Weight loss would be atypical, and x-rays are generally unremarkable unless mucus plugging causes atelectasis. Choice E (Pulmonary parenchymal necrosis) may result from infarction, vasculitis, or infection, typically presenting acutely. A subacute to chronic presentation with weight loss would be atypical. Choice F (Pulmonary vascular obstruction) describes pulmonary embolism, presenting with acute chest pain, dyspnea, or hemoptysis in the setting of thromboembolism or predisposing conditions. Collapsed lung and weight loss would be unlikely features. Educational Objective: Advanced lung cancer can obstruct a bronchus, causing atelectasis, hemoptysis, and post-obstructive recurrent pneumonia. When large, invasive, or metastatic, lung cancer has worse prognosis. Screening with low-dose chest CT is recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force for patients aged 50 to 80 years with a 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years to promote early detection.
▶Respiratory System Pneumoconiosis1 questions
Source: 7A #25
A 70-year-old man comes to the office because of a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath with exertion. Six months ago, he was able to walk five blocks before having shortness of breath. He now has shortness of breath after walking one block. He has not had chest pain, palpitations, swelling of his legs, or shortness of breath at night. He has hypertension. His medications are lisinopril and aspirin. He does not smoke cigarettes. He is a retired foundry worker. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². His pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows no other abnormalities. There is no edema of the extremities. Results of pulmonary function testing show an FVC of 65% of predicted and an FEV₁:FVC ratio of 70%. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Asbestosis B) Aspergillosis C) Asthma D) Bronchiectasis E) Chronic bronchitis F) Pneumoconiosis
Correct Answer: F) Pneumoconiosis
Pneumoconiosis describes interstitial lung disease arising from inhalation of small solid particulate matter such as dust or powder (talc, silica, beryllium, and ores) that leads to fibrosis with resultant restrictive lung disease. It is commonly seen in patients with chronic occupational exposures, such as foundry workers, miners, shipyard workers, cotton workers, farmers, stone drillers, and sandblasters. The disease's progression is often worsened by smoking. It typically presents with chronic symptoms of cough and shortness of breath on exertion; when severe or advanced, it can be associated with the need for supplemental oxygen and symptoms of heart failure (cor pulmonale). Diagnosis is based on clinical history, symptoms, examination, occupational exposure history, characteristic imaging tests showing fibrosis (x-ray may show honeycombing and fibrosis, especially in the apices), and pulmonary function tests disclosing a restrictive pattern of lung disease marked by decreased overall volumes and capacities but a preserved or increased FEV₁:FVC ratio. This ratio is a key distinguishing feature from obstructive lung disease, which presents with a decreased ratio. Choice A (Asbestosis): While asbestosis also arises from chronic exposure to inhaled asbestos and causes restrictive lung disease with similar pulmonary function tests showing a restrictive pattern, imaging typically shows fibrosis of dependent and inferior portions of lung and is associated with pleural thickening and nodularity, not the apical predominance typical of other pneumoconioses. Choice B (Aspergillosis): This presents with various clinical manifestations including aspergillomas (fungal masses within existing cavitary lesions such as those from tuberculosis, emphysematous blebs/bullae, or cavitary lung carcinoma), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, chronic necrotizing aspergillosis, and invasive aspergillosis. The clinical presentation and imaging findings differ significantly from this patient's presentation. Choices C, D, E (Asthma, Bronchiectasis, Chronic Bronchitis): All present with an obstructive pattern on pulmonary function testing, characterized by decreased FEV₁, decreased FEV₁:FVC ratio, and preserved FVC. These conditions typically present with wheezing and air trapping on examination, not the diffuse bilateral crackles seen in this patient. The patient's preserved FEV₁:FVC ratio of 70% rules out these obstructive diseases. Educational Objective: Pneumoconiosis is interstitial lung disease resulting from inhalation of small solid particulate matter leading to fibrosis and restrictive lung disease. Diagnosis relies on clinical features, occupational exposure history, imaging showing fibrosis, and pulmonary function tests demonstrating a restrictive pattern. A critical distinguishing feature of restrictive lung disease on pulmonary function testing is the preserved or increased FEV₁:FVC ratio.
▶Gastrointestinal System Sialadenitis1 questions
Source: 7A #28
A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of progressive left-sided facial pain and swelling. Initially, the pain was only precipitated by eating, but now it has been constant for the past 3 days. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 136/80 mm Hg. Examination shows an area of edema over the lateral left face that is warm, tender, and erythematous. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Mumps B) Sarcoidosis C) Sialadenitis D) Sjégren syndrome E) Temporomandibular joint dysfunction
Correct Answer: C) Sialadenitis
Sialadenitis refers to inflammation of the salivary gland and typically presents with acute onset of pain and swelling over the affected gland. Acute sialadenitis often persists for several weeks and most commonly occurs because of obstruction of the gland caused by sialolithiasis but may also occur secondary to viral infection (e.g., mumps or Epstein-Barr virus), bacterial infection (most commonly with S. aureus), or strictures following radiotherapy. The presence of constitutional symptoms may be indicative of a viral cause, while the expression of purulent discharge from the glandular orifice may indicate a bacterial infection. This patient's history of pain initially precipitated by meals is most suggestive of the presence of a salivary gland stone causing intermittent obstruction. Further evaluation with ultrasonography or CT may help establish the diagnosis. Treatment is primarily conservative with analgesics, application of heat and massage, and hydration. Patients that fail to improve with conservative management sometimes require removal of a sialolith, if present, usually by sialoendoscopy. Choice A (Mumps): Presents with salivary gland swelling, which is typically bilateral and accompanied by other signs and symptoms, such as fever, headache, malaise, and myalgia. Mumps typically presents in children and is rare in the United States because of widespread vaccination. Choice B (Sarcoidosis): May present with parotid gland inflammation as part of the classic Heerfordt syndrome, along with anterior uveitis, facial nerve palsy, and fever. This manifestation of sarcoidosis is uncommon, and this patient lacks the other typical signs of Heerfordt syndrome. Choice D (Sjégren syndrome): An autoimmune disorder characterized by chronic inflammation and destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands. Salivary involvement presents with chronic, painless, bilateral salivary gland enlargement, which does not fit this patient's acute presentation. Choice E (Temporomandibular joint dysfunction): May produce symptoms of periauricular pain and popping sensations with chewing but does not cause facial swelling. Educational Objective: Sialadenitis presents with acute onset of pain and swelling over the affected salivary gland. It most commonly occurs due to obstruction from sialolithiasis but may also result from viral infection, bacterial infection (particularly S. aureus), or post-radiotherapy strictures. A history of pain precipitated by eating is characteristic of salivary gland obstruction. Treatment is primarily conservative with analgesics, heat application, massage, and hydration.
▶Gastrointestinal System Cholelithiasis1 questions
Source: 7A #29
An obese 42-year-old woman has an episode of colicky pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen that lasts 2 hours and subsides spontaneously. She has no fever or leukocytosis and no signs of peritoneal irritation in the right upper quadrant. Liver function tests show no abnormalities. Ultrasonography shows gallstones. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the abdominal pain? A) Bacterial growth in bile within the common hepatic duct B) Bacterial invasion of the gallbladder wall C) Transitory chemical irritation of the gallbladder wall D) Transitory obstruction of the common hepatic duct by gallstones E) Transitory obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones
Correct Answer: E) Transitory obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones
This patient's presenting symptom of colicky pain in the right upper quadrant is consistent with biliary colic secondary to transitory obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones. The pain is typically dull, severe, triggered by meals, and may radiate to the right shoulder. Most episodes of biliary colic last for several hours before subsiding spontaneously. Biliary colic can be distinguished from cholecystitis by a lack of fever, a normal abdominal examination, and a lack of leukocytosis. Choice A (Bacterial growth in bile within the common hepatic duct) may result from an ascending infection of the biliary tree, known as cholangitis, which typically occurs in the setting of biliary instrumentation or choledocholithiasis. Acute cholangitis presents with fever and jaundice in addition to abdominal pain (Charcot triad) and possibly shock and altered mental status (Reynolds pentad). This patient lacks these findings. Choice B (Bacterial invasion of the gallbladder wall) results in acute cholecystitis, which presents with fever, abdominal pain, and tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant, often in a patient with a history of gallstones. Patients typically present with leukocytosis and fever, which this patient lacks. Choice C (Transitory chemical irritation of the gallbladder wall) may occur in the setting of intra-arterial chemotherapeutic embolization of hepatic metastases. The presence of gallstones and the colicky nature of this patient's pain are more consistent with biliary colic. Choice D (Transitory obstruction of the common hepatic duct by gallstones) refers to choledocholithiasis, which would present with increased bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. This patient's liver function tests are normal. Additionally, obstruction of the cystic duct (not the common hepatic duct) is the mechanism of biliary colic. Abdominal ultrasonography can aid diagnosis by identifying gallstones. The acute management of biliary colic is generally conservative with oral analgesics. Elective cholecystectomy is recommended to prevent future complications from the gallstones. If symptoms progress to show features of jaundice, hepatic injury, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, choledocholithiasis, or cholangitis, operative (cholecystectomy) or interventional (e.g., endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) management should take place.
▶Gastrointestinal System Chronic pancreatitis1 questions
Source: 7A #30
A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of loose, foul-smelling stools; during this period, he has had a 6.3-kg (14-lb) weight loss despite a good appetite. He also has had urinary frequency and urgency for 3 weeks. He has not had fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting. He has a 10-year history of recurrent alcoholic pancreatitis that required hospitalization once or twice each year because of severe abdominal pain. He has not been hospitalized since he abstained from drinking alcohol 2 years ago, but he has had chronic mild midepigastric pain since that time. During his last hospitalization 2 years ago, an x-ray of the abdomen showed calcifications in the pancreas. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 69 kg (153 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Examination shows temporal wasting. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows midepigastric tenderness with no masses or hepatosplenomegaly; bowel sounds are normal. There is no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 39%, Mean corpuscular volume 84 µm³, Leukocyte count 9000/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 72%, Lymphocytes 18%, Monocytes 10%, Platelet count 230,000/mm³, Serum urea nitrogen 17 mg/dL, Glucose 280 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, Protein total 5.8 g/dL, Albumin 2.7 g/dL. Which of the following sets of findings is the most likely explanation for this patient's increased serum glucose concentration? Insulin Production | Glucagon Production | Peripheral Insulin Response A) Decreased | Decreased | Normal B) Decreased | Increased | Normal C) Increased | Decreased | Decreased D) Increased | Increased | Decreased E) Increased | Normal | Decreased F) Normal | Normal | Decreased
Correct Answer: A) Decreased | Decreased | Normal
Recurrent episodes of acute pancreatitis may lead to chronic pancreatitis and insufficiency of both the exocrine and endocrine pancreatic functions. The exocrine pancreas produces digestive enzymes; their absence leads to malnutrition, cachexia, muscle wasting, weight loss, vitamin deficiencies, and frequent, loose, foul-smelling, sometimes oily stools (steatorrhea). This patient's 4-month history of loose, foul-smelling stools and weight loss despite good appetite are classic signs of exocrine insufficiency. The endocrine pancreas produces insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin. In chronic pancreatitis, there is loss of endogenous insulin production, leading to development of diabetes mellitus with symptoms including polyuria, polydipsia, and polyphagia. This patient's urinary frequency and urgency for 3 weeks combined with his serum glucose of 280 mg/dL reflect new-onset diabetes from pancreatic endocrine insufficiency. Additionally, he has decreased glucagon production due to loss of pancreatic alpha cells, while peripheral tissue response to insulin remains normal (the problem is lack of insulin production, not resistance). Choice B corresponds to the normal fasting state, where glucagon normally increases to counterregulate hypoglycemia, but this does not explain the elevated glucose. Choice C characterizes type 2 diabetes mellitus, wherein chronic hyperinsulinemia occurs in response to poor peripheral tissue insulin resistance. However, this patient's problem is pancreatic insufficiency with insufficient insulin production, not insulin resistance. Choice D suggests both increased insulin and glucagon production with decreased peripheral insulin response. While both insulin and glucagon concentrations may be transiently increased in acute pancreatitis, this does not occur in chronic pancreatitis. Additionally, decreased peripheral insulin response is not a feature of chronic pancreatitis. Choice E suggests increased insulin with normal glucagon and decreased peripheral response, which may occur in type 2 diabetes but not in pancreatic insufficiency. Choice F suggests normal production of both hormones with decreased peripheral response, which may occur in early type 2 diabetes but not in the setting of chronic pancreatitis with pancreatic endocrine failure. The diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic insufficiency is established through clinical history, imaging (showing pancreatic calcifications as in this patient), and biopsy. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is treated with oral pancreatic enzyme and fat-soluble vitamin replacement. The diabetes mellitus caused by loss of pancreatic insulin requires insulin replacement therapy. Any modifiable inciting causes of pancreatitis (gallstones, alcohol abuse, hypertriglyceridemia, or hypercalcemia) should be mitigated to delay disease progression and preserve remaining native pancreatic function.
▶Endocrine System Hashimoto thyroiditis1 questions
Source: 7A #37
A 28-year-old woman comes to the office because of an 8-week history of fatigue and cold intolerance. She has a 2-year history of bipolar disorder. At the age of 4 years, she was hospitalized for 2 days for treatment of meningitis. At the age of 16 years, she had loss of consciousness after a motor vehicle collision. Her medications are divalproex, an oral contraceptive, and a daily multivitamin. Her brother has type 1 diabetes mellitus. The patient does not smoke cigarettes. She drinks two 12-oz beers daily and smokes marijuana four times monthly. She appears well developed and well nourished. Her temperature is 36.4°C (97.5°F), pulse is 54/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 120/74 mm Hg. The thyroid gland is nontender and cannot be palpated. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+. The remainder of the examination, including cardiac examination, shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 23 uU/mL and free thyroxine concentration of 0.5 ng/dL (N=0.8–2.4). Which of the following historical factors has most likely increased this patient's risk for her current condition? A) Alcohol consumption B) Childhood illness C) Current medications D) Family history E) History of motor vehicle collision F) Illicit drug use
Correct Answer: D) Family history
This patient presents with clinical and biochemical evidence of primary hypothyroidism (elevated TSH of 23 uU/mL and low free thyroxine of 0.5 ng/dL), with symptoms of fatigue and cold intolerance. The most important historical risk factor is the family history of type 1 diabetes mellitus in her brother, which indicates familial autoimmune disease. The most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-replete parts of the world is Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic autoimmune thyroiditis). This autoimmune condition is characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland leading to cytotoxic destruction and subsequent fibrosis. The elevated TSH with decreased free thyroxine indicates adequate pituitary function but inadequate thyroid hormone production. Patients may present with either a goiter or normal-sized thyroid gland. Some patients have antibodies against thyroid peroxidase or thyroglobulin, though these are not required for diagnosis.
