As an autoimmune disease, patients with family histories of other autoimmune conditions such as type 1 diabetes mellitus or primary adrenal insufficiency are at significantly higher risk for developing chronic autoimmune thyroiditis. The disease is more common in women. Treatment involves thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine. Choice A (Alcohol consumption): Does not increase the risk for hypothyroidism. Choice B (Childhood illness): Meningitis at age 4 is not associated with hypothyroidism development, though it may increase risk for hearing loss and seizure disorders. Choice C (Current medications): Divalproex, oral contraceptives, and multivitamins are not associated with increased hypothyroidism risk. While divalproex may rarely cause amenorrhea, it is not directly associated with hypothyroidism. Choice E (History of motor vehicle collision): While traumatic brain injury can cause central hypothyroidism through hypopituitarism, this would present with decreased TSH and decreased free thyroxine (opposite pattern from this patient). Additionally, isolated central hypothyroidism without other pituitary hormone deficiencies would be unusual. Choice F (Illicit drug use): Marijuana is not known to be associated with hypothyroidism. Educational Objective: Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-replete regions. The disease is more prevalent in women and shows higher prevalence in patients with family histories of autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes mellitus or primary adrenal insufficiency.
▶Endocrine System Prolactinoma1 questions
Source: 7A #39
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because she has not been able to conceive for 12 months. Her son was born 4 years ago. Her menses were normal until 1 year ago when they became irregular. She has not had a menstrual period for the past 6 months. She has also had a small amount of milky secretion from her breasts. She does not take medications. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities except for galactorrhea. Her serum prolactin concentration is 200 ng/mL. A pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Cytologic examination of breast secretions B) Measurement of serum estradiol concentration C) Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormone concentrations D) Mammography E) MRI of the pituitary gland
Correct Answer: E) MRI of the pituitary gland
MRI of the pituitary gland is the most appropriate next step in evaluation of this young woman with amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and markedly increased serum prolactin concentration. Prolactin is produced and secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. Pathologic increases in prolactin concentration are commonly the result of pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas) resulting in hypersecretion of prolactin from lactotroph cells. While dopamine antagonists such as antipsychotic medications or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors may lead to mild increases in prolactin concentration, they do not approach the concentrations seen in pituitary adenomas. Prolactin inhibits the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and thereby reduces concentrations of follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone, leading to amenorrhea and infertility. Prolactin also acts directly on mammary glands and induces lactation. After medications are excluded as the potential cause, patients should undergo MRI of the pituitary gland to assess for the presence of a mass. First-line treatment is typically with cabergoline, a dopamine agonist that decreases prolactin secretion, or bromocriptine as an alternative. Transsphenoidal resection may be required in rare circumstances. Choice A (Cytologic examination of breast secretions) is incorrect. While unilateral galactorrhea may be concerning for breast cancer, the constellation of bilateral galactorrhea and amenorrhea is more consistent with a prolactinoma. Choice B (Measurement of serum estradiol concentration) is not necessary. Estradiol concentrations fluctuate throughout the menstrual cycle, but the markedly increased prolactin concentration indicates a more likely cause of amenorrhea. Choice C (Measurement of serum FSH and LH concentrations) is unlikely to be helpful. Prolactin suppresses GnRH secretion, which will lead to suppression of both FSH and LH. The elevated prolactin is the primary finding that guides diagnosis. Choice D (Mammography) is used to screen for breast cancer in women over 40 years or to evaluate palpable masses. This patient's galactorrhea is more likely the result of a prolactinoma and does not represent primary breast pathology. Educational Objective: Markedly increased prolactin concentrations, especially when seen in combination with amenorrhea and galactorrhea, represent autonomous secretion of prolactin from an anterior pituitary adenoma. MRI of the pituitary gland is the appropriate diagnostic imaging to identify a prolactinoma.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Toxic Shock Syndrome1 questions
Source: 7A #40
A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 12 hours after the sudden onset of fever, diffuse muscle and bone pain, and dizziness. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg while supine. Her palpable systolic blood pressure is 70 mm Hg while sitting. Examination shows a diffuse, erythematous, macular rash over the face, trunk, hands, and feet. There is desquamation over the palms of the hands. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs or gallops. There is 1+ peripheral edema bilaterally. Pelvic and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatment? A) Oral prednisone B) Intravenous dopamine C) Intravenous fluids D) Intravenous metronidazole E) Intravenous penicillin
Correct Answer: C) Intravenous fluids
This patient presents with classic signs and symptoms of toxic shock syndrome (TSS). Toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST-1), produced by Staphylococcus aureus, causes a cytokine storm that leads to dysfunction of multiple organs and can result in distributive shock and death. Patients typically present with fever, hypotension, diffuse erythematous rash, desquamation, and clinical and laboratory evidence of end organ dysfunction such as altered mental status, myalgia, thrombocytopenia, azotemia, and transaminitis. The most appropriate initial intervention is aggressive hemodynamic support with intravenous fluid resuscitation, which should be initiated immediately to address the hypotension and distributive shock. Once hemodynamic stability is achieved with fluids, further interventions such as vasopressors and appropriate antibiotics (such as nafcillin or oxacillin for methicillin-sensitive S. aureus, or vancomycin for methicillin-resistant strains) can be administered. Source control measures, such as a pelvic examination to remove a retained tampon if present, are also important to limit further toxin release. Choice A (Oral prednisone) is a glucocorticoid ineffective against Staphylococcus aureus infection. Choice B (Intravenous dopamine) is a vasopressor that could be considered if shock persists despite appropriate fluid resuscitation, but it should not be used initially and is not first-line due to its proarrhythmic potential; norepinephrine is preferred as the initial pressor in septic shock. Choice D (Intravenous metronidazole) is an antibiotic used for anaerobic infections (such as Clostridium difficile and Giardia lamblia) and is inappropriate for S. aureus. Choice E (Intravenous penicillin) is inappropriate because Staphylococcus aureus is resistant to most penicillins due to its penicillinase enzyme that cleaves the beta-lactam ring. Educational Objective: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by toxic shock syndrome toxin produced by Staphylococcus aureus and causes a full body erythematous eruption with fever, vital sign instability, and signs of end organ dysfunction related to systemic shock. Treatment requires aggressive fluid resuscitation for hemodynamic support, appropriate antibiotics targeting the inciting staphylococcal infection, and supportive care for end organ failure.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Raynaud Disease1 questions
Source: 7A #42
A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of her hands and fingers becoming tender and turning white on exposure to cold. The symptoms occur four times monthly. She has not had any other symptoms. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 8 years. Examination shows no abnormalities. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference range. In addition to smoking cessation, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation? A) Avoidance of cold exposure B) Doxazosin therapy C) Prednisone therapy D) Propranolol therapy E) Sympathectomy
Correct Answer: A) Avoidance of cold exposure
Raynaud phenomenon refers to vasospasm that causes intermittent loss of blood flow to the distal extremities in response to cold, stress, or emotional upset, resulting in sequential white, blue, and red discoloration of the affected areas. The vasospasm can be triggered and exacerbated by cold temperature, stress, or emotional upset. Activities such as cigarette smoking, injury, trauma, or chemical exposure increase the risk for Raynaud phenomenon. It may be idiopathic or associated with mixed connected tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, or CREST syndrome. When severe or prolonged, ischemic injury can result in digital ulcerations. The most appropriate recommendation is avoidance of cold exposure and keeping hands warm in cold weather, which directly addresses the primary trigger of vasospasm. Doxazosin (Choice B) is an alpha-adrenergic blocker used for hypertension, post-traumatic stress disorder, and urinary retention from benign prostatic hyperplasia, but has not been conclusively shown to improve symptoms of Raynaud phenomenon. Prednisone therapy (Choice C) is a glucocorticoid used in systemic inflammatory conditions such as scleroderma, which can be associated with Raynaud phenomenon, but would not directly address the mechanism of vasospasm. Propranolol therapy (Choice D) is a non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker used for hypertension, hyperthyroidism, anxiety disorders, and portal hypertension, but is not generally employed in the treatment of Raynaud phenomenon. Sympatectomy (Choice E) refers to removal of a sympathetic nerve root and is used in hyperhidrosis, reflex sympathetic dystrophy, and severe Raynaud disease, but is an invasive surgery reserved for refractory, treatment-resistant, severe cases.
▶Social Sciences Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infections1 questions
Source: 7A #46
A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever and chills. He received the diagnosis of small cell carcinoma of the lung 1 month ago and is undergoing chemotherapy. A right subclavian central venous catheter is in place. His temperature is 38.9°C (102.1°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg. Examination shows warm, flushed skin. The catheter site is slightly erythematous, and there is tenderness over the subcutaneous pocket. His leukocyte count is 12,300/mm³. A chest x-ray shows a nodule in the right upper lobe. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Candida albicans B) Clostridium perfringens C) Escherichia coli D) Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Correct Answer: E) Staphylococcus epidermidis
This patient presents with signs of bacteremia (fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, leukocytosis) in the context of a central venous catheter with signs of local infection (erythema and tenderness at the insertion site). Central line-associated bloodstream infections are commonly caused by skin flora, particularly staphylococcal species. Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common cutaneous organism that can translocate and seed the bloodstream through discontinuities in the skin at line insertion sites, especially in immunocompromised patients undergoing chemotherapy. Treatment includes intravenous antibiotics and removal of the infected line. Choice A (Candida albicans): While candidemia can occur in immunocompromised patients with central lines, it is rare and typically presents with severe sepsis accompanied by skin and ophthalmologic lesions, which this patient does not demonstrate. Choice B (Clostridium perfringens): This organism causes necrotizing skin infections characterized by fever, severe pain out of proportion to examination findings, erythema, ecchymosis, edema, and bullae. It progresses rapidly over hours to days and requires emergent surgical debridement. This clinical presentation does not match the patient's presentation. Choice C (Escherichia coli): While E. coli can cause bacteremia, it is typically associated with urinary or gastrointestinal sources and is not the typical pathogen for central line-associated infections. Choice D (Pseudomonas aeruginosa): Although Pseudomonas can cause line infections in hospitalized patients, it is less common than staphylococcal species as a cause of central line-associated bacteremia. Educational Objective: Recognize that central line-associated bloodstream infections are most commonly caused by skin flora such as Staphylococcus epidermidis, particularly in immunocompromised patients, and that clinical findings of catheter site infection (erythema, tenderness) in the setting of bacteremia strongly suggest line infection requiring line removal and antibiotic therapy.
▶Biostatistics Epidemiology Population Health Case-Control Study1 questions
Source: 7A #48
A study is conducted to assess a possible association between regular use of alcohol and colon cancer. Cases consist of patients hospitalized with colon cancer; controls consist of age- and gender-matched patients admitted to the same hospital for treatment of an acute injury. Cases and controls are interviewed after their conditions stabilize. The researchers conclude that regular use of alcohol reduced the risk of colon cancer. Which of the following is the most important reason to be concerned about the authors' conclusion? A) Confounding by age B) Inappropriate case group C) Inappropriate control group D) Lack of incidence rates for alcohol users and nonusers
Correct Answer: C) Inappropriate control group
This case-control study has a critical methodological flaw in the selection of the control group. While age and gender matching were appropriately performed to eliminate these confounding variables, the choice of controls (patients admitted with acute injuries) introduces a significant bias. The problem is that regular alcohol use can lead to acute injuries during intoxication, meaning the control group likely has a higher baseline prevalence of alcohol use compared to the case group (colon cancer patients). This inflates the alcohol exposure in controls relative to cases, artificially making it appear that alcohol use is protective against colon cancer when this conclusion is actually due to the inappropriate selection of controls. Choice A is incorrect because age confounding was eliminated through age and gender matching of cases and controls. Choice B is incorrect because selecting patients with colon cancer as the case group is entirely appropriate for studying the relationship between alcohol use and colon cancer development. Choice D is incorrect because incidence rates would be more appropriately evaluated in a prospective cohort study rather than a case-control study. The more fundamental concern here is the biased control group selection, not the lack of incidence data. Educational Objective: When designing and interpreting case-control studies, careful selection of both case and control groups is essential to minimize confounding variables and selection biases. Controls should be representative of the population that gave rise to the cases and should not have exposure patterns systematically different from the source population due to the nature of their hospitalization or condition.
▶Social Sciences Medical negligence and malpractice1 questions
Source: 7A #50
A 54-year-old man is hospitalized because of a 5-day history of chills and moderate pain, edema, and erythema of the right foot. His symptoms began 2 days after he stepped on a nail. He has coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. He has no known drug allergies. His medications are metformin, insulin, lisinopril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, and aspirin. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 145/92 mm Hg. Examination of the right lower extremity shows erythema, warmth, and tenderness to palpation from the proximal aspect of the ankle to the dorsum of the foot. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam therapy is begun, and the patient's home medication regimen is continued. While filling the prescription, the pharmacist notices a problem in the medication order. Investigation shows that the physician wrote the prescription in an immediate-release formulation instead of an extended-release formulation. Which of the following best characterizes this type of medical error? A) Active failure B) Adverse event C) Latent condition D) Near miss event E) Sentinel event
Correct Answer: D) Near miss event
Medical errors are common in healthcare and result from an interplay of individual and systemic factors. They range from medication administration errors to equipment failures and may or may not reach the patient. The key distinction in this case is that the pharmacist caught the prescribing error before it reached the patient, making this a near miss event. Active failure (Choice A) is a medical error caused by human error such as negligence, misinformation, incompetence, or a technical mistake that directly causes patient harm. While the physician's mistake of writing immediate-release instead of extended-release was likely an honest error, it was caught by the pharmacist before reaching the patient, making it a near miss rather than an active failure. Adverse event (Choice B) occurs when a medical error reaches the patient and causes unintended harm. If the immediate-release formulation had been dispensed and administered, it could have led to hypoglycemia or hypotension, qualifying as an adverse event. However, the error was prevented from reaching the patient. Latent conditions (Choice C) are systemic or organizational conditions inherent in the design of a system that can lead to medical mistakes and patient harm. While this error could have resulted from latent system weaknesses, it was prevented by existing safeguards (pharmacist verification), making it a near miss. Sentinel event (Choice E) is a medical error that reaches a patient and leads to permanent disability or death. Examples include operating on the wrong patient or wrong site, or administering a known allergen resulting in death. This error did not reach the patient. Near miss events are medical errors that are prevented from reaching the patient through safeguards in place, such as the multiple checkpoints in medication dispensing (physician order, pharmacist verification, nurse verification at bedside). In this case, the pharmacist's catch of the formulation error exemplifies the healthcare system's safety mechanisms working effectively. Educational Objective: Medical errors in healthcare range from active failures by providers to latent systemic conditions and are commonly caused by an interplay of individual and systemic factors. When errors are prevented from reaching the patient through safeguards, they are referred to as near miss events. Errors that reach the patient are classified as adverse events if they cause temporary harm or sentinel events if they result in permanent disability or death.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura1 questions
Source: 10A #2
A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of an 8-hour history of temperatures to 38.9°C (102°F), confusion, and intermittent headache. His wife says that he also has had increased bruising over his forearms today. He has not had difficulty breathing or urinating. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. His medications are lisinopril and pravastatin. On arrival, he is oriented to person but not to place or time. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/78 mm Hg. Examination, including neurologic examination, shows no other abnormalities. One month ago, his serum creatinine concentration was 1 mg/dL. Laboratory studies today show: Hemoglobin 6 g/dL, Hematocrit 34%, Leukocyte count 6400/mm3, Platelet count 44,000/mm3, Prothrombin time 13 sec (INR=1), Partial thromboplastin time 28 sec, Serum Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, Bilirubin total 1.9 mg/dL, Indirect 1.5 mg/dL, Lactate dehydrogenase 660 U/L. Blood smears show schistocytes. A CT scan of the head shows age-related atrophy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Aspirin therapy B) Hemodialysis C) Plasmapheresis D) Splenectomy E) Transfusion of platelets
Correct Answer: C) Plasmapheresis
This patient presents with the classic pentad of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP): fever, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, and neurologic dysfunction (confusion/altered mental status). TTP is a thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, and progressive organ dysfunction due to microvascular thrombi. The disease is caused by deficiency in ADAMTS13, a von Willebrand factor cleaving protease. The presence of schistocytes on blood smear confirms hemolytic anemia. The laboratory findings show anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelet count 44,000/mm3), elevated indirect bilirubin and LDH indicating hemolysis, and acute kidney injury (creatinine increased from 1 to 2.8 mg/dL). The first-line treatment for acquired TTP is plasmapheresis, which removes autoantibodies against ADAMTS13. Choice A (Aspirin therapy) is used for myocardial and cerebral infarction, not TTP. Choice B (Hemodialysis) is not indicated as the patient lacks indications such as severe volume overload or life-threatening metabolic derangement. Choice D (Splenectomy) may be used in refractory immune thrombocytopenia but is not indicated in TTP. Choice E (Transfusion of platelets) is contraindicated in TTP except in life-threatening situations, as platelet transfusion can worsen the consumptive process and increase microthrombi formation.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Paraneoplastic Neurologic Syndromes1 questions
Source: 10A #4
A 67-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital from the general medicine clinic because of a 3-month history of progressive nonproductive cough, intermittent fever and sweating, vomiting, and fatigue. During this time, she has had a decreased appetite resulting in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss. She has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. She has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 45 years. She appears to be in mild respiratory distress. Her temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Rhonchi are heard over the upper lobe of the right lung field. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 48%, Leukocyte count 15,600/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 85%, Lymphocytes 10%, Monocytes 5%, Serum Ca²⁺ 12.9 mg/dL, Urea nitrogen 59 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, Phosphorus 2.7 mg/dL, Albumin 2.9 g/dL. A chest x-ray shows a 5-cm right hilar density and a right upper lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's hypercalcemia? A) Granulomatous disease B) Increased vitamin D concentration C) Parathyroid hormone-related peptide D) Primary hyperparathyroidism E) Thiazide diuretics
Correct Answer: C) Parathyroid hormone-related peptide
This patient with a 45-year smoking history presents with a 3-month history of progressive nonproductive cough, weight loss, fever, and systemic symptoms, combined with imaging findings of a right hilar density and upper lobe infiltrate. These clinical features are most consistent with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. The hypercalcemia in this case is due to paraneoplastic parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) production, a hallmark of squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common type of primary lung cancer after adenocarcinoma and characteristically presents with central location, pulmonary cavitations, and hypercalcemia due to PTHrP production. The histologic characteristics include polygonal cells with intercellular bridges, eosinophilic cytoplasm, keratin pearls, and extensive necrosis. Risk factors include tobacco use, secondhand smoke, asbestos or radon exposure, and family history of lung cancer. Choice A (Granulomatous disease): While sarcoidosis, a noncaseating granulomatous disease, can present with cough and lung involvement and may cause hypercalcemia through unregulated 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol production, this would typically increase both calcium and phosphorus concentrations. This patient has normal-low phosphorus (2.7 mg/dL), and her extensive 45-year smoking history with new weight loss and systemic symptoms are far more suggestive of malignancy than granulomatous disease. Choice B (Increased vitamin D concentration): While increased vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia, this patient shows no evidence of elevated vitamin D activity. The clinical presentation with an extensive smoking history, new-onset weight loss, and decreased appetite is most consistent with a paraneoplastic cause rather than vitamin D-mediated hypercalcemia. Choice D (Primary hyperparathyroidism): Primary hyperparathyroidism, typically caused by parathyroid adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma, would present with elevated serum intact parathyroid hormone and an undetectable PTHrP concentration. This is inconsistent with the paraneoplastic presentation in this case. Choice E (Thiazide diuretics): Although thiazide diuretics can cause hypercalcemia by inhibiting sodium chloride absorption in the distal convoluted tubule, this patient's presentation with significant constitutional symptoms, weight loss, and imaging findings of a lung mass makes PTHrP production from lung cancer the most likely explanation for her hypercalcemia. Educational Objective: Recognize that squamous cell carcinoma of the lung commonly presents with hypercalcemia due to paraneoplastic PTHrP production in patients with significant smoking history, constitutional symptoms, and imaging evidence of lung malignancy.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Delirium1 questions
Source: 10A #6
A 55-year-old man with a history of benzodiazepine dependence is admitted to the intensive care unit after sustaining an acute myocardial infarction. Approximately 18 hours later, he has visual and auditory hallucinations, labile affect, and a coarse tremor in all extremities; he is anxious and cannot sleep. His level of consciousness fluctuates over time. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Delirium B) Frontotemporal dementia C) Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition D) Schizoaffective disorder E) Substance-induced psychotic disorder
Correct Answer: A) Delirium
Educational Objective: Withdrawal from benzodiazepines presents with confusion (delirium), hallucinations, autonomic instability (hyperadrenergic states), and tremor, usually beginning 12 to 24 hours after discontinuation of benzodiazepines. This patient's benzodiazepine dependence plus time without the medication while in the intensive care unit led to withdrawal-induced delirium. Definition: Benzodiazepines, like alcohol and barbiturates, increase the central nervous system activity of gamma-aminobutyric acid, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Abrupt discontinuation of benzodiazepines therefore leads to sympathetic (excitatory) excess. Uncomplicated withdrawal typically presents with tremor, anxiety, restlessness, headache, nausea, and diaphoresis, which can occur hours after cessation. Benzodiazepine withdrawal can be complicated by seizures and hallucinosis (auditory or visual hallucinations). Severe benzodiazepine withdrawal can present with life-threatening complications such as delirium and can include confusion and disorientation, fluctuations in consciousness, agitation, visual hallucinations, and autonomic instability (fluctuations in heart rate and blood pressure). Evaluation: Benzodiazepine withdrawal is a clinical diagnosis based on symptoms and signs plus history of cessation of benzodiazepines within 12 to 24 hours of the onset of symptoms. Prevention: Prevention of benzodiazepine withdrawal includes continuing baseline, stable doses of benzodiazepines, and if cessation is desired, benzodiazepines should be tapered in a controlled hospital setting. Treatment: Benzodiazepine withdrawal is managed supportively with replacement of benzodiazepines. Differential: This patient's inadvertent discontinuation of benzodiazepines, followed by hallucinations, tremor, anxiety, and insomnia is consistent with benzodiazepine withdrawal-induced delirium. Dementia, psychosis, and mood disorders would present with forgetfulness, poor self-care, agitation, and negative symptoms, not seen in this case. Choice B (Frontotemporal dementia) is incorrect. Frontotemporal dementia presents with loss of memory and executive function, along with behavioral dysregulation and mood disturbances. This patient has not clearly lost memory or executive functioning. Choice C (Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition) is incorrect. Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition, such as hyperthyroidism, presents with hallucinations, agitation, and negative symptoms. An acute myocardial infarction is not a common precipitant of psychosis. Choice D (Schizoaffective disorder) is incorrect. Schizoaffective disorder presents with hallucinations, paranoia, delusions, and poor self-care (symptoms of psychosis) along with mood symptoms (e.g., depression or mania). These symptoms must be present for weeks. This patient's symptoms began within a few hours following discontinuation of benzodiazepines. Choice E (Substance-induced psychotic disorder) is incorrect. Substance-induced psychotic disorder presents with psychosis (hallucinations, agitation, paranoia, delusions) following ingestion of, not withdrawal from, a substance, commonly a sympathomimetic or hallucinogen.
▶Gastrointestinal System Hepatic encephalopathy1 questions
Source: 10A #14
A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of confusion and lethargy. She says she found him at home confused and not oriented to person, place, and time earlier today when she returned from a 3-day out-of-town trip. He keeps repeating, "I am hungry." The patient consumed three to four glasses of whiskey daily for 35 years but stopped drinking alcoholic beverages 6 months ago on the advice of his primary care physician. He has no other history of serious illness and takes no routine medications. He switched to a high-protein diet 2 weeks ago because he felt his stomach was growing bigger, and protein now makes up half of his diet. He is 185 cm (6 ft 1 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m². Temperature is 36.3°C (97.3°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild scleral icterus. On mental status examination, the patient is oriented to time but not to person or place. He is unable to spell "world" backward. The remainder of the examination is most likely to disclose which of the following? A) Asterixis B) Dupuytren contracture C) Gynecomastia D) Kayser-Fleischer rings E) Painful blisters on sun-exposed areas of the skin
Correct Answer: A) Asterixis
This patient presents with hepatic encephalopathy secondary to decompensated cirrhosis from chronic alcohol use. The clinical clues include a 35-year history of heavy daily alcohol consumption, abdominal distention (ascites), scleral icterus, and acute altered mental status with disorientation and inability to perform cognitive tasks. The recent switch to a high-protein diet represents a precipitating factor that increased ammonia production via protein catabolism, triggering hepatic encephalopathy. Asterixis (flapping tremor) is a hallmark finding of hepatic encephalopathy caused by hyperammonemia. It presents as involuntary lapses of sustained muscle contraction resulting from accumulation of ammonia and neurotoxins that the liver cannot clear due to hepatic dysfunction. Asterixis is an acute neurologic finding directly related to the pathophysiology of hepatic encephalopathy. Choice B (Dupuytren contracture) is incorrect. While Dupuytren contracture is associated with chronic alcohol use and stems from fibroproliferation in the palmar fascia causing flexion contractures, it is not related to neurologic changes or hepatic encephalopathy and does not result from hyperammonemia. Choice C (Gynecomastia) is incorrect. Gynecomastia can occur in cirrhotic patients due to disruption of sex hormone metabolism, but it is a chronic finding, not an acute manifestation of hepatic encephalopathy or hyperammonemia. Choice D (Kayser-Fleischer rings) is incorrect. These copper deposits in the cornea are pathognomonic for Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), not alcoholic cirrhosis. This patient's cirrhosis is from alcohol use, not copper metabolism disorder. Choice E (Painful blisters on sun-exposed areas) is incorrect. While porphyria cutanea tarda can be associated with alcohol use and presents with photosensitive bullae, it is unrelated to decompensated cirrhosis and hyperammonemia. Educational Objective: A history of heavy alcohol use, abdominal distention (ascites), and worsening mental status after starting a high-protein diet is consistent with decompensated cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy from hyperammonemia. Asterixis is the characteristic neurologic finding. Hepatic encephalopathy results from accumulation of ammonia, a byproduct of protein catabolism via the urea cycle, which the liver cannot adequately clear. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by elevated serum ammonia levels and imaging studies. Treatment involves lactulose and rifaximin to decrease ammonia absorption and production, along with avoiding precipitating factors such as gastrointestinal bleeding, infection, and excessive protein consumption.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Folliculitis1 questions
Source: 10A #17
A patient presents to the urgent care center because of a 12-hour history of an itchy, bumpy rash that is most prominent over his chest and thighs. He has not had fever or chills. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He has no known allergies. There is no family history of serious illness. He is sexually active with two female partners and uses condoms inconsistently. Two days ago, he returned from a skiing trip with his friends, during which he spent time in a hot tub at a rental property. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows perifollicular, erythematous papules and pustules; the rash is more highly concentrated on the trunk and bilateral upper thighs. There is no lymphadenopathy. Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause of this patient's condition? A) Molluscum contagiosum B) Neisseria gonorrhoeae C) Pseudomonas aeruginosa D) Scabies E) Staphylococcus aureus F) Vibrio vulnificus
Correct Answer: C) Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most likely infectious agent causing this patient's hot tub folliculitis. P. aeruginosa thrives in warm, moist environments such as hot tubs and swimming pools. Folliculitis presents with perifollicular, erythematous papules and pustules affecting the face, trunk, or extremities, often with pruritus or irritation. The diagnosis is clinical with no specific diagnostic test required. This patient's history of recent hot tub exposure in combination with the characteristic rash distribution on the trunk and thighs is pathognomonic for hot tub folliculitis. In healthy patients, hot tub folliculitis is self-limited and resolves within days to weeks without specific treatment. In immunocompromised patients, treatment with antipseudomonal quinolones may be indicated. Prevention includes adequate chlorination of hot tubs and showering immediately after exposure with antibacterial soap. Choice A (Molluscum contagiosum) is incorrect because molluscum contagiosum is caused by a superficial epithelial poxvirus transmitted by skin-to-skin contact and presents with characteristic dome-shaped, umbilicated papules with central hyperkeratotic cores, not the perifollicular pustules seen here. Choice B (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) is incorrect because N. gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhea, a sexually transmitted infection involving the genitals, anal canal, or oral mucosa, not a trunk and thigh rash following hot tub exposure. Choice D (Scabies) is incorrect because scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei mites transmitted by direct skin-to-skin contact and characteristically presents with pruritic papules and burrows in interweb spaces, intertriginous folds, and flexural surfaces, not the distribution seen in this patient. Choice E (Staphylococcus aureus) is incorrect because while staphylococcal folliculitis is common and presents with pustules at sites of involvement often with honey-colored crusting, P. aeruginosa is the classic causative agent of hot tub folliculitis, making it the most likely answer given this patient's specific exposure history. Choice F (Vibrio vulnificus) is incorrect because V. vulnificus is a bacterium found in shellfish and saltwater that causes watery diarrhea, wound infections, and septicemia primarily in patients with underlying liver disease or diabetes mellitus, not folliculitis from hot tub exposure. Wound infections present with fever, severe pain, erythema, crepitus, and bullous lesions progressing to necrotizing fasciitis.
▶Musculoskeletal System Pathologic fracture1 questions
Source: 10A #18
A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician 3 days after the sudden onset of back pain while vacuuming a carpet. The pain is localized to the mid back and increases with deep inspiration. Use of aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs has provided no relief. She underwent hysterectomy at the age of 50 years. Her mother died of an acute myocardial infarction at the age of 72 years, and her father died of lung cancer at the age of 75 years. Her 65-year-old brother has hypertension. She is in mild distress. She was 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall at the age of 40 years. Today, she is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2. Examination shows kyphosis and pain on palpation over T7 and T8 posteriorly. Serum studies show: Ca2+ 8.9 mg/dL, Phosphorus 3 mg/dL, Total protein 6.5 g/dL, Alkaline phosphatase 146 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) DEXA scan B) X-ray of the spine C) Bone scan D) MRI of the spine E) Bone biopsy after tetracycline labeling
Correct Answer: B) X-ray of the spine
Vertebral compression fractures are common in older postmenopausal patients with osteoporosis and typically occur from minimal trauma such as coughing, bending, or lifting. X-ray of the spine is the most appropriate initial imaging modality for evaluating acute or subacute vertebral compression fractures. This patient presents with classic features suggestive of compression fracture: 62-year-old postmenopausal woman (hysterectomy at age 50), acute onset focal back pain over T7-T8 with tenderness on palpation, 2.5 cm loss of height since age 40, and kyphosis on examination. All of these findings raise concern for an acute compression fracture requiring imaging evaluation. Choice A (DEXA scan) is used to diagnose osteoporosis by measuring bone mineral density, which may be indicated for screening in this patient, but it is not the appropriate next step when acute fracture is suspected. Choice C (Bone scan) may be used to determine chronicity of a fracture or when MRI is contraindicated, but X-ray is more appropriate initially. Choice D (MRI) is more sensitive and useful for evaluating soft tissue involvement and neurologic complications, but it is not necessary in this patient without neurologic deficits and is more costly than plain radiography for initial evaluation of suspected acute compression fracture. Choice E (Bone biopsy with tetracycline labeling) is used to evaluate osteoblast and osteoclast activity in metabolic bone disease, not for diagnosis of acute fractures. X-ray provides rapid, cost-effective initial imaging to confirm the presence and location of compression fracture and assess severity.
▶Gastrointestinal System Gastroparesis1 questions
Source: 10A #19
A 77-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of nausea and vomiting undigested food 1 to 6 hours after eating. He has a 25-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus that had been previously well controlled with insulin, but he reports frequent episodes of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia during the past year. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 116 kg (255 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m². His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. Fundoscopic examination shows a few hemorrhages and exudate in both eyes. Sensation is decreased below the knees. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Duodenal ulcer B) Esophageal stricture C) Gastric outlet obstruction D) Gastroparesis E) Pharyngoesophageal (Zenker) diverticulum
Correct Answer: D) Gastroparesis
Gastroparesis is a functional obstruction caused by delayed gastric emptying, often seen in patients with long-standing diabetes mellitus and autonomic neuropathy. This patient presents with classic features consistent with this diagnosis: nausea and vomiting of undigested food occurring 1-6 hours after eating (early satiety), bloating, and evidence of diabetic complications including retinopathy (hemorrhages and exudate on fundoscopy) and peripheral neuropathy (decreased sensation below the knees). His 25-year history of type 2 diabetes with poor glycemic control in the past year increases his risk for microvascular complications including autonomic neuropathy. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy impairs the autonomic nerve function that controls gastric motility, resulting in slow emptying of stomach contents. The diagnosis is confirmed with a gastric emptying scan using radiolabeled tracer. Treatment involves medications that enhance gastric motility, such as metoclopramide (a D2 receptor antagonist) or erythromycin (a motilin agonist). Adequate glycemic control can help prevent or slow progression of this complication. The other options are less likely: duodenal ulcer would present with more epigastric pain; esophageal stricture would cause dysphagia; gastric outlet obstruction is an anatomic obstruction rather than a functional one; and Zenker diverticulum would cause dysphagia and regurgitation of undigested food from the esophagus, not from the stomach.
▶Cardiovascular System Hypercholesterolemia1 questions
Source: 10A #20
A healthy 24-year-old man has a family history of cardiovascular disease. Physical examination is normal. Serum cholesterol concentration is 240 mg/dL. A fasting serum lipid profile shows an LDL-cholesterol concentration of 190 mg/dL, an HDL-cholesterol concentration of 39 mg/dL, and a triglyceride concentration of 150 mg/dL. Overnight refrigerated plasma is clear. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the laboratory findings? A) Abnormal cellular uptake of LDL-cholesterol B) Abnormal forms of apolipoprotein E C) Defective formation of lipoprotein lipase D) Inability to synthesize apolipoprotein C-II E) Increased catabolism of apolipoprotein A-I
Correct Answer: A) Abnormal cellular uptake of LDL-cholesterol
This patient with a family history of cardiovascular disease and an abnormal lipid panel (elevated LDL-cholesterol at 190 mg/dL, low HDL-cholesterol at 39 mg/dL, and normal triglycerides at 150 mg/dL with clear overnight refrigerated plasma) likely has familial hypercholesterolemia. The clear refrigerated plasma rules out type I hyperlipoproteinemia (which would show lipemic plasma due to chylomicrons). The LDL receptor is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum and transported to the cell surface via the Golgi complex. At the cell surface, the LDL receptor binds circulating LDL via apolipoprotein B particles. Bound LDL-cholesterol receptor complexes are then endocytosed and degraded, with recycling of the LDL receptor protein. Defects at any of these steps—synthesis, surface transport, LDL binding, endocytosis, or recycling of LDL receptor proteins—can result in abnormal cellular uptake of LDL, leading to increased circulating LDL-cholesterol. Absence or dysfunction of the LDL receptor complex results in familial hypercholesterolemia, a known risk factor for cardiovascular disease as noted in this patient's family history. Choice B (Abnormal forms of apolipoprotein E) is incorrect because apolipoprotein E is expressed in cholesterol and lipoproteins other than LDL-cholesterol. Apolipoprotein E plays an important role in the uptake of chylomicron remnants, not LDL-cholesterol, which is this patient's primary laboratory derangement. Abnormalities of apolipoprotein E are associated with Alzheimer's disease, not familial hypercholesterolemia. Choice C (Defective formation of lipoprotein lipase) is incorrect because lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes type I hyperlipoproteinemia with severe hypertriglyceridemia and lipemic plasma, neither of which is present in this patient. Choice D (Inability to synthesize apolipoprotein C-II) is incorrect because apolipoprotein C-II deficiency causes type I hyperlipoproteinemia, not the pattern seen in this patient. Choice E (Increased catabolism of apolipoprotein A-I) is incorrect because this would primarily affect HDL metabolism and is not the primary pathophysiology of familial hypercholesterolemia. Educational Objective: Familial hypercholesterolemia arises from mutations affecting the LDL receptor pathway, resulting in abnormal cellular uptake of LDL-cholesterol. Recognition of the clinical presentation (elevated LDL with low HDL, family history of early cardiovascular disease, clear plasma) combined with understanding the LDL receptor synthesis, transport, binding, endocytosis, and recycling pathway allows proper diagnosis.
▶Female Reproductive Breast Antihistamines Adverse Effects on Female Reproductive System and Breast1 questions
Source: 10A #21
A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of nonproductive cough, nasal congestion, and runny nose for 36 hours. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.4°F), and respirations are 16/min. Examination of the nose shows boggy, erythematous turbinates, and mucoid rhinorrhea. A few rhonchi are heard in the upper lobes bilaterally. Treatment with diphenhydramine and guaifenesin every 3 to 4 hours is prescribed. Twenty-four hours later, he is unable to void. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for this patient's urinary symptom? A) Decreased bladder muscle tone B) Delayed neuromuscular maturation C) Ectopic insertion of the ureters D) Renal calyceal obstruction E) Stenosis of the urethral meatus F) Trigonal inflammation G) Uninhibited detrusor muscle contractions
Correct Answer: A) Decreased bladder muscle tone
Diphenhydramine is an H1-receptor blocking agent prescribed for treatment of allergic rhinitis and nasal decongestion. However, it has significant anticholinergic adverse effects, including urinary retention. The mechanism involves competitive blocking of bladder muscarinic receptors, primarily M3 receptors, which decreases bladder muscle tone and results in an inability to void. This adverse effect developed 24 hours after the patient started diphenhydramine therapy, establishing a clear temporal relationship between drug exposure and symptom onset. Choice B (Delayed neuromuscular maturation) is incorrect. Typical symptoms of neuromuscular disorders include muscle pain, cramping, atrophy, and weakness. Moreover, delayed neuromuscular maturation is a developmental condition, not an acute adverse effect of medication in a 62-year-old. Choice C (Ectopic insertion of the ureters) is incorrect. Ectopic ureteral insertion is a congenital abnormality resulting in abnormal ureter location. This patient is 62 years old with new-onset urinary symptoms 24 hours after starting medication, making this congenital diagnosis highly unlikely. Choice D (Renal calyceal obstruction) is incorrect. Renal calyceal obstruction may occur secondary to kidney stones, renal tumors, or congenital abnormalities. This acute presentation following diphenhydramine administration points to decreased bladder muscle tone as the more likely mechanism. Choice E (Stenosis of the urethral meatus) is incorrect. Urethral meatal stenosis may occur after inflammation or irritation of the urethral opening. In the absence of reported trauma or urethritis, this diagnosis is less likely in this acute presentation. Choice F (Trigonal inflammation) is incorrect. Trigonal inflammation typically occurs secondary to urinary tract infection and would present with urinary frequency and dysuria, not inability to void. Choice G (Uninhibited detrusor muscle contractions) is incorrect. Uninhibited detrusor contractions lead to overactive bladder syndrome, characterized by urinary frequency and urgency, not by inability to void. Other anticholinergic adverse effects of diphenhydramine include dry mouth, constipation, hallucinations, delirium, ataxia, flushed skin, and visual disturbances. Treatment involves cessation of diphenhydramine and, if necessary, bladder catheterization for decompression if the patient remains unable to void. Urinary retention might have been avoided by using H2-receptor blocking agents such as famotidine, which have fewer anticholinergic adverse effects.
▶Respiratory System Acute Upper Respiratory Infection1 questions
Source: 10A #26
A previously healthy 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 5-day history of runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, scratchy throat, and a nonproductive cough. The nasal discharge is clear to yellow. He has not had facial pain or toothache. He takes no medications and has no allergies. He does not smoke. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. There is no conjunctival erythema or eye discharge. The nasal mucosa and throat are mildly erythematous and swollen. There is no sinus tenderness. The posterior cervical lymph nodes are shotty. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment? A. Amoxicillin B. Azithromycin C. Pseudoephedrine D. Rimantadine E. Vitamin C
Correct Answer: C. Pseudoephedrine
A viral upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. The clinical presentation is classic for the common cold, characterized by clear rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, sneezing, postnasal drainage, sore throat, and nonproductive cough. While low-grade fever may accompany viral URTIs, it is less common than in bacterial infections. The absence of fever, leukocytosis, purulent drainage, productive cough, facial pain, sinus tenderness, or conjunctival findings argues strongly against bacterial infection. Viral URTIs are diagnosed clinically and are self-limited conditions managed with supportive care and symptomatic treatment. Pseudoephedrine is the correct choice as it is a decongestant that provides symptomatic relief of nasal congestion in viral URTIs. Symptomatic treatment is the foundation of viral URTI management, as antibiotics are ineffective and inappropriate without evidence of bacterial superinfection. Choice A (Amoxicillin) is incorrect. This is a penicillin-based antibiotic used for bacterial infections such as bacterial rhinosinusitis and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia. This patient has no clinical features suggestive of bacterial infection, making empiric antibiotic therapy inappropriate. Choice B (Azithromycin) is incorrect. This is a macrolide antibiotic also used for bacterial infections. Like amoxicillin, it has no role in treating uncomplicated viral URTI and would not address this patient's symptoms. Choice D (Rimantadine) is incorrect. Rimantadine is an antiviral agent used to treat and prevent influenza A infection. While influenza can present with respiratory symptoms, it classically includes prominent systemic manifestations such as high fever, chills, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, and gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). This patient's clinical picture is more consistent with a typical viral URTI rather than influenza. Choice E (Vitamin C) is incorrect. Although vitamin C plays an important role in immune function, it is not a treatment for viral URTI and has no proven efficacy in reducing symptom duration or severity in this clinical context. Educational Objective: Recognize viral URTIs as common, self-limited infections typically managed with supportive care and symptomatic treatment such as decongestants. Understand that antibiotics are inappropriate without evidence of bacterial superinfection, and distinguish viral URTIs from influenza and bacterial respiratory infections based on clinical presentation.
▶Female Reproductive Breast Pelvic Inflammatory Disease1 questions
Source: 10A #30
A previously healthy 23-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of vaginal discharge and right-sided abdominal pain that has gradually worsened during the past 3 days. Menses occur at regular intervals and last 5 days. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She is sexually active with multiple partners; they use condoms inconsistently. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows cervical motion tenderness, right adnexal tenderness and fullness, and a white vaginal discharge. Her leukocyte count is 17,000/mm3 (17 x 109/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Blood cultures B) CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis C) HIV antibody testing D) Ultrasonography of the pelvis E) Urinalysis
Correct Answer: D) Ultrasonography of the pelvis
This patient presents with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) characterized by fever, vaginal discharge, cervical motion tenderness, and adnexal tenderness. The presence of right adnexal fullness raises concern for a tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA), a serious complication of PID. The most appropriate next step in diagnosis is ultrasonography of the pelvis to assess for the presence of an abscess, its location, and size. In suspected cases of TOA, ultrasonography is essential to visualize the abscess and guide further management. PID results from ascending migration of bacteria from the lower genital tract and involves inflammation of the upper genital tract and pelvis. Risk factors include multiple sexual partners, inconsistent barrier contraception use, and young age. Pathogens are often polymicrobial, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and gram-negative enteric flora. TOA represents a collection of pus involving the ovary and fallopian tube, and while palpable fullness may be noted on examination, ultrasonography is required for definitive diagnosis. Untreated PID can lead to serious complications including Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis), TOA, and chronic infertility from tubal occlusion. Patients under evaluation for PID should generally receive ultrasonography to rule out TOA except in clearly uncomplicated cases. Additionally, laboratory studies including sexually transmitted infection testing should be obtained. Choice A (Blood cultures) would be an appropriate adjunct to assess for bacteremia and sepsis, but would not visualize the abscess. Choice B (CT scan) is more resource-intensive and not the first-line imaging for this clinical scenario. Choice C (HIV antibody testing) while relevant to sexually active patients with multiple partners, is not the most appropriate immediate diagnostic step for assessing TOA. Choice E (Urinalysis) would not identify the gynecologic pathology. Treatment of TOA involves intravenous antibiotics and operative or radiologic-guided drainage, typically followed by longer courses of oral antibiotics.
▶Biostatistics Epidemiology Population Health Selection Bias1 questions
Source: 10A #31
A study is conducted to assess the risk for hospitalization resulting from respiratory complications of a highly contagious viral infection in 100 elderly patients residing in a nursing care facility. Group A consists of 50 patients ages 65 years and older who have had known exposure to the virus confirmed by polymerase chain reaction testing. Group B is an age-matched control that consists of 50 patients who have twice tested negative for the virus. In the 6 weeks that followed testing, Group A had a 15% incidence of hospitalization resulting from respiratory complications while the control, Group B, had a 7.5% incidence. The risk ratio for Group A was 1.5 (confidence interval (CI) 1.2-1.6), and the risk ratio for Group B was 1.1 (CI 0.9-1.2). Which of the following biases is most likely to invalidate the findings of this study? A) Allocation B) Detection C) Publication D) Recall E) Selection
Correct Answer: E) Selection
Educational Objective: Selection bias, the most likely bias to invalidate this study, occurs when there is nonrandom (biased) selection of individuals for inclusion in a particular study group. Key Concept: Selection bias occurs when the participants studied are not representative of the target population. Explanation: This study is attempting to assess the risk for hospitalization secondary to complications from a highly contagious viral infection. However, the patients selected were older individuals who were residing in a nursing care facility, who are likely less healthy than the general population. In addition, bias may have been introduced as testing for the viral infection occurred during group assignment. There is a risk that the age-matched controls may have contracted the highly contagious virus between testing negative and the 6-week follow-up to evaluate for incidence of hospitalization. Selection bias is the most likely bias to invalidate the findings of the study, as the older patients residing in a nursing care facility are likely less healthy than the general population and may be at a higher risk for hospitalization from a viral infection. Incorrect Answers: Choice A (Allocation) is incorrect because allocation bias occurs when the likelihood of being assigned to a study group is not equal for all participants being studied. Selection bias is the most likely invalidating feature of this study. Choice B (Detection) is not the most likely bias to invalidate the study. Detection bias, also known as surveillance bias, occurs when one group is more likely to have a disease or condition identified as a result of increased surveillance or testing. The groups in this case were both screened for the viral infection at the beginning of the study, making this bias less likely. Choice C (Publication) is incorrect because publication bias occurs when the likelihood of a study being published or distributed depends on the nature or direction of the findings (i.e., positive or significant findings are more likely to be published). The most likely bias present in this study is selection bias. Choice D (Recall) is not applicable in this study design.
▶Cardiovascular System Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm1 questions
Source: 10A #32
A 68-year-old man comes to the office for a routine examination. He feels well. He has hypertension well controlled with hydrochlorothiazide and hyperlipidemia well controlled with atorvastatin. His last colonoscopy 5 years ago showed no abnormalities. He received the pneumococcal vaccine 3 years ago. He has an active lifestyle and is an avid hunter and fisherman. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 50 years. He drinks one glass of wine with dinner five times weekly. He is a retired schoolteacher. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test at this time? A) Colonoscopy B) Colonoscopy and measurement of serum prostate-specific antigen concentration C) Pulmonary function testing D) Ultrasonography of the abdominal aorta E) No screening tests are indicated
Correct Answer: D) Ultrasonography of the abdominal aorta
The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends using ultrasonography to screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) in men aged 65 to 75 years who have a history of tobacco use. This 68-year-old patient's 50-year history of smoking one pack daily places him at significantly higher risk for AAA and makes ultrasonography of the abdominal aorta the most appropriate screening test at this time. AAAs are most commonly seen in male smokers with atherosclerotic disease, as in this patient. Additional risk factors include hypercholesterolemia, hypertension, and trauma—all relevant to this patient. AAAs typically occur in the infrarenal abdominal aorta and may present as a palpable, pulsatile abdominal mass in large aneurysms in thin patients, but are often undetectable on clinical examination since examination maneuvers are insensitive. Ruptured aneurysms require emergent surgical intervention. Chronic AAAs are typically asymptomatic, making screening to detect subclinical disease paramount. Ultrasonography allows direct visualization and measurement of the aorta. Aneurysms that are large, rapidly expanding, or otherwise at high risk for rupture require preemptive repair. Choice A (Colonoscopy) is incorrect. Colonoscopy for colorectal cancer screening is recommended every 10 years beginning at age 45 in average-risk patients without other indications. This patient had a normal colonoscopy 5 years ago with no risk factors warranting more frequent screening. Choice B (Colonoscopy and PSA measurement) is incorrect for two reasons. First, colonoscopy is not indicated at this time as discussed above. Second, the USPSTF does not recommend routine prostate-specific antigen testing for prostate cancer screening, as it results in increased false-positive results with associated morbidity from unnecessary medical intervention. Choice C (Pulmonary function testing) is incorrect. There is no recommendation for routine pulmonary function testing screening in asymptomatic patients, even with significant smoking history. PFT would only be indicated if the patient develops symptoms such as shortness of breath or signs of parenchymal or stromal lung disease. Choice E (No screening tests indicated) is incorrect given this patient's significant risk factors for AAA.
▶Gastrointestinal System Giardia infection1 questions
Source: 10A #34
42-year-old woman comes to the office 5 days after the acute onset of diarrhea. She has had four to six daily bowel movements of greasy, foul-smelling stool; there has been no blood or mucus. She also has had abdominal cramps and bloating, nausea, malaise, and a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss during this time. Two weeks ago, she returned from a cruise to Eastern Europe. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. On examination, the abdomen is mildly tender to palpation. Bowel sounds are normal. Which of the following is the most likely causal agent? A) Campylobacter jejuni B) Cryptosporidium hominis C) Escherichia coli O157:H7 D) Giardia lamblia E) Salmonella enteritidis
Correct Answer: D) Giardia lamblia
Educational Objective: This patient with a 5-day history of greasy, foul-smelling stool 2 weeks after travel to Eastern Europe likely has infection with Giardia lamblia, a flagellated protozoan that colonizes the small intestine. Definition: Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan that colonizes the small intestine. Infection typically presents with foul-smelling diarrhea, flatulence, and nausea. Patients may exhibit steatorrhea and malabsorption as a result of small intestine mucosal injury. Evaluation: Patients suspected of having Giardia lamblia infection generally have a history of travel involving consumption of contaminated water, such as to a location with poor public water quality or having consumed still water while hiking or camping. The gold standard for diagnosis is a stool ova and parasite examination which will identify cysts or trophozoites. Prevention: Prevention of Giardia lamblia infection includes avoidance of untreated water and proper hygienic food handling. Treatment: First-line treatment of Giardia lamblia infection is with the antibiotic metronidazole. Differential Diagnosis: The initial differential diagnosis for this patient with a 5-day history of diarrhea after traveling is broad and includes infectious causes such as viral and bacterial gastroenteritis, along with other causes such as celiac disease or irritable bowel syndrome. The features of recent travel and steatorrhea narrow the differential to a malabsorption diarrhea, which in the setting of infection often results from Giardia lamblia. Incorrect Answers: Choice A (Campylobacter jejuni): Campylobacter jejuni is incorrect. This bacterium typically presents with bloody, acute diarrhea. This patient's symptom time course since exposure along with greasy, foul-smelling stool makes infection with Giardia lamblia the most likely cause. Choice B (Cryptosporidium hominis): Cryptosporidium hominis is incorrect. Cryptosporidium hominis typically infects immunocompromised hosts and presents with watery diarrhea. This patient is not immunocompromised. Choice C (Escherichia coli O157:H7): Escherichia coli O157:H7 is incorrect. This bacterium typically presents with bloody, acute diarrhea. This patient's symptom time course since exposure along with greasy, foul-smelling stool makes infection with Giardia lamblia the most likely cause. Choice E (Salmonella enteritidis): Salmonella enteritidis is incorrect. This bacterium typically presents with bloody, acute diarrhea. This patient's symptom time course since exposure along with greasy, foul-smelling stool makes infection with Giardia lamblia the most likely cause.
▶Cardiovascular System Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy1 questions
Source: 10A #36
A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of shortness of breath with exertion. She becomes short of breath after using the treadmill for 15 minutes. She has had no pain with exertion, but over the past 4 weeks, she has had intermittent vague chest discomfort in the evening. Her mother died suddenly of unknown causes at the age of 32 years. Her pulse is 82/min and regular, and blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg in the right arm and 128/80 mm Hg in the left arm. Cardiac examination shows an accentuated point of maximal impulse just left of the midclavicular line in the fifth intercostal space. There is an S4. A grade 2/6, harsh, crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is heard best along the left sternal border that decreases with sustained handgrip. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Aminophylline B) Enalapril C) Isosorbide dinitrate D) Propranolol E) Spironolactone F) No pharmacotherapy indicated
Correct Answer: D) Propranolol
This patient presents with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM), evidenced by: (1) exertional dyspnea and chest discomfort in a younger patient, (2) family history of sudden cardiac death at young age, (3) a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that decreases with sustained handgrip (increased afterload), (4) accentuated S4 and displaced PMI, and (5) ECG showing left ventricular hypertrophy. HOCM is caused by autosomal dominant inherited myocyte hypertrophy resulting in left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The murmur characteristically decreases with maneuvers that increase afterload (handgrip) and increases with maneuvers that decrease preload (Valsalva, standing), distinguishing it from aortic stenosis. Treatment of HOCM focuses on preventing symptoms and reducing mortality risk from arrhythmias. Beta-adrenergic blockers like propranolol are first-line agents because they: slow heart rate, decrease the force of myocardial contraction, reduce ectopic beats, and prevent dangerous arrhythmias. Choice A (Aminophylline): A bronchodilator; has no role in HOCM management. Choice B (Enalapril): An ACE inhibitor; while used in systolic heart failure, it may worsen HOCM by reducing preload and increasing outflow obstruction. Choice C (Isosorbide dinitrate): A nitrate; causes vasodilation and reduced preload, which worsens LVOT obstruction in HOCM. Choice E (Spironolactone): An aldosterone antagonist; used in heart failure but not indicated as monotherapy for HOCM. Choice F (No pharmacotherapy): Incorrect because symptomatic HOCM with family history of sudden death requires pharmacotherapy to prevent sudden cardiac death. Educational Objective: Recognize HOCM in a patient with exertional dyspnea, a dynamic systolic murmur that decreases with increased afterload, left ventricular hypertrophy, and family history of sudden cardiac death. Understand that beta-adrenergic blockers are the first-line pharmacotherapy for HOCM as they reduce arrhythmia risk and decrease mortality.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Metabolic Acidosis1 questions
Source: 10A #37
A 42-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of nausea and vomiting, and diarrhea associated with abdominal cramps. During this period, she has vomited each time she has tried to eat; she has been able to drink broth and water without vomiting. During the past 12 hours, her vomiting and cramps have been less severe, but she has had eight episodes of profuse watery diarrhea. She has a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glyburide and metformin. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. On arrival, she appears fatigued and dehydrated. Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 104/60 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Serum studies show: Na+ 140 mEq/L, K+ 3.5 mEq/L, Cl- 114 mEq/L, HCO3- 18 mEq/L, urea nitrogen 30 mg/dL, glucose 130 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: pH 7.34, PCO2 36 mm Hg, PO2 90 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these serum electrolyte abnormalities? A) Adverse effect of metformin B) Bowel ischemia C) Diabetic ketoacidosis D) Diarrhea E) Starvation ketoacidosis
Correct Answer: D) Diarrhea
This patient presents with nonanion-gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) characterized by hyperchloremic acidosis. NAGMA is identified by pH less than 7.35 (acidemia) with decreased PCO2 and HCO3-. The anion gap ([Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-])) is normal, indicating unmeasured anions are not contributing to acidity. NAGMA results from excess supply of protons or chloride, retention of protons or chloride by the kidneys, or failure to secrete bicarbonate buffers. In diarrheal illness, bicarbonate normally secreted in the small intestine is reclaimed in the large intestine in exchange for chloride ions. When diarrhea occurs, the colon cannot reclaim bicarbonate, resulting in increased serum chloride and decreased serum bicarbonate. The patient's clinical history of profuse watery diarrhea combined with laboratory findings of hyperchloremic acidosis directly indicates diarrhea as the cause. Choice A (Adverse effect of metformin) is incorrect because metformin causes high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) from excess lactate, not hyperchloremic acidosis. Choice B (Bowel ischemia) is incorrect because ischemia presents with HAGMA from excess lactate due to anaerobic respiration in ischemic cells. Additionally, bowel ischemia causes acute severe abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea, not profuse watery diarrhea, and this patient has a soft, nontender abdomen. Choice C (Diabetic ketoacidosis) is incorrect because it presents with HAGMA from accumulation of ketoacids (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate, acetate, and lactate). Diabetic ketoacidosis typically occurs in insulin-dependent patients with physiologic stress, not in noninsulin-dependent type 2 diabetics with simple diarrheal illness. Choice E (Starvation ketoacidosis) is incorrect because starvation ketosis presents with HAGMA from accumulation of lactate and ketoacids, similar to diabetic ketoacidosis. This patient has hyperchloremic (nonanion-gap) acidosis, not the high-anion-gap pattern seen in starvation ketosis.
▶Respiratory System Pharyngitis1 questions
Source: 10A #38
A 42-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a worsening sore throat over the past 3 days; she is now unable to swallow liquids or solids. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Examination is limited because she is unable to fully open her mouth but shows asymmetric swelling and white exudate covering the tonsils. Which of the following is the most likely infectious agent? A) Candida albicans B) Clostridium tetani C) Haemophilus influenzae D) Herpes simplex virus E) Streptococcus pyogenes (group A)
Correct Answer: E) Streptococcus pyogenes (group A)
This patient presents with the classic constellation of findings consistent with streptococcal pharyngitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) infection. The key clinical features include fever (38.5°C), sore throat, odynophagia (pain with swallowing), trismus (difficulty opening mouth), and tonsillar exudates with swelling. Streptococcal pharyngitis typically presents with fever, sore throat, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, odynophagia, trismus, palatal petechiae, and swollen red tonsils with purulent exudate. The likelihood of group A streptococcal pharyngitis can be predicted using the Centor Score, which incorporates age, tonsillar exudates or swelling, lymphadenopathy, fever, and absence of cough. Diagnosis is confirmed with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for S. pyogenes, with throat culture and streptococcal antigen testing as alternative options. Treatment involves antibiotics, most commonly penicillin or amoxicillin. Complications of untreated infection include rheumatic fever, peritonsillar abscess, bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, reactive arthritis, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Choice A (Candida albicans) is incorrect. While C. albicans causes oral thrush and esophagitis presenting with loss of taste and pain during eating, it typically occurs in immunocompromised patients (HIV/AIDS, immunosuppression, inhaled corticosteroid use). This patient lacks these risk factors and has the classic presentation of acute pharyngitis. Choice B (Clostridium tetani) is incorrect. C. tetani causes tetanus, resulting in spastic paralysis following bacterial inoculation through penetrating traumatic wounds. Physical examination findings include trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonos, and rigid abdominal muscles. Acute sore throat and odynophagia are not common presentations of tetanus. Choice C (Haemophilus influenzae) is incorrect. H. influenzae classically causes epiglottitis rather than pharyngitis with tonsillar exudates. Choice D (Herpes simplex virus) is incorrect. Viral causes of pharyngitis, including herpes simplex virus and adenovirus, do not classically produce tonsillar exudates with the purulent appearance seen in this patient.
▶Cardiovascular System Stasis Ulcers1 questions
Source: 10A #39
An 82-year-old man is brought to the physician because of a large ulcer on his lower right leg for the past 3 months. He has coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a history of deep venous thrombosis. He had a cerebral infarction 2 years ago, and he underwent coronary artery bypass grafting 6 months ago. He uses a wheelchair for ambulation. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 130/75 mm Hg. Examination shows left hemiparesis. There is 2+ brawny edema of the right ankle extending to the middle of the anterior edge of the shin; brown hyperpigmentation is noted in the same area. A 3-cm, circular ulcer with good granulation tissue is present above the medial malleolus. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the ulcer? A) Arterial insufficiency B) Diabetes mellitus C) Pressure D) Vasculitis E) Venous stasis
Correct Answer: E) Venous stasis
Correct Answer: E) Venous stasis Educational Objective: This patient with a large ulcer on the right leg and a history of deep venous thrombosis and chronic leg edema likely has a venous stasis ulcer. Evaluation: Venous stasis ulcers should be suspected based on clinical history including chronic lower extremity edema, skin hyperpigmentation, and hyperkeratosis, skin breakdown, and location (venous ulcers are often on the distal lower leg above the ankle and generally have irregular borders). The diagnosis is clinical but supported further by venous ultrasonography of the lower extremity showing increased venous pressure and evidence of venous stasis. Definition: Venous stasis ulcers occur in areas of chronic edema as a result of impaired venous return. The lower extremity is a common location, and patients often have a history of venous obstruction or valvular insufficiency from chronic venous thrombosis, tumor, trauma, inflammation, or other inciting condition. Comorbid right-sided heart failure is common. Venous stasis ulcers generally occur proximal to the ankle on the lower leg in the setting of chronic, pitting, lower extremity edema, skin hyperpigmentation, and hyperkeratosis. Chronic increased tissue edema results in inflammation and impaired perfusion, resulting in skin breakdown and ulceration. Ulcers may be painful, and the compromised skin barrier increases the risk for infection. Ulcers may chronically weep serous fluid. Treatment: Treatment of venous stasis ulcers involves wound care to prevent infection and promote the development of granulation tissue to support epithelialization and healing. Venous stasis ulcers will not resolve unless the underlying cause of venous insufficiency is also managed, which generally involves compression stockings, diuretics, anticoagulants, and management of heart failure/any associated triggering cause. Incorrect Answers: Choice A (Arterial insufficiency): Arterial ulcers are generally distal, involving the toes or foot, accompanied by cyanosis, shiny skin, a lack of edema, and hair loss.
