Pulses may be diminished or detectable only by Doppler ultrasonography. This patient lacks these features and instead has signs of chronic edema with skin hyperpigmentation. Choice B (Diabetes mellitus): Diabetes mellitus is an independent risk factor for micro- and macroscopic vascular disease, both of which increase the risk for arterial and venous ulcers. However, diabetes mellitus is an indirect cause of ulcerations by virtue of increased risk for both vascular disease and neuropathy. Ulcers directly associated with diabetic neuropathy are usually located on the feet and heels, occurring in proximity to bony prominences such as the calcaneus and metatarsal heads. Choice C (Pressure): Pressure ulcers result from chronic direct pressure on skin and are most often found on skin adjacent to the sacrum, coccyx, and ischial tuberosity in patients who are bedridden. Although this patient does have paralysis, it is of his left leg, not right. This would place the patient's left leg at risk for pressure ulceration, not the right leg where the ulcer is located. Choice D (Vasculitis): Vasculitis can cause multiple cutaneous manifestations including rash, purpura, or ulcerations. This patient has no history or signs of active vasculitis.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Parvovirus1 questions
Source: 10A #42
A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of persistent pain in her wrists and knees. Two months ago, she had fever, sore throat, malaise, and muscle pain in her upper arms and calves that resolved spontaneously. At that time, her 18-month-old son had a fever followed by a facial rash; he is well now. Today, the patient's temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 106/68 mm Hg. On examination, active and passive range of motion of the wrists and knees is limited by pain. There are no effusions. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in pharmacotherapy? A) Amoxicillin B) Ciprofloxacin C) Famciclovir D) Ibuprofen E) Prednisone
Correct Answer: D) Ibuprofen
Erythema infectiosum is caused by human parvovirus B19. In children, it presents with the characteristic 'slapped cheeks' appearance (pink patches on bilateral cheeks) followed by a lacy, macular eruption over the trunk and extremities. In adults, the infection is associated with a viral prodrome followed by development of migratory, symmetric polyarthritis involving the small joints of the hands, wrists, knees, and feet. This patient's clinical presentation—recent viral prodrome with fever and myalgias, exposure to a child with a rash consistent with erythema infectiosum, and current migratory symmetric polyarthritis—is classic for parvovirus B19 infection. Treatment for virally induced polyarthritis involves supportive care with NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and analgesics such as acetaminophen. In refractory cases, systemic corticosteroids may be considered. Ibuprofen represents the most appropriate initial step in pharmacotherapy for this patient's migratory polyarthritis. Choice A (Amoxicillin) is incorrect. While amoxicillin is used in treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis and rheumatic fever (which is associated with migratory polyarthritis and carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules), this patient's clinical presentation with documented exposure to a child with a characteristic rash is more consistent with parvovirus B19. Choice B (Ciprofloxacin) is incorrect. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for bacterial infections and is not indicated for viral polyarthritis. Choice C (Famciclovir) is incorrect. Famciclovir is an antiviral agent used for herpesvirus infections and is not indicated for parvovirus B19. Choice E (Prednisone) is incorrect. While systemic corticosteroids may be considered in refractory cases of parvovirus-induced polyarthritis, NSAIDs are the appropriate first-line therapy and should be tried initially before escalating to corticosteroids. Educational Objective: Recognize that erythema infectiosum in adults presents with migratory polyarthritis rather than the characteristic 'slapped cheeks' rash seen in children, and understand that initial treatment of viral polyarthritis involves NSAIDs such as ibuprofen for supportive care.
▶Immune System Selective Immunodeficiency (IgA)1 questions
Source: 10A #43
37-year-old woman comes to the physician for evaluation of recurrent infections. During the past 25 years, she has had several infections annually, including sinusitis, bronchitis, and gastroenteritis with diarrhea. Currently, her only medication is inhaled fluticasone for allergies. Her mother and sister have a history of frequent infections. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows boggy nasal turbinates. Urinalysis and an x-ray of the chest show no abnormalities. Dysfunction of which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's recurrent infections? A) Cell-mediated immunity B) Complement C) Immunoglobulins D) Myeloperoxidase E) Neutrophil chemotaxis
Correct Answer: C) Immunoglobulins
This patient, with a 25-year history of recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections, most likely has dysfunction of immunoglobulins, specifically IgA deficiency. IgA deficiency results from an impairment in B lymphocyte differentiation into IgA-secreting plasma cells. IgA primarily acts on mucosal surfaces, hence the predilection for sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections—areas of prominent mucosal tissue that are also exposed to airborne, droplet, and foodborne pathogens. The gold standard for diagnosis is measurement of serum immunoglobulin concentrations, which show decreased or absent IgA. Treatment involves prompt management of infections, ensuring applicable immunizations are given, and monitoring closely for complications. Patients with known IgA deficiency must receive washed or IgA-depleted blood products because of the risk for anaphylaxis from anti-IgA antibodies. Choice A (Cell-mediated immunity) is incorrect because patients with impaired cell-mediated immunity, such as those with severe combined immunodeficiency, often present in childhood with failure to thrive and severe infection. Choice B (Complement) is incorrect because complement deficiencies often present with recurrent infections from encapsulated bacteria. Choice D (Myeloperoxidase) is incorrect because myeloperoxidase deficiency decreases the neutrophilic granule reaction and can present with increased susceptibility to Candida species infection. Choice E (Neutrophil chemotaxis) is not the primary cause in this clinical presentation.
▶Behavioral Health Opioid Intoxication1 questions
Source: 10A #44
Four days after admission to the hospital because of worsening renal function, a 66-year-old woman is somnolent and difficult to arouse. She has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, osteoarthritis, hypertension, and major depressive disorder. Her home medications are metformin, amlodipine, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, continuous-release oxycodone, and citalopram. On admission, metformin, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide were discontinued, and short-acting insulin was started. Her other medications were continued. Today, she is oriented to person but not to place or time. She is arousable but immediately falls back to sleep. Her temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 6/min, and blood pressure is 148/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows myotonic jerking of the upper extremities. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show: On Admission / Today: Sodium: 136 mEq/L / 134 mEq/L Creatinine: 1.7 mg/dL / 3.4 mg/dL Urea nitrogen: 35 mg/dL / 46 mg/dL Glucose: 110 mg/dL / 92 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's change in mental status? A) Hypoglycemia B) Nonconvulsive status epilepticus C) Opioid intoxication D) Serotonin syndrome E) Uremia
Correct Answer: C) Opioid intoxication
Opioid intoxication is the most likely cause of this patient's somnolence and bradypnea in the setting of worsening renal function. Oxycodone is metabolized primarily via the cytochrome P450 (CYP450) system and produces active metabolites including oxymorphone and noroxymorphone. Like many opioids, oxycodone acts on μ-opioid receptors causing analgesia, sedation, diminished gastrointestinal transit, and respiratory depression. Most opioids are variably metabolized by the liver and/or kidneys, and worsening renal function can result in inadvertent overdose through accumulation of the drug or its metabolites, even at the same baseline doses the patient typically takes. In this case, the patient's creatinine doubled from 1.7 to 3.4 mg/dL and renal function worsened significantly. The clinical presentation of oversedation (somnolence, arousable but immediately falls back to sleep), respiratory depression (respirations 6/min), and worsening renal function narrowly points to relative opioid overdose. Additionally, the discontinuation of other potentially offending medications (metformin, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide) on admission makes opioid accumulation the primary culprit. Choice A (Hypoglycemia) is incorrect because the patient's glucose concentrations are normal (92 mg/dL today), and hypoglycemia typically causes tremors, sweating, agitation, tachycardia, and in severe cases seizures and coma—not sedation and bradypnea. Choice B (Nonconvulsive status epilepticus) is not the best choice. While nonconvulsive status epilepticus can cause altered mental status, this patient's history of worsening renal function, bradypnea, and continued use of opioids with declining renal clearance is more consistent with relative opioid overdose. Nonconvulsive seizures typically present with more rhythmic brain activity patterns and would not explain the bradypnea. Choice D (Serotonin syndrome) is incorrect. Serotonin syndrome occurs from excess serotonergic stimulus, typically from overdose of a serotonergic agent. It presents with hyperreflexia and/or clonus, autonomic instability (tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, hyperthermia), and tremors. This patient does not have the classic presentation of serotonin syndrome. Choice E (Uremia) is incorrect. While uremia can present with confusion and tremors, it typically requires urea nitrogen concentrations greater than 80 to 100 mg/dL, though it can occur at lower levels. This patient's urea nitrogen is only 46 mg/dL. Additionally, bradypnea is far more consistent with opioid intoxication than uremia. Key concept: Relative overdoses of medications can occur due to medication interactions that impair metabolism or enhance effects, or from diminished capacity for metabolism or accumulation of metabolites in acute or worsening liver or kidney disease.
▶Uncategorized Gastric outlet obstruction1 questions
Source: 10A #46
A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department for the second time in 24 hours because of repeated vomiting. The vomiting began 3 days ago, and since that time, she has been unable to keep anything down. She has not had diarrhea or abdominal pain. She has recurrent peptic ulcer disease, schizophrenia, and chronic bronchitis. Medications include famotidine, olanzapine, and inhaled albuterol. She has not taken any medications for 2 months because she believes her doctors are trying to poison her. She has smoked two and a half packs of cigarettes daily for 12 years and drinks beer occasionally. She appears agitated. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and increased tympany in the epigastrium. There is epigastric and left upper quadrant discomfort but no rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are normal. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Her hemoglobin concentration is 14.2 g/dL, and leukocyte count is 14,200/mm³. An x-ray of the abdomen shows no abnormalities except for marked distention of the stomach. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Alcohol-induced gastritis B) Gastric outlet obstruction C) Gastroesophageal reflux disease D) Psychogenic vomiting E) Viral gastroenteritis
Correct Answer: B) Gastric outlet obstruction
Correct Answer: B) Gastric outlet obstruction. Educational Objective: A history of peptic ulcer disease with medication nonadherence, now with inability to tolerate food or fluids and recurrent nausea and vomiting is consistent with a bowel obstruction, likely at the level of the stomach (gastric outlet obstruction). This patient's abdominal x-ray with marked distension of the stomach is consistent with a gastric outlet obstruction. Definition: Gastric outlet obstruction occurs from obstruction at the level of the distal stomach, pylorus, or proximal duodenum. Gastric outlet obstruction can result from a wide range of causes, the most common in adults being malignancy and peptic ulcer disease. Peptic ulcer disease causes chronic ulceration, scar formation, and potential stricture formation which results in blockage. Evaluation: Gastric outlet obstruction results from narrowing in the gastroduodenal region that blocks passage of gastric contents forward. The gold standard for diagnosis is direct visualization with esophagogastroduodenoscopy. This patient's clinical presentation of inability to tolerate food or fluids for 3 days with recurrent vomiting, combined with marked gastric distention on abdominal x-ray, is highly suggestive of gastric outlet obstruction. Choice A (Alcohol-induced gastritis): While this patient does drink beer occasionally, her presentation is not consistent with simple gastritis, which typically presents with epigastric pain and dyspepsia. The inability to tolerate any intake and marked gastric distention point to obstruction rather than inflammation alone. Choice C (Gastroesophageal reflux disease): GERD would not cause the degree of vomiting, inability to tolerate any intake, or the marked gastric distention seen on imaging. Choice D (Psychogenic vomiting): Although the patient has schizophrenia and does not take her medications, psychogenic vomiting would not explain the objective findings of marked gastric distention on x-ray, positive stool occult blood, and leukocytosis. Choice E (Viral gastroenteritis): Viral gastroenteritis typically presents with diarrhea, which this patient does not have. The duration of symptoms (3 days) and lack of improvement also make this less likely. Differential: This patient's gastric outlet obstruction is likely due to peptic ulcer disease with stricture formation. Her documented history of recurrent peptic ulcer disease, combined with 2 months of medication nonadherence (not taking famotidine), predisposed her to continued ulceration and scarring. Other potential causes of gastric outlet obstruction include foreign body blockage, caustic ingestion, or malignancy. Treatment: Treatment includes endoscopic or surgical clearance of the obstruction and dilatation of the narrowed area. Additionally, patients should receive proton pump inhibitors and antiemetics, and may benefit from initial gastric decompression with a nasogastric tube. Prevention: Prevention of gastric outlet obstruction caused by peptic ulcer disease involves treating the peptic ulcer disease in order to minimize mucosal injury and resultant scarring and stricture formation.
▶Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Toxoplasma gondii infection in pregnancy1 questions
Source: 10A #48
A 47-year-old woman who is HIV positive is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-day history of a progressive headache and a 1-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure. On arrival, she is confused. Neurologic examination shows mild left facial weakness and hemiparesis. A CT scan of the head shows multiple, cortical, ring-enhancing lesions bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Albendazole B) Amphotericin B and flucytosine C) Ciprofloxacin D) Ganciclovir E) Metronidazole F) Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine G) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Correct Answer: F) Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine
This patient with HIV infection, new seizure, neurologic deficits, and ring-enhancing lesions on CT scan of the brain has cerebral toxoplasmosis, which is treated with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine as first-line therapy. Toxoplasma gondii is a ubiquitous organism that typically does not cause severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. However, in patients with HIV infection and CD4+ T-lymphocyte counts less than 100/mm³, reactivation can occur. Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an AIDS-defining disease that typically presents with seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, nausea, and vomiting. The diagnosis is supported by imaging showing ring-enhancing brain lesions on CT or MRI, and definitive diagnosis is made through brain biopsy. The patient's clinical presentation—immunocompromise, headaches, focal neurologic deficits, seizure, and ring-enhancing lesions—is characteristic of cerebral toxoplasmosis. Maintaining a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count greater than 200/mm³ is the most effective means of preventing toxoplasmosis infection. Standard treatment is supportive care plus pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine in nonallergic patients. Choice A (Albendazole) is incorrect because it is an anthelmintic used for parasitic worm infections, not protozoan infections like toxoplasmosis. Choice B (Amphotericin B and flucytosine) is incorrect because this combination is used for fungal infections such as cryptococcal meningitis, not toxoplasmosis. Choice C (Ciprofloxacin) is incorrect because it is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for bacterial infections, particularly urinary tract and diverticular infections. Choice D (Ganciclovir) is incorrect because it is used for CMV infections, not toxoplasmosis. Choice E (Metronidazole) is incorrect as it is used for anaerobic bacterial and certain parasitic infections, not toxoplasmosis. Choice G (Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is incorrect because while it provides some coverage against toxoplasmosis, pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine are the first-line agents.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Hemochromatosis1 questions
Source: 10A #49
A 62-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He has a 6-month history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Examination shows hepatomegaly. There are no cutaneous stigmata of hepatic disease. Serum studies show a bilirubin concentration of 1.3 mg/dL, AST activity of 150 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase activity of 90 U/L. A liver biopsy specimen shows massive iron deposition and fibrotic changes. Without treatment, he is most likely to have which of the following complications over the next several years? A) Cardiomyopathy B) Cerebellar degeneration C) Interstitial pneumonitis D) Polycythemia E) Renal failure
Correct Answer: A) Cardiomyopathy
Hemochromatosis develops because of abnormally increased intestinal absorption of iron, which may be demonstrated on tissue biopsy as iron deposition on Prussian blue stain. This condition may be acquired or inherited secondary to mutations in the HFE gene. Iron accumulates in several organs including the liver, pancreas, skin, heart, and joints, which may result in cirrhosis, portal hypertension, diabetes mellitus, arthritis secondary to calcium pyrophosphate deposition, darkening of the skin, gonadal atrophy, and cardiomyopathy. This patient presents with new-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus, hepatomegaly, and liver biopsy showing massive iron deposition, which is diagnostic of hemochromatosis. Without treatment, progressive iron overload is most likely to result in cardiomyopathy over the next several years. Treatment involves serial phlebotomy and management of secondary disorders such as heart failure and diabetes mellitus. Choice B (Cerebellar degeneration) is incorrect. While hemochromatosis has been associated with generalized cognitive impairment and movement disorders such as Parkinson disease, chorea, myoclonus, and ataxia, cardiomyopathy is the most likely complication to develop in this patient over the next several years. Choice C (Interstitial pneumonitis) is incorrect. While hereditary hemochromatosis may result in pulmonary hemosiderosis, this is a rarer occurrence compared to cardiomyopathy. Choice D (Polycythemia) and Choice E (Renal failure) are not characteristic complications of hemochromatosis.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Seborrheic Dermatitis1 questions
Source: 4A #1
A 42-year-old man has had the gradual onset of greasy, diffuse scaling of the scalp with variable itching over the past year. Yellowish red scaling papules appear along the hairline and behind the ears; there is no hair loss. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Exfoliative dermatitis B) Lichen simplex chronicus C) Pediculosis capitis D) Psoriasis E) Seborrheic dermatitis
Correct Answer: E) Seborrheic dermatitis
Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease that occurs in regions containing sebaceous glands. In adults, it typically presents as yellowish-red, scaly patches of the scalp and forehead, around the ears, nasolabial folds, and chest. In infants, it presents as 'cradle cap,' with the appearance of a diaper rash and yellow scaling on the scalp. Diffuse, severe seborrheic dermatitis can occur in immunosuppressed patients. Treatment consists of zinc pyrithione or selenium sulfide shampoo applied to the scalp along with topical antifungals such as ketoconazole. Topical corticosteroids can also be used for severe cases to decrease the inflammatory reaction and pruritus. Exfoliative dermatitis (Choice A) is a severe inflammatory skin condition characterized by generalized, diffuse erythema and scaling with desquamation involving large areas of the body, often occurring in the setting of pre-existing skin disorders (eg, psoriasis, eczema), cancer (eg, leukemia, lymphoma), or after administration of certain medications (eg, sulfa, penicillin, phenytoin). Lichen simplex chronicus (Choice B) is a localized region of skin thickening (lichenification) that results from repetitive rubbing or itching of the skin. Pediculosis capitis (Choice C) refers to infestation of the scalp and hair by Pediculus humanus capitis (human louse), which can cause severe pruritus. Treatment includes permethrin, pyrethrins, ivermectin, or malathion lotions. Psoriasis (Choice D) results in erythematous plaques with silvery scales typically located on extensor surfaces (e.g., knees, elbows). While it can involve the scalp, this is less common compared to seborrheic dermatitis.
▶Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Dermatophytosis1 questions
Source: 4A #2
A 24-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Two months ago, he was seen for a red, scaly rash over his groin. A 6-week course of topical clotrimazole resolved the rash completely, but it recurred 2 days ago. He is sexually active with one partner and uses condoms consistently. Examination shows an erythematous, excoriated rash over the groin and a similar rash over the instep of the left foot. A KOH preparation of a skin scraping shows hyphae. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's recurrent infection? A) Autoinfection B) Clotrimazole resistance C) Impaired cellular immunity D) Impaired humoral immunity E) Reinfection from a sexual partner
Correct Answer: A) Autoinfection
Tinea (dermatophytosis) refers to cutaneous fungal infection with organisms such as Microsporum, Trichophyton, and Epidermophyton, characterized by branching septated hyphae on KOH preparation. This patient initially presented with tinea cruris (groin rash) treated with clotrimazole, which resolved completely. However, he also has tinea pedis (rash on left foot instep) that was not treated. The untreated tinea pedis served as a reservoir for autoinfection, leading to recurrent tinea cruris when the patient inadvertently transferred fungal organisms from his foot to his groin through scratching or contact. This is the most likely scenario because treatment addressed only the groin but left another infected body region untreated. Concurrent treatment of all affected areas is necessary to prevent recurrence. Clotrimazole resistance (Choice B) is uncommon in dermatophytosis, and the initial course of treatment was successful, indicating drug efficacy. Impaired cellular immunity (Choice C) and impaired humoral immunity (Choice D) would present as risk factors for disseminated dermatophytosis, but this patient has localized infections in anatomically distinct areas without other evidence of immunocompromise. While reinfection from a sexual partner (Choice E) is theoretically possible through skin-to-skin contact, the patient uses condoms consistently and has an untreated tinea pedis as an obvious alternative source of infection, making this less likely.
▶Gastrointestinal System Pancreatic pseudocyst1 questions
Source: 4A #9
A 32-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital 8 hours after the onset of nausea and vomiting and epigastric abdominal pain that radiates to her back. She has had two similar episodes during the past 2 months. She has no other history of serious illness. She does not drink alcohol. Abdominal examination shows moderate epigastric tenderness. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, Hematocrit 38%, Leukocyte count 15,400/mm³, Platelet count 326,000/mm³, Serum amylase 1450 U/L. Ultrasonography of the gallbladder shows no abnormalities. A CT scan of the abdomen demonstrates a pseudocyst in the pancreatic parenchyma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) HIDAscan B) Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography C) Esophagogastroduodenoscopy D) Mesenteric angiography E) Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography
Correct Answer: B) Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is the most appropriate next diagnostic and therapeutic step for this patient. The clinical presentation of recurrent episodes of nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain radiating to the back, combined with elevated serum amylase and a CT-demonstrated pancreatic pseudocyst, indicates recurrent acute pancreatitis with pseudocyst formation. Pancreatic pseudocysts are granulation tissue-lined collections of fluid located in the pancreatic parenchyma or peripancreatic region that develop as a complication of acute pancreatitis. They cause persistent elevation of pancreatic enzymes and recurrent epigastric pain. Intervention is indicated for pseudocysts larger than 5 cm or those that are symptomatic. ERCP allows for both diagnosis and therapeutic drainage via transpapillary approach or by creating cystogastrostomy or cystoduodenostomy, which establish drainage pathways between the cyst and gastrointestinal tract. HIDAscan (Choice A) is used for diagnosing acute cholecystitis by detecting cystic duct obstruction from impacted gallstones. This is not indicated here since the gallbladder ultrasound is normal and the clinical picture is consistent with pancreatitis, not cholecystitis. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (Choice C) alone does not provide definitive diagnosis or therapeutic intervention for pancreatic pseudocysts. While ERCP involves endoscopic access, EGD without the capability to access the pancreatic duct would be insufficient. Mesenteric angiography (Choice D) is indicated for evaluating mesenteric vessels in cases of mesenteric ischemia or gastrointestinal bleeding, neither of which is the clinical problem in this patient. Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (Choice E) is used for visualizing the biliary tree when ERCP fails or is unsuccessful, or for therapeutic placement of biliary drains or stents. It is not the first-line intervention for pancreatic pseudocyst drainage.
▶Gastrointestinal System Diverticulitis1 questions
Source: 4A #11
A 72-year-old nursing home resident is brought to the emergency department because of abdominal pain and bloody stools for 3 days. She has dementia, Alzheimer type, and a long-standing history of constipation treated with psyllium and docusate. She is in no apparent distress. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/80 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows left lower quadrant tenderness and distention. Rectal examination shows blood and no masses. She is not oriented to place or time. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Campylobacteriosis B) Celiac disease C) Clostridium difficile colitis D) Colon cancer E) Diverticulitis F) Diverticulosis G) Irritable bowel syndrome H) Ischemic colitis I) Salmonellosis J) Shigellosis K) Ulcerative colitis
Correct Answer: E) Diverticulitis
Diverticulitis is the most likely diagnosis in this elderly patient presenting with left lower quadrant abdominal pain and tenderness, fever, and hematochezia. Diverticulitis results from inflammation and infection involving pre-existing diverticula and is a common presentation in older adults with a history of constipation. The clinical constellation of fever (39°C), focal left lower quadrant tenderness with distention, and bloody stools is classic for acute diverticulitis. Hematochezia can occur secondary to concomitant diverticular bleeding. Complications include perforation leading to peritonitis, abscess formation, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation. Treatment involves bowel rest, symptomatic control, and antibiotics covering enteric flora. Choice A (Campylobacteriosis), Choice I (Salmonellosis), and Choice J (Shigellosis) cause bloody diarrhea but typically present with diffuse diarrhea rather than focal left lower quadrant pain without watery diarrhea. Choice B (Celiac disease) is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the proximal small bowel in response to gluten ingestion, presenting with chronic diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, and malnutrition—not acute fever and localized abdominal pain. Choice C (Clostridium difficile colitis) is an opportunistic infection typically following antibiotic use, presenting with severe watery diarrhea rather than the focal pain and hematochezia seen here. Choice D (Colon cancer) can cause hematochezia but does not typically present acutely with fever and focal tenderness. Choice F (Diverticulosis) refers to the presence of colonic diverticula without inflammation. While diverticulosis can result in painless hematochezia, it does not cause acute abdominal pain, fever, and tenderness—these symptoms indicate active inflammation (diverticulitis). Choice G (Irritable bowel syndrome) presents with intermittent abdominal pain relieved by bowel movements and associated with alternating diarrhea and constipation, not acute fever and focal tenderness. Choice H (Ischemic colitis) results from inadequate blood supply to the colon, most commonly occurring with atherosclerosis or hypercoagulable states (atrial fibrillation). While it can present with abdominal pain and hematochezia, the localized left lower quadrant tenderness with fever is more typical of diverticulitis. Choice K (Ulcerative colitis) is an inflammatory bowel disease presenting with chronic bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, and abdominal pain, typically with a more chronic course rather than acute presentation with fever.
▶Respiratory System Pneumothorax1 questions
Source: 4A #12
A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after the sudden onset of shortness of breath while scuba diving. He reports that he had to ascend rapidly from a 70-foot depth because he was running out of compressed air. During the ascent, he had the sudden onset of midchest pain; he had shortness of breath by the time he reached the surface. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He is in moderate respiratory distress and unable to speak in complete sentences. His respirations are 28/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. He is using accessory muscles of respiration. The trachea is midline. Pulmonary examination shows decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion on the left. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Measurement of serum D-dimer concentration B) Chest x-ray C) ECG D) Echocardiography E) CT scan of the thorax
Correct Answer: B) Chest x-ray
Chest x-ray is the most appropriate next diagnostic step for evaluating this patient's suspected pneumothorax. The clinical presentation is classic for decompression sickness (the bends) following rapid ascent from scuba diving. Decompression sickness occurs when dissolved gases precipitate out of solution in the body and form bubbles, or when gas expands due to rapid decrease in ambient pressure. These mechanisms increase risk for air emboli, arthropathy, tympanic membrane rupture, and pneumothoraces. The physical examination findings of decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion on the left hemithorax are pathognomonic for left-sided pneumothorax. Chest x-ray is the standard diagnostic modality for confirming pneumothorax and determining its size, which guides management decisions regarding need for thoracostomy. Choice A (D-dimer measurement) is used for evaluating DVT or pulmonary embolism in patients with low pretest probability, but this patient's clinical picture is clearly consistent with pneumothorax, not thromboembolism. Choice C (ECG) would be indicated for evaluating cardiac arrhythmias or acute coronary syndromes, but the patient's midchest pain is secondary to the pneumothorax, not myocardial ischemia, and he lacks risk factors for ACS. Choice D (echocardiography) evaluates cardiac pathology and pericardial disease, not pulmonary conditions; lung ultrasound, not cardiac ultrasound, may assist in pneumothorax evaluation but is not the standard first-line modality. Choice E (CT scan of the thorax) can evaluate various thoracic pathologies but is unnecessary here since plain chest x-ray provides rapid, adequate evaluation for nontension pneumothorax and is more efficient than CT.
▶Endocrine System Diabetic nephropathy1 questions
Source: 4A #14
A 47-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Six weeks ago, her fasting serum glucose concentration was 177 mg/dl; urine protein was 1+. She has been taking metformin and following a low-carbohydrate diet for the past 4 weeks. She has no other medical problems and is taking no other medications. Her father died of end-stage renal disease secondary to type 2 diabetes mellitus. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 30 kg/m². Her weight is unchanged from her last visit. Today, her blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg; at her last examination 4 weeks ago, it was 128/80 mm Hg. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin A1c 7.3%, Serum Urea nitrogen 17 mg/dl, Glucose 169 mg/dl, Creatinine 1.1 mg/dl, Urine protein 180 mg/24 h. Which of the following measures is most likely to slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy in this patient? A) Calorie-reduced diet B) Dietary protein restriction to 0.6 g/kg daily C) Maintenance of a hemoglobin A1c of less than 6% D) Addition of lisinopril to the medication regimen E) Switching from metformin to insulin therapy
Correct Answer: D) Addition of lisinopril to the medication regimen
Addition of lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) is the most effective measure to slow progression of diabetic nephropathy. Diabetic nephropathy develops following nonenzymatic glycosylation of the glomerular basement membrane and efferent arterioles, resulting in abnormally increased glomerular filtration rate and progressive hyperfiltration injury. This manifests as microalbuminuria progressing to macroalbuminuria and eventually end-stage kidney disease. ACE inhibitors like lisinopril decrease angiotensin II production, causing relative efferent arteriole dilatation and reducing efferent arteriole constriction secondary to glycosylation. This decreases hyperfiltration injury and directly slows nephropathy progression. The patient's urine protein of 180 mg/24 h indicates early diabetic kidney disease. Choice A (Calorie-reduced diet) may improve glucose control and weight loss but does not directly affect nephropathy progression. Choice B (Dietary protein restriction to 0.6 g/kg daily) does show some evidence for slowing nephropathy progression but is less effective than ACE inhibitor therapy. Choices C (Hemoglobin A1c <6%) and E (Switching to insulin) would improve overall diabetes management and slow microvascular complications including nephropathy, but ACE inhibitors remain the most effective specific intervention for slowing diabetic nephropathy progression.
▶Cardiovascular System Atrial Septal Defect1 questions
Source: 4A #15
A 20-year-old woman comes for a routine health maintenance examination. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. The S2 is split and fixed. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard at the third intercostal space. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Aortic insufficiency B) Atrial septal defect C) Mitral insufficiency D) Patent ductus arteriosus E) Pulmonic insufficiency F) Tetralogy of Fallot G) Tricuspid insufficiency H) Ventricular septal defect
Correct Answer: B) Atrial septal defect
Atrial septal defect (ASD) is a defect in the interatrial septum. The most common type is an ostium secundum defect, although ostium primum defects are commonly associated with trisomy 21. The ASD results in a left-to-right shunt with abnormal flow of blood from the left atrium to the right atrium, causing relative volume overload of the right atrium and ventricle. This increased stroke volume of the right ventricle results in delayed closure of the pulmonic valve, presenting as a fixed, split S2 and a low-grade physiologic ejection murmur on cardiac auscultation. If the ASD remains uncorrected, it can result in the development of Eisenmenger syndrome secondary to prolonged pulmonary vasculature remodeling, resulting in pulmonary arterial hypertension and shunt reversal leading to cyanosis. Choice A (Aortic insufficiency) presents with an early diastolic decrescendo murmur best heard in the right second intercostal space and is most commonly associated with endocarditis, rheumatic fever, and aortic root dilation. Choice C (Mitral insufficiency) presents with a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left fourth or fifth intercostal space along the midclavicular line and radiates to the left axilla. It is commonly associated with mitral valve prolapse and prior myocardial infarction. Choice D (Patent ductus arteriosus) results in a continuous, machine-like murmur best heard in the left second intercostal space and radiates to the clavicle. Choice E (Pulmonic insufficiency) presents with a diastolic murmur best heard in the left second intercostal space. Choice F (Tetralogy of Fallot) consists of pulmonary infundibular stenosis, overriding aorta, ventricular septal defect, and right ventricular hypertrophy, resulting in a right-to-left shunt with cyanosis first noted in infancy. The murmur heard with Tetralogy of Fallot relates to the underlying ventricular septal defect. Choice H (Ventricular septal defect) is characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard in the lower left sternal border. Choice G (Tricuspid insufficiency) demonstrates a holosystolic murmur best heard in the lower left sternal border. The clinical presentation of fixed, split S2 with a low-grade systolic ejection murmur at the third intercostal space in an asymptomatic young woman is pathognomonic for atrial septal defect.
▶Biostatistics Epidemiology Population Health Life Expectancy1 questions
Source: 4A #19
The life table shown compares the natural disease history of groups A and B. Which group at which time has the poorest 1-year survival rate? A) Group A at Time 0-1 B) Group B at Time 0-1 C) Group A at Year 2-3 D) Group B at Year 3-4 E) Group B at Year 4-5
Correct Answer: D) Group B at Year 3-4
Group B at Year 3-4 demonstrates the largest decrease in percent survival for a 1-year time span, representing the poorest 1-year survival rate. The life table plots the natural disease progression for the percent of individuals alive over time (years) for Group A and Group B. At Year 3, Group B demonstrates a percent survival of approximately 80%. By Year 4, this decreases to approximately 50%, indicating a 1-year drop in percent survival of 30%. Incorrect Choices: Choice A (Group A at Time 0-1): Demonstrates a linear decrease in percent survival of approximately 10% per year. Choice B (Group B at Time 0-1): Demonstrates no appreciable decrease in percent survival. Choice C (Group A at Year 2-3): Demonstrates a linear decrease in percent survival of approximately 10% per year. Choice E (Group B at Year 4-5): Demonstrates a percent survival decrease of approximately 5%, less than Group B at Year 3-4. The educational objective is to understand how to interpret life tables and identify the time period with the steepest decline in survival, which reflects the poorest survival rate during that interval.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Cauda Equina Syndrome1 questions
Source: 4A #20
A 67-year-old man had the acute onset of bilateral weakness of the lower extremities and urinary incontinence 2 days ago. He has had carcinoma of the prostate for 2 years and bone metastases to the pelvis for 6 months. His temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3°F), pulse is 86/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 160/86 mm Hg. There is tenderness to palpation over the lumbosacral spine most prominent at S1. He is unable to lift his legs against gravity; deep tendon reflexes are absent at the knees and ankles. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in diagnosis? A) Radionuclide bone scan B) Electromyography and nerve conduction studies C) CT scan of the head D) MRI of the lumbosacral spine E) Lumbar puncture
Correct Answer: D) MRI of the lumbosacral spine
MRI of the lumbosacral spine is the most appropriate initial diagnostic step for evaluation of acute onset neurological deterioration from cauda equina syndrome. The patient presents with classic features of cauda equina syndrome: acute bilateral lower extremity weakness, loss of deep tendon reflexes, urinary incontinence (bowel or bladder dysfunction), and lumbosacral spine tenderness. Given his history of osseous metastatic prostate cancer with pelvic bone metastases, spinal cord compression from metastatic disease is a medical emergency. Cauda equina syndrome occurs from acute compression of the cauda equina nerve roots in the lumbosacral spinal canal, most commonly from acute disc herniation, traumatic or pathologic vertebral column fracture, or in this case, metastatic disease. Emergent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is indicated to identify the cause of compression and determine the necessity of urgent surgical decompression or other intervention. Choice A (Radionuclide bone scan) uses technetium 99m-methyl diphosphonate (Tc-99m MDP) to evaluate for osteoblastic osseous metastases, particularly in breast and prostate cancer, but is not appropriate for emergent evaluation of acute neurological symptoms requiring urgent diagnosis. Choice B (Electromyography and nerve conduction studies) are used to differentiate myopathic and neuropathic causes of extremity weakness and assess chronic nerve and muscle function, but are not indicated in the emergent evaluation of acute neurological deterioration. Choice C (CT scan of the head) evaluates intracranial pathology, but this patient's clinical presentation clearly localizes to the lumbosacral spine, not the brain. Choice E (Lumbar puncture) evaluates cerebrospinal fluid composition and is indicated for meningitis, encephalitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and conditions like Guillain-Barré syndrome, but is not the initial diagnostic study for suspected spinal cord compression. Additionally, lumbar puncture may be contraindicated in the setting of significant spinal cord compression.
▶Multisystem Processes Disorders Pulmonary Osteoarthropathy1 questions
Source: 4A #21
A 72-year-old man has had burning, aching pain in the distal extremities for 3 weeks; the pain is exacerbated by lowering the extremities and relieved by elevation. Examination shows tenderness and swelling of the fingers and wrist, knee, ankle, and toe joints; the overlying skin is warm and erythematous. There is clubbing of the fingers and toes. Which of the following is most likely to be abnormal? A) Serum creatinine concentration B) Serum ferritin concentration C) Serum protein electrophoresis D) X-ray of the abdomen E) X-ray of the chest
Correct Answer: E) X-ray of the chest
This patient presents with paraneoplastic hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, a syndrome characterized by digit clubbing and long-bone periostitis. The clinical presentation includes burning, aching pain exacerbated by dependency and relieved by elevation, along with tenderness, swelling, and warmth of distal joints (fingers, wrists, knees, ankles, toes), and clubbing of fingers and toes. The most common cause of paraneoplastic hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is non-small cell lung cancer, particularly adenocarcinoma. Therefore, chest X-ray is the most appropriate initial imaging study to evaluate for a primary lung mass. Choice A (Serum creatinine concentration): Used to evaluate for acute or chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease. While chronic kidney disease can cause renal osteodystrophy, this presents with subperiosteal bone thinning, not digit clubbing, making it unlikely in this clinical context. Choice B (Serum ferritin concentration): Used in the evaluation of anemias and iron metabolism disorders. While elevated ferritin may be seen in hemochromatosis, which can present with joint pain and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, this does not explain the constellation of symptoms and clubbing present in this patient. Choice C (Serum protein electrophoresis): Used to evaluate hemoglobinopathies and monoclonal gammopathies. Multiple myeloma presents with lytic bone lesions from abnormally increased osteoclast activation, not the clinical picture of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy with clubbing. Choice D (X-ray of the abdomen): Typically used for evaluation of acute abdominal pathology such as small bowel obstruction. It would not assist in the workup for a primary malignancy causing paraneoplastic syndrome. The key clinical features pointing to paraneoplastic hypertrophic osteoarthropathy are the combination of distal joint pain, swelling, warmth, erythema, and digit clubbing in an elderly patient. Chest imaging is essential to identify the underlying malignancy.
▶Gastrointestinal System GERD1 questions
Source: 4A #22
A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of heartburn for 4 months and difficulty swallowing solids for 1 month. She has daily episodes of epigastric burning radiating to her chest and neck, especially at night or after ingestion of large meals. Treatment with ranitidine over the past 3 months has been ineffective. She has not had nausea, vomiting, change in bowel habits, or weight loss. She takes no other medications. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. She appears well nourished. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 136/86 mm Hg. Examination shows no scleral icterus, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Her hemoglobin concentration is 13 g/dL, serum AST activity is 18 U/L, and serum lipase activity is 224 U/L (N=14-280). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Add metoclopramide to the medication regimen B) Add omeprazole to the medication regimen C) Switch to famotidine therapy D) Switch to omeprazole therapy E) Upper endoscopy F) No further testing or pharmacotherapy indicated
Correct Answer: E) Upper endoscopy
Upper endoscopy is the most appropriate next step in management for GERD that is resistant to medication therapy and presents with alarm symptoms, specifically solid food dysphagia. GERD typically presents with burning epigastric and lower chest pain that radiates superiorly and is exacerbated by ingestion of large meals. First-line therapy for GERD is an empiric trial of proton pump inhibitors or H2 receptor blockers. However, when a patient demonstrates reflux that is nonresponsive to medication therapy and develops dysphagia, an upper endoscopy should be performed for definitive evaluation of the esophagus. Dysphagia may indicate development of reflux-associated sequelae such as erosive or eosinophilic esophagitis, Barrett esophagus, or esophageal carcinoma, necessitating direct visualization. Choice A (Add metoclopramide) is incorrect because while metoclopramide can increase lower esophageal sphincter tone and may be used for persistent GERD, its potentially severe adverse effects (parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia) restrict its use to only severe, resistant cases. Additionally, metoclopramide is primarily used for gastroparesis and as an antiemetic, not as a first-line GERD agent. Choice B (Add omeprazole) and Choice D (Switch to omeprazole therapy) are inappropriate because the patient has already failed empiric H2-receptor blocker therapy with ranitidine and has developed the alarm symptom of solid food dysphagia. Simply escalating or adding proton pump inhibitor therapy without investigating the cause of dysphagia would be inadequate management. Choice C (Switch to famotidine) is incorrect for similar reasons—the patient has already failed H2-receptor blocker therapy, so switching to a different agent in the same class is unlikely to be beneficial and delays necessary investigation. Choice F (No further testing or pharmacotherapy) is inappropriate because medication-resistant GERD with development of dysphagia requires definitive evaluation to exclude serious complications or alternative diagnoses. The esophagus must be directly visualized to assess for reflux-associated sequelae or alternative culprit lesions.
▶Cardiovascular System Complications of Artificial Valves1 questions
Source: 4A #24
A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of episodes of vomiting blood. He has no history of similar episodes. He has esophageal adenocarcinoma, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, osteoarthritis, and coronary artery disease. He has a prosthetic, mechanical aortic valve. He is receiving radiation therapy. He notes that the therapy makes him tired and he naps several hours daily. His other medications are lisinopril, metformin, glipizide, simvastatin, warfarin, and aspirin. Which of the following is the strongest indication for anticoagulant therapy in this patient? A) Adenocarcinoma B) Coronary artery disease C) Decreased activity D) Prosthetic aortic valve E) Radiation therapy
Correct Answer: D) Prosthetic aortic valve
The prosthetic mechanical aortic valve is the strongest indication for anticoagulant therapy. Mechanical prosthetic valves carry a substantial risk for thrombus formation without anticoagulation therapy. Thrombus formation at the site of a mechanical aortic valve places the patient at risk for acute arterial thromboembolic events including stroke, myocardial infarction, and acute peripheral arterial occlusions, all of which result in significant morbidity and mortality risk. For patients with mechanical aortic valves, the target international normalized ratio (INR) with warfarin therapy is 2.5 to 3.5. Choice A (Adenocarcinoma) increases the patient's risk for venous thromboembolic disease, most commonly deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary emboli. However, patients with underlying adenocarcinoma are not recommended to start anticoagulation without evidence of thromboembolic disease. Choice B (Coronary artery disease) increases the risk for myocardial infarction. Patients with CAD are recommended to take aspirin, an irreversible antiplatelet medication, to reduce myocardial infarction risk. Anticoagulation is not indicated for patients with CAD without acute coronary syndrome. Choice C (Decreased activity/immobilization) increases risk for thromboembolism, and prophylactic anticoagulation is often utilized in immobilized hospital and institutionalized patients using subcutaneous heparin or enoxaparin. However, this patient is indicated for therapeutic anticoagulation due to the mechanical aortic valve, which is a stronger indication. Choice E (Radiation therapy) is not an indication for anticoagulation therapy as it does not directly increase the risk for thromboembolic disease.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Hodgkin lymphoma1 questions
Source: 4A #25
A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of swelling of the neck for 1 month and malaise, fever, fatigue, night sweats, and generalized pruritus for 2 weeks. Acetaminophen has provided only minimal relief of his symptoms. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 100/67 mm Hg. There is a 3 x 4-cm left anterior cervical lymph node. Conjunctivae are not injected, and the tympanic membranes and pharynx are not erythematous. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 1/6, nonradiating systolic murmur is heard best at the upper right sternal border. Bowel sounds are slightly hyperactive. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 14 g/dL, Leukocyte count 6000/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 60%, Bands 2%, Eosinophils 1%, Lymphocytes 33%, Monocytes 4%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute lymphocytic leukemia B) Cat-scratch disease C) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia D) Drug reaction E) Gastric carcinoma F) HIV infection G) Hodgkin disease H) Infectious mononucleosis I) Rubella J) Sarcoidosis K) Syphilis L) Systemic lupus erythematosus M) Tuberculosis
Correct Answer: G) Hodgkin disease
Hodgkin disease is a type of lymphoma, predominantly B-cell in origin, that occurs most commonly in patients ages 20-30 years and 55-65 years. This patient's age of 22 fits the classic presentation. Patients typically present with lymphadenopathy along with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and weight loss (B symptoms), hepatosplenomegaly, and pruritus. The patient demonstrates classic B symptoms (fever, night sweats, malaise, fatigue) and generalized pruritus. The anterior cervical lymphadenopathy is a typical presentation, as the most common sites for lymphadenopathy are the neck and mediastinum. Pel-Ebstein fevers refer to recurrent high fevers for 1-2 weeks followed by 1-2 week afebrile periods and are characteristic of Hodgkin disease. A specific sign for Hodgkin disease associated lymphadenopathy is alcohol-induced pain at the enlarged lymph node sites. Definitive diagnosis requires excisional lymph node biopsy demonstrating Reed-Sternberg cells. The most common subtype is nodular sclerosing, and the worst prognosis occurs in the setting of the lymphocyte-depleted subtype. Choice A (Acute lymphocytic leukemia) most commonly occurs in pediatric patients and is defined as greater than 20% lymphoblasts on peripheral blood smears and bone marrow biopsies. Down syndrome patients demonstrate increased risk. Choice B (Cat-scratch disease) is caused by Bartonella henselae transmission through cat scratches, typically presenting with lymphadenitis in the lymphatic drainage pattern of the scratch location. Choice C (Chronic lymphocytic leukemia) most commonly occurs in adults greater than 60 years of age and patients are often asymptomatic with slow progression and characteristic "smudge" cells on peripheral blood smears. Choice D (Drug reaction) would not typically present with a 1-month duration of malaise, fevers, and night sweats and is typically following administration of the causative drug. Choice E (Gastric carcinoma) may present with early satiety and abdominal pain along with generalized malaise but lacks the lymphadenopathy and B symptoms pattern. Choice F (HIV infection) can present with systemic constitutional symptoms during acute HIV syndrome, but this patient does not demonstrate behaviors or features placing him at risk for HIV infection. Choice H (Infectious mononucleosis) commonly presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly along with pharyngitis, but the lymphadenopathy typically involves posterior cervical lymph nodes and would show atypical lymphocytes. Choice I (Rubella) is a togavirus resulting in fever, arthralgias, and lymphadenopathy (most often postauricular) with a confluent rash that spreads from head to trunk and centrifugally to extremities. Choice J (Sarcoidosis) is a chronic noncaseating granulomatous disease most commonly presenting with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and possible upper lobe-predominant reticular pulmonary opacities. Choice K (Syphilis) demonstrates multiple stages with varying symptoms including primary chancre, secondary fever and lymphadenopathy, and tertiary manifestations. Choice L (Systemic lupus erythematosus) is an autoimmune disease resulting in fever, rash, photosensitivity, renal disease, and nonerosive arthritis. Choice M (Tuberculosis) is a mycobacterial infection presenting with fever, night sweats, and weight loss but is typically associated with cough and/or hemoptysis.
▶Gastrointestinal System Intestinal obstruction1 questions
Source: 4A #29
A 47-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 24 hours after the onset of severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She says her pain improves somewhat with vomiting and rates her current pain as a 9 on a 10-point scale. At first, her vomitus consisted of partially digested food, but now it contains yellow fluid. She also has noticed increased abdominal girth. Her last bowel movement was 24 hours ago. She has not had fever or chills. She underwent an endodontic surgical procedure 4 days ago and has been taking acetaminophen with codeine for pain. She underwent an appendectomy at the age of 17 years and a total abdominal hysterectomy at the age of 45 years for dysfunctional uterine bleeding. She appears uncomfortable. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), and respirations are 17/min. Her pulse is 120/min and blood pressure is 110/82 mm Hg while supine; her pulse is 130/min and blood pressure is 100/76 mm Hg while sitting. Examination shows dry oral mucosa. The abdomen is distended and tympanitic; there is mild diffuse tenderness to palpation. Bowel sounds are high pitched. Rectal examination shows no stool in the rectal vault and no masses. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 47%, Leukocyte count 13,000/mm³, Platelet count 450,000/mm³, Serum Na⁺ 145 mEq/L, K⁺ 3.4 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 103 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 35 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 62 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL. An abdominal x-ray shows distended loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. There is no air in the rectum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cecal volvulus B) Ileus C) Obstruction of the small bowel D) Pseudo-obstruction of the colon E) Sigmoid volvulus
Correct Answer: C) Obstruction of the small bowel
Small bowel obstruction (SBO) occurs from partial or complete blockage of the small bowel lumen and typically presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Partial small bowel obstructions allow continued flatus with diminished stooling, while complete obstructions result in obstipation. The most common causes are post-surgical peritoneal adhesions and hernias. This patient has significant risk factors for SBO including prior appendectomy and total abdominal hysterectomy. On physical examination, SBO typically presents with abdominal tenderness, distention, tympany to percussion, and borborygmi (high-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds)—all present in this patient. The progression from bilious vomitus (green/yellow fluid) indicates gastric contents have moved into the small bowel, supporting mechanical obstruction. Laboratory abnormalities reflect dehydration and electrolyte loss from prolonged vomiting: elevated hematocrit, elevated BUN/creatinine ratio, hypernatremia, and hypokalemia. The abdominal x-ray demonstrating distended small bowel loops with air-fluid levels is classic for SBO. The absence of air in the rectum suggests a complete obstruction. Management requires bowel rest and intravenous hydration. Partial obstructions are managed conservatively with monitoring and supportive care, while complete obstructions require exploratory laparotomy to relieve the obstruction and prevent complications such as bowel rupture and necrosis. Choice A (Cecal volvulus) results from twisting of the cecal mesentery causing large bowel obstruction. It is less common than sigmoid volvulus and is associated with a hyper-mobile cecum. This patient's imaging shows small bowel obstruction, not large bowel obstruction. Choice B (Ileus) refers to intestinal hypomotility without mechanical obstruction, most commonly occurring following surgery or with electrolyte abnormalities. While this patient has had recent surgery and some electrolyte derangements, ileus typically presents with diffuse small and large bowel dilatation without air-fluid levels. The high-pitched bowel sounds and localized small bowel dilation with air-fluid levels are inconsistent with ileus. Choice D (Pseudo-obstruction of the colon/Ogilvie syndrome) results in large bowel dilatation without mechanical obstruction. It most commonly occurs in elderly patients or those with severe comorbidities and electrolyte derangements. This patient presents with small bowel obstruction findings, not large bowel dilatation. Choice E (Sigmoid volvulus) results from twisting of the sigmoid mesentery causing large bowel obstruction. It typically demonstrates a characteristic coffee-bean appearance on abdominal x-rays. This patient's imaging shows small bowel loops with air-fluid levels, and sigmoid volvulus is less common than post-surgical small bowel obstruction from adhesions.
▶Blood Lymphoreticular System Neutropenia1 questions
Source: 4A #32
A 42-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever, chills, headache, and joint and muscle pain. She says that she was recently hospitalized in another city for treatment of an overactive thyroid and was given two medications on discharge. She recalls no further details. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 132/70 mm Hg. Examination shows lid lag, exophthalmos, a prominent goiter, and a supple neck. The lungs are clear to auscultation. There are no skin or joint abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 45%, Leukocyte count 1400/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 5%, Lymphocytes 95%, Platelet count 287,000/mm³. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Autoimmune neutropenia B) Cyclic neutropenia C) Drug-induced neutropenia D) Radioactive iodine-induced neutropenia E) Thyroid storm
Correct Answer: C) Drug-induced neutropenia
Drug-induced neutropenia is an adverse effect of both propylthiouracil and methimazole, which are thioamides used in the treatment of hyperthyroidism. The patient exhibits classic symptoms of hyperthyroidism secondary to Graves disease, including exophthalmos, goiter, and lid lag. These medications inhibit thyroid peroxidase, while propylthiouracil also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 by blocking 5'-deiodinase. A rare adverse effect of these medications is agranulocytosis, resulting in insufficient production of segmented neutrophils (as evidenced by the markedly elevated leukocyte count of 1400/mm³ with only 5% segmented neutrophils and 95% lymphocytes). This results in susceptibility to a variety of infections and increased risk for sepsis in the setting of neutropenic fever. Autoimmune neutropenia (Choice A) is a rare hematologic disorder characterized by autoantibody-induced destruction of neutrophils, but this patient's clinical presentation and recent medication history point toward drug-induced etiology. Cyclic neutropenia (Choice B) is a rare disease resulting in recurrent episodes of neutropenia, typically every 3 weeks, with patients presenting with lethargy, fever, and mucosal ulcerations. The acute presentation following drug initiation makes this less likely. Radioactive iodine-induced neutropenia (Choice D) can occur due to myelosuppressive effects of radioactive iodine, although this is rare given the low doses used for the treatment of hyperthyroidism secondary to Graves disease. Importantly, the patient received medical therapy for her hyperthyroidism, not radioactive iodine therapy. Thyroid storm (Choice E) is a serious potential complication of hyperthyroidism following an acute stress such as trauma or infection. Characteristic presenting symptoms include fever, diarrhea, tachyarrhythmia, altered mental status (delirium, agitation), and potential coma or death if not emergently treated. While this patient has fever and signs of hyperthyroidism, the laboratory findings showing severe neutropenia are not consistent with thyroid storm and instead point to a medication side effect.
▶Nervous System Special Senses Multiple Sclerosis1 questions
Source: 4A #33
A previously healthy 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of progressive sensory loss. Initially, only her feet felt numb, but the loss of sensation has slowly ascended symmetrically to the umbilicus. She also has had urinary urgency and frequency, nocturia, and the perception of a tight band-like sensation around her midabdominal region. Examination shows slowing of left eye adduction during saccadic movement of the eyes to the right. There is diffuse hyperreflexia. Sensation to pinprick is decreased to the level of the umbilicus. The most likely explanation for the slowing of left eye adduction is a lesion at which of the following sites? A) Left cerebral hemisphere B) Left medial longitudinal fasciculus C) Left paramedian pontine reticular formation D) Right cerebellar hemisphere E) Right sixth cranial nerve nucleus
Correct Answer: B) Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
The patient presents with multiple focal neurologic deficits occurring in separate neurologic pathways including ascending sensory loss, urinary symptoms, hyperreflexia, and impaired eye adduction. In a younger female, this clinical presentation raises suspicion for multiple sclerosis, an inflammatory demyelinating disease that can affect multiple white matter tracts throughout the central nervous system. The left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) is the anatomic structure responsible for coordinating horizontal eye movements. Specifically, it allows communication between the right abducens nerve nucleus (CN VI) and the left oculomotor nerve nucleus (CN III), enabling conjugate horizontal eye movement in the same direction. A lesion affecting the left MLF results in impaired left eye adduction during rightward saccadic eye movement, a finding called internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). This occurs because the signal from the right abducens nucleus cannot reach the left oculomotor nucleus via the damaged left MLF. The most common cause of MLF lesions is inflammatory plaques from multiple sclerosis. Choice A (Left cerebral hemisphere): Lesions here produce varied deficits including contralateral motor and sensory loss and aphasia depending on location. Frontal eye field involvement would cause conjugate gaze deviation toward the lesion, not selective impairment of one eye's adduction. Choice C (Left paramedian pontine reticular formation): This structure coordinates horizontal gaze. A left PPRF lesion would cause conjugate gaze deviation to the right (toward the lesion), affecting both eyes equally, not selective left eye adduction impairment. Choice D (Right cerebellar hemisphere): Cerebellar lesions produce ipsilateral signs including extremity ataxia, intention tremor, and loss of balance, not isolated eye movement abnormalities. Choice E (Right sixth cranial nerve nucleus): This nucleus provides motor innervation to the lateral rectus muscle via CN VI. Damage results in horizontal gaze palsy with medial deviation of the ipsilateral eye, not selectively impaired adduction of the contralateral eye. The combination of sensory level, urinary symptoms, hyperreflexia, and INO strongly suggests demyelinating disease, with the MLF lesion being characteristic of MS.
▶Respiratory System Epiglottitis1 questions
Source: 4A #34
A 20-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a severe sore throat, hoarseness, and dysphagia for 8 hours. She appears toxic. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). She has severe pharyngitis and stridor. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Assay for diphtheria toxin B) Culture and Gram stain of sputum C) X-ray of the chest D) Barium swallow E) Laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation
Correct Answer: E) Laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation
Epiglottitis is an acute infection of the epiglottis that presents with fever, severe pharyngitis, drooling, hoarseness, dysphagia, and stridor. The clinical presentation of a toxic-appearing patient with acute severe pharyngitis and stridor is classic for epiglottitis. Although on lateral neck x-rays it appears as a 'thumbprint sign,' the immediate priority in epiglottitis is airway management, not diagnosis. Because patients with epiglottitis can exhibit rapid respiratory decompensation and airway obstruction, the most appropriate next step is to emergently establish a protected airway through endotracheal intubation. Endotracheal intubation should take place in the operating room under direct visualization with a laryngoscope. This condition was commonly caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b prior to widespread pediatric vaccination, though other organisms can be responsible. Choice A (Assay for diphtheria toxin) would evaluate for Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection, which presents with acute pharyngitis and gray oropharyngeal pseudomembranes but would not explain the stridor and acute airway compromise seen here. Choice B (Culture and Gram stain of sputum) can characterize respiratory infections but does not address the immediate life-threatening airway emergency. Choice C (X-ray of the chest) is appropriate for primary pulmonary pathology but offers no pertinent findings in acute pharyngitis and delays critical airway management. Choice D (Barium swallow) evaluates swallowing function and is utilized for causes of dysphagia but should not be used for acute pharyngeal pathology and would be dangerous in the setting of acute airway compromise.
▶Respiratory System Mycoplasma pneumoniae Pneumonia1 questions
Source: 4A #35
A 21-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an 8-day history of sore throat, cough, and fever. The cough is nonproductive but keeps her awake at night. She subsequently develops hoarseness. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Crackles are heard over the right posterior lower chest. X-rays of the chest show patchy, lower right alveolar infiltrates with increased interstitial markings. Her leukocyte count is 10,000/mm³ with 75% segmented neutrophils and 1% bands. For each patient with pulmonary infection, select the most likely infectious agent. A) Cytomegalovirus B) Haemophilus influenzae C) Klebsiella pneumoniae D) Legionella pneumophila E) Mycoplasma pneumoniae F) Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carinii) G) Pseudomonas aeruginosa H) Respiratory syncytial virus I) Streptococcus pyogenes (group A)
Correct Answer: E) Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most likely infectious agent for this patient's infection. The patient presents with a fever, nonproductive cough, and crackles along the right posterior lower chest. Her x-ray demonstrates patchy, lower right alveolar infiltrates along with increased interstitial markings. This constellation of findings is consistent with community-acquired pneumonia secondary to an atypical infection, especially given the patient's young age. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most common infectious agent for pneumonia in patients of this age and is best treated with a macrolide antibiotic. Key distinguishing features of atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae include: nonproductive cough, constitutional symptoms (sore throat, fever), young age, patchy infiltrates with interstitial markings on imaging, and lack of lobar consolidation. Choice A: Cytomegalovirus (HHV-5) is transmitted through sexual contact, urine, respiratory droplets, and transplacental routes. While it can cause pneumonia, this occurs primarily in immunocompromised patients, not in immunocompetent young adults. Choice B: Haemophilus influenzae is an encapsulated gram-negative bacterium that causes various mucosal infections including conjunctivitis, otitis media, bronchitis, and pneumonia. It was the leading cause of epiglottitis in children prior to widespread immunization, but is less common in pneumonia in this age group. Choice C: Klebsiella pneumoniae is an encapsulated gram-negative bacterium that typically presents with lobar pneumonia, particularly in patients with diabetes mellitus or alcohol use disorder. It can also cause nosocomial urinary tract infections but is not the most common cause of pneumonia in healthy young adults. Choice D: Legionella pneumophila is a gram-negative rod transmitted primarily through aerosols from water sources. It causes Legionnaires disease characterized by fever, pneumonia, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Legionnaires disease most commonly occurs in chronic smokers or those with chronic underlying lung disease, not in otherwise healthy young women. Choice F: Pneumocystis jirovecii is a yeast-like fungus that primarily affects immunosuppressed patients. It results in bilateral pneumonia with diffuse reticulogranular (ground-glass) opacities on imaging. Treatment includes TMP-SMX, atovaquone, or pentamidine. Choice G: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative rod causing various infections including urinary tract infections, osteomyelitis, otitis externa, folliculitis, hospital or ventilator-associated pneumonia, and sepsis. It is not a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia in immunocompetent hosts. Choice H: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) commonly causes respiratory tract infections in infants such as bronchiolitis or pneumonia. Palivizumab can be used for prevention in premature infants. Choice I: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) is a gram-positive bacterium causing cellulitis, pharyngitis, scarlet fever, necrotizing fasciitis, glomerulonephritis, and rheumatic fever, but is not a typical cause of pneumonia.
▶Respiratory System Legionella Pneumonia1 questions
Source: 4A #36
In September, 5 days after returning from a business trip, a 57-year-old woman develops fever, abdominal cramps, and watery diarrhea followed by a cough 24 hours later. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), and pulse is 90/min. Crackles are heard diffusely over both lung fields. Her leukocyte count is 16,000/mm³ with a predominance of segmented neutrophils. X-rays of the chest show alveolar infiltrates in the right upper and lower lobes and in the left lower lobe. Gram stain of sputum shows many segmented neutrophils but no predominant microorganism. A) Cytomegalovirus B) Haemophilus influenzae C) Klebsiella pneumoniae D) Legionella pneumophila E) Mycoplasma pneumoniae F) Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carinii) G) Pseudomonas aeruginosa H) Respiratory syncytial virus I) Streptococcus pyogenes (group A)
Correct Answer: D) Legionella pneumophila
Legionella pneumophila is a gram-negative rod transmitted primarily through aerosols from water sources such as air conditioning systems. It causes Legionnaires disease, which most commonly occurs in patients who are chronic smokers or have underlying chronic lung disease. This case presents the classic features of Legionnaires disease: fever, atypical pneumonia with diffuse alveolar and interstitial opacities, and prominent gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea and abdominal cramps). The temporal relationship to travel, the smoking history, and the clinical presentation of fever followed by respiratory symptoms with GI complaints are hallmark features. Legionnaires disease may also be associated with hyponatremia. In healthy adults, Legionella pneumophila can cause mild flu-like symptoms called Pontiac fever. First-line therapy includes macrolides or respiratory fluoroquinolones. Cytomegalovirus (Choice A) is transmitted through sexual contact, urine, respiratory droplets, and transplacental routes. It causes mononucleosis in immunocompetent patients and pneumonia, retinitis, and infectious esophagitis in immunocompromised patients—this patient is immunocompetent. Haemophilus influenzae (Choice B) is an encapsulated gram-negative bacterium causing conjunctivitis, otitis media, bronchitis, and pneumonia. It was the leading cause of epiglottitis in children prior to immunization, but does not present with the prominent GI symptoms seen here. Klebsiella pneumoniae (Choice C) is an encapsulated gram-negative bacterium presenting with lobar pneumonia, especially in patients with diabetes or alcohol use disorder. This patient has no such risk factors, and Klebsiella does not characteristically cause diarrhea and abdominal cramps. Mycoplasma pneumoniae (Choice E) is a common atypical bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia in young adults with alveolar and interstitial infiltrates. However, it does not typically present with significant gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea and abdominal cramps. Pneumocystis jiroveci (Choice F) is a yeast-like fungus primarily affecting immunosuppressed patients, causing bilateral pneumonia with diffuse reticulogranular opacities. This patient has no evidence of immunosuppression. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Choice G) causes hospital or ventilator-associated pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and osteomyelitis, not community-acquired pneumonia in this clinical context. Respiratory syncytial virus (Choice H) commonly causes bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, not this presentation in an adult. Streptococcus pyogenes (Choice I) is a gram-positive bacterium causing cellulitis, pharyngitis, scarlet fever, and necrotizing fasciitis, not this pneumonia presentation with GI symptoms.
▶Renal Urinary System Chlamydial Urinary Tract Infection1 questions
Source: 4A #37
A 19-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 5-day history of pain with urination and a watery urethral discharge. He has not had fever. He has no history of sexually transmitted diseases. He was sexually active with a female partner 3 weeks ago and another female partner 2 weeks ago, and he did not use condoms. He is not sure if his partners have had genitourinary symptoms. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 122/70 mm Hg. Examination shows no lymphadenopathy. The penis and testes appear normal. There is a mucopurulent, whitish urethral discharge. Rectal examination shows a normal-sized, nontender prostate. A Gram stain of the urethral discharge shows segmented neutrophils without intracellular organisms. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
